en: The Section on Conduct [1] First Chapter
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by saluting whom at the commencement of all undertakings, Vāgīśa and the other wise ones become successful in their aims. (1)

Thus, having reached the station of the sacred ford of solitude, bathing in the supreme sacred ford of the Vedic tradition, skilled in association with the sacred ford of the virtuous, and resorting to the sacred ford of noble conduct,
I received from Śrī Bhāratītīrtha a wave of splendor that I have now come to realize.
Taking refuge at the ford of knowledge, I worship Śrīkaṇṭha, the unimpeded, within my heart. || 2 ||

[2] He who guards the single vow of truth, whose intellect is twofold, who seeks the three goals, who is learned in the four Vedas, who has mastered the five aggregates, who is firm in the sixfold lineage, who endures all through the seven limbs,
who possesses the eight manifest arts, who is the treasure of the nine, and who nourishes the ten causal conditions.
Victorious is the illustrious King Bukkaṇa, who bears the burden of upholding the traditions of the Smṛtis. || 3 ||
[3] Aṅgiras was the priest of Indra; Sumati, of Nala; Medhātithi, of Śaibya; Dhaumya, of the son of Dharma; Svaujas, of King Vainya; Gautami, of Nimi;
and Arundhatī’s companion, Pratyagdṛṣṭi, was the priest of the meritorious Rāma.
Just as that sovereign had a family preceptor who was his minister, so too did Mādhava. || 4 ||

[4] With wisdom as its root and soil, sprinkled with the waters of solitude, nourished by the spells that destroy the [enemy's] strength, possessing vast branches through the six measures of policy beginning with conciliation at dawn,
budding with power, made fragrant by sacrifice, and bearing uplifted fruit through success— this tree of sovereignty stands firm.
Having arrived upon this earth, the creeper of political ethics shines forth, surpassing all others in its excellence. || 5 ||
He whose illustrious mother was Śrīmatī, whose father was Māyaṇa,
and whose brothers were Sāyaṇa and Bhoganātha— born of his mind and intellect.
He whose Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana, whose Vedic branch is the Yajurveda, and whose lineage is Bhāradvāja—he indeed is the omniscient Mādhava. (7)
That Mādhava, the promoter of all Purāṇa compendiums, is Parāśara, the supreme excellence of the Smṛtis;
he now proceeds with this commentary on the Parāśara-smṛti for the attainment of the welfare desired by the world. (8)
The Parāśara-smṛti has not been commented upon by previous authors; therefore, an effort is being made by me, the noble Mādhava, toward its exposition. (9)

But surely this *smṛti* does not deserve such an explanation, because its authority is difficult to establish. As for the reason for the authority of the Veda set forth by Jaimini in the sūtra: “That is authoritative, according to Bādarāyaṇa, because it is independent of anything else” (PMS 1.1.5), that cannot be applied to human-authored texts which depend upon an original source of authority (*mūlapramāṇa*). Well then, let its authority be based on its dependence upon such an original source.

That is not so, because the root source is difficult to establish. First of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*) cannot be the root, because that [source] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Nor can it be inference (*anumāna*), because inference is dependent upon perception. Nor can it be the word of another person (*puruṣāntaravākya*), because a deceptive person lacks the quality of speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived, and even for one who is non-deceptive, doubt and error are possible. Nor can it be Vedic injunction (*codanā*), because such an injunction is not apprehended. Indeed, we do not perceive through direct observation any Vedic injunction that serves as the root for the practices of purity and so forth that are currently being remembered. Nor can it be inferred, for that would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [finding such a root] even in the worship of shrines (*caityavandana*) and other practices composed by the Śākyas and others.

Now, it might be argued: there is a great disparity between the *smṛtis* of Manu and others and the *smṛtis* of Śākya and others, because the authority of Manu and his peers is directly accepted by the perceived Veda itself. For it is recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "Whatever Manu said is indeed medicine" (TS 2.2.6.2). However, there is no Vedic statement whatsoever that supports the *smṛtis* of Śākya and others. Therefore, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not apply.

That is not so; for the passage beginning with "whatever [is said]" (*yad vai kiṃ ca*) is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) and thus lacks any intentionality regarding its own literal meaning. This is because the passage beginning with "whatever [is said]" is recited as a praise of the injunction: "One should employ two *ṛc* verses of Manu as *dhāyyā*s" (*TS* 2.2.6.2). And the meaning of that injunction is this: among the *sāmidhenī* verses which are obtained by extension (*atideśataḥ*) for the *caru* offerings to Soma and Rudra—which are modifications of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice—one must insert those two mantras designated as *dhāyyā*s, and those two should be composed by Manu. In that context, the fact that they are "composed by Manu" (*mānavatva*) is extolled by the aforementioned explanatory eulogy. Therefore, the authority of the Smṛti is not stated by the Veda; thus, like the Smṛtis of Śākya and others, the Smṛtis of Manu and others are indeed devoid of authority. As it has been said:

"Because men generally speak untruth, because errors and the like are possible, and because there is no direct Vedic injunction (codanā), their authority rests merely on faith. Or, even if the *Manusmṛti* were somehow authoritative, what follows for the *Parāśarasmṛti* under discussion? For the Veda nowhere proclaims the greatness of Parāśara as it does that of Manu. Therefore, the authority of his Smṛti is difficult to establish.

To this it is replied: Smṛtis are authoritative because validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and because there is no cause for invalidity. As for the three reasons—such as being a speaker of falsehood—that were adduced to prove invalidity, they are unestablished (*asiddha*). This is because, regarding Manu, Parāśara, and others who have been established since birth, speaking falsehood and error are utterly beyond suspicion; thus, the very nature of the reason is unestablished. Nor should one dispute their establishment from birth, for the mantras, *arthavādas*, histories, and Purāṇas that inform us of the existence of Parāśara and others are precisely what establish their reality. Furthermore, if the mantras and other texts were invalid, who could prevent the fallacy of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) due to the non-existence of Parāśara and the rest? The validity of mantras and the like with respect to their own objects—provided they are not contradicted by other means of knowledge and are not mere restatements (*ananuvādin*)—was established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (UMS 1.3.9) of the Uttara-mīmāṃsā. However, the denial of intrinsic validity in the *Arthavādādhikaraṇa* (PMS 1.2.1) applies only to those cases involving contradictions or restatements that find scope elsewhere. Therefore, since the *arthavāda* passage "whatever [is spoken]" (*yad vai kiṃ ca*), which praises the injunction, possesses an intention toward its own literal meaning as well, the comparison (*pratibandī*) with the words of the Śākyas and others is not tenable. It was with this very intent that the *Caturviṃśatimata* stated that the words of the Śākyas and others are not to be respected.
"One should avoid all those words of the Arhat and the Cārvākas, as well as those recited by the Buddhists and others, for they are the words of deceivers."

Nor is the greatness of Parāśara un-Vedic, for in the Śruti it is said, "Vyāsa Pārāśarya spoke" (TS 1.1.3.37), whereby Vyāsa is praised by virtue of being the son of Parāśara. If even Vedavyāsa, whose greatness is universally acknowledged, is praised by relying on his status as the son of Parāśara, then what need is there to mention that Parāśara’s own greatness is inconceivable? Furthermore, in the Vājasaneyi Śākhā, within the Vaṃśabrāhmaṇa, in the lineage of teachers and disciples who transmitted the Veda, the son and grandson of Parāśara are heard of: "Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśaryāyaṇa; Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya" [11]. Therefore, Parāśara also is indeed equal to Manu.

This same principle should be applied to Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Yājñavalkya, and others, since their respective *śruti* sources are found. For instance, there are such *śruti* passages as: “The sages did not see Indra face-to-face; Vasiṣṭha saw him face-to-face” (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 3.5.2.5); “Atri gave [the earth] to Aurva, who desired offspring” (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 7.1.8.1); and “Now Yājñavalkya had two wives,” and so forth. Nor should it be suspected that, this being the case, why there should be a lack of respect for the *smṛti* texts of Manu and others; for the *smṛtis* of Manu and others have been commented upon by Medhātithi and other authorities.

Furthermore, the non-perception of the injunctions that serve as the basis for these [Smṛtis] which you have put forward is itself unestablished. This is because we do perceive such injunctions that form the basis of Smārta dharma, such as: “These five great sacrifices proceed continuously and conclude continuously—the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to Brahman” (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.10.7). The word *satati* means “continuously,” that is, eternally. Even in cases where an injunction is not perceived regarding matters such as ritual purity (*śauca*), it is nonetheless to be inferred there as well. Thus it has been stated by the Bhaṭṭācāryas:
"Because they are remembered by those learned in the Vedas, because of the firmness with which they are accepted,
and because it is possible that the Smṛtis have their root in the Veda, the authority of the Smṛtis is appropriate.
This very point was also stated by Manu.
Sages perceive the Śruti and likewise remember the Smṛti;
therefore, both are authoritative, as they are established by means of valid cognition upon this earth.
“He who would despise both of these by relying on treatises of logic—that nihilist and reviler of the Vedas—should be excluded by the virtuous. (Manu Smṛti 2.11).
Also, in the *Ānuśāsana-parvan*:
"For those desiring to know Dharma, the first authority is the Śruti;
the second is the Dharmaśāstra, and the third is the consensus of the world.
Therefore, it is established that the Parāśara-smṛti is fit to be explained.
[14] In this Parāśarasmṛti, the composition of the work is analyzed:
it consists of two sections (kāṇḍas), twelve chapters (adhyāyas), and five hundred and ninety-two verses (ślokas).
The first section concerns the preceptor and so forth, and the last section concerns expiation;
from these two, respectively, follow the attainment of the desired and the cessation of the undesired.
"All these become worlds of merit," so the Śruti proclaimed;
that from the performance of the duties of one's stage of life (āśrama) comes the attainment of desired rewards in the world beyond.
The undesirable hell that results from the performance of prohibited acts is clearly averted by that which the scripture prescribes under the heading of "expiation" (prāyaścitta).
For dharma, which has the other world as its primary goal, there are these two paths:
expiation and customary practice, because they are so observed in the revealed dharma.
Dharma based on revelation consists of the agnihotra and other rites; conduct is their performance.
When performed contrary to the rules, expiation is prescribed in the revealed scripture.
Those who composed the Kalpasūtras performed expiation according to the Śrauta rites;
however, those who did not compose Sūtras did not prescribe expiation for both types of conduct.
In the very same way, this Teacher, desiring to proclaim the Dharma based on the Smṛtis which has the next world as its primary concern, spoke two sections [of the treatise].
Now, if it is argued that even in conventional usage understood through injunction there exists suchness (dharmatā), let it be so; however, that [suchness] is what is functional in this world.
Just as Vedic rituals such as the Kārīrī sacrifice have only visible results,
so too worldly activity has only the results of gain, honor, and fame.
Likewise, the victor gains profit and the like, while the vanquished suffers punishment;
these two alone constitute heaven and hell, arising from what is enjoined and what is prohibited.
[16] But surely— since there is sin incurred by the king, the members of the court, and the witnesses if they act otherwise, legal procedure has its purpose in the world beyond.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell as well.
One should not enter an assembly, nor should one speak what is improper; by remaining silent or by speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
Speaking untruthly as a witness, one is bound tightly by the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred future births while rendered powerless; therefore, a witness should speak the truth.
[Verse 82] Let there be sin for the king and others regarding the procedure in the legal process;
the legal process itself belongs to the plaintiff and the defendant, not to the king and others.
In this matter, no sin is recorded for either the defendant or the plaintiff;
nor is any penance prescribed on account of defeat.
[17] Even that statement regarding hell on account of debts and the like is based upon established custom;
or rather, let there be hell for one who conducts himself in a manner contrary to the scriptures.
We only refute the primacy of the next world for one who makes this world primary and treats the next world as secondary.
That dharma would be conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), whereas right conduct (*ācāra*) occurs in its opposite case;
even though this world is characterized by predominance [of worldly custom], it must nonetheless have its root in sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
From the auxiliary sciences (upavedas) such as that of music (gāndharva), through his observation of them,
he mastered the recitation from the Ṛgveda and the chanting from the Sāmavedas.
[18] From the Yajurveda he derived the dramatic gestures, and from the Atharvaveda the aesthetic sentiments;
what need is there for further words? This teacher has his gaze fixed solely upon the world beyond.
But he did not speak of legal procedure; rather, while protecting the earth according to dharma in the course of discussing the duties of kings, he merely indicated it.
Thus speaking, while indicating legal procedure visible to the king,
customary conduct (*ācāra*) is treated first because it is the direct cause for attaining what is desired.
But when conduct deviates from its norm, there is the search for expiation;
here, three chapters on conduct have been proclaimed, and nine on expiation.
Based on conduct, the duties of the four castes are both common and specific;
therein, the duty associated with the conduct of the virtuous is remembered as the common one.
[19] The six duties, beginning with the protection of the earth, are recorded as being common to all social classes (*varṇas*).
These matters have been proclaimed in the first chapter on conduct (*ācāra*).
The means of livelihood, such as agriculture and so forth, were explained in the second chapter;
and the duties of the four stages of life (āśramas) were indicated by the mention of those stages.
The third [section], consisting of the detailed exposition on impurity (āśauca) and the summary of ancestral rites (śrāddha), has been declared;
thus have the topics contained within the three chapters belonging to the section on conduct (ācārakāṇḍa) been explained.
In the fourth [chapter], the expiation for miscellaneous sins has been explained in detail;
and incidentally, the various types of sons and the practice of marrying before an elder brother have also been described.
[20] The purification for miscellaneous remnants is the same as that for an *āhitāgni* in the fifth [case],
as well as for those involving impurity, mixed castes, and likewise for minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Expiation was taught in the sixth [chapter], as well as purification regarding food and liquids;
the purification of remaining substances is declared in the seventh chapter.
The expiation for killing a cow is generally prescribed in the eighth [chapter],
while that for specific cases such as confinement and so forth is declared in the ninth.
The expiation for approaching [a woman] after having understood [her status] is declared in the tenth [chapter];
that for eating forbidden food and so forth is declared in the eleventh.
There should be twelve supplements for both of those sections;
here, let the inclusion of other [topics] not mentioned be observed.
[21] Regarding the principal secondary sins (anupātaka), the expiation has not been stated in every instance;
likewise, the secret expiation has also been described.
Certain mild colors and other such difficult conditions have not been mentioned here, nor has the ripening of karma been stated; all of that is nonetheless implied.
Thus, the expiation has been elaborated upon through nine chapters;
this detailed exposition of expiation is undertaken because it is intended for the Kali age.
For in the Kali age, an abundance of evil is both seen and recorded in tradition;
since men are for the most part of little capacity, [this work is composed] out of a desire to favor them.
He contracted the rules of conduct, the penances, and the vows;
one should not censure them, for those twice-born ones were indeed shaped by the [degenerate] age.
[Par. Smṛ. 1.33;
11.51] [22] Thus, this compassion was previously mentioned at both the beginning and the end:
the study of a portion of the Veda and the livelihood of Brahmins and others through agriculture.
By such statements, a restriction in practice is clearly manifested:
"For the killing of a cow, there shall be a *pārājāpya* penance; for the slayer of a Brahmin, the pilgrimage to Setu."
Thus, because it is stated that this is the primary vow, a restriction is understood here as well;
the determination of its scope is established in accordance with another Smṛti.
If you say they must be postulated, then tell me of another proof for an omniscient being,
following the lead of all those various traditions that exist.
If it is argued that our own capacity does not extend to the entirety [of those objects],
then the claim that "it refers to as many as have been perceived by oneself" is likewise illogical.
[23] Because it is sometimes and in some cases seen to be otherwise, the mind is unstable; that cognition is merely a small amount of conceit, and it does not remain fixed.
For this very reason, a lack of consistency is observed in the commentaries;
alas, if this were so, the entire treatise would be as good as consigned to the depths.
Do not obstruct or contradict those who consider themselves wise;
hear now the conclusion on this matter from us, who maintain the doctrine of self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*).
When a matter is already established, all means of knowledge are authoritative provided there is no sublation;
nowhere, however, is there any sublation of the words of Parāśara by another Smṛti.
[24] Furthermore, the instruction regarding other vows does not constitute a contradiction, because it is not a prohibition;
for there are many [grains], such as priyaṅgu, kodrava, vrīhi, godhūma, and so forth.
Just as means of accomplishment for a single satisfaction are observed without contradiction,
and just as the Viśvajit sacrifice and the Agnihotra lead to a single heaven.
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, the New Moon sacrifice, and many other such causes are heard of in scripture,
just as there are various means for attaining the single world of Brahmā.
The meditations on Śāṇḍilya, the Dahara, and others are differentiated;
likewise, many means are recorded for the removal of a single sin.
[25] Let the various types of vows be conceptualized; however, your dullness of faith is in vain.
Indeed, where is the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth, and where is that which ends only with death?
For you who claim that these two are equally devoid of conceptual construction, this is an extreme audacity:
how can the Viśvajit sacrifice and the Agnihotra be equal when they both accomplish heaven?
Or how is it not an act of extreme audacity for you to speak of conceptual construction,
given that you rely on the principle that "an abundance of fruit results from an abundance of action"?
[26] "Violence must be avoided"—this applies equally to both sides.
But why is the established rule we have stated, which relies upon justice, being opposed?
If you say this, then a lack of consistency has been stated by you; therefore, I dislike your words, for they vary from one way to another due to differences of place, time, and person.
I have previously stated that the meaning of the treatise is subject to inversion;
therefore, in the case of prescriptive statements (*vidhi-vākya*), one should discard whatever portion constitutes an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) according to its respective nature.
That which is well-known should be accepted as such, unless there is a contradiction in the explicit scriptural statement;
for all commentators on the Smṛtis have established this principle regarding the interpretation of the words.
For those of dull intellect are merely instructed by those who speak thus;
otherwise, for the sake of a minor sin, there would be a twelve-year penance.

There would be no cessation [of suffering] as you have taught it, because such a system would exist; therefore, tell me: if a small [cause] were to destroy the great, then why would the other not be destroyed by a small [cause]?
What is your criterion for determining that "this is small" and "this is large"?
If it were the smallness of effort and the greatness of effort that constituted smallness and largeness [of the result], [then your position would be untenable].
[28] In that case, farmers and the like would be "Great Vow-holders" (mahāvrata),
because they involve a great deal of exertion in matters such as the urine of lions, tigers, and other animals.
For you, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) shall possess both excellence and the status of being an auxiliary to the vow;
whereas if [the former] were great, then [the latter] would be small due to the abundance of its required procedures.
Otherwise, there would follow the [unintended] consequence that entering water, fire, and so forth would constitute another vow;
therefore, that for which praise is declared by the scripture is the "Great Vow" (mahāvrata).
Or rather, let there indeed be a "Great Vow" because of the abundance of suffering;
for as a small loss is [compensated] by a great one, so too is a great loss [compensated] by a small one.
[29] Why should it not be so? For a heap of grass is indeed burned by a spark;
as that spark grows, it continues to burn, but such is not the case with a vow.
If this great destruction increases so that nothing remains, then let there be the destruction of only one part; let the remainder be enjoyed.
Even though sin is formless, it possesses divisions according to its nature;
otherwise, how could manifold suffering arise from a single sin?
Likewise, even when a small portion of a great vow has been ruined,
one remembers abundant happiness through the ripening of the remainder of that vow.
Therefore, whether it be small or even great, a vow that turns one away from evil is entirely consistent with the words of all those who remember [the truth].
The Great Vow is not rendered futile in the complete destruction of evil,
because it is useful for the destruction of minor faults and for the attainment of future happiness.
And thus, when vows have been prescribed for even a single sin,
this man proceeds out of confidence toward whichever one he desires.
[31] Otherwise, there can be no confidence in this established object,
whether for one who does not know it or even for one who knows it, due to the suspicion that there may be another statement.
Among all the vows that are esteemed, a person who engages in a great vow undoubtedly attains the highest good.
In the Kali age, the vows prescribed by Parāśara alone are paramount;
even by performing those briefly, that sin is completely eliminated.
Intending to explain this very point in detail,
he made a formal promise regarding the penance that was thus proclaimed by Parāśara.
According to the principle previously stated, there may be the practice of even small or great vows prescribed for other sages in the Kali age.
[32] What has been spoken by one sage is not refuted by another; on the contrary, he would rather cite it in support. Therefore, the word of everyone is agreed upon by all.
Alas, this being the case, your Mīmāṃsā would result in being fruitless,
since even the virtues prescribed in other scriptures would not be incorporated.
Listen, O you who are skilled in dialectical inquiry: what force is there in the words of the sages? Even by creating contradictions yourself, you merely manifest your own cleverness.
No contradiction arises merely from the mention of another vow;
whether there is a combination or an option, what loss would there be for you in that case?
Just as bathing, giving, recitation, and fire-offerings are to be combined on specific occasions,
so too is the combination of vows to be performed at the conclusion [of the eclipse].
[33] If one evil has been destroyed by one [act], the second would be useless;
for it is not possible that its nature as austerity could serve as a cause for heaven [in that case].
Let it be so in the case of the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such rites because they are perceived as forms of austerity;
but how could it be so for the begging bowl, the skull of Brahmā, and so forth, in the case of one whose sins have already been destroyed?
In that case, let there be such a conceptual construction (vikalpa) in this matter according to one's own wish;
as for the doubt regarding deficiency or excess, an answer has already been given previously.

[34] In every respect, we do not accept the established doctrine you have propounded, for it is rootless, a mere construction of the intellect, and differentiated by such categories as desire and lack of desire.
If the distinction between desire and the other [afflictions] is obtained only within the [scriptural] statements themselves,
then we, who take the word as our sole refuge, accept this with ease.
"If Kapila is omniscient, what proof is there that Kaṇāda is not?"—
such a logical consequence would follow if omniscience were established based on mere intelligence alone.

That which consists in establishing [the meaning] by following the literal sequence of the sentences would be the mark of a Mīmāṃsaka; anything else, however, is merely a display of one's own scholarship.
"This purification has been declared for having killed a twice-born man unintentionally" (MDh 11.89);
thus, the complete destruction of sin committed unintentionally is stated.
[35] However, it is not said that purification is ineffective when performed out of desire,
because other Smṛti texts state that purification occurs in general terms.
As long as there is no perception of particulars, so long is there perception of the universal;
otherwise, your authority would consist merely in being an omniscient being.
And thus, the synthesis of qualities should be accepted according to what is observed;
for if there is no synthesis of what has not been observed, it would be of no use to you at all.

To whatever extent a statement is observed, and to whatever extent its capacity exists therein, to that extent the effect must be produced; it is not proper to neglect it out of a suspicion of deficiency.
Having cited those other Smṛtis which I have observed regarding penance and conduct,
I shall thereafter collect their essential qualities.
And for the sake of establishing the subject matter and for the attainment of clear understanding,
I shall explain it just as previous authors of treatises have done.
Whatever has been stated regarding a particular subject is intended as a praise of that very thing; here, no negation of anything else is intended.
For the sake of discerning that [truth], I shall here compose a commentary on the Pārāśara-smṛti.
(Thus begins the author of the commentary.

In order to focus the minds and intellects of the listeners upon the work he intends to compose, he first sets forth the fourfold preliminary inquiry (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*)—consisting of the connection (*saṃbandha*), the qualified student (*adhikārin*), the subject matter (*viṣaya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*)—in the following two verses:
Then, in ancient times, the sages questioned Vyāsa as he sat with one-pointed concentration at the summit of the Himālayas, in a dwelling within a forest of Devadāru trees.
O son of Satyavatī, please describe in due detail the Dharma beneficial for human beings and the rules of purification and conduct as they pertain to the current Kali Yuga.

Regarding the word *atha*: the term *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*). This is because it is appropriate to construe it as “immediately thereafter they asked. If it were intended to signify the commencement of an action (*ārambha*), there would be a lack of syntactic connection in the phrase “having begun, they asked. The same fault applies even if it were intended to mean “questioning” (*praśna*), as in “they asked by means of questioning,” which would be a tautology. If it were intended to mean “entirety” (*kārtsnya*), as in “they asked completely,” even if the construction were possible, the relationship between the two parts would not be indicated. However, when it signifies immediate succession, the causal relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) between the preceding event (the antecedent) and the subsequent question is indicated. [38]

Now, if it is argued that in the passage, "First he cuts from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest" (TS 6.3.11), there is no relationship of cause and effect despite the sequence; then [we reply]:

This is not a fault, because in that case, only the mere sequence of performance required therein is being stated. In the present context, however, the specific sequence between the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and its effect is what is adopted, because it is primary (*mukhya*). It is indeed primary precisely because there is no delay or deviation; for when the causal complex is present, the effect neither delays nor deviates. This has been explained in detail by the author of the *Vivaraṇa* regarding the phrase "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*, *Brahmasūtra* 1.1.1). And the causal complex for a question consists of a general knowledge of the subject matter to be asked about, since questions are not observed when the object is either entirely unknown or already known in its specific details. General knowledge concerning Dharma, however, arises from the study of Vedic passages such as "One removes evil through Dharma" (*Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* 22.1) and "Practice Dharma" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 1.11.1). Therefore, the meaning of the word *atha* is "immediately after the study [of the Vedas]. Alternatively, because of the qualification "in the current Kali age," let it be understood as "immediately after the knowledge of the Dharma of other ages. [39]

Now, one might ask: since the performance of an auspicious invocation at the beginning of a work is established by the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), why is auspiciousness not explicitly denoted by the word *atha*? We reply that the attainment of auspiciousness occurs merely by hearing the word *atha*, just like the sound of a drum or similar instruments. For this very reason it has been said:
"The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the mouth of Brahmā after piercing his throat; therefore, both are auspicious."
If it is argued that, in that case, the syllable *oṃ* should be employed here:

No, because that [the syllable *oṃ*] has as its sole object the Veda. For this very reason, it was stated by the Teachers in the *Prapañcasāra*: “Because this is the beginning of the Vedas, everything belonging to the twice-born (*anūnām*) is indeed preceded by the two [the *oṃ* and *atha*]. Consequently, the word *atha* alone is employed by the great seers (*maharṣis*) in the *Smṛtis* and other such works. Furthermore, by considering the qualified recipients (*adhikārin*), the established distinction between the subject matter of the *oṃ* and the *atha* is proven. For the *Śruti* is well known to have as its qualified recipients only those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), and the *oṃ* is likewise so. According to the *Śruti*: “They do not desire the *Sāvitrī*, the *Praṇava*, the *Yajus*, or *Lakṣmī* for a woman or a *Śūdra*” (*Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanī* 1.3). Since the word *atha* and human-authored texts (*pauruṣeya-grantha*) have as their scope all castes, that [word *atha*] alone is appropriate for them.

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since those who study only a single recensional branch (*śākhā*) do not possess knowledge of all dharmas, and since there is no comprehension of the dharma of the Kali age through the comprehension of the dharma of other ages, this should be understood as the reason.

Since the infinite Vedic statements, which constitute the root of all dharmas without exception, are to be grasped only through the vision of a yogin, and since that vision is possible only in the state of yoga, he indicates with two words a specific location suitable for that state: "on the peak of the snowy mountain, in a dwelling in the Devadāru forest. There, by the phrase "on the peak of the snowy mountain," he expresses its seclusion due to its inaccessibility to all living beings. Thus it is heard in the Kaivalyopaniṣad: "Seated in a comfortable posture in a secluded place" (Kaiv. Up. 4). It is also heard in the Kṣurikopaniṣad: "Having resorted to a noiseless place, having taken his seat there" (Kṣu. Up. 2). By the phrase "in a dwelling in the Devadāru forest," he expresses its suitability for the mind. For this very reason, it is heard in the Mantra-upaniṣad of the Śvetāśvataras:

"In a clean place, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, which is agreeable to the mind and not distressing to the eyes, and which is sheltered from wind in a cave or similar location— one should practice. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10)
A place infested with mosquitoes is distressing to the eyes.

But surely, in this section (UMS 4.1, adhikaraṇa 6), beginning with the sūtra “Wherever there is one-pointedness, there [practice may be done], because there is no distinction” (UMS 4.1.7), the restriction of direction, place, and time for the practice of yoga has been refuted.
Certainly; however, even though there is no restriction regarding the unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa*), the restriction concerning the visible cause—namely, one-pointedness of mind—is not precluded.

By the term "one-pointed" (*ekāgram*), the fourth of the five stages of consciousness (*cittabhūmi*)—which is capable of perceiving supersensuous objects—is indicated. For instance, in the *Vaiyyāsikabhāṣya*, a commentary on the *Yogasūtras* of Patañjali, five stages of consciousness are demonstrated: "The stages of consciousness are the distracted (*kṣipta*), the dull (*mūḍha*), the scattered (*vikṣipta*), the one-pointed (*ekāgra*), and the restrained (*niruddha*)" (YBh 1.1). Among these: the mind is *distracted* when it is driven moment by moment toward various objects of enjoyment by the winds of karma; it is *dull* when possessed of sleep and lethargy; it is *scattered*—distinguished from the distracted—when it is occasionally joined with meditative absorption (*samādhi*). It is *one-pointed* when, through proficiency in the practice of the eight limbs beginning with restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*), it remains established upon a single object in the form of a continuous flow of mental modifications (*vṛtti*). It is *restrained* when devoid of modifications and consisting of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone. In this regard, it is well known that the distracted and dull states are useless for yoga. Even in the scattered mind, absorption that has become subordinate to distraction does not belong to the side of yoga; because it is included among opposing factors, it is as ineffective as a seed placed within fire. "That which, in a one-pointed mind, illuminates the true object, attenuates the afflictions (*kleśa*), loosens the bonds of karma, and brings about opposition [to them], is called cognitive yoga (*saṃprajñāta-yoga*)" (YBh 1.1). Through specific forms of constraint (*saṃyama*) therein, various kinds of yogic sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) manifest. Constraint is defined as the triad of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*) focused on a single object. As Patañjali stated: "When there is constraint upon the word, the object, and the cognition—which are mutually distinct—and there is direct perception of all words and so forth, the speech of birds and other beings becomes known. By that same principle, the knowledge of the various branches of the Vedas is intended; it is with this in mind that the term "one-pointed" is used.

Considering that the posture (*āsana*) serves as a limb for one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*), [the author] says "seated" (*āsīnam*). Thus, there is the *Vyāsasūtra*: "He is seated, because of its possibility" (UMS 4.1.7). For one who is lying down, sleep may suddenly overcome him; for one who has risen, the mind is occupied with maintaining the body; and for one who is walking or running, there is an abundance of distraction. By process of elimination, since one-pointedness of mind is possible only for one who is seated, the meaning is that one should practice yoga while seated.

Intending to show that questioning is a means for attaining understanding through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he said "he questioned. The positive concomitance is expressed in [Bhagavad Gītā 4.34]: "Know that by prostration, by inquiry, and by service. The negative concomitance is expressed in [Manu Smṛti 2.110]: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked."

The word *ṛṣi* denotes the perception of objects beyond the reach of the senses. The status of being a seer (*ṛṣitva*) occurs subsequent to the practice of those dharmas that are yet to be known. This is just as one uses the expression "make a mat" by employing a designation that refers to what is yet to come. Otherwise, if they were already seeing supersensuous objects, their inquiry would not be appropriate, as they would have no desire to know [what they already perceive]. Alternatively, let the inquiry be for the purpose of teaching proper conduct, or for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect who, though not themselves desirous of knowledge, require instruction.

By using the word "pure" (formerly), he indicates that although the past tense is already established by the verb "apṛcchan" (asked), such a tradition of the *Dharmaśāstra* has existed in all *kalpas*. This serves as a cause for generating an extraordinary degree of confidence. Furthermore, the intention behind the seers' choice to question Vyāsa alone, while disregarding other sages, is that Vyāsa is preeminent in the Vedic *dharma*.

Thus, in this verse, two types of relationship are presented: the direct relationship of the work intended to be composed with the question of the Sage, and the relationship with the study [of the work] by way of generating the desire to inquire. However, the triad beginning with the qualified student (adhikārī) is set forth in the second verse.

Now, an objection: just as specific qualifications for those entitled to perform rites are heard in such injunctions as, "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava; a King should sacrifice with the Rājasūya; a Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," there is no such statement regarding the duties taught by Parāśara that they are to be performed by such [specific classes]. How, then, is this to be determined?

Therefore, he says: "Of human beings. Because those who are inferior, such as animals and the like, lack the capacity, and because for the highest beings, such as the gods, there is no purpose in the performance of dharma, only humans remain. Since no specific distinction has been determined, let the entitlement belong to all humans.

But surely, the entitlement of the gods is heard of in the Nakṣatreṣṭi and other rites: "Agni indeed desired, 'May I be the eater of food among the gods. He offered this cake of eight potsherds, mixed with earth, to Agni Kṛttikā" (TB 3.1.4).

Not so; for the word "Agni" in the nominative case is used by relying on the future designation of a certain human sacrificer. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of two fires being simultaneously conflated.

Now, one might object: let there be an entitlement for deities (*devatādhikāra*) in those cases where the fault of doubling (*dvaiguṇya*) does not exist; for it is heard in scripture: “Bṛhaspati desired, ‘May the gods have faith in me; may I attain the office of domestic priest (*purodhā*). He saw this twenty-four-night sacrifice (*caturviṃśatirātra*); he took it up and performed it with it. Then indeed, the gods had faith in him and attained the office of domestic priest” (TS 7.1.1). Here, *śrat* means trust; *me* means in me; *purodhām* means the priesthood (*paurohitya*); and *caturviṃśatirātram* means a sacrificial session (*satrayāga*) of that name.

Not so; for even here, it is the future designation that must be accepted. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that Bṛhaspati would lack both trustworthiness and the office of domestic priest (*purohita*) for some period of time. And that would contradict another Vedic text: "Bṛhaspati was indeed the domestic priest of the gods" (TS 6.4.11), by which the existence of Bṛhaspati is revealed as being preceded precisely by his office as *purohita*.

Alternatively, even if there is no personal utility for themselves, let the gods perform ritual acts in order to incite human beings, according to the maxim: "Whatever the best man practices, that very thing other people do" (BhG 3.21). Or, let there indeed be personal utility as well, because those gods who are appointed to the maintenance of the world must practice austerity as the cause thereof. If it is argued that the consecration of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), which is prescribed by the rule "In autumn, a Vaiśya should establish the fires" (TB 1.1.2), is impossible for gods—just as it is for those outside the three higher castes (*atraidharmika*)—we say no, for it is possible in the same manner as the case of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*).

Now, you might think: there exists for the chariot-maker a scriptural injunction prescribing the installation of the fires accompanied by mantras, because of the Vedic text, “‘O Lord of Vows, I install thee with the vow of the Ṛbhus, the gods’—this is for the chariot-maker” (TB 3.1.6.15). But there is no such injunction for the gods. If that is so, then let the principle of the Niṣāda-sthapati apply. Just as the status of the Niṣāda chief is accepted even though no injunction for his own installation of the fires is heard, so too should it be accepted for the gods. If it is argued that there is a statement concerning the Niṣādas, namely, “One should cause the Niṣāda-sthapati to win by means of this [offering],” [then the same applies here].

Have you forgotten those statements concerning the realm of the gods cited previously? Even if they were considered *arthavāda* (explanatory passages), why should they not have an intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding their own literal sense, given that they do not contradict other means of valid cognition and are not merely restatements of what is already known?

Now, it might be argued: "Since the *Smṛtis* are treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), the *Dharmamīmāṃsā* must be followed in them; and in that [system], it is not accepted that any *arthavāda* has authority regarding its literal meaning. This statement, while supporting the *Smṛtis*, would be for the benefit of one [party] but for the total detriment of another. It falls under the maxim: "The house was burned out of fear of mice. Out of fear that some *arthavāda* might have authority in its own sense, one would have to abandon the very existence of the *Smṛti*-composers such as Manu and others—who are renowned solely for their *arthavādas*—as well as Jaimini, the author of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtras*. Furthermore, this would lead to the loss of all history (*itihāsa*). Therefore, an *arthavāda* that describes an actual fact (*bhūtārtha*) is indeed authoritative. And this being the case, why could even the gods not have performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), based on the *arthavāda*: "Pūṣan performed it; Tvaṣṭṛ performed it; Manu performed it; Dhātṛ performed it"? If there were an absence of Brāhmaṇa-status and so forth, then certainly there would be no restriction to specific times such as spring; but what does that have to do with the act of consecration itself? Moreover, a sacrifice is observed even in a worldly fire without a formal consecration, according to the *Jaiminisūtra*: "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), likewise, because the time for the consecration has not arrived" (PMS 6.8.22). The animal sacrifice for the breaker of vows is defined as: "He who, being a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), approaches a woman is a *avakīrṇin*; he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal" (BDh 2.1.1.30–31). The meaning of the *sūtra* is that just as the initiation-oblation (*upanayanahoma*) is performed in a worldly fire, so too is this animal sacrifice. Having expended so much effort to establish the eligibility of the gods for ritual action, what will be the fruit for you? What is cut away in the *Mīmāṃsā* by this? Only your dogmatic attachment remains. As for the result, it is simply the sustenance of the world (*jagannirvāha*), as was stated previously. In this way, the entire corpus of the *Purāṇas* and other texts is upheld. Let there be no rituals for the gods toward heaven as there are for humans; rather, they shall exist for the sustenance of the world. If it is argued that the world is sustained by austerity alone—[we reply: no.

No, for austerity is not observed as anything distinct from bathing, giving, sacrifice, oblation, silence, meditation, and so forth. For this very reason, although the Supreme Lord possesses the power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*), he sustained the world through the performance of worldly and Vedic actions alone during his incarnations as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others.
If it is argued that the gods likewise should act as performers, even so, you must admit that they possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the actions to be performed.
If it is asked, "In that case, why was it said 'of humans'?

we reply: it was said with reference to human-authored texts. Indeed, for the gods, whose entire Vedas are self-manifesting, there is no need for human-authored texts to know the Dharma; however, because humans are not of such a nature, they do have such a need.

But surely, the eligibility for *dharma* is also heard of even among animals. For the Śruti states: "The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session (*sattra*), thinking with the desire, 'Though we are hornless, may horns grow upon us. They remained seated for months, and then horns grew. They arose, saying, 'We have succeeded! Then those whose horns did not grow arose after completing a year, saying, 'We have succeeded! (TS 6.5.1.1). By this scriptural passage, it is declared that even animals, such as cows, are performers of the sacrificial session. The phrase "we have succeeded" (*arāt sma*) means that they attained the fulfillment of their desired object.

This is not a fault, because this scriptural passage is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). In order to enjoin the year-long sacrificial session (*saṃvatsarasattra*) for one desiring prosperity—via the statement, “Those who, knowing thus, undertake the year-long session” (TS 7.5.1.2)—there is first made a commendation: “The year-long session is indeed the *gosattra*” (TS 7.5.1.12). To substantiate that [praise], the passage beginning with “Cows, indeed... is recited. Furthermore, it is impossible to maintain that this *arthavāda* has its own literal meaning as its primary purport, as in the case of such passages as “Whatever Manu said is medicine,” because it contradicts both direct perception and other scriptural texts. For the lack of capacity in animals for the utterance of mantras and the performance of ritual acts is established by direct perception. Moreover, another scriptural text demonstrates the lack of discernment in animals: “Now, they say that hunger and thirst are the only signs of knowledge for other animals; they do not see what is unknown, nor do they know the morrow. Or, let us grant that this *arthavāda* does have its own literal meaning as its purport, on the grounds that by the word “cows” (*go*), the presiding deities (*abhimānin-devatā*) of the cows are intended. For this very reason, in the Sūtra, “But there is designation by way of the presiding deities” (Brahmasūtra 2.1.5), the venerable Bādarāyaṇa established that all things, such as clay and the like, have presiding deities based on the authority of Śruti. Therefore, the Smṛti scripture has human beings alone as its qualified audience in every respect.

By the word "beneficial" (*hitam*), the purpose is indicated. For the quality of being beneficial (*hitatvam*) consists in being a means to achieve a desired result. And that result is twofold: pertaining to this world (*aihika*) and pertaining to the next world (*āmuṣmika*). That which is accomplished through the *Aṣṭakā* and other rites, such as nourishment and so forth, is pertaining to this world. That pertaining to the next world is twofold: prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Among these, [dharma] is a direct means to prosperity, but to the supreme good it is a means by way of generating the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). And thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:

[53] "From dharma, happiness and knowledge arise; from knowledge, liberation is attained. Regarding this, some say: "There is no fruit at all for obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). They are performed merely out of fear of the transgression incurred by non-performance. In that case, how can they be the cause of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) or the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)?"

Others, however, say otherwise: "Since the arising of an entity from non-existence is not observed, the claim that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for non-performance is not logically tenable; nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it. But surely, a transgression for the non-performance of enjoined acts such as initiation (*upanayana*) and Vedic study is recorded in tradition (*smṛti*): "Beyond this age, if these three have not been consecrated at the proper time, they become fallen from the *Sāvitrī*, outcasts (*vrātyas*), despised by the noble ones" (MDh 2.39).
(54) That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still living, along with his progeny.
By failing to perform prescribed duties and by practicing what is censured, [he likewise falls].
And through the lack of restraint of the senses, a man undergoes downfall. [55]

Not so. For these scriptural passages indicate the existence of previously accumulated demerit (*durita*) caused by laziness on the part of one who fails to perform obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). This has been established by both the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) and the Author of the Vārttika in their exegesis of the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*. Whether non-performance produces demerit or merely indicates it, in either case, through the performance of obligatory duties, there is achieved both the preservation of the antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*) of demerit and the production of its subsequent absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Furthermore, the power to destroy demerit is clearly manifest in the mantras recited at the three junctions of the day: "And the Sun" (MNU 14.4), "May the Waters Purify" (MNU 14.2), and "And Fire" (MNU 14.3). This being the case, it is difficult to maintain that obligatory duties—which lack any fruit to be enjoyed—are causes for worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). [56]

To this it is replied: Let there be opposition to the incurrence of sin (*pratyavāya*); yet, by this much alone, there is no absence of a fruit, because that fruit is understood from the indicative power of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*), as well as from Śruti and Smṛti statements. The indicative power of the mantra is: “Bestow upon me luster, strength, and vigor” (*mayi varco balam ojo vidhatta*). And the Chāndogya statement shows that the three stages of life (*āśrama*) are the cause of the worlds, while the fourth stage is the cause of liberation: “There are three branches of duty (*dharma-skandha*): sacrifice, study, and charity; the first is austerity itself; the second is the student living in the teacher’s house; the third is one who settles himself completely in the teacher’s house. All these attain the worlds of merit; he who is established in Brahman attains immortality” (ChU 2.23.1). That this statement refers to the stages of life has been established by the Vyāsa-sūtras beginning with “Jaimini [thinks] it is a reference” (UMS 3.4.18). And this is a Smṛti statement: “Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of fruit, shade and fragrance are produced as secondary results; so too, when dharma is practiced, worldly benefits are produced as secondary results. And Viśvarūpācārya cited this statement in his Vārttika as referring to obligatory duties (*nityakarman*).

"The statement from the *Āpastamba-smṛti* beginning with 'In the mango tree, for the sake of fruit' indeed declares that even obligatory rites possess fruitfulness. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārttika 1.1.97)
And so Manu says:
"One should constantly perform, without sloth, one's own duty as prescribed by the Veda;
for performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal" (MDh 4.14).
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"One should perform action according to one's ability and avoid censurable acts;
having shaken off the turbid mass of delusion and attained the unsurpassed yoga."

"A householder is liberated from bondage; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (KūP 1.2.28–29) Now, one might object: let it be so. However, its being a cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is not possible, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). On the contrary, it is prohibited by both Śruti and Smṛti: the Śruti says, "Not by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth" (MNU 10.5); and the Smṛti says, "Liberation (*kaivalya*) comes only from knowledge."

It is not so; for within the context of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), sacrifices and other rites are enjoined as means for the desire to know—that knowledge which is the cause of supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), according to the scriptural text: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, and through charity. The prohibition, however, will refer to [the idea that these rites are] direct means to supreme liberation. Therefore, there is no requirement for liberated souls to perform rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*); such a requirement exists only for the arising of that knowledge. Both of these points have been established by the two sections [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "And for this very reason, there is no dependence on the kindling of the fires and so forth" (UMS 3.4.25), and "And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse" (UMS 3.4.26). Accordingly, the fact that ritual actions are causes of liberation through a mediated succession has been declared in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*.

Having attained a preeminence of karma, there occurs the destruction of the fetters of the bound soul. Thus, for one whose sins have been gradually exhausted over many births, detachment from sense objects arises; from detachment comes the purification of one's inner disposition.
For one endowed with purity of being, there is the attainment of the knowledge of Śiva.
For a person devoted to knowledge and meditation, yoga proceeds;
through yoga, however, supreme devotion arises, and immediately thereafter, grace. (70, 75)
"Through grace, a living being is liberated; once liberated, he becomes equal to Śiva. (Śiva Purāṇa 5.1.2.69–76).

Now, one might object: for the sake of avoiding transgression, for the attainment of meritorious worlds, and for the knowledge of Brahman, it follows that the daily obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) should be performed three times each day.

That is not so; for just as in the case of the *khadira* wood, since the action is performed only once, the non-difference of the result is established through the difference in the connection of the scriptural injunctions. The statement, “The sacrificial post is made of *khadira* wood” (*TB* 2.4.24), pertains to human goals. These two statements together constitute the reason for the twofold utility of the single *khadira* wood, according to Jaimini’s sūtra: “But when one thing has a dual purpose, there is a separation of connections” (*PMS* 4.4.31). Likewise, here too, by the force of the three previously cited statements, even though there is a threefold utility, the performance occurs only once. And this has been determined in the section beginning with: “And because it is enjoined, the duties of the stages of life are also [to be performed]” (*UMS* 3.4.32). Nor should it be suspected that if the obligatory (*nitya*) rite also possesses a fruit, there would be no distinction between the obligatory and the optional (*kāmya*). For although the results are equal when the rite is performed, they differ in that the obligatory rite entails sin (*pratyavāya*) if not performed, whereas the optional does not. Indeed, no sin is heard of in scripture regarding the non-performance of rites such as the *Āyuṣkāma* or *Vṛṣṭikāma* sacrifices. This same principle of the obligatory applies to the occasional (*naimittika*) as well. That which is associated with specific conditions—such as the Vedic injunctions, “He offers when [the ladle] has spilled,” or “He offers when it has broken”—is the occasional rite.

If it is argued that even optional rites (*kāmya*) possess the status of a means to liberation because, being prescribed as obligatory (*nityavat*), they cause purification, we say no; for passion (*rāga*) is predominant. Purification, however, being subordinate, is exhausted once it has produced enjoyment as the object of that passion. For this very reason, the Blessed One in the *Gītā* prohibited Arjuna, who was seeking liberation, from attachment to results: "Established in yoga, perform actions, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment."
"Being the same in success and failure, equanimity is called yoga. (BhG 2.48) "Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits;
let not the fruit of action be your motive... (BhG 2.47) [62]

By such statements as these, it is shown that in the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), the purification of the intellect (*buddhiśuddhi*) is primary, while the fruit (*phala*) is secondary. For this very reason, even while the fruit is being experienced, one’s discernment (*viveka*)—which consists in perceiving the defects of impermanence and excessiveness in that fruit—is not obstructed. As stated by the author of the *Vārttika*: "In obligatory rites, because purity is primary, even enjoyment does not constitute an obstruction; those who follow the purification of the intellect regard enjoyment as fragile."

(From Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārttika 1.1.608) Furthermore, obligatory action (*nitya-karma*) is of two kinds: that which is purificatory (*saṃskāraka*) and that which generates the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-janaka*). That which is performed with the mere understanding that it is prescribed is purificatory. And thus it is recorded in Smṛti: "He for whom these forty-eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) exist goes to union with Brahman (*sāyujya*) and to the same world (*salokatā*). That which is performed with the understanding of offering it to the Lord (*īśvara-arpaṇa-buddhi*) is that which generates the desire for knowledge. And this has been shown by the Blessed One: "Whatever one does, whatever one eats, whatever one offers in sacrifice, and whatever one gives..."

"Whatever austerity you perform, O son of Kuntī, do that as an offering unto Me" (BhG 9.27). Thus it is also stated in the *Gītā*. In that regard, through *saṃskāra* (purification), the mind merely attains the capacity for knowledge (*vedanā-yogyatā*). However, the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), by generating activity, necessarily brings about realization (*vedana*). Therefore, for one seeking liberation, offering everything to the Lord is praiseworthy. Precisely because that [offering] is designated by the word "beneficial" (*hita*) as being a means to the desired end of dharma, it is said that the "attainment of the desired goal" is the purpose (*prayojana*).

The word *dharma* indicates the subject matter. It is called *dharma* because it sustains (*dhārayati*) both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by being their means. And that [subject] has been established through its definition and its means of valid cognition by the aphorisms concerning *codanā*. Now, an objection: that which is to be understood through *codanā* cannot be the object of *smṛti* (tradition/memory), because it is understood that the object [of a means of knowledge] must be something not obtainable through any other means. If you think that even though it is to be known through *codanā*, it is nevertheless compiled—setting aside the *arthavādas* and by way of synthesizing specific details found in other recensions—for the sake of facilitating the order of performance, [we reply: [This is accepted. However, the *smṛti* is not a separate means of valid cognition for that which is already established by *codanā*; rather, it serves as a reminder (*smāraka*) of what has already been known. For example, just as one who has previously seen a cow remembers her when seeing a gavaya, so too does one remember the *dharma* previously known through *codanā* by means of the *smṛti*. Thus, there is no contradiction between *śruti* and *smṛti*. Furthermore, since the *smṛti* is based on a *codanā* that is inferred (*kalpyamāna*), it is indeed a means of valid cognition for that which is not otherwise established. Therefore, the *smṛti* is authoritative insofar as it is not contradicted by perception or *śruti*. As for the *ācāra* (conduct) of virtuous men, it is authoritative as a source of inference for a *codanā*. Thus, all these are means of valid cognition for the *dharma*. This is the conclusion.

That is not so, because they are included in that manner within the *Kalpasūtras*. Anticipating the objection that, for this reason, purity (*dharma*) would not fall within its scope, he says: "purity and conduct" (*śaucācāram*). This is the intended meaning: Dharma is twofold—based on revelation (*śrauta*) and based on tradition (*smārta*). Among these, the *śrauta* consists of rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), which are preceded by the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) and are rooted in the Veda as directly perceived and studied. The *smārta* consists of practices such as ritual purity (*śauca*) and sipping water (*ācamana*), which are rooted in branches of the Veda that are inferred and beyond direct perception. Now, although the establishment of the fires and other such rites are included in the *Kalpasūtras*, purity and the like are not; therefore, they do fall within its scope.

Now, one might object: "Purity and other such practices are also mentioned in other Smṛtis. To this he replies: "In the present Kali age. Since in the present Kali age activities such as officiating at sacrifices and teaching are insufficient for a livelihood, that dharma—consisting of agriculture and the like performed by Brāhmaṇas—which is beneficial, easy to perform, and conducive to human life, prosperity, and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), is what is primarily expounded here. The meaning is that its status as the subject matter [of this work] arises from the fact that it cannot be obtained elsewhere.

By the word "yathāvat" (according to reality), he expresses completeness and thereby precludes any contraction [of the meaning]; however, it does not preclude the possibility of speaking otherwise, for such a thing is impossible given that the authors of the tradition are free from error and deception. For this very reason, there is the address "son of Satyavatī. When even a woman who was virtuous, truthful, and spoke the truth was called Satyavatī, her mother; then what need is there to say that her son, the teacher of the Vedas, is a speaker of truth? By the particle "ca" (and), he conjoins the quality of being easily understood.

In this regard, the mutual relationship between the aforementioned qualification (*adhikārin*), purpose (*prayojana*), and subject matter (*viṣaya*) is clear. Among these, the purpose and the qualified person stand in the relation of the sought object and the seeker; for it is the qualified person who seeks the purpose. Furthermore, there is a relationship of produced and producer between the purpose and the subject matter, because when the Dharma is known, prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) are accomplished through its practice. And there is a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor between the qualified person and the subject matter; the subject matter, having brought about the purpose, benefits the qualified person. Finally, there is a relationship of the expounded and the expounder between the subject matter and the text. Thus, since the fourfold preliminary conditions (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*) are easily established, listeners with concentrated minds should apply themselves to this treatise—this is the intended meaning of the two verses. (1–2)
Now, fearing that the question addressed to Vyāsa in the introduction to the *Parāśarasmṛti* might be inconsistent with its subject matter, he refutes this objection with two verses:
"Having heard those words of the sage, he—who was like fire and the sun, possessed of great luster, and learned in the Śruti and Smṛti—replied together with his disciples. (3)
"And since I am not an omniscient knower of all truths, how could I speak on the Dharma?
My father alone should be questioned," thus Vyāsa, the son, replied. (4)

Regarding the passage beginning with *tad* and so forth: he is "with his disciples" (*saśiṣya*) because he is accompanied by Sumantu, Vaiśampāyana, Jaimini, and Paila—his disciples who were the propagators of the four Vedas and were joined by Sūta, the propagator of the Purāṇas. Just as fire is endowed with flames and the sun with rays, so too is he endowed with disciples whose learning is equal to his own; for this very reason, he possesses "great splendor" (*mahātejas*). By the word *tejas*, what is intended here is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), since there is no need for any other kind of physical brilliance. He clarifies this very intention with the phrase "learned in the Śruti. The analogies of fire and the sun should be applied respectively to the Śruti and the Smṛti. Fire burns only what is near to it, yet it burns without distinction both day and night. Likewise, although only a few *dharmas* are known from the directly studied Śruti texts, they are known without distinction whether one is in a state of formal application (*yukta*) or not. The sun, while illuminating only during the day, illuminates everything—both near and far. Similarly, although the *dharmas* recorded in the Smṛtis are remembered only when one is in a state of application, all of them—even those scattered across various branches (*śākhās*)—are remembered. Alternatively, the analogy of fire is used in the sense that he is utterly purified by austerity, according to the Vedic text: "Agni is the most pure in his vows" (RV 6.3.40.1). The analogy of the sun is used for his capacity to manifest a vast range of subjects. || 3 ||
But surely—if this were the case, the statement "I am not omniscient" would be contradicted.

No—because that statement is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) intended to glorify his father. Just as the statement, "All other animals are indeed not cattle (*apaśavaḥ*) except for cows and horses" (*TS* 5.2.9.4), is primarily for the purpose of praising cows and horses, yet does not negate the status of goats and others as cattle—since that would contradict direct perception and conflict with injunctions regarding sacrificial animals such as those dedicated to Agni-Soma—so too this statement by Vyāsa does not negate Vyāsa’s omniscience; rather, it praises his father. Alternatively, this was said for the purpose of instructing him in proper conduct, such as that one must show humility toward one's teacher. Or else, the intention of Vyāsa—who says "nor do I"—is this: "Now the duties of the Kali age are being asked about. In that regard, I do not personally know the true nature of the Kali-age duties, because my father alone is proficient in them. For this very reason, it will be stated later: 'In the Kali age, the followers of Parāśara are remembered [as authorities]' (*ParSm* 1.24). If my knowledge of them comes through my father's grace, then that father himself should be questioned. Indeed, when the original speaker is available, it is not appropriate to resort to an indirect channel."

He is called "Father" (*pitā*) because he protects. And his role as protector here should be understood in accordance with the context as being through the instruction of the *dharma* of the Kali age. With this very intention, he employs the word "father" (*pitṛ*), setting aside terms such as "progenitor" (*janaka*) or "grandfather" (*tātā*). By the use of the particle "only" (*eva*), other traditionalists (*smartāraḥ*) are excluded. Although Manu and others were also conversant with the *dharma* of the Kali age, nevertheless, in this matter, a certain extraordinary excellence due to the power of Parāśara’s specific asceticism (*tapas*) is to be recognized. This is to be understood just as the unique status of Kaṇva and others is recognized within their respective recensions (*śākhā*), such as the Kāṇva, Mādhyandina, Kāṭhaka, Kauthuma, and Taittirīya.

The intention behind the statement “Vyāsa is the son” is this: if even Parāśara’s son—who was endowed with the tradition of the *dharma* of the Kali age—felt hesitation in proclaiming the secrets of that *dharma*, then what need is there to mention others? Thus, it should be understood that in order to generate an awareness of extreme reverence for Parāśara by means of Vyāsa, the question addressed to Vyāsa regarding the introduction of the *Parāśarasmṛti* is not irrelevant (*avyadhikaraṇa*). || 4 ||
Intending to show that the acquisition of knowledge occurs through approaching a guru according to the prescribed rule, he demonstrates that approach:
"Then all those sages, desiring the true meaning of the principles of Dharma, went to Badarikāśrama, placing the sage Vyāsa at their head. (5)

Thus, in every case, when an object is known in its general aspect (*sāmānya*) but unknown in its specific details (*viśeṣa*), there arises a desire for knowledge. Here, the word *dharma* denotes the general aspect, while the word *tattvārtha* denotes the specific detail. Among these, the general aspect is understood by a person who has studied the Veda, mastered grammar, and is skilled in the definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the Veda defines the general nature of Dharma: "Dharma is the foundation of the entire world" (MNU 1.22). However, those who study other recensions (*śākhā*) come to know it through the science of grammar, since it has been shown that [the term] is derived from the etymology: "it upholds prosperity and the supreme good" (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*). If one is skilled in the *auṇādika* derivations, let him know it by that definition. As for the specific meaning, the definition is: "Dharma is that which is to be known through Vedic injunction (*codanā*). In this context, the word "meaning" (*artha*) excludes non-beneficial acts such as the *śyena* sacrifice and others. Regarding the killing of an enemy, which is the fruit of the sacrifice named *śyena* as stated in the Vedic text, "One desiring to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the *śyena*," this is a non-beneficial act because it falls under the prohibition: "One must not harm any living beings. Consequently, the *śyena* itself, being the cause of that [harm], is also non-beneficial. Since the *śyena* is not prohibited in its own essential form (*svarūpa*), its status as something to be performed (*vidheya*) does not negate its non-beneficial nature.

Nor should it be suspected that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*), because even the killing of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*āgnīṣomīyavadha*)—as being the object of a prohibition—is excluded by the word "artha" (purpose/meaning). This is because, in that case, the general prohibition is set aside by a specific injunction. Furthermore, by the word "codanā" (Vedic injunction), perception and other means of knowledge are excluded. If it is argued that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to worldly injunctions such as "Make a pot," [the answer follows].

No, because the word *codanā* is well-established in the context of the Veda; for, as in the case of words like *paṅkaja*, the meaning of its constituent parts serves merely as the occasion for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). By the very statement of the definition given above, it is effectively asserted that "with respect to dharma, *codanā* is the means of valid cognition. Thus, even though [dharma] is known in a general sense through its definition and other such means, the sages certainly still possess a desire to know its specific details.

In this regard, Vyāsa is honored because of his skill in asking specific questions. His residence at Badarikāśrama is due to its being the cause for liberation from the impurities of the Kali age and the cause for inexhaustible fruit. As it is said in the Kūrmapurāṇa:
"Having reached Badaryāśrama, one is liberated from the impurities of the Kali age;
there dwells the eternal Lord Nārāyaṇa together with Nara."
Whatever is given there, or likewise whatever is recited as a prayer, becomes inexhaustible;
for that sacred ford is dear to Mahādeva and is especially purifying.
And by especially offering the śrāddha rite, one shall cause all one's ancestors to cross over.
Thus [ends the citation from] Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.36.48–49.
It was strewn with various flowering creepers, adorned with fruit-bearing trees,
provided with rivers and springs, and graced by sacred bathing places.
Abounding with the cries of wild beasts and birds, surrounded by divine abodes, and adorned with the dances and songs of yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas. (7) Thus.

The fruit of exceedingly intense austerity manifests in this very world. This being so, one must determine the excellence of the austerity by the kind of superior fruit that is obtained. And here, a continuous profusion of various kinds of flowers blooming in their respective seasons is observed. From this, it is understood that the austerity characterized by the worship of the gods has reached its fruition. Likewise, from the excellence of the fruit-bearing trees, the perfection of the restriction regarding food is determined. Furthermore, even during the season for religious rites (*dharmakāla*), the ripening of the restriction regarding ritual bathing is known from the uninterrupted flow of the river. A "sacred ford" (*puṇyatīrtha*) refers to the Viṣṇugaṅgā and others. And the beauty of such a sacred ford is presented as the reason for this hermitage’s capacity to produce a superior merit over others. (6)

The cry of wild animals and others, free from fear due to their mutual abandonment of enmity, demonstrates the successful accomplishment of the practice of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). Accordingly, Patañjali, in his *Yogaśāstra*, while formulating the signs of success for the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) in their proper sequence, set forth the accomplishment of non-violence in the sūtra: "In his presence, there is the abandonment of enmity" (Yogasūtra 2.35).

In former times, great seers (*maharṣi*) performing austerities here constructed each of these divine abodes at its respective time. The fact that this hermitage is surrounded by all of them is a sign universally recognized as being caused by an excess of ascetic heat (*tapas*). Alternatively, it is stated that the hermitage is surrounded by abodes marked by the gods—such as the Moon, the Sun, and others—with the intention of expressing that in a previous birth they were human beings who, having performed austerities right here in various shrines, attained divinity. Even Yakṣas and others, though experiencing the state of a divine womb as the fruit of austerities performed in a previous life, come here and, seeing the excellence of this [hermitage’s] austerity, dance and sing in joy. By this, it is shown that even the gods seek after this hermitage; and this is appropriate, because even for those born as gods, the highest fruit can be accomplished here. Or again, Yakṣas and others, being seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*), come here and worship the Lord through dance and song as a means to liberation. For this very reason, it was said by Yājñavalkya:
"One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, is proficient in the *śruti*s and *jāti*s, and understands musical rhythm (*tāla*), attains the path to liberation without effort.
(Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.115) Thus [ends the section].
He shows the specific manner in which service to the guru is to be performed:
"In that assembly of sages, [he approached] Parāśara, the son of Śakti, who was seated comfortably, possessed of great splendor, and surrounded by a host of preeminent sages. (8)
Then Vyāsa, together with the sages, having joined his palms in reverence, honored him with circumambulations, salutations, and hymns of praise. (9) Thus.

The word "in that" (*tasmin*) is an expression referring to the hermitage (*āśrama*).
