The phrase "assembly of sages" (*ṛṣisabhā*) is stated in order to demonstrate that the duties about to be described are approved by all sages without exception. Furthermore, with the intention of expressing the excellence of the authors of the *Smṛtis* and the founders of lineages (*gotra*) among the sages, such as Atri, Yājñavalkya, and others, he says: "the chief of sages" (*munimukhya*). He states "son of Śakti" (*śaktiputra*) to show that Parāśara’s greatness arises not only from the power of his asceticism, but also from his distinguished birth. This greatness is clearly understood by reflecting upon the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the name Parāśara, which has been cited by the great authorities.
Because he warded off the arrows of the Rākṣasas who sought to slay him,
the wise have called that seer by the name Parāśara.
Since the arrows of the other Kāmadeva— such as those that cause infatuation and the like—
do not exist [in him], for that reason the sage is called Parāśara.
Because he did not harbor even a sign of anger toward others who harbored evil intentions,
that sage was therefore called Parāśara.
"Having uttered a *ṛc*, this Parāśara emerged, having burst through her own mother's womb.

By the word "mouth" (*mukha*), one-pointedness (*ekāgrya*) is intended; the meaning is that he sat in such a way that one-pointedness was achieved by abandoning all distractions of the mind. The terms "one-pointedness," "seated," and "of great splendor" have been explained previously. (8)

The state of palms joined in reverence (*añjalipada*) illuminates the excellence of devotion. Through supreme devotion, the reality of the meaning taught by the Guru becomes manifest. Thus it is heard in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"For one who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and for the Guru as for the Lord—for such a great soul, these meanings that have been declared truly shine forth" (ŚveUp 6.23).
[75] Thus, even if a subject is taught, it becomes fruitless without devotion to the guru. This is also heard in some places:
"Those Brahmins who, though instructed, do not honor their gurus in word, thought, or deed—just as they are not to be fed by their gurus, so too that sacred learning does not nourish them."

(VaDh 2.11) The meaning is that just as disciples who show no respect for their teacher cannot be sustained by him, so too that [knowledge] which has been heard from him does not sustain those disciples by bestowing its own fruit. Since the teacher is to be honored like a god, acts such as circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) are appropriate toward him.
If it is then asked: "In that case, would ritual services (*upacāra*) such as invitation (*āvāhana*), offering a seat (*āsana*), and welcome (*svāgata*) also be required?"

Let them indeed be attained, since "circumambulation" and so forth are used as illustrative examples (*upalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, for those who have come from afar to behold the Guru, circumambulation and the like are what is appropriate; thus, that many [acts] are specified here. (9)
In order to demonstrate that the aforementioned service was performed according to the prescribed rule, he shows the special grace of the Guru, preceded by his satisfaction:
"Then the great sage Parāśara, his heart satisfied, the bull among sages, said while seated: 'Welcome; speak! (10).
[76] That the satisfaction of the guru is the cause of spiritual welfare has been declared in the *Purāṇasāra* through both positive and negative concomitance:
"If the guru is dissatisfied, all the gods and the best of the twice-born will be dissatisfied."
Since [the deities] are pleased when he is pleased, the Guru is therefore composed of all the gods.
"If one who seeks the highest good should not transgress the guru's command even in thought, for by obeying the guru's command, one attains the perfection of knowledge. Thus it is said.

By means of a greeting preceded by great respect, a special degree of compassion was shown. The repetition of the word *su* is for the sake of emphasizing respect. Alternatively, with the first *su*, worldly well-being regarding his arrival is expressed; with the second, the excellence characteristic of scriptural propriety, namely approaching according to rule, is stated. He dispels the doubt that Parāśara ought to rise when the sages have arrived by saying, "seated" (*āsīnaḥ*). As the reason for this, Parāśara is qualified by the two terms *mahāmuni* and *munipuṅgava*. These two terms respectively indicate his seniority in terms of age and learning. Because of this twofold seniority, he [the sage] should not rise for him. || 10 ||

Just as a welcome is asked of one who has arrived while he is seated, so too, when he has arrived and is standing, his welfare must be inquired after. Therefore, having first asked that and once the teacher has declared his own well-being, he subsequently asks about the matter he wishes to know;
thus it is said:
"Having replied, 'I am well,' Vyāsa then asks."
Having said this, one should supply the phrase "and having heard what is beneficial from the mouth of the guru" and connect it [to the preceding].
He shows the manner of questioning regarding the matter he wishes to know: "If you know my devotion, or out of affection for me, O you who are kind to your devotees... (11)
"O father, speak to me of the Dharma, for I am worthy of your grace."

Thus: only a dear disciple or a son is worthy of receiving secret instruction, and no one else. This point is recorded by the Chandogas in the Madhu-vidyā: "A father should indeed impart this Brahman-knowledge to his eldest son or to a well-disciplined student (*antevāsin*), but to no one else whatsoever" (ChU 3.11.5–6). Therefore, with the intention that Vyāsa possesses both the status of a son and a disciple in this matter, two alternatives are presented: [78] "If my particular devotion toward you is inferred from these signs, then, because of your affection for devotees, favor me with the thought that I am your disciple. Even if there is no such inference, I am to be favored out of paternal affection. In any case, the Dharma must certainly be taught. || 11 ||

Now, one might object: "There are many dharmas proclaimed by Manu and others; among those, which dharma do you wish to know? Anticipating this, [the author] sets forth various dharmas in order to specify that which he intends to seek: "I have heard the dharmas of Manu, as well as those of Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa. (12)
Those of Garga and Gautama, as well as those recorded by Uśanas, and those of Atri, Viṣṇu, Saṃvarta, Dakṣa, and likewise Aṅgiras; 13.
And likewise from Śātātapa, Hārīta, and Yājñavalkya;
the Dharmas composed by Āpastamba, as well as those of Śaṅkha and Likhita. (14)
And likewise those composed by Kātyāyana and those of the sage Prācetasa. Thus [it is said].

[79] “*Me śrutāḥ*” means “heard by me. This is because the genitive case, which generally expresses a relationship (*saṃbandhasāmānya*), is restricted here to the specific sense of the agent or the author. The words ending in the fifth case, such as *atreḥ* and so forth, are connected with the word *śrutāḥ* supplied from the previous context. The meaning is that they were composed or proclaimed by Āpastamba; thus, the *dharmas* are related to Śaṅkha and Likhita, and their status as being related to them consists in their having been proclaimed by those two. *Prācetasaḥ* is simply *pracetāḥ*; the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), as in the case of *vāyasa-* or *rākṣasa-*. Alternatively, there may have been some author of a Dharmaśāstra named Pracetas’s son. (12, 13, 14)

Now, one might object: "If the Smārta duties such as those prescribed in the *Mānava-dharma-śāstra* have been heard, then let them remain uninvestigated; however, the Śrauta rites such as the *agnihotra* will surely be sought after.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For these which you have spoken have indeed been heard by me; the meanings of the Vedas (*śruti*) have not been forgotten. (15)
In this Manvantara, the dharmas [prevail] during the Kṛta, Tretā, and other Yugas.

Thus: "Those duties (*dharma*) such as the *agnihotra* and others, which are the objects of the directly perceived *śruti*, have been heard by me from you. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of indicating that this is well known even to you. The reason for this is stated as "proclaimed by you. According to the *Paurāṇikas*, Vyāsa studied [the Vedas] from Parāśara. Anticipating the objection that if there were forgetfulness of what has been heard, one would require a further reminder, it is said that they have not been forgotten. With the intention that the *agnihotra* and other rites are generally difficult to perform in the *kali* age, it is said "in the *kṛta*, *tretā*, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *dvāpara* age is included. The specification "in this *manvantara*" is for the sake of illustration; it does not, however, exclude past or future *manvantaras*, because there is no purpose in such an exclusion. Indeed, we do not find the *dharma* differing in any way across the various types of *manvantaras*. Those duties—the objects of the directly perceived *śruti*—which are generally capable of being performed in the three ages beginning with *kṛta* within this *manvantara*, are not [separately] desired to be known [here], because they are already established as *śruta* like the *smārta* duties of Manu and others. (15)
Now he asks about the remaining matter he wishes to know:
"All dharmas were born in the Kṛta age; all have perished in the Kali age. (16)

"Tell me something common regarding the conduct of the four castes. The word "all" (*sarva*) indicates the manifold nature of duties (*dharma*) due to differences in place, time, condition, and so forth. This has been explained in detail in the *Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda* within the *Anuśāsana-parvan* of the *Mahābhārata*:
"In this world, there are many kinds of duties arising from the various openings of the Vedas."
The laws of the country are seen, and likewise the laws of the family.
O beautiful one, there are the laws of birth, the laws of age, the laws of qualities,
the laws of the body and time, and likewise the laws of calamity.
"This diversity of Dharma is created by those dwelling in the world.

And all those Dharmas were practiced correctly by living beings in the Kṛta Yuga, because even though Dharma has four feet, they do not perish due to the power of that age. In the Tretā and subsequent ages, the Dharmas gradually diminish and, at the end of the Kali Yuga, they become completely destroyed. All of this is demonstrated in detail in the *Purāṇasāra*:
"In the Kṛta [Yuga], it is complete with all four feet and free from deceit and conditions."
In ancient times, Dharma existed among human beings as a bull firmly established.
In the Tretā age, Dharma stands upon three parts, being deprived of one foot;
in the Dvāpara age, it is held that Dharma is mixed with only half.
"In the Tiṣya age, [Dharma] stands with three quarters diminished, existing merely as a presence.
Here, Tiṣya is Kali. And likewise Bṛhaspati says:
"In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete; in the Tretā age, it stood on three feet."
A quarter of unrighteousness, born of envy and hatred, has entered.
"Having become equal, *dharma* and *adharma* stood on two feet in the *dvāpara* age;

in the *tiṣya* [kali] age, *adharma* stands on three feet and *dharma* remains established on one foot. Likewise, in the *Laiṅgapurāṇa*, having introduced the destruction of *dharma* in the *kali* age, the fault of man is presented as its cause.
[83] But the dharma that was established in the first age proceeds in the Tretā; it becomes disordered in the Dvāpara and perishes in the Kali age.
In the Tiṣya age, there is illusion, malice, and even the killing of ascetics.
"Men there accomplish [their goals] with their senses agitated by darkness.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"In the Kali age, the conduct of men does not possess the observances of the social classes and stages of life."
"It is not caused by the production of Sāmans, Yajus, or groups of Ṛks.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the Āditya Purāṇa:
"That dharma which belongs to the Kṛta Age is not to be performed in the Kali Age."

"For in the Kali age, women as well as men are addicted to sin. Therefore, since it is impossible for people in the Kali age to engage in dharma that is achievable only through great effort, the dharma sought here is one that is easy to perform. And that is of two kinds: common to the four castes and specific to each. Among these, the common dharma has been defined by Bṛhaspati:
"Compassion, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness..."
"Freedom from miserliness and absence of covetousness—these are common to all.
Likewise, it was said by Viṣṇu as well:
"Forbearance, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, charity, and control of the senses..."
Non-violence, service to the teacher, following the sacred fords, and compassion.

Self-control, freedom from greed, worship of the deities, and likewise freedom from malice— this is declared to be the common dharma. (ViDh 2.16–17) [85] It is also recorded by Bṛhaspati as being non-common.
Vedic study and teaching, as well as performing sacrifices and officiating at sacrifices,
giving gifts and receiving them— these are the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Sacrifice, study, giving, the protection of subjects,
the bearing of weapons and missiles, and service— these are the duties of the Kṣatriya.
Vedic study, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, as well as the protection of cattle,
money-lending, agriculture, and trade— these indeed are the seven duties of a Vaiśya.

"Purity, service to Brāhmaṇas, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—these are the duties of a Śūdra; likewise, the mantra prescribed for him is the utterance of 'namas'. Thus it is said. The Blessed One also said in the Gītā: [86]
O scorcher of foes, the duties of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras have been divided according to the qualities arising from their own natures.
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness,
as well as knowledge, realization, and faith in the Vedas— these are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of a Vaiśya, born of his own nature;
while bravery, majesty, fortitude, skill, and not fleeing from battle are the duties of a Kṣatriya.
"Giving, sovereignty, and the duty of a Kṣatriya are born of their own nature;
likewise, service-oriented duty is born of the Śūdra’s own nature" (BhG 18.41–44).

Since there is thus a twofold division, the common [duty] is asked about in this verse. "Something" (*kiñcit*) is an adverbial modifier. This being so, because the interrogative *kim* has a restrictive sense, the meaning becomes "in brief. And this is appropriate, for [the question] regarding the uncommon duties would otherwise be extensive. || 16 ||
Then he asks about the uncommon duty: (87) "The duty that must be performed by those learned in dharma for all four castes. || 17 ||
"Speak at length, O knower of the true nature of *dharma*, concerning its subtle and gross aspects.

Thus, because there are conflicting views among disputants regarding the nature of *dharma* and because its precise discernment is difficult to achieve, he is addressed as "knower of the true nature of *dharma*" with the intention of expressing proficiency in that regard. First, the logicians (*tārkika*) say that *dharma* and *adharma* are qualities (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*):
"Dharma is considered a quality of the person, to be accomplished through enjoined action."

"Adharma is said to be a quality of the person accomplished through prohibited actions. However, the Mīmāṃsakas formulated the sūtra: "Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction" (PMS 1.1.2). Regarding this, the Bhāṭṭas hold the view that the status of dharma will be established for substances, actions, qualities, and so forth.
Even though these are objects of the senses, they do not possess the nature of reality (dharmatā) by virtue of that very form.
"For it is from the Veda alone that their status as the means to the highest good (*śreyas*) is eternally understood;
and since their nature as *dharma* consists in that very status, they are therefore not within the range of the senses" (TV 1.1.2.13–14).

[88] However, the Prābhākaras maintain that *dharma* is an attribute of the self (*ātmaguṇa*), which is denoted by the terms "kārya," "niyoga," and "apūrva," is to be accomplished through the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and serves as the means for attaining results such as heaven. Furthermore, the difficulty of discerning [this *dharma*] was stated by Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the *Mahābhārata*.

"O Brahmin, it is not possible for those like us to determine whether something is unrighteousness or righteousness; therefore, I do not make such a determination. [Mahābhārata, Ādi-parvan 196.11-12] Thus, even regarding such a dharma, there exists proficiency therein, as he knows its true nature without confusion. And Viśvāmitra spoke of the true nature of dharma:
That purpose which those who know the scriptures praise when it is being performed is Dharma;
that which they censure, they declare to be Adharma.
"For even regarding such a dharma, its true nature is not confused; thus, those who possess the dharma have mastery therein as well. So too says Manu: [89]

"Understand that Dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are ever free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart. (MDh 2.1) Now, one might object: in this way, the essential nature of Dharma would remain undefined. For indeed, from the verses of Viśvāmitra and Manu, only its general form is perceived, but not its specific form consisting of substances, qualities, and so forth. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that disputants are divided on this point. It is with this very intention that the *Mahābhārata* records the duties of kings (*rājadharma*).
"Neither variegated, nor tawny, nor black, nor red;
subtler than the edge of a razor—who is fit to speak of Dharma? Thus it is said.

This is not a fault. For in the statements already mentioned, a specific form distinct from non-dharma (*adharma*) is clearly perceived; furthermore, the conflicting views of disputants can be resolved, as there is universal agreement that *dharma* is a transcendental excellence (*atiśaya*)—the means for attaining heaven and other goals—which is accessible through the scriptures alone. That excellence is of two kinds: residing in substances and the like, and residing in the self (*ātman*). Regarding this, the Naiyāyikas and Prābhākaras maintain that *dharma* is a quality of the self denoted by the term "apūrva" (the unprecedented), because such an excellence residing in the self is the direct means of producing the fruit and persists for a long time until the completion of that result. The Bhāṭṭas, however, hold that *dharma* is the excellence residing in substances and so forth which serves as the means to produce that aforementioned *apūrva*, intending by "apūrva" the state at the moment the fruit arises. This view is not even contradictory to the Vedāntins, since they accept the principle: "In worldly transaction, the system of the Bhāṭṭas. Thus, when the nature of *dharma* has been defined in this way, it is possible to possess expertise in it without confusion.

"Among the four castes, please explain in detail that which must be performed by those who are experts in *dharma* and possess knowledge of its unique characteristics. That *dharma* to be performed is of two kinds: gross (*sthūla*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*). The gross *dharma*—such as ritual purity (*śauca*), sipping water (*ācamana*), and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*)—is easily understood even by those of dull intellect. The subtle *dharma*, however, is fit to be understood only by scholars who have mastered the scriptures; it is the subject of the misconception of unrighteousness (*adharman*) on the part of others, such as the marriage of Draupadī. Accordingly, in the *Mahābhārata*, Drupada censured [the act], considering the state of one woman having many husbands to be contrary to both worldly custom and the Vedas. In this regard, the contradiction with worldly custom is quite evident, for even among animals, one sees two bulls fighting over a single cow. It is likewise heard in the Veda: 'One man may have many wives, but one woman does not have many husbands at once' (TS 6.5.4). And: 'Because he winds two ropes around a single sacrificial post, therefore one man finds two wives; because he does not wind a single rope around two posts, therefore one woman does not find two husbands. Regarding this—"
"This dharma, O best of the upholders of dharma, is contrary to both the world and the Vedas," said Drupada. To dispel his delusion, Yudhiṣṭhira replied:
"Dharma is subtle, O Great King; we do not know its course. (MBh Ādi 195.29)

And the nature of *dharmatva* regarding the state of having many wives has been elaborated upon in many ways in that very same [text]. Likewise, in the narrative of the hunter Dharmavyādha, it is established that service to one’s mother and father is weightier than the practice of knowledge (*vidyā*), because knowledge arises for him through that very service even without study; having thus demonstrated this, he concludes by stating the subtlety of *dharma*:
"O best of the twice-born, *dharma* is seen in many ways, yet it is indeed subtle" (MBh Va. 206.42).
Thus, since both the gross and the subtle exist, a question concerning both is appropriate. || 17 ||

To ensure that the previously stated question and the answer about to be given do not become confused, he introduces the answer: "But at the conclusion of Vyāsa’s speech, Parāśara, the chief of sages... (18).
"He has declared the determination of Dharma, both subtle and gross, in detail.

By the qualification "the chief of sages," his skill in determining the subtle is demonstrated. Now, one might ask: whose verse is this? It cannot be Vyāsa's, because it lacks the form of a question; nor can it be Parāśara's, because it lacks the form of an answer. But is this not stating too little? This same objection applies even to the first verse. If that is so, then a solution must be sought for all such cases.

It is said: it should be understood that Parāśara himself composed such verses to inform his own life story for the sake of settling the understanding of his future disciples; for there is universal consensus that the verses concerning Vyāsa’s life at the beginning of the Mahābhārata were indeed composed by Vyāsa himself. (18)
He enjoins heedfulness for the sake of grasping the secret of the Dharma that is about to be taught:
"Listen, O son, I shall speak; let the sages likewise listen" (19).

In this regard, although the addressing of the son is already established by the very addressing of the sages, he addresses him specifically because he is the one who will propagate the tradition. (19)

In order to inspire an excess of faith in the Dharma and to state that the Dharma is beginningless by way of its continuous flow, he briefly describes the creation and dissolution of the Smṛti scriptures and their authors:
"In every Kalpa, through destruction and rebirth, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, as well as those who determine the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous, always [reappear]. (20)

A *kalpa* is that period of time during which the world is conceived (*kalpyate*), beginning from the initial creation up to the commencement of dissolution; thus, it is the uninterrupted duration of the world. It is of two kinds: the *mahākalpa* (great eon) and the *avāntarakalpa* (intermediate eon). A *mahākalpa* is measured by the lifespan of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), beginning from the creation of the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). An *avāntarakalpa* is merely a single day of the Four-faced One. As it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "One day of Brahmā is called a *kalpa*, and his night is said to be of equal duration.
The wise declare that a *kalpa* consists of a thousand cycles of the four ages (*caturyuga*)."

This is the intermediate *kalpa*. However, it is well known in the *Purāṇas* and other texts that a *mahākalpa*, according to the measurement of Brahmā, is limited to one hundred years. By the repetition [in the phrase] “in each and every small [kalpa],” it is intended to express the incalculability (*asaṃkhyatva*) of both types of *kalpas*. Thus, it is said in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
“In this way, O best of sages, the *kalpas* of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, are incalculable; there are thousands of millions upon millions of *kalpas*” (LiPu 1.4.49).

In that regard, between each pair of kalpas, there occurs a dissolution (*kṣaya*). And that dissolution is fourfold: constant (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), elemental (*prākṛtika*), and absolute (*ātyantika*). Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The constant, the occasional, the elemental, and likewise the absolute—this dissolution is declared to be fourfold in the Purāṇas."
[95] This which is constantly seen in the world as the destruction of beings is perpetually designated by the name "re-absorption" (pratisaṃcara) by the sages.
The Brahma dissolution is called occasional;
it will occur at the end of a kalpa when everything from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa) undergoes total destruction.
"This is called the primary dissolution (*prākṛta-pratisarga*) by those who contemplate time;
for the yogi, it is declared to be absolute through knowledge of the Supreme Self. Thus [it is said].
Therein, the primary dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*) is described in the *Sūtasaṃhitā* of the *Skandapurāṇa* as follows:
Three hundred and sixty kalpas are declared to be one year of Brahmā;
a hundred of such years is here called a parārdha.
O best of sages, at the end of Brahmā, the world dissolves into Māyā;
likewise, Viṣṇu and Rudra also go to dissolution within Prakṛti.
O you of excellent vows, the various forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra likewise underwent dissolution into those causes.

"And Māyā [dissolves] at the time of dissolution into the Supreme Lord, who is designated as the Absolute Brahman—consisting of truth, consciousness, bliss, and infinity—and as Rudra and others. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, following the dissolution of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the rest, the dissolution of the five elements and so forth is recited.
Then, when the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the wielder of the Pināka bow—
have withdrawn, the earth, along with all its qualities, goes to dissolution within the waters.
The fire devours that reality of water together with its quality;
then the light, conjoined with its quality, goes to dissolution in the wind.
The all-sustaining wind, endowed with its qualities, undergoes dissolution into space;
and likewise, space, together with its qualities, dissolves into the principle of ego (bhūtādi).
All the sense organs, however, go to dissolution in the Taijasa;
O best of men, the hosts of gods go to their destruction in the Vaikārika.
O virtuous ones, this threefold ego— namely, the vaikārika, the taijasa, and the bhūtādi—
dissolves into the mahat.
"O twice-born ones, Prakṛti devours the Great One (Mahat) together with these [other principles]. (KūP 1.2.44.14–19)

In this manner, the dissolution of nature (*prākṛtapralaya*) is to be understood from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other such texts. With this very dissolution in mind, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa composed the aphorism: [97] “But the sequence is by way of reversal; for it is logical from that” (UMS 2.3.14). Therefore, the sequence of dissolution must be accepted as the reverse of this sequence of creation. Since the sequence of creation was examined in the preceding sutras, it is referred to here by the word “from that” (*ataḥ*). Indeed, this reversed sequence is logical, because when the clay—which serves as the material cause—is present, the effect, the jar, undergoes dissolution. If the very same sequence of creation were to be respected even in dissolution, then one would have to conclude that the clay perishes while the jar still remains; however, such a thing is never observed anywhere. Therefore, the reversed sequence is logical. This being so—since the sequence of creation, beginning with the Supreme Self and ending with this body, will be described [later], the sequence in dissolution is appropriately the reverse of that, beginning with our own bodies and ending with the Supreme Self. If it is argued that in the dissolution of nature, the sequence should end with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), [the answer follows].

"Certainly. That very thing is indeed stated, because the Supreme Self is the material cause (*prakṛti*). And thus, in the *Bahvṛca-Upaniṣad*, the status of the Supreme Self as the material cause of the world is heard: 'In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: "Let me create the worlds. He created these worlds' (AitUp 1.1). [98] But surely, in the *Śvetāśvatara-Upaniṣad*, it is heard that *māyā* is the material cause and the Supreme Self is its controller:
'One should know *māyā* as the material cause, but the Great Lord as the wielder of *māyā*' (ŚveUp 4.10)."

This is not a fault, because since *māyā* is a power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it necessarily follows that the Self, as the possessor of that power (*śaktimat*), is also its material cause (*prakṛti*). This is seen in the case of fire, which, though endowed with the power of burning, is conventionally referred to as "the burner. Furthermore, that *māyā* is a power of the Self is heard in that very Upaniṣad: "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3).

Furthermore, in the penultimate section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the first chapter, Bādarāyaṇa established that Brahman—qualified by *māyā*—possesses both the nature of material cause (*prakṛti*) and efficient cause (*nimitta*). Its status as an efficient cause arises from its sentience, like a potter; its status as a material cause arises from its persistence within its own effects, just as clay persists in a jar. Indeed, Brahman qualified by *māyā* is perceived throughout the universe. In this regard, existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*) are the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, whereas changeability (*vikāritva*) belongs to *māyā*. We observe both of these in the world: "The jar exists" indicates the form of existence; "The jar appears" indicates the form of consciousness; "The jar is pleasant" indicates the form of bliss; and "The jar is produced and perishes" indicates changeability. This very point is heard in the *Uttaratāpanīya*: "All this is of the nature of existence, for all this is existent, existent, existent; all this is of the nature of consciousness, for it shines," and so forth (*Nṛ Utt Tā* 7). Thus, according to the Upaniṣadic view, since Brahman is the root material cause, and since the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* follow the *Śruti*, it should be understood that what is intended here is the dissolution of the universe into Brahman alone. However, the dissolution established in the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others is not elaborated upon by us here, because, being rooted in mere reasoning based on human intellect, it can be inferred by the wise themselves.

Now, the process of origination is described in accordance with the Śruti. For there are many scriptural passages that set forth the creation. Among them, the passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad beginning with “In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone” (AitUp 1.1) has already been cited. There is also the passage from the Taittirīya Upaniṣad beginning with “Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite” (TaitUp 2.1.3) and continuing with “From that very Self, space was produced” (TaitUp 2.1.7). Furthermore, there is the passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad beginning with “Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning” (ChUp 6.2.1) and continuing with “It thought: ‘May I be many, may I procreate,’ and it emitted heat” (ChUp 6.2.3).
Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks of the same nature fly forth by the thousands, even so,
my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable and into it they also go.

(Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1) — this is a statement from the Atharva Veda. “At that time, this was indeed unmanifest; it was then manifested by means of name and form” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7) — this is a statement from the Vājasaneyins. Now, one might object: in these passages, the process of creation cannot be definitively established because of the great abundance of conflicting views. Entities denoted by such terms as *ātman*, *brahman*, *sat*, *akṣara*, and *avyākṛta* are heard in scripture as being the cause. Yet, it is not logical for a single world to have many distinct material causes (*upādāna*).

This is not a fault, because a single reality is denoted by such terms as "Self" (*ātman*) and so forth. To begin with, the identity of meaning between the words *ātman* and *brahman* is clear, since in the supplementary passage to the [Taittirīya] *Brahma-sūtra*, it is stated: "From that very Self, space was produced. Furthermore, the identity of meaning between the words *sat* (Being) and *ātman* is logical, because the word *ātman* can denote both self and other, and because the Upaniṣadic thinkers accept that Being (*sattā*) is the essential nature of all things. Indeed, the fact that Being is the essential nature of all things is experienced, for even things like a human horn are admitted to have the nature of Being (*satsvarūpatva*) by virtue of their capacity to produce a cognition. The word *akṣara* denotes the Supreme Self either as "the unheard" (*a-śruta*) or as "that which does not perish" (*na kṣarati*). The word *avyākṛta* (the Undifferentiated) can also be applied to that same reality. According to its etymology—*vi-spaṣṭam ā-samantāt kṛtam* ("made clearly and completely")—*vyākṛta* refers to the state of the world when it has reached a grossness capable of being perceived. Therefore, *avyākṛta* expresses the subtle state. Thus, the two states—the gross and the subtle—of one and the same reality are expressed by the words *jagat* (world) and *brahman*. This is because it is accepted that the Brahman, which is partless and of a single essence, appears in the form of the world through the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) and the like. Consequently, these five terms—*avyākṛta*, *brahman*, and the others—have one and the same referent.

Now, an objection is raised: Is it not heard in some places that the non-existent (*asat*) is the cause of the world? For instance: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent was born" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.7.1.2). Not so. In that passage, the words "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) denote the manifested (*vyākṛta*) and the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) respectively. Furthermore, another Śruti text denies that emptiness (*śūnya*) can be the cause: "How could the existent be born from the non-existent? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2). If it is asked: "If Brahman is distinct even from emptiness, being devoid of the form of the world as it is perceived, then in what manner should it be conceived in the intellect? [The answer follows:]

Fix your mind on the understanding that whatever you have now asked about is exactly as it has been described. If you ask for an illustration, we are unable to provide one, because there exists no other entity equal to it. Thus says the Śruti:
"Of Him there is neither effect nor instrument;
neither is anyone seen who is equal to Him or superior to Him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).

If, for the sake of instructing the disciple, a semblance of an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) is required, then deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the illustration for the nature of non-duality; and for its being the very essence of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), the bliss of sense-objects (*viṣayānanda*) is to be cited as the illustration, based on such scriptural passages as: "He understood that bliss is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.5.1) and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28). If there is a requirement for the removal of all doubts, then study the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*; enough with this excessive elaboration.

For as long a time as Brahman previously existed endowed with the manifested form of the world, for that very same duration it remains in the state of non-manifestation, and only thereafter does it strive toward manifestation.
Now, one might ask: how can either time or its measure be possible during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)?

It is replied: To whom is this objection addressed? It is certainly not against the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*). In his view, what burden is there in merely postulating the notion that Māyā—which projects the perception of a universe divided by endless distinctions such as ether and so forth—existed for a duration limited to this much time during some great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)? Even in the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇuvāda*), eternal time certainly exists. In the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhānavāda*), since there is no principle of time existing outside the twenty-five principles, let primordial matter itself be designated by the word "time. Therefore, at the conclusion of the period of dissolution, the Supreme Lord desires creation. And thus say the Śrutis: "Desire first arose within Him" (*Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīya Upaniṣad* 1.1); "He desired: 'May I become many, may I procreate'" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.6.1); "He thought: 'May I become many, may I procreate'" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.3); "He performed reflection" (*Praśna Upaniṣad* 6.3), and so forth.

Now, an objection is raised: desire (*kāma*) is indeed a particular modification of the mind, according to the Śruti: “Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are nothing but the mind” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.5.3). Furthermore, the mind is material, according to the Śruti: “For the mind, my dear, consists of food” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4). This being the case, since the mind does not exist prior to the origination of the elements, from where could desire arise?

It is replied: First of all, this objection does not arise at the time of creation, because that mind is not composed of material elements (*bhautika*), and because the eternal will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) is independent of the mind. Furthermore, the state of "desiring to create" (*sisṛkṣātva*) is established in the eternal will by way of its being conditioned by the impulse toward creation. In the Upaniṣadic view, however, although the will of the individual soul (*jīvecchā*) is an effect of the material mind, the will of the Lord—being of the nature of a transformation of *māyā*—has no dependence on the mind. Indeed, it is understood from the Śrutis that the Supreme Lord possesses inconceivable power for all worldly activity even without a body or sense organs:
For him there exists neither effect nor instrument;
neither one equal to him nor superior to him is seen. His supreme power is heard of as indeed manifold.
"And its power of knowledge and action is inherent" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8),
and "He who is handless and footless, yet swift and a grasper."
He sees without eyes; he hears without ears. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19)

And so it is said. This being the case, such objections as: "How can that which is unattached be a producer? or "How could things yet to be produced, such as space (*viyat*) and the rest, arise without a suitable causal complex (*sāmagrī*)?"—have no place, for all such objections have been answered by the very fact of inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*). Therefore, one should accept creation without hesitation according to the sacred texts (*śruti*). And the scripture says thus: "From this very Self (*ātman*), space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, the person (*puruṣa*)" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1–4). In this context, by the word "person," the body endowed with the form of a head, hands, and so forth, is denoted. And that body is of many kinds, ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. Among these, because the body of Brahmā consists of the fruit of an unsurpassed mass of merit, it is beginningless (*anādi*) by virtue of being the cause of all other bodies. And so it is said:
"In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists"—
so says the Śruti.
"Brahmā was born as the first of the gods; the creator of the universe and the protector of the world" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1).
Thus it is said.
"He is indeed the first embodied one; he is called Puruṣa.
He is the original creator of beings; as Brahmā, he existed in the beginning"—thus says the Smṛti. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.5.38)

By this, the primordial nature (*āditva*) of the bodies of Viṣṇu and Maheśvara is also explained, because a single conscious being has assumed three bodies for the sake of the distribution of the three qualities (*guṇa*). Thus it is heard in the Maitrāyaṇī Śākhā: “His declared forms are Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu. Now, that which is indeed his *rājasa* portion is this Brahmā; now, that which is indeed his *tāmasa* portion is this Rudra; now, that which is indeed his *sāttvika* portion is this Viṣṇu. He, though one, has become threefold. (MaitU 5.2). Likewise, in the Uttara-tāpanīya, concerning *māyā*, it is heard: “This [māyā] is variegated, very firm, and possesses many sprouts; she herself is divided by the qualities, and even within the sprouts she is divided by the qualities; everywhere she takes the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, illumined by consciousness. Therefore, the threefold nature belongs to the Self alone everywhere. (NṛU 9). Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Śiva alone is manifest for the sake of accomplishing creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
he unfolds himself through the conceptual manifestations known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Thus it is established that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara perish at the conclusion of that great aeon (*mahākalpa*), and are born again at the beginning of each subsequent great aeon.

The literal meaning, however, is as follows: "destruction-and-arising" (*kṣayotpatti*) refers to arising accompanied by destruction; they are characterized by these two. Thus, at the conclusion and the commencement of each respective intermediate *kalpa*, those who determine the *Śruti* and other scriptures are characterized by destruction and arising. Among them, the determiners of the *Śruti* include Vyāsa, the arranger of the Vedas; Kaṭha, Kauthuma, and others, who established the traditions of the various Vedic branches (*śākhā*); Baudhāyana, Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba, and others, the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*; and Jaimini and others, the authors of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtras*. The determiners of the *Smṛti* are well known to be Manu and others. In this regard, Paiṭhīnasi says:
Among them are Manu, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Gautama, Atri, Uśanas,
Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara.
Viṣṇu, Āpastamba, Hārīta, Śaṅkha, Kātyāyana, Bhṛgu, Pracetas,
Nārada, Yogī, Baudhāyana, and Pitāmaha.
Sumantu, Kaśyapa, Babhru, Paiṭhīna, Vyāsa,
Satyavrata, Bharadvāja, Gārgya, and likewise Kārṣṇājini.
Jābāli, Jamadagni, Laugākṣi, and Brahmasambhava— these,
along with thirty-six other sages, are likewise the promulgators of Dharma.

Now, is this an *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification)? Not so; for if that were the case, there would be no authorship of Dharmaśāstras by Vatsa, Marīci, Devala, Pāraskara, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Likhita, Chāgaleya, Āreya, and others. Furthermore, in the *Aśvamedhika* Parvan, because of the enumeration of the Dharmas proclaimed by those respective sages, they are understood to be the authors of Dharmaśāstras. Beginning with "The Dharmas of Manu have been heard by me," it is recited thus:
"The *Umāmaheśvara* [Dharmas] and the purifying *Nandidharmas*... [109]
I have heard those spoken by Brahmā as well as the Kaumāras;
likewise the Dharmas composed by Dhūmrāyana, and those of the Kāṇvas, Vaiśvānaras, Bhārgavas, Yājñavalkyas, Mārkaṇḍeyas, and Kauśikas. (17–18)
Those composed by Bharadvāja and those composed by Bṛhaspati;
those composed by Kuṇi and Kuṇivāha, and those composed by Viśvāmitra;
likewise those composed by Sumantu and Jaimini, as well as those by Śākuneya. (19)
Those sung by Pulastya and Pulaha, as well as those by Pāvaki;
those sung by Agastya, the Saudhanvans, the Śāṇḍilyas, and the Saulabhāyanas;
those composed by the Vālakhilyas, and those composed by the Seven Sages. (20–21)
[110] Those sung by Vyāghra, those sung by Vyāsa, and those composed by Vibhāṇḍaka;
likewise the words of Vidura, as well as those of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras; those sung by Vaiśampāyana, and others such as these. Thus it is said. (26)

"Good conduct (*sadācāraḥ*) consists of the Holi festival, the bull sacrifice (*vṛṣabha-yajña*), the *ahnivuka* rite, and so forth. Its determiners are the elders of the respective families. The word 'and' (*ca*) serves to include both what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned. Those already mentioned are Manu and others, as well as Brahmā and others—the authors of the *Smṛti* scriptures. But there is also Dharma that has not been mentioned; even that, having perished at the end of the previous cosmic cycle (*kalpa*), undergoes creation at the beginning of the subsequent cycle. Accordingly, in the *Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa*, within the section on creation, after recounting the creation of Prajāpati and Manu, as well as all living beings from humans down to ants, and the presiding deities of the four castes, the creation of Dharma is recorded—Dharma which is capable of restraining even the most formidable Kṣatriyas and others: "He did not find sufficient rest. He created Dharma, a form superior to that. This Dharma is the sovereign power (*kṣatra*) of the Kṣatriya. Therefore, there is nothing higher than Dharma" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.14). The meaning of this is as follows: The Supreme Lord, the creator of the world who assumes the forms of Prajāpati, Manu, and others, even after creating the subjects, did not attain the glory of having fulfilled his purpose because there was no one to restrain them. Thereupon, having reflected, he created Dharma as a supreme restrainer. Oh, how great is this power of Dharma! For even a fierce Kṣatriya or similar person, though capable of killing, does not kill a Brahmin or other supplicant who is useless for purposes such as paying taxes, out of fear of Dharma; instead, he gives him wealth. And even hundreds of thousands of soldiers, exceedingly brave and bearing bows, swords, and other weapons, though being insulted and beaten by their fierce, unarmed master, still fear treachery against him. Therefore, there is no restrainer whatsoever superior to Dharma."

If it is argued that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), when even *dharma* is withdrawn, the future creation—which has *dharma* as its causal factor—would be impossible, we say no; for we do not accept the destruction of the "unseen" (*apūrva*) seed of fruit accumulated through the performance of rituals in previous cycles (*kalpas*). Indeed, it is only *dharma* in the form of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) that is withdrawn and subsequently produced again. By the word "always" (*sarvadā*), he demonstrates that the stream of creation and dissolution is beginningless and endless. || 20 ||
Having briefly stated the purpose for which creation and dissolution occur, he now describes their eternal continuity in the flow [of time]:
"No creator of the Veda exists; rather, the four-faced Brahmā, having remembered the Veda, likewise remembers the Dharmas just as they were in another interval between Kalpas," (verse 21).

Having observed that Manu and others, the determiners of the *smṛtis*, are regarded as the authors of those *smṛtis*, one might likewise suspect that those who determine the *śruti* are the authors of the Veda; therefore, he refutes this. First of all, Vyāsa is not the author of the Veda, because he merely performed its division. Nor is the Four-faced One (Brahmā), because the Veda was bestowed upon the Four-faced One by the Lord (*Īśvara*). Nor is the Lord of the World (the Creator), because he is the manifestor of the already established Veda. As it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "At the beginning of the Kalpa, the omniscient Supreme Lord [revealed] this Veda..."
O Brahmins, it is merely a manifestor; it is certainly not the creator, there is no doubt.
Having first created Brahmā, Maheśvara gave him all the Vedas that reside within his own self, O Brahmins.

"O best of the twice-born, impelled by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, in the form of Vyāsa, effects the divisions of the Vedas for the welfare of all beings. Thus [it is said]. As for others, however, their authorship of them is far removed from possibility; the arguments for this should be seen in the section concerning the non-human origin of the Vedas (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 1.1.27).

Now, an objection may be raised: in the section concerning the Scripture as the Source (*śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*, Brahma Sūtra 1.1.3), Vyāsa established that Brahman is the author of the Veda in order to strengthen the proof of Brahman’s omniscience and omnipotence.

But surely, in the very same work, in the section concerning the Deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*), the eternity of the Veda was also demonstrated by the sūtra, "And for this very reason, its eternity" (1.3.29). If this is so, then the contradiction must be resolved.

It is said: The Vaiśeṣikas and others describe the non-eternality of phonemes (*varṇa*), as well as words (*pada*), their meanings and relations, and sentences (*vākya*); in response to them, the Mīmāṃsakas, in the first chapter (*pāda*), described the eternality of time, space, and so forth, as well as phonemes and the like. To indicate the accepted principle that "in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the Bhaṭṭa view prevails," that very same conventional eternality was set forth in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*. Therefore, since there is no composition of sentences in the Vedas—unlike in the works of Kālidāsa and others—which proceeds from the addition and removal of specific words based on a prior understanding of meaning, their lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is logical. Thinking that the Vedas, like the ether (*viyat*) and other elements, are an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, the author of the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa* demonstrated that Brahman is the author of the Vedas. For this very reason, the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda denied independence [of the Veda] even though there is a connection with a person.
"Human independence must be strenuously refuted by us.
Therefore, there is no agent of the Veda characterized by the definition [given in Pāṇini's Sūtra 1.4.54]: "The independent one is the agent."

The word *tu* (but), functioning in the sense of the particle *tu*, expresses a distinction. For there are many authors of *smṛtis*, such as Caturmukha, Manu, and others; however, there is no author of the Veda—this is the distinction. In the sentence "having remembered the Veda," the three words found in the second half [of the verse] must be connected by the principle of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying an ellipsis). This principle of *anuṣaṅga* is described in the first section (*pāda*) of the second chapter (*adhyāya*). To illustrate: in the procedure for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, three mantras are heard regarding the *upasat* oblations: "O Agni, that body of yours which rests on the earth (*ayāśayā*), that which rests on the mid-region (*rajāśayā*), that which rests on heaven (*harāśayā*)—which is most excellent, dwelling in the deep, has warded off harsh speech, has warded off injurious speech, *svāhā*" (VS 5.8.8). In this regard, because of the distinctness of the words "resting on the earth," "resting on the mid-region," and "resting on heaven," there is a distinction between the mantras. Among them, the first mantra requires the remainder of the sentence beginning with "that body" (*tanūr*); the final mantra requires the opening of the sentence "O Agni, that which..."; and the middle mantra requires both the beginning and the end. In this context, the doubt arises: should some portion of a worldly sentence be supplied (*adhyāhāra*) to complete the required meaning, or should the collection of words already heard be supplied (*anuṣañjana*)? The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there should be a worldly supply, because the beginning of the sentence is connected only with the first mantra, and the remainder of the sentence is connected only with the final mantra.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since the expectancy of a Vedic passage must, whenever possible, be fulfilled by Vedic words alone, and because words connected with other mantras—being present in the mind—are more proximate than words that would have to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*), one should perform *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a word from a neighboring context) rather than *adhyāhāra* (invention of a new word).

This being the case, even in the present context, the three words from the first half-verse—“remembers the dharma in another kalpa”—must be supplied. Having remembered the Veda bestowed upon him by the Supreme Lord during that great kalpa, Caturmukha compiled the dharmas pertaining to the castes, stages of life, and so forth, which were scattered therein, and composed them in the form of Smṛti texts. Accordingly, the words of Pitāmaha are cited here and there by the authors of legal digests (nibandhakāras). Furthermore, Manu also states that Caturmukha is the author of the Smṛti scriptures:
"Having composed this treatise himself, he first caused me alone to learn it according to the rule; I, in turn, [taught] the sages beginning with Marīci. (MDh 1.58)

Just as the four-faced [Brahmā], so too Svāyaṃbhuva Manu compiles the duties declared in the Vedas during that intermediate kalpa (*avāntarakalpa*). By the mention of Manu, others such as Atri, Viṣṇu, and Yājñavalkya are implied. Thus, because the Smṛtis are composed by various four-faced Brahmās at the beginning of every great kalpa (*mahākalpa*) and by various Manus and others at the beginning of every intermediate kalpa, the eternal continuity of Dharma and the rest is established. With this very intention, it is recited in the *Aśvamedhika* Parvan: "As the ages revolve, Dharma also revolves again."

"When the dharmas revolve, the world also revolves again. With this in mind—referring to the distinct characteristics of the dharmas according to the divisions of the ages (yugas)—the plural designation "dharmān" is employed. || 21 ||
[117] He declares that very distinction: "The dharmas in the Kṛta age are different from those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages."
Others [are born] in the Kali age according to the characteristics of that age. || 22 ||

In this context, the word "other" (*anya*) does not denote a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the *dharma*, but rather a difference in its mode (*prakāra*). Otherwise, there would follow a difference even in the injunctions (*codanā*) that constitute the means of knowing *dharma* according to the different ages (*yuga*), for there is no restrictive rule stating, "This injunction is to be studied in the Kṛta age, but this one in the Tretā," and so forth. However, regarding a difference in mode, there is an illustrative example: since even for the single Agnihotra sacrifice, a difference in the mode of performance is heard in scripture according to the distinction between evening and morning times: "With the words 'I sprinkle you with Ṛta through Satya,' he sprinkles in the evening; with the words 'I sprinkle you with Satya through Ṛta,' [he sprinkles] in the morning" (TB 2.1.1.5).

Now, an objection may be raised: in that case, the distinction between the types of mantras has already been established by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): “Agni is indeed *ṛta*; yonder Āditya is *satya*. Thus, in the evening, he sprinkles Agni with Āditya; and in the morning, [he sprinkles] Āditya with Agni” (TB 2.11). If this is so, then here too, the distinction between types is justified by the phrase “in accordance with the nature of the age” (*yugarūpānusārataḥ*). The essential character of the ages (*yugas*) is endowed with varying degrees of capacity in the persons who perform the rites. Accordingly, a diversity in the performance of rituals is possible, since it has been determined regarding obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) that “one should act in such a way as one is able. For instance, this was deliberated upon at the beginning of the third quarter of the sixth chapter of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* (PMS 6.3.1): “One should offer the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives”—so it is heard in scripture. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: does the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the rite require the inclusion of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), or is one entitled to perform the principal act (*pradhāna*) when one performs it accompanied by as many auxiliaries as one is capable of including? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the principal act endowed with all auxiliaries is the means to the result, and because the result does not arise when there is a deficiency in the auxiliaries, there must be an inclusion of all parts. However, in this context, living is heard in scripture specifically as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the *agnihotra*, for otherwise its status as an occasion would be impossible. Therefore, the principal act must be performed even by omitting those auxiliaries that cannot be carried out; by that much alone, the attainment of the result follows from the authority of the scripture. And Baudhāyana also records this in his *Smṛti*: [The text continues with the citation of Baudhāyana’s rule.]

"In whatever way possible, one should never cause the eternal rites to be omitted, in accordance with one's state of capacity, by means of whatever [method] available. Here, the word "of men" (*nṛṇām*) is used with the intention of expressing that there is a disparity in the performance [of rites] caused by the varying degrees of human capacity. [22]

Now, he presents the previously promised distinction through six verses. Therein, he classifies the dharmas that are the causes for the supreme goal of man (puruṣārtha), which are easy to practice primarily during the four ages:
"Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age; in the Tretā, knowledge is said [to be supreme];
in the Dvāpara, they say sacrifice alone [is supreme]; and in the Kali age, charity alone. (23)

[120] Thus: austerity (*tapas*) consists of the avoidance of food in the form of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances, according to the Vedic revelation: “There is no austerity higher than fasting” (MNU 21.2). Although the nature of giving (*dāna*) is also heard to be austerity—“They say that this indeed is austerity: he who gives” (TS 6.1.6.3)—nevertheless, that is not intended here, because giving is mentioned separately.
Now, an objection: Vyāsa records austerity otherwise: “Austerity is abiding in one’s own duty; purity is the destruction of attachment.”

This is not a fault, because even the *kṛcchra* penance and others are specific forms of one’s own duty (*svadharma*). The word *tapaḥ*, derived from the verbal root *tap* (to heat), has its primary meaning in the emaciation of the body. For this very reason, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The wise declare that the emaciation of the body by means of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such rites according to the method prescribed in the Vedas is called *tapaḥ*."
However, it is stated in that very same place:
"The wise who know the meaning praise as austerity the contemplation: 'Who am I? What is liberation? How and by what means have I entered into saṃsāra?'"

Thus, this is indeed another word for *tapas*, because it is derived from the verbal root √*tap* in the sense of "perception" (*ālocane*). That *tapas* is here subsumed under the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*). As for the word "supreme" (*para*), it indicates that [this form of *tapas*] is to be practiced as the primary duty. If it is argued: "In that case, would one not disregard *tapas* in the Tretā and subsequent ages? And in the Kṛta age, would one not disregard knowledge, sacrifice, and charity? [The answer follows:]

No, for an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) consisting of the exclusion of others is not intended here. Indeed, no injunction regarding performance has been commenced at this point, such that one might suspect an exclusive specification as a particular type of injunction. However, its commencement will occur later with the words "devoted to the six duties" (ParSm 1.38) and so forth. What is being defined here is simply the capacity of the ages (*yuga*). Just as there is an abundance of flowers in spring and an excess of heat in summer—such being the capacity of the seasons—likewise, an abundance of austerity and other qualities is intended here by virtue of the capacity of the Kṛta and subsequent ages. For this very reason, he will state: "In each age, however, there is a [specific] capacity" (ParSm 1.64). Furthermore, the purpose of knowing this capacity will be explained:
"One should not speak ill of them, for those twice-born ones are indeed the embodiments of the [respective] ages.
Thus [it is said]. Bṛhaspati also demonstrates this capacity:
"In the Kṛta age, austerity is the dharma; in the Tretā age, knowledge is established."
"In the Dvāpara age, sacrifice is proclaimed; in the Tiṣya age, charity, compassion, and self-restraint. (23)
[122] Having analyzed the phenomena, he analyzes their measures:
one should abandon the country in the Kṛta age, and in the Tretā age, one should leave the village.

"In the Dvāpara [age], however, it is the family; but in the Kali age, the individual perpetrator. (25) In this regard, when a man has fallen [from his status], the entire country—in which he resides as a primary factor, consisting of a collection of villages and governed by a single king—becomes, by implication, a source of unrighteousness (*adharma*) even during the Kṛta age. The same principle should be applied to the village as well. "Exclusion of the family" (*kulatyāga*) means the cessation of marriage, dining, and other social interactions with the family of the fallen person. "Exclusion of the agent" (*kartṛtyāga*) refers to the avoidance of conversation and other forms of contact with him. (25)
[123] He now classifies the occasions for abandonment, just as he did the places to be abandoned:
"In the Kṛta age, by mere conversation; and in the Tretā, by touch."
"In the Dvāpara age, however, one falls by taking food; in the Kali age, one falls through action.

(26) Thus, unlike in the Kṛta and other ages, in the Kali age one does not fall by oneself merely through conversation with a fallen person and so forth; rather, one becomes fallen through an act such as killing. (26)
He divides the time that serves as the cause for the ripening of the curse resulting from the insult to a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa) and so forth:
"In the Kṛta age, the curse takes effect immediately; in the Tretā, after ten days;
in the Dvāpara, after one month; but in the Kali age, after one year. (27) Thus it is said.
He analyzes the causes that bring about the relative gradations of the Dharma:

"In the Kṛta age, a gift is given after approaching [the recipient]; in the Tretā, it is given upon being invited; in the Dvāpara, it is given to one who asks; and in the Kali, it is given through service. (28) Thus.

Where the recipient resides, the donor goes there in person, approaches him as if he were a guru, and performs the gift. But in the Tretā age, the gift is given after having summoned the recipient. The plural form "in the Tretās" (*tretāsu*) is intended to indicate that the singular is used for the class [of ages], such as the Kṛta, Dvāpara, and so forth. In the Dvāpara age, the gift is given to the recipient who comes to him and makes a request. In the Kali age, it is not given merely by means of a request, but rather through service. Bṛhaspati also states this division.

"In the Kṛta age, [the gift] is given after going [to the recipient]; in the Tretā ages, it is brought to the house; in the Dvāpara, it is given when [the recipient] requests; and in the Kali age, it is given while following [the recipient]. Thus [it is said]. 28.
He demonstrates the gradation based on the specific circumstances:
"Giving to one who approaches is superior; giving to one who merely calls out is middling; giving to one who begs is inferior; but giving as a reward for service is fruitless. (29) Thus it is said.
The specific distinctions regarding excellence and so forth are established by way of their results in the *Purāṇasāra*:
"A gift that is given after one has gone [to the recipient] is remembered as having infinite fruit;
that which is given after summoning [the recipient] is said to be a thousandfold; but that which is given when requested is half of that."
"Whether it be a gift given after being approached, or a gift given unasked, there may be an end to the depths of the ocean, but no end at all to that [merit]. (29)
Since the characteristics of the Kali age will be described primarily in this work, he elaborates specifically on the power of Kali:
"In the Kali age, dharma is indeed conquered by adharma, and truth by falsehood; kings are conquered by thieves, and men by women. (30)
[125] "The Agnihotra sacrifices fail, reverence for the guru perishes, and maidens give birth [to children] constantly in this Kali Yuga. Thus it is said.
The "victory of unrighteousness" (adharma) consists in its being endowed with three feet; the "defeat of dharma" consists in its existing with only one foot. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"In the Tiṣya [age], unrighteousness (*adharma*) will stand with three feet, and righteousness (*dharma*) with one foot.

Although truth and falsehood consist of the nature of *dharma* and *adharma*, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of illustrating them by citing *dharma* and *adharma* specifically. There is an abundance of examples such as thieves because of the intention to show that to the extent that the Kali age increases, to that same extent unrighteousness increases. This has been stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Whenever there is a decline of the virtuous who follow the path of the Vedas..."
At each such time, the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the wise.

"When there is no delight in the teachings of the Vedas and no essence of compassion toward heretics, then and then the increase of the Kali age is to be inferred by the best of the twice-born. (ViP 6.1.45–46).
Thus [ends the section on] verses 30–31.
Thus it has been said: "Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age," and so forth; therein he states the reason:
"In the Kṛta age, however, the vital breaths reside in the bones; in the Tretā, they reside in the flesh; in the Dvāpara, in the blood; but in the Kali, they are situated in food and such. (32)

The word *prāṇa* denotes a specific vital air (*vāyu*) that resides in locations such as the heart and is endowed with the fivefold functions. And the nature of *prāṇa* is clearly heard in the Maitreya recension:

In the beginning, Prajāpati alone existed. He did not delight in being alone. Meditating upon himself, he created many offspring. They were like stones—unawakened, insentient, standing still like pillars. He beheld them; he did not delight in them. He thought, "I shall enter within these to awaken them. Making himself like the wind, he entered within. Being one, he is called the fivefold self, consisting of non-breath (*an-ātman*), divided as follows: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. Now, that which moves transversely and upward, causing [the breath] to ascend, is indeed the prāṇa. That which moves downward is indeed the apāna. That which places the coarsest food-element in the apāna and leads it evenly to the finest part of the body is indeed the samāna. That which vomits up and swallows what has been drunk and eaten is indeed the udāna. And that by which these channels are pervaded is indeed the vyāna. (MaitU 2.6)

The meaning is "like a stone" (*aśmeva*), that is, like a rock. Furthermore, the sense organs such as speech and sight are also designated by the term "prāṇa" because their functions are dependent upon prāṇa. For this very reason, the Chandogas declare: "They do not call them 'speeches,' nor 'sights,' nor 'hears,' nor 'minds'; they call them simply 'prāṇa'" (ChU 5.1.15).

Therefore, it is the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), consisting of a collection of the senses and vital airs (*indriyavāyu*), which is capable of traveling to and returning from other worlds, that is intended by the term "prāṇa. And this [subtle body] is bound to the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*)—composed of bone, flesh, and so forth—by the ropes of karma. Furthermore, that binding remains fixed within the bones and other parts according to the specific power of each respective age (*yuga*). Thus, in the Kṛta Age, austerity (*tapas*) is easy to perform; for even when flesh and the like waste away due to the abandonment of food for the sake of penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, the vital airs do not suddenly fail because the bones do not immediately decay, and thus the prāṇas remain undisturbed. In the Tretā and subsequent ages, however, because the vital airs become disturbed through the wasting away of flesh and so forth, austerity is difficult to perform. Although it is difficult to state precisely how the vital airs have a specific utility in knowledge and other pursuits by depending upon the support of flesh and the like, nevertheless, that description was given to show the impossibility of performing austerity [in later ages]. For this very reason, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, austerity is described immediately after [the description of] the other ages with reference to those intervening ages.
[128] "Non-violence, truthful speech, kindness, self-restraint, and compassion—this the wise know to be austerity, not the emaciation of the body. Thus [ends verse 32].

Now he states the purpose of describing the power of the ages (yugas): "The duties that exist in each age, and the twice-born who exist in each respective place—one should not censure them, for those twice-born ones are indeed the very forms of the ages. (33) Thus.
"Corresponding to the ages" means conforming to the ages; that is to say, they are dependent upon time. As it is said in the Āraṇyaparvan:
"The earth, rivers, trees, mountains, as well as the Siddhas and celestial rishis, follow that Time, just as all things do in age after age."
"O bull among men, having encountered their respective times, the strength, stature, power, and other qualities of human beings arise and manifest. (33)

Now, one might object: if, in this Kali age, sinners are thus beyond reproach, the scripture that establishes the entire system of dharma and adharma would fall into ruin. For instance, regarding the statement, "Dharma has indeed been conquered by adharma" (PārSm 1.30), the injunction heard there, "Practice dharma" (TaitUp 1.11.1), would be contradicted.
Furthermore: "There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood;
for the stability of dharma rests upon truth, therefore one must not violate the truth."
Thus it is stated among the duties of kings (*rājadharma*). And that [statement] would be contradicted if falsehood were not blameworthy:
"A king who punishes those who should not be punished, and fails to punish those who should be punished, incurs great infamy and goes to hell" (MDh 8.128).
Otherwise, this statement would contradict the fact that the thief is blameless;
for there is the declaration of Yājñavalkya: "The word of the husband must be carried out by women; this is the supreme duty of a woman" (YDh 1.77).
"But a woman who, arrogant on account of her kinsmen or her own virtues, should transgress against her husband—
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public assembly," so says the statement of Manu (MDh 8.371).
"A wife who transgresses her husband's command must be abandoned by you;
that there is no fault in this, you indeed know exactly as it is."
[130] Even if she possesses all auspicious marks, she who commits transgression against her husband must be abandoned; this is the eternal law.

Thus is the statement of the great seers in the *Brahma Purāṇa*. These three statements would be contradicted if one were to avoid censuring a man who is ruled by his wife. In the *Acchidrakāṇḍa*, the expiation for the *agnihotra* has been heard of in many ways; and it is also stated in the *Aśvamedhika Parvan*: "O King Yudhiṣṭhira, he who desires the higher goal should perform the *agnihotra* according to the rules; this *agnihotra* shall be as if it were a lifelong sacrificial session (*satra*) from birth. (88)
This must not be abandoned for even a moment; it should be accepted by the twice-born.
For whatever consciousness exists on earth, whether moving or unmoving, all that was created by the Self-existent One for the sake of the Agnihotra. (89, 56)
"And those men who do not understand this, being shrouded in darkness,
go to the terrible hell well-known by the name Raurava. (79) Thus,
these two [scriptural] texts from the Śruti and Smṛti would be contradicted if the neglect of the Agnihotra were not censured.
Acting against the will of the guru, neglecting what is pleasing to the guru,
and failing to perform service for the guru are causes for the non-arising of knowledge.
[131] Hearing disparagement of the teacher, witnessing his defeat,
and likewise engaging in debate with him are causes for the non-arising of knowledge.
Thus says the *Skanda Purāṇa*. And this [statement] would be contradicted if it were not a censure of the failure to honor the guru. For it is said:
"When the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter—month after month, her father drinks her menstrual blood" (*Yama Smṛti* 22).
Thus says Yama:
"If an unmarried maiden sees her menses while in her father's house, her father incurs the sin of foeticide; that maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 24.41)
Such is the statement. Both of these [statements] would be contradicted if there were no censure of giving birth to a daughter. || 33 ||
To the question, "How then is there no censure?", he says:
"In every age, however, the remaining capacity [of penance] has been declared by the Sage;
and the expiation also spoken of by Parāśara is prescribed. (34) Thus.
The remainder—that is, the specific efficacy of each respective age—has been described in detail by other sages. Thus it is recited in the Āraṇyaparvan:
"The age named Kṛta is the most excellent, wherein the eternal Dharma exists;
in that supreme age, everything is already accomplished and nothing remains to be done. (11)

In that age, the *dharmas* do not falter, nor indeed do the people perish; therefore, it is called the Kṛta Yuga, which by the power of time has attained its excellence. In the Kṛta Yuga, Dharma has four feet, is white in color, and is imperishable (*acyuta*).

This is called the Kṛta-yuga, which is entirely devoid of the three qualities (guṇas). (22) Dharma declines by one quarter, and Acyuta departs from those who are attached to the world. (23) Men are devoted to truth and dedicated to the dharma of ritual action.
From that, sacrifices proceed, as do various righteous rites.
(24) In the Tretā Yuga, people were established in their own duties and were devoted to ritual action.
Viṣṇu attains a yellow hue, and the Veda itself becomes fourfold. (27)
In this world, there is a falling away from truth, yet some remain established in truth. For those who deviate from truth, many diseases arise;
likewise, there are desires, calamities, and those brought about by the gods. (30–31)
For others, desiring pleasure and desiring wealth, perform sacrifices;
thus, having reached the Dvāpara age, living beings decline through unrighteousness.
O son of Kuntī, in the Kali age, dharma stands upon only a single foot.
The practices prescribed by the Vedas cease, as do the performance of dharma-sacrifices; likewise, calamities, diseases, lethargy, faults, anger, and the like [subside]. (34) (MBh Vana 149.11–34)
[133] Thus it is said in that very same work:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, becoming intermingled with one another, will become equal to Śūdras, devoid of austerity and truth. (17–18)
"When the destruction of the age has arrived, all men will be cruel by nature and suspicious of one another" (MBh Vana 199.17–57),
and so forth. Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:

Prolonged practice of celibacy, the breaking of a water-pot, marriage with a woman from one's own maternal lineage or a sapinda relative, and likewise the killing of a cow; [these are causes for loss of caste].
"In the Kali age, human sacrifice, horse sacrifice, and liquor must be avoided by the twice-born. Thus [says] Kratu as well:
"The procreation of a son through the husband's brother [is forbidden], and a daughter once given away is not to be given again."
In the Kali age, the slaughter of a cow should not be performed at a sacrifice, nor should the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) be used.

[134] Thus it is said; and also in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "In the Kali age, one should not perform these five things: the remarriage of a woman already married, the granting of the eldest son's special share, the killing of a cow, approaching a brother’s wife, and carrying a water-pot."
Likewise, there are others as well who take the conventions of those who know the Dharma as their authority. For example:
the appointment of a brother-in-law for the procreation of offspring by a widow;
and the marriage of a girl and of women whose virginity has been violated by another man.
The marriage of twice-born men with girls of a different caste,
and the killing of even eminent twice-born men who are aggressors in a righteous war.
[135] The taking on board of a twice-born man traveling by boat upon the ocean, even if he has been purified;
the initiation for a sacrificial session (*sattra*) for all castes; and the carrying of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
The journey on the Great Departure, the collection of the Surā-graha,
the licking of the Agnihotra ladle, and the non-acceptance of what has been licked.
The entry into the forest-dwelling stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama) is likewise enjoined by the sacred law;
it depends upon one's conduct and Vedic study, and serves to diminish sin.
The ordinance for expiation for Brahmins ending in death,
the fault of association with thieves and others, and the atonement for mortal sins (mahāpātaka).
