The performance of the act of cooking animals for the sake of a boon, for guests, or for the ancestors; the formal acceptance of sons other than the *datta* (given) and *aurasa* (legitimate) types as one's own offspring;
and sexual intercourse with women of the same caste who are otherwise forbidden—even if they have been purified by penance—[are all grounds for loss of caste].
If an improper union occurs, there shall be abandonment of the teacher’s wife;
furthermore, after the collection of the bones, there shall be no touching of his body.
Serving as a slaughterer for Brahmins, likewise selling Soma,
eating at the six meal-times, fasting, and taking food from one of low-caste occupation;

Among Śūdras, the food of slaves, cowherds, family friends, and those who share half the harvest from their plowing may be eaten by a householder; however, he must stay very far away from visiting their sacred bathing places.
The conduct toward the wife of one's teacher is said to be as toward the teacher himself;
likewise, for the foremost of the twice-born, there is the mode of conduct in times of distress, as well as the practice of not storing more than a day's supply.
For the sake of progeny, the foremost of the twice-born take wives from among their own kind;
for Brahmins, there is the practice of living abroad and the act of blowing upon the sacrificial fire with the mouth.
[137] The seduction of a woman by force or other such wicked means is forbidden by the sacred law;
however, for an ascetic, the practice of begging alms from among all social classes is prescribed according to the rules.
In the case of new water, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed for ten days by the Guru;
likewise, for a Śūdra, even activities such as cooking may be performed for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
Likewise, there is death by leaping from a cliff or into fire, as well as death by fasting;
and the learned perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) upon water that is sufficient only to satisfy a cow.

In disputes between father and son, the determination of punishment for witnesses and the rule regarding their being present in the evening at home have been established by the learned who are intent upon the truth.
At the beginning of the Kali age, these actions were restricted by great-souled sages for the sake of protecting the world, according to established rules.
"And the consensus (*samaya*) of the virtuous shall also be authoritative, like the Veda" [138].

This was also stated by Āpastamba: "The consensus of those who know the Dharma and the Vedas are authoritative" (ĀpDh 1.1.1). Other examples may be cited in the same way; for instance, how the specific capacities of various ages were described by the sages through injunctions and prohibitions. Likewise, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for both the transgression of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited was also declared by the ancient Parāśara. Indeed, the words of the elder Parāśara are recited:
Living beings born from a womb, from an egg, and those born from moisture—all these are indeed not to be killed; so it has been described by the wise.
For the sake of certainty regarding those who have awakened [to the truth], an expiation is prescribed:
if one should deprive even a single boneless creature of its life.
Having fasted for one day and performed sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
and having bathed three times in water, one is liberated from that sin.
But for the killing of a vertebrate creature, double the penance is prescribed;
by this same rule, there is no doubt regarding stationary beings as well.
"One is released from offense through the body by means of the feet and hands;
it is fourfold when committed through action, twofold when corrupted by speech,
and likewise remembered as singlefold when mental sin is committed."

The word *ca* (and) serves to include Yājñavalkya, Manu, and others, for the chapters on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) are indeed well-known in their respective works. However, the mention of Parāśara is intended with reference to the Kali age; for among all the *kalpas*, the *Parāśarasmṛti* is partial toward the duties of the Kali age. Even regarding expiations, Parāśara is to be primarily respected in matters pertaining to the Kali age. Therefore, the expiation prescribed by Parāśara, Manu, and others is ordained by an assembly of learned men (*vidvat-pariṣad*) for the removal of specific sins. This is what is meant: since various sages have elaborated upon both the capacities of the respective ages and the corresponding expiations, one must deliberate upon both and establish a systematic rule (*vyavasthā*) regarding praise and censure. Those censure statements such as, "That girl who does not perform the prescribed rites nor avoid prohibited acts according to the capacity of the age, that daughter of his is considered a *vṛṣalī* [outcaste]" (Viṣṇu Smṛti 24.41), apply to those persons who, though capable of performing prescribed duties, avoiding prohibited ones, and undertaking expiation for sins committed through negligence, nevertheless fail to do so. Conversely, the statement "No censure should be directed at them" applies to those who are incapable. For this very reason, it is recited in the Śaiva Āgama: [139] ... [The text continues with the citation from the Śaiva Āgama].
"In cases of being afflicted by extreme illness, fear of kings or thieves, and so forth;
during the performance of duties toward gurus, fire, or deities; and when there is a constant neglect [of other duties], one does not incur sin.
Therefore, there is no subversion whatsoever of the *dharmaśāstra*. 34.

Now, one might object: since the entire power of the *yugas* is difficult to comprehend without familiarity with numerous texts in the manner described, how can those of dull intellect and short lifespan determine the conduct of the four castes according to the power of the *yugas*? To this he says:
[140] "I shall tell you all of that today, having recollected it;
O best of sages, listen to the conduct of the four castes. (35) Thus.

Because everything previously mentioned is summarized here, this [work] is easily grasped even by those of dull intellect. By the phrase "not by fate" (*adaiva*), which prohibits delay in time, a definitive conclusion is easily obtained in this treatise even for those of short lifespans. The four castes constitute the *cāturvarṇya*. Its proper conduct is *dharma*. The word "conduct" (*ācāra*) denotes worldly behavior, which is synonymous with "character" (*śīla*). That *dharma* characterized by rites such as sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices, for which proper conduct—meaning conduct approved by the learned (*śiṣṭa*)—serves as the cause, is this *dharma* known as "proper conduct" (*samācāra*). For this very reason, he will later state the distinction between conduct and *dharma* in the form of cause and effect: "Conduct is the protector of *dharma*" (PārSm 1.37). Furthermore, the *Śruti* designates *dharma* and conduct as distinct: "As one acts, as one conducts oneself, so does one become" (BṛĀ Up 4.4.5). And in another *Śruti*, the distinction between ritual action (*karman*) and conduct (*vṛtta*) is recorded: "Now, if you should have any doubt regarding action or doubt regarding conduct... (TaitUp 1.11.3). Although heedfulness was already enjoined previously in the words, "Listen, O son, I shall speak; let the best of sages listen," nevertheless, because that point had been interrupted by the detailed exposition of the power of the *yugas*, it is reminded once again. Alternatively, the previous statement concerned the subject of hearing about the power of the *yugas*, whereas this concerns the subject of hearing about *dharma*; thus, there is no tautology. (35)

In order to state, by way of a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, that the knowledge of the Dharma about to be taught is the cause of the supreme goal of man, he praises the recitation of the text and the knowledge of its meaning:
"The meritorious, purifying, and sin-destroying doctrine of Parāśara has been composed for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas and for the establishment of Dharma. (36)

The collection of texts proclaimed by Parāśara is the *Parāśaramata*. It bestows merit (*puṇya*) merely through its recitation. Merit is of two kinds: that which brings about the desired (*iṣṭaprāpaka*) and that which averts the undesired (*aniṣṭanivartaka*). Both of these are intended by the terms "purifying" (*pavitra*) and "destroying sin" (*pāpanāśana*). Thus, when this collection of texts is "contemplated"—that is, when it is investigated according to its meaning—it becomes a bestower of merit as before. The purpose of investigating the meaning is twofold: one's own practice (*svānuṣṭhāna*) and the instruction of others (*paropadeśa*). Both of these are expressed by the two words beginning with "brāhmaṇa. The meaning of "brāhmaṇa" is the performance of one's own duty (*svadharma*) for the sake of brahminhood. "Establishment of Dharma" (*dharmasaṃsthāpana*) means causing others to perform [Dharma] through the instruction of Dharma. If such is the greatness even of the recitation of the text and the knowledge of its meaning, then what need is there to say that practice is the cause of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)? And this is indeed appropriate, for Parāśara—having obtained boons through the grace of Pulastya and Vasiṣṭha—possessed mastery over the heart of all scriptures. Thus says the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: [142] ...[text of Viṣṇupurāṇa]... *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific verse from the Viṣṇupurāṇa.*
"Even in the midst of great enmity, you have resorted to forgiveness toward your teacher at my word;
therefore, you shall know those scriptures as being equal [to all]."
Therefore, even when you were angry, you did not bring about the annihilation of my continuum;
for that reason, O illustrious one, I grant you another boon.
"My child, you shall become the compiler of the Purāṇa-saṃhitās,
and you shall come to know the ultimate reality of the deities exactly as it is."
And regarding both active and withdrawn action, O child, your stainless intellect shall become free from doubt through my grace.
Thereupon, the Blessed Vasiṣṭha, our grandfather, said:
"All that was spoken to you by Pulastya shall come to pass. (ViP 1.1.28–31).
Thus [ends the section]. 36.
Thus ends the introduction to proper conduct in the first chapter of the section on conduct.
And the table of contents of the book is completed.
[143] Now, conduct is being examined. As it was asked:
"Tell me something common regarding the conduct of the four castes" (PārSm 1.17).
To this, he gives the following reply:
"The conduct of all four castes is the protector of Dharma;
for those whose bodies have fallen away from right conduct, Dharma turns its back. (37) Thus it is said.

Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that right conduct (*ācāra*) is the cause of welfare in this world and the next. Furthermore, the definition of right conduct is stated in the *Anuśāsana-parvan*:
"For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct one obtains prosperity;
through right conduct a person attains fame both in this world and after death."
For a man of evil conduct does not attain a long life in this world;
living beings tremble before him and likewise treat him with contempt.
Therefore, one should practice proper conduct in this world if one desires one's own prosperity;
for even in the case of one with a sinful body, right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
"Dharma is characterized by conduct, and the virtuous are characterized by conduct;
the way of life of the righteous—this is the characteristic of conduct. Thus it is said.
Hārīta also records:
"The virtuous (sādhu) are those whose defects have been destroyed; the word 'sat' denotes the virtuous. That which is their conduct is called *sadācāra* (the conduct of the good). Thus [it is said].
Manu also says:

"In whatever region a particular custom has been handed down through traditional succession for the social classes (*varṇa*) and the intermediate castes (*antarāla*), that is called 'right conduct' (*sadācāra*). (MDh 2.17). "The virtuous" (*santaḥ*) refers to the refined (*śiṣṭa*). Regarding their nature, the venerable Baudhāyana says: "The refined are indeed those who are free from envy, devoid of egoism, possessing only as much grain as fits in a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*), not covetous, and exempt from hypocrisy, pride, greed, delusion, and anger. (BDh 1.1.5). [Also stated] in the Āraṇyaparvan.
Free from anger and malice, devoid of egoism and envy,
upright and endowed with tranquility, they become those who follow the conduct of the disciplined.
Those who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, possessed of good conduct, renowned,
devoted to the service of their gurus, self-controlled, and disciplined in their behavior— such are they.

[145] Thus, in all these cases, it is meant that "conduct" (*ācāra*) is a specific mode of behavior characterized by compassion, courtesy, modesty, and so forth, which is approved by the learned (*śiṣṭas*). That good conduct protects the *dharma* based on revelation (*śrauta*) and tradition (*smārta*), because when good conduct exists, there is an absence of cruelty, anger, and other such factors that obstruct *dharma*. However, when conduct is absent, because of the presence of opposing factors, *dharma* itself would not proceed; even if it were somehow set in motion, it would turn back. This conduct, which protects *dharma*, is common to all four [classes].

If it is objected: "The question 'Tell me something common' asked regarding *dharma* does not cohere with an answer concerning *ācāra*," we say no; for the intention is to express the non-difference between *ācāra* and *dharma*, which stand in the relation of cause (*nimitta*) and effect (*naimittika*). || 37 ||
Now he shows the unique duty of the Brāhmaṇa:
"Constantly devoted to the six duties, worshipping the deities and guests, and eating only the remains of the oblation, the Brāhmaṇa does not come to ruin. (38) Thus.
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, studying, teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts are the six duties. As Manu has said:
"Teaching, studying, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving gifts and receiving gifts—these are the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa). (MDh 10.75)
In that regard, teaching has been explained in detail in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"One should constantly teach the Veda, the Dharma, the Purāṇas, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) to one who is endowed with good conduct, self-possessed, and free from hypocrisy."
If a teacher does not impart knowledge to a student who has resided with him for a year,
that teacher takes upon himself the misdeeds of the student living with him.
One who is devoted to service, the youngest son of the teacher, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, and virtuous— these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma.

"Grateful, likewise free from malice, intelligent, most virtuous, trustworthy, and dear—one who possesses these six qualities should be taught by the best of the twice-born according to the rule. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.14.37–40).
Viṣṇu also said: "One should not officiate at a sacrifice for, nor teach, nor initiate one who has not been examined. (Viṣṇu Dharma-sūtra 29.4–6). And Vasiṣṭha [said]:
[147] Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: "Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak me to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained; thus shall I be potent. (VaDh 2.8).
Yama states the rule regarding teaching:
"Rising constantly at dawn, having first cleansed his teeth,
bathed, and offered oblations, a man should engage in teaching his disciples.
Thus [says] Manu as well.
But when the student is about to begin his lesson, the teacher, always alert, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should stop when [the student] says, "May there be a pause. (MDh 2.73)

The disciple who is about to be initiated: desiring to recite the Veda to him, being unwearied at the commencement of the daily teaching, he should begin by saying, "Recite, sir! At the conclusion, for the sake of pleasing the Lord, he should cease by saying, "May there be a pause. With all this in mind, the Śruti says: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age; one should teach him."

On this point, Prabhākara maintains: Pāṇini has prescribed the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *nī* in the sense of "acting as a teacher" (Pāṇ 1.3.36). Since the acts of initiation (*upanayana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*) stand in the relationship of subordinate and principal and thus share a single agent, one who desires the status of a teacher is the qualified person for the act of teaching. For this very reason, it is recorded by Manu:
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret portions (*rahasya*), him they call a teacher (*ācārya*)" (MDh 2.140).

Thus, since the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana*) is well-established, it will not be necessary to postulate a separate injunction for studying (*adhyayana*). This is because the purpose of studying is already accomplished through the fact that the enjoined act of teaching is otherwise impossible without study.

[Objection: But surely there is no fault of postulation regarding an injunction for studying, because such an injunction already exists in the Vedic revelation: "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.11). [Reply: Not so. Because this injunction lacks a stated qualification (*adhikārin*), it cannot function as an impeller to performance.

Now, it might be argued: let an eligible person (*adhikārī*) be postulated either by the logic of the Viśvajit sacrifice or the logic of the Rātri-sattra. In the injunction “One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit,” since no specific qualification for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—such as “desiring this”—is heard, and because heaven is desired by all when no other performance is established, heaven itself is postulated as that qualification. Likewise, in this case, let the boy desiring heaven be the person to be enjoined. In the Rātri-sattra, based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, “Those who perform these night-sacrifices indeed find firm standing,” since “firm standing” is heard in the text and is more proximate than heaven—which is not explicitly mentioned—the person entitled to the rite is postulated as one desiring firm standing. Similarly, in this case, let the person entitled to the rite be one desiring streams of milk and so forth, based on the explanatory passage: “When he studies the Ṛg-veda, streams of milk carry the *svadhā* offerings to his ancestors; when he studies the Yajur-veda, streams of ghee; when he studies the Sāman-veda, Soma flows for them” (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.11).

Not so; for the streams of milk and the like are subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) to the injunction for the *brahmayajña*, and because the student (*māṇavaka*), being unawakened, cannot possibly possess the desire for heaven (*svargakāmatva*). Even if such a desire were somehow possible, the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) would be unavoidable: the comprehension of the injunction to study occurs after one has studied the Veda, yet the study itself depends upon that comprehension. Therefore, since study is prompted by teaching, it is teaching alone that is enjoined, not study.

Other disputants do not accept this view of the Teacher (Guru), because it is impossible for eternal study to be prompted by non-eternal teaching; and teaching is indeed non-eternal, since the qualification for it belongs to one who desires a livelihood. Thus Manu says:
"Of his six duties, three are means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons" (MDh 10.76).
[150] Study, however, is obligatory, because Manu has recorded that there is a transgression in its non-performance:
"The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other matters,
quickly becomes a Śūdra even while living, along with his lineage" (MDh 2.168).

Therefore, study is indeed prompted by its own injunction (*vidhi*). Nor is there a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*), because even prior to study, the meaning of the injunction is understood through the mouth of the father or others, as in the case of the *saṃdhyāvandana* and other rites. Precisely because the boy is regulated by his father and others, the fault of being unawakened (*aprabuddha*) does not apply to him. Although in the Taittirīya recension the sentence “One’s own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied” is read within the context of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and thus has the form of an injunction for the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), nevertheless, since study preceded by initiation (*upanayana*) is elaborately described in all the *smṛtis*, the underlying *śruti* must be inferred. The author of the *Vivaraṇa*, however, maintained that even in the phrase “he should cause [the student] to study” (*adhyāpayīta*), since the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇij-artha*) is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*) for the sake of livelihood, he intended the root-meaning—study itself—to be the object of the injunction; thus, having modified the sentence to “An eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa should approach [the teacher]; O, let him study,” he established his position. In every respect, there exists an eternal scriptural injunction for the study of one’s own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*) consisting of the words “One’s own Veda is to be studied. Likewise, there is also a *smṛti* to this effect.
[151] “The entire Veda, together with its secret portions (*rahasya*), must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities (*tapas*) and vows prescribed by rule” (MDh 2.165).

Here, “mastery” (*adhigati*) refers to study that extends up to the investigation of the meaning. Accordingly, it is recorded in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in the absence of both study and the investigation of its meaning.
That twice-born man who exerts effort in other matters without having studied the Veda is indeed a fool; he is outside the Veda and should not be conversed with by those of the twice-born classes.
A twice-born man should certainly not be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Vedas;
for one who rests content with recitation alone sinks like a cow in the mud.

"He who, having studied the Veda according to the rules, does not investigate the meaning of the Veda—he, along with his lineage, is equal to a Śūdra and does not attain the status of a worthy recipient. Thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya states the procedural requirements for study:
One should also attend upon the teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study;
one should study when summoned and offer whatever has been obtained to him.
"And one should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body. Thus [it is said].
Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O King, with a concentrated mind, one should likewise worship both twilights, the Sun, and the Fire."
One should attend upon him and likewise perform even the salutation to the guru.

O best of men, when the teacher stands, the disciple should stand; when he walks, he should walk; when he sits low, he should sit; and when he is silent, he should remain silent. A disciple should never act in opposition to his teacher.
Addressed by him, he should recite the Veda with undistracted mind while standing before his teacher; and then, permitted by the teacher, he should eat the food obtained as alms.
"One who has perfected his intellect, while observing the vows, should master the Veda. Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Being summoned, he should engage in study, gazing at the face of the guru."

"One should always have the hand uplifted, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.14.1–2) "Study" (*adhyayana*) is the recitation of the specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*) inherited through one's own family lineage. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Those for whom the Veda, along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*), has been handed down through tradition..."
"One should perform the ritual acts according to that branch and likewise study that branch" (VaDh 6.43).
He himself prohibits the abandonment of one's own branch:
"He who, having abandoned his own branch, masters that of another..."
He should be excluded from all activities by virtuous people, like a Śūdra.

[153] "By whomsoever one's own branch is abandoned, by him the Supreme Brahman is abandoned; he should be known as a slayer of Brahman (brahmahā), eternally censured by the virtuous. Thus it is said. However, the study of another branch preceded by the study of one's own branch was accepted by that very same authority.
"Having studied his own branch [of the Veda], he should likewise study another branch. Thus, one should study the *Dharmaśāstra* just as one studies the Veda. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Having thus consecrated his son with the staff and other rites, the father..."
Afterwards, one should teach the Veda, as well as the treatises of Manu and others.
The Brahmin is rooted in the Veda; he is traditionally held to be equal in authority regarding both Śruti and Smṛti.
Likewise, this triad should always be understood as including the conduct of the virtuous (Sadācāra).
"Having studied the four Vedas, along with their limbs (aṅgas), sub-limbs (upāṅgas), padapāṭha, and kramapāṭha, those devoid of memory do not shine, just as a night without the moon.
Here, by the term "study," the fivefold practice of the Vedas is indicated. To this effect, Dakṣa says:
"First, the acquisition of the Veda; then reflection, practice, recitation, and its impartation to disciples—thus the study of the Veda is fivefold. So says Hārīta as well.
A twice-born man who knows the meaning of the mantras, while muttering them, offering oblations, and likewise teaching them, attains the heavenly world; but in the opposite case, he goes to hell.
[154] Thus, it should be studied only from the mouth of the guru, and one must not engage in study from written texts. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"That which is studied relying solely on a book, and not studied in the presence of the guru, does not shine in the midst of an assembly, like the offspring of an adulteress. (Nā Śi 2.13)
Manu states those things to be avoided during study:
"One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night, one who is exhausted should not go back to sleep. (MDh 4.99)
Nārada also says:
"But he who studies [the Veda] while deprived of his hands, or devoid of proper accents and phonemes, being consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman verses, enters a low birth. (Nā. Śi. 2.27)

Vyāsa also says: "That which is studied during forbidden periods of study, that which is studied in the presence of a Śūdra, and that which is studied for the sake of receiving gifts— this is said to lead to hell."

Thus concludes the section on studying and teaching. Now, the occasions when study is prohibited (*anadhyāya*). These are of two kinds: constant (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*). Regarding the constant ones, Hārīta says:
"On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the fourteenth day, on the eighth day, and on both the junction days (*parvan*)."
"One should never study on a day that is not a day of study, nor during the night.
[155] Yājñavalkya speaks of the occasional (naimittika) occasions [for suspension]:
"When there is the sound of a dog, a jackal, a donkey, an owl, the Sāman chants, or a distressed cry..."
Near impure things, corpses, Śūdras, outcastes, cemeteries, or those who have fallen [from their caste].
In an impure place, or when one is personally impure; during a downpour of lightning and thunder;
after eating while the hands are still wet; while in the midst of water; at midnight; or during an excessively violent wind.
During a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mist,
while running, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at the house.

"Traveling by donkey or camel, on an elephant, horse, or boat; climbing a tree or ascending a mountain—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary suspensions of study. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.148–51).
Other such occasions for non-study are recorded here and there in the Smṛtis. Regarding this, Nārada says:

"One must observe a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) during the solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and during the sleeping and waking of Hari, as well as on the anniversaries of the Manus (*manvādi*) and the beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*).
The anniversaries of the Manus are specified in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, likewise the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of the month of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada.
[156] The new moon day of Phālguna, as well as the eleventh of Pauṣa,
then the tenth of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
and the fifteenth bright day of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha.
"And these beginnings of the Manvantaras cause what is given to become inexhaustible.
Thus [it is said]. The beginnings of the Yugas are described in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"The third day of the month of Vaiśākha, and that ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika..."
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, on the thirteenth and fifteenth days, and in the month of Māgha" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.14.13).
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"At the Upākarma and the Utsarga, a three-night suspension [of Vedic study] is prescribed."
But on the days of the Aṣṭakās and on the nights at the ends of the seasons, one should observe impurity for a full day and night.
"Likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, and similarly in Māgha—these three Aṣṭakās are proclaimed by the wise in the dark fortnight. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.14.77–78)

Gautama also states: “The full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha, as well as the three Aṣṭakās—these constitute a period of three nights of non-study” (GDh 16.7). This means that starting from the aforementioned full moon days, there is a three-night interval of non-study. Likewise, regarding the three Aṣṭakās beginning with the seventh lunar day, the meaning is that there is also a three-night period of non-study on those occasions. Paiṭhīnasi says: “There are three Aṣṭakās occurring in the dark fortnight; some say they begin with Mārgaśīrṣa. Āpastamba, however, prescribes a month of non-study during the evening (*pradoṣa*) starting from the *upākarma* ceremony: “Having performed the commencement of study on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the evening for one month” (ĀpDh 9.1). By the word *pradoṣa*, the early part of the night is intended here. One should also not study during the evenings of the thirteenth lunar day and so forth. Thus says the *Ādityapurāṇa*.
"One who desires intelligence should not remember nor recite [the mantra] on the thirteenth lunar day, especially on the seventh, and on the fourth during the evening twilights.
Thus says Prajāpati regarding the two types of lunar days beginning with the fourth.

"One should not study during the sixth and the twelfth [lunar days], nor when it is less than half a *nāḍikā* before midnight; nor during the evening twilight (*pradoṣa*), nor on the third [lunar day] for nine *nāḍikās*.
Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.
There is a suspension of study for three days in the case of deaths among pupils, officiating priests, teachers, or kinsmen;
likewise at the commencement (upākarmaṇi) and conclusion (utsarge) of the Vedic term, and when a person learned in one's own Vedic branch (svaśākhā-śrotriya) has died.
In the event of thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor;
and upon completing the Veda during the day or having studied the Āraṇyaka.
On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during an eclipse of Rāhu, at the junctions of the seasons, or after eating, or having accepted an offering at a Śrāddha ceremony; [158]

"When an interval is created by a domestic animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a rat, it is a day and night; likewise when there is the falling or the rising of Indra's banner. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:

"When a village is plundered by thieves, or in the event of a panic caused by fire, one should know that there is a suspension of study for the remainder of the day; this applies to all extraordinary portents as well. (MDh 4.118). In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"One should never study under the shade of the *śleṣmātaka*, the *śālmali*, or the *madhuka*, nor under the *kovidāra* or the *kapittha* tree" (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.14.79).
Manu states an exception even to these aforementioned occasions for non-study:

"And indeed, there is no restriction regarding the study of the Vedas (*vedopakaraṇa*), the daily recitation (*svādhyāya*), and the obligatory rites (*naityaka*), as well as the *mantras* for the fire-oblation (*homa*). Here, "the Vedas' auxiliaries" refers to the *aṅgas*. "Daily recitation" refers to the *brahmayajña*. Śaunaka also says:

"In the case of daily recitation, optional recitation, a sacrificial rite, or even the complete study of the Vedas, there is no prohibition against the study of the Vedas, nor likewise when teaching them. Thus it is stated;
and also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

"But there is no suspension of study regarding the ancillary sciences (*aṅga*), nor for the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, nor for the other *Dharmaśāstras*. On the festival days (*parvan*), one should avoid these [latter categories]. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.14.84).
Thus ends the section on the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*).

Previously, the duties pertaining to study and teaching were described. Now, we shall describe those pertaining to sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices. Regarding that, the Blessed Lord spoke of the creation and purpose of sacrificing:
"Having created beings together with sacrifice in the beginning, Prajāpati said:
'By this you shall propagate; let this be the cow of plenty for your desired objects.'"
Nourish the gods with this; let those gods nourish you. Nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good.
"For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you desire.
He who enjoys what is given by them without giving to them in return is truly a thief" (BhG 3.10–12).
And he [the Lord] himself has stated that this sacrifice is threefold, according to the division of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*.

That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits, with the mind concentrated on the thought that "sacrifice must simply be performed," is characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
But that sacrifice which is performed with a view toward a reward, and even for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas— know that sacrifice to be rajasic.
"A sacrifice devoid of prescribed rules, in which no food is distributed, lacking mantras and sacrificial fees, and bereft of faith, is declared to be tāmasa" (BhG 17.11–13).
In the *Aśvamedhika* Parvan, this is introduced by demonstrating that the creation of the twice-born and other beings was for the purpose of sacrifice.
The twice-born were created for the purpose of sacrifice, as were the stars in the sky and the deities;
likewise, cows were produced for the sake of sacrifice and for the purpose of sacrificial fees.
For the purpose of vessels and jars, as well as for sacrificial fuel and the sacrificial post, Brahmā created the trees of the forest, including gold and silver.
"Domestic and wild animals are born for the sake of sacrifice.
Thus [it is said]. Hārīta also demonstrates the greatness of sacrifice through both positive and negative concomitance:
"By sacrifice the worlds shine forth stainless; by sacrifice the gods attained immortality."

"By means of sacrifice, one is liberated from many sins and attains the worlds of the undecaying Viṣṇu. Indeed, there is no world for one who does not perform sacrifice; one who does not sacrifice finds no auspiciousness.
Having failed to perform sacrifice, his soul unpurified, he perishes like a withered leaf. Thus it is said.

The specific sacrifices (*yajñaviśeṣa*) are the *agnihotra* and so forth. Thus it is heard in scripture: "Prajāpati created the sacrifices: the *agnihotra*, the *agniṣṭoma*, the *paurṇamāsī*, the *ukthya*, the *amāvāsyā*, and the *atirātra*. Since the *agnihotra* and other rites are to be accomplished by means of consecrated fires (*saṃskṛta-agni*), the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), which effects that consecration, must be performed first. Regarding this, [it is said]: "One who has installed the fires (*āhitāgni*) shall have the entitlement to all sacrificial forms (*saṃsthā*) provided he possesses wealth. Even one without wealth, a twice-born man, should install the fire constantly out of fear of sin."
The sin incurred by failing to perform [this duty] is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"He who, out of atheism or laziness, does not desire to establish the sacred fires,
or does not sacrifice with a sacrifice, goes to many hells."
Therefore, with every effort— and especially so for a Brāhmaṇa—
one whose self is purified should, having established the sacred fires, worship the Supreme Lord.

[162] Thus it is said. Furthermore, the Śruti prescribes the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) as qualified by time and other factors: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring; for spring is the season of the Brāhmaṇa. Having established them in his own season, he becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). A Rājanya should establish the fires in summer; for summer is the season of the Rājanya. Having established them in his own season, he becomes possessed of sensory power and vigor. A Vaiśya should establish the fires in autumn; for autumn is the season of the Vaiśya. Having established them in his own season, he becomes possessed of cattle. This is also stated in the *Āśvamedhika* [Parvan].
O lord of men, the fire should be established by a Brāhmaṇa in the spring;
for the Brāhmaṇa is said to be the spring, as he is called the source of the Vedas.
O King, for that Brahmin by whom the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) is performed in the spring, his prosperity and spiritual growth increase.
O King, for a Kṣatriya, the installation of the sacred fires is best performed in the summer;
indeed, for him by whom the installation is performed in the summer, his prosperity increases.
Prosperity, progeny, cattle, wealth, strength, and fame— indeed,
in the autumn season, the Vaiśya may also establish the sacrificial fire.
The autumn night is indeed the Vaiśya himself; he is called the source of the Vaiśya.
O Pāṇḍava, it is in this way that the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is performed in autumn.

"Indeed, for him, prosperity, progeny, longevity, cattle, and wealth increase. Thus it is said. And sacrifices such as the *darśa* and others are preceded by the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*). Likewise, Vasiṣṭha states: "A Brāhmaṇa must necessarily establish the sacred fires; he should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, *cāturmāsya*, animal, and *soma* sacrifices. Hārīta also says: "One should constantly perform the *pākayajñas*, and one should constantly perform the *haviryajñas*."
"But he who desires the imperishable Brahman should [worship] the Saumyas according to the prescribed rule. Thus [it is said].

And they were enumerated by Gautama: “The Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa-śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āṣāḍhī, the Prauṣṭhapadī, the Caitrī, and the Āśvayujī—these are the seven forms of the *pākayajña*. The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and the *sautrāmaṇī*—these are the seven forms of the *haviryajña*. The *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*—these are the seven forms of the *soma-saṃsthā*” (GDh 8.18–20). Furthermore, Devala has pointed out other great sacrificial rites (*mahāyajñakratu*): “The horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), the royal consecration (*rājasūya*), the *pauṇḍarīka*, the *godāna*, and so forth, are the great sacrificial rites. All these sacrifices are of three types according to their respective application: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*).
Human action is threefold: obligatory, occasional, and optional. (MāPu 34.4)

Thus, according to the statement of Madālada. Regarding that, the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of sacrifices is heard in the Kauthuma branch: "The rituals which the seers beheld in the mantras, those were spread out in many ways during the Tretā age; perform them constantly" (MunUp 1.2.1). Also in the Vājasaneyi branch: "Only performing actions here in this world should one desire to live for a hundred years" (ĪśāUp 2); and also: "This Agnihotra sacrifice indeed lasts until old age; for by old age or by death one is released from it" (MNUp 25.1). Furthermore, the connection with living and so forth in the injunctive statements (*vidhivāka*) indicates their obligatory nature. For example: "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives," "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring. Moreover, the sin incurred by non-performance is an indicator of the obligatory nature. Thus it is heard in the Atharvaṇa: "He whose [sacrifice] is without the Agnihotra, without the New and Full Moon sacrifices, without the Cāturmāsya, without the Āgrayaṇa, devoid of guests, unoffered, without the Vaiśvadeva, or offered contrary to rule—his worlds [of merit] he destroys up to the seventh generation" (MuṇUp 1.2.3). Likewise, another Śruti says: "He whose father or grandfather does not drink Soma is a *vrātya*. The occasional (*naimittika*) rite is that which proceeds based on an indefinite cause such as the burning of one's house, distinct from the desire to live. Thus the Śruti says: "If fire burns one's house, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat. The optional (*kāmya*) rite is that which proceeds from desire. For example: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu"—these and others are the optional animal sacrifices. "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"—these and others are the optional offerings (*iṣṭi*). Among these, the fruit of the optional rites is the attainment of the desired object. However, regarding the obligatory and occasional rites, when performed according to the rules, the attainment of the world of Indra is heard in the Atharvaṇa: [text continues].
Kālī, Karālī, Manojava, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarucī— the goddess Leelāyamānā— these are the seven tongues of flame.
[167] Those who move among these blazing fires, duly offering oblations,
are led by these rays of the sun to where the sole lord of the gods has his dwelling.

"Come, come!"—thus do the resplendent oblations carry the sacrificer by the rays of the sun, speaking endearing words and gladdening him: "This is your holy world of Brahman, earned by meritorious deeds."
Thus [it is said in] Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.4. Also in the Ānuśāsana-parvan:
"It is the settled conclusion that the sacrifice must be performed by very pure sacrificers and likewise by such officiating priests, using pure materials and implements."
When sacrifices are performed in this manner, there shall be satisfaction for the gods;
when the hosts of gods are satisfied, the sacrificer shall obtain the fruit of the sacrifice.
The gods, being gratified by sacrifices, cause the worlds to prosper;
O Goddess, the prosperity of both worlds is seen in sacrifice.
Therefore, from that sacrifice one goes to heaven and rejoices with the immortals.
There is no gift equal to sacrifice; there is no rite equal to sacrifice.
O Goddess, the exposition of all dharmas is contained within sacrifice.

[168] Thus it is said. If, for some reason, the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) should be omitted, Prajāpati has stated the remedy for that: "Having omitted either the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) or the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*), or both, purification is achieved by one quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance for one omission, and by half for two."

For one who is unable to perform the *havis* sacrifices, even if one [rite] is omitted from the beginning, he may be purified by the *prājāpatya* penance; for the same applies to the *pākasaṃsthā* sacrifices as well.
But upon the omission of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana),
as well as the loss of the daily bath and the regular fire-oblation (homa), one becomes pure by reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
At the end of the year, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance upon the omission of Soma sacrifices,
or if one fails to perform any of the sacrifices for which one is qualified.
"One is indeed purified by fasting in the case of the *pākasaṃsthā* sacrifices.
Kātyāyana also says:
"In the event of the omission of the *pitṛyajña* and also in the event of the omission of the *vaiśvadeva*."
Likewise, one who has not performed the New Moon sacrifice (navayajña) when partaking of new grain for the first time;

"Whatever food falls into the meal becomes the *caru* offering for Vaiśvānara. Thus it is said. Even in the absence of sufficient wealth to provide the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one must not omit the obligatory rite. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
"He whose obligatory rites, as well as those performed on special occasions, have been omitted..."
Even if he should fail, he would not go to heaven, for he is indeed fallen.
"Therefore, one should always perform the daily rites with bulbs, fruits, roots, honey, or the essence of ghee, and one must not omit the daily rites.
Now, it may be argued that the Soma sacrifice should only be performed when there is a complete abundance of all required materials. To this, Manu says:
"He who possesses wealth sufficient for three years' maintenance of his dependents, or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma. (MDh 11.7). Yājñavalkya also says:

"A twice-born man who possesses more than three years' worth of grain may indeed drink the Soma juice" (YDh 1.124). Thus, when there is a supply of food sufficient for three years, only the Darśa and other sacrifices that precede the Soma sacrifice should be performed. On this point also, the same author says:
"One whose food lasts for one year should perform the rites preceding those of the Soma sacrifice" (YDh 1.124).
A sacrifice by one of small means is forbidden by Manu.
One who is faithful and has conquered his senses should perform other meritorious deeds,
but he should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices with insufficient sacrificial fees.

"A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses, heaven, longevity, fame, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice. (Manu Smṛti 11.39–40).
Thus it is stated. Also, in the Matsya Purāṇa:
“A sacrifice devoid of food burns the kingdom; likewise, one devoid of mantras burns the officiating priests;
one devoid of sacrificial fees burns the self. There is no enemy equal to a sacrifice [thus performed]. (MDh 11.41).
If it is argued that this being so, these statements would contradict such injunctions as “with bulbs and roots,” and so forth—then [the answer follows].

Not so; for these statements concern optional sacrifices (*kāmyayāga*). It was deliberated upon in the sixth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā that "an optional rite must be performed only when there is the capacity for its complete performance. To illustrate: regarding the injunction, "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," a doubt arises as to whether one has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) even by performing it according to one's capacity, or only by including all the constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*). Since it was determined in the preceding section that optional rites may be performed according to capacity—just as in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) rites—it might be argued that the same applies here. To this we reply: In the case of obligatory rites, because they must not be abandoned even by one who lacks full capacity, performance according to capacity is permitted; for obligatory rites are not to be abandoned, as their engagement is necessitated by causes such as being alive. If they did not apply to the occasional (*naimittika*) rites, their very status as a cause would be lost. However, desire (*kāmanā*) is not a cause in the sense that it would necessarily impel one toward the sacrifice. Therefore, an optional rite is not something that must be undertaken regardless of capacity. This being the case, since an optional rite is to be performed solely for the sake of achieving a result, and a result cannot be produced unless the principal act is assisted by all its constituent parts, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: an optional rite is to be performed only when there is the capacity to perform all its constituent parts.

Thus ends the section on performing sacrifices (yajana). In this manner, the performance of sacrifice has been described. Regarding the officiating at sacrifices (yājana), however, the following injunction is heard in scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa, while acquiring wealth, may accept gifts, officiate at sacrifices, or teach. This is not a mandatory injunction (nityavidhi), because there is an absence of the characteristics of a mandatory rite, such as the occurrence of sin (pratyavāya) from its non-performance. Rather, it is an optional injunction (kāmyavidhi), since the qualification for it belongs to one who desires the acquisition of wealth. Even in that case, it is not an original injunction (apūrvavidhi), because officiating at sacrifices is already established as a means of livelihood. And its status as a cause for livelihood is demonstrated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
"Sacrificing for others and teaching are pure, as is the acceptance of gifts from the pure;
this is correctly declared to be his various means of livelihood" (MārPu 28.4).

Nor is this an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), because there is no possibility of its being already established as a constant requirement. Therefore, since it is only optionally established, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). And this restriction is solely for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), not for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), because the injunction regarding the acquisition of wealth was discussed in the *Lipsāsūtra* as being for the sake of the person.
For instance—the doubt arises as to whether the acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is for the sake of the sacrifice; for only in that case is the restrictive rule (*niyama*) purposeful. There is a restriction such that for a Brāhmaṇa [wealth is acquired] through officiating at sacrifices and so forth, for a Kṣatriya through conquest and so forth, and for a Vaiśya through agriculture and so forth. That restriction would be meaningless under the view that it is for the sake of the person, because wealth acquired by other means can also accomplish human purposes such as the warding off of hunger. However, the sacrifice cannot be accomplished otherwise. Therefore, in that context, the restriction is purposeful.

This being the position, we reply: for it is the substance, once acquired, that gratifies the person; therefore, its status as serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) is directly perceived. Its status as serving the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*), however, must be inferred because otherwise the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would be inexplicable. And what is directly perceived is stronger than what is merely to be inferred. Furthermore, since it serves the purpose of the person, the sacrifice also—just like eating and so forth—attains the status of being for the sake of that [person], insofar as it is an activity of the person, even by implication. Let there be a restriction even in the injunction for acquiring wealth which serves the person’s purpose; it will produce some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). For the proponent of its being for the sake of the sacrifice, the sacrifice itself would not be accomplished due to the loss of livelihood. Therefore, it is established that sacrificing and the like serve the purpose of the person.
If it is argued that there is no one else who can perform the sacrifice except for the officiating priests (ṛtvij), then:

Not so; for in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, after describing the selection of sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there is a separate mention of the selection of the seventeenth, the sacrificer (*yājitṛ*): “The Kauṣītakins record the Sadasya as the seventeenth; he is the supervisor of the rituals. For this very reason, in the Taittirīyaka Brāhmaṇa, the role of Devabhāga as the officiant for the Sṛñjaya Brahmins is heard in the question of the great sage named Sātyahavya, born of the Vasiṣṭha lineage: “Sātyahavya, the descendant of Vasiṣṭha, asked Devabhāga: ‘Sacrifice for the Sṛñjayas, who perform many sacrifices’” (TB 6.6.2). Likewise, in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, the role of Śvetaketu as the officiant for one named Citra is recorded: “Citrodbhava Gārgyāyaṇi, being about to sacrifice, chose Āruṇi. He sent his son Śvetaketu, saying, ‘Let him officiate. Therefore, the Sadasya is distinct from the officiating priests, or perhaps the officiating priests themselves are the ones who officiate. In any case, officiating (*yājana*) exists as a means of livelihood for Brahmins.

In the Taittirīyaka, the state of wearing the sacred thread (*upavītitva*) by means of either a black antelope skin or a garment, in the form of a specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*), is prescribed: “Therefore, one should study, officiate at sacrifices, or sacrifice while wearing the sacrificial thread; for the successful performance of the sacrifice, having draped over the right shoulder either a skin or a garment” (TaitĀ 2.1). Furthermore, the knowledge of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other such details regarding mantras is recorded in the *Chandoga-brāhmaṇa* as an auxiliary element of officiating at sacrifices: “Whoever, indeed, officiates at a sacrifice or teaches with a mantra whose seer, meter, deity, and explanatory passage (*brāhmaṇa*) are unknown, he strikes against a wooden post, falls into a pit, or dies, and becomes worse off. His meters become exhausted (*yātayāman*). But he who knows [these] for every mantra attains everything and becomes superior. His meters do not become exhausted. Therefore, one should know these for every mantra” (ChBrā 3.7.5).

[Objection: But surely, since officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) is censured in some places and accepting gifts (*pratigraha*) in others, for one who performs those acts, the recitation of the *svādhyāya* and the *gāyatrī* is prescribed: "He who officiates at a sacrifice or accepts a gift is as if emptied out; he is indeed emptied out. Having officiated at a sacrifice or accepted a gift, he should recite the Veda, his own *svādhyāya*, three times without eating. Or he should extend the *sāvitrī gāyatrī* for three nights" (TĀ 2.15). Likewise elsewhere: "He who officiates at a sacrifice milks the *chandas* [metres]. Whatever sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) he may officiate at, having gone to the forest and sat in a pure place, he should remain reciting that very *svādhyāya*. For him, fasting is the initiation (*dīkṣā*); standing [in silence] is the *upasad* rites; sitting is the *sutyā*; speech is the *juhū* ladle; mind is the *upabhṛt* ladle; fortitude is the *sruva* spoon; breath is the oblation (*havis*); the *sāman* is the *adhvaryu* priest. This sacrifice of his has breath as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it has an infinite fee, and it is more perfect" (TĀ 2.16). If this is argued: [Response: ... (The response follows in the next section).

This is not a fault, because that [prohibition] refers to officiating at sacrifices for those who are ineligible (*ayājya*). Even officiating for those ineligible may be permissible when one has fallen into a life-threatening situation for the sake of preserving one's life. Thus says the *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa*: “O King, it is indeed for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that one officiates for those for whom one should not officiate, or accepts what should not be accepted” (*Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad* 4.1.3). Regarding this, the *Chāndogas* prescribe an expiation: “In that case, having abandoned the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for officiating for the ineligible, he should eat only at every fourth mealtime for a month and chant those mantras” (*Chāndogyabrāhmaṇa* 5.1.3). Likewise, Sumantu also records: “One who officiates for a *śūdra* becomes pure by renouncing all property. Those who sacrifice for a *śūdra*, as well as the accursed, the outcaste, the son of a remarried woman, the killer of an embryo, the unchaste woman, the impure, the blacksmith, the oil-presser, the wheelwright, the standard-bearer, the goldsmith, the armor-maker, the dyer, the carpenter, the group-leader, the courtesan, the butcher, the hunter, the *niṣāda*, the washerman, the basket-maker, and the leather-worker—their food is not to be eaten, gifts from them are not to be accepted, and they are not to be officiated for. Similarly, Vasiṣṭha states: “It is known that one becomes pure by abandoning the sacrificial fee. Likewise, Baudhāyana also says: “Having accepted many things that should not be accepted, or having officiated for those for whom one should not officiate, one should not eat. Having eaten their food, one should mutter the *taratsamandīya* hymn” (*Vasiṣṭhadharmaśāstra* 2.2, 5, 8). The definition of one who officiates for the ineligible is shown by Devala: [The text here provides the definition of the *ayājya-yājaka*. Thus, there is no contradiction. "He who, for the sake of wealth, performs sacrifices for Śūdras or even for outcasts,
or who, having been so sacrificed for, acts as a priest for those two— such a Brāhmaṇa is one who sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice.
Thus ends the section on officiating at sacrifices.

Thus, officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) has been described. Now, giving (*dāna*) and receiving (*pratigraha*) are being described. Regarding that, there is a Vedic revelation concerning giving: "All beings praise 'giving. There is nothing more difficult to practice than giving; therefore, they delight in giving" (MNU 21.2). Likewise, there is another passage: "Giving is the protection of sacrifices; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is its essence. In this world, all beings depend upon the giver. By giving, they drive away enemies; by giving, those who hate become friends. Everything is established in giving; therefore, they say that giving is supreme" (MNU 22.1). This is also stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*.
Nothing superior to generosity is seen anywhere in the three worlds;
by generosity heaven is attained, and by generosity alone is prosperity obtained.
Through generosity one conquers enemies; through generosity disease is destroyed.
Through generosity knowledge is obtained; through generosity one gains the company of young women.
"It is remembered as the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Thus, through both Śruti and Smṛti, the injunction regarding the giving of gifts has been established with praise. Yājñavalkya, however, explicitly prescribed the act of giving:
"One should give daily to a worthy recipient (pātra), especially on specific occasions (nimitteṣu)."
Even when requested, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith.
"Goats, land, sesame, gold, and so forth should be given to a worthy recipient who has been honored;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise man desiring his own welfare. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.203, 201).
Of these two [verses], one is an injunction regarding the essential nature (*svarūpavidhi*), while the other is an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). Manu also says:

"One should practice the duty of giving, known as the obligatory and occasional rites, with a spirit of complete contentment, having encountered a worthy recipient according to one's capacity" (MDh 4.227).
And in the *Vahni Purāṇa*, the practice of giving is enjoined, preceded by the statement that wealth is useless if not given away.
The wealth of that embodied being which is not for giving, nor for enjoyment,
nor for fame, nor for dharma, is useless.
Therefore, having acquired wealth—whether by fate or through human effort—
"One should give properly to the twice-born, but one should not cause [them] to perform recitations. Thus it is said.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, it states the fault regarding the absence of giving:
"He who does not give to a preeminent twice-born who is in distress and seeking wealth..."
"Even when possessing capability, one of evil intellect is reborn in hell. Thus it is said; and also in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"Those of good conduct, of noble birth, handsome, and pleasant of speech..."
Though they are learned, knowers of the Dharma, and seeking alms at the houses of others.
"O Sage, all living beings are seen to be suffering at all times; those who do not give gifts are born dependent upon the fortune of others. Thus [it is said]; Vyāsa also says:
Those two syllables, "not," "not," which were practiced in the past,
have now appeared in reverse as "give," "give."
[179] Thus it is said. Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The suppliant who says 'Give me' seems to awaken the person [to their duty];
for this painful state of begging is indeed the fruit of not having given in the past."
With one standing below and the other standing above,
the distinction between the giver and the beggar was indicated by their very hands.
"But that evil-minded person who, out of delusion, prevents what is being given to cows, Brahmins, fire, or deities, shall go to the womb of an animal. Thus says Śātātapa as well.
"He who says 'do not give' regarding a cow, fire, or Brahmins,
having passed through a hundred births as an animal, is born among the Cāṇḍālas.
Thus Devala shows the essential nature of giving (*dāna*) and its procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
The faithful bestowal of objects upon a worthy recipient when [the latter] has appeared is designated as "giving" (dāna); its explanation will now be stated.
Giving is said to have two causes, six bases, six limbs, and to be endowed with six ripenings; it is of four types, three kinds, and has three ways of destruction.
Neither the smallness nor the greatness of a gift brings about its exaltation;
rather, it is faith and devotion that truly cause gifts to increase and lead to the highest good.
[180] Virtue, wealth, and pleasure; as well as modesty, joy, and fear—these six are declared to be the foundations of gifts.
That which is given constantly to worthy recipients without regard for any personal motive,
solely with the intention of renunciation, is called the gift of Dharma.
That which is given incidentally, having disregarded the primary purpose, they call *arthadāna*; it has its fruit in this world as its cause.
That which is given out of attachment to women, drinking, hunting,
and gambling, or out of passion for unworthy objects, is called "desire-giving" (kāmadāna).
When wealth is requested from those who are one's equals in an assembly out of a sense of shame,
and that gift is subsequently bestowed, it is known as the "gift of shame."
Whatever one bestows out of joy upon seeing or hearing pleasant things,
those who contemplate Dharma call that gift "the gift of joy."
That which is given out of fear for the sake of countering abuse, loss,
or injury from those who have done harm is called "the gift of fear."
The giver, the recipient, faith, the object to be given,
the place, and the time— these six are known as the constituent factors of gifts when conjoined with the Dharma.
Free from disease, righteous in nature, desirous of giving, free from vice, pure, and one whose livelihood and actions are beyond reproach— a giver who possesses these six qualities is praised.
"One who is pure in three ways, of frugal livelihood, compassionate, with all faculties intact, and free from the defects of birth—such a Brāhmaṇa is called a worthy recipient (*pātra*).
Regarding the term "pure in three ways" (*triśukla*), it means being pure by virtue of having been instructed by three: mother, father, and teacher.
Purity, cleanliness, great joy at the sight of those who seek [one's help],
as well as hospitality, freedom from envy, and faith in giving— these are declared to be [the qualities of a donor].
Wealth acquired by one's own effort, without harming others or causing distress—
whether it be small or vast— is said to be what ought to be given.
Whatever object is difficult to obtain in a particular place, or whatever time it may be,
those two— place and time— are the most excellent for giving, and not otherwise.
Through the excellence of circumstances, place, time, and the qualities of both the recipient and the donor,
even that which is inferior may become superior, or that which is superior may become otherwise.
[The gift] to an atheist, a thief, a violent person, a paramour, and one who has fallen from his caste yields bad fruit, no fruit, or is inferior, equal, vast, or inexhaustible [respectively].
Six are taught as pairs of karmic results; these six arise from maturation.
A wicked fruit shall be bestowed by those who practice slander and those who kill an embryo.
Even a great gift is fruitless when devoid of faith;
a gift that causes harm to others, though abundant, shall come to naught.
As it has been said: "Even if a gift is given with a defiled mind, that gift will have a result equal [to its cause] due to the fault of the intention."
A gift given with all six constituent factors is of vast fruit;
a gift given out of compassion attains imperishability.
The Vedic path of giving is described by the wise as being fourfold, in this order: obligatory, constant, optional, and occasional.
Water-stations, groves, ponds, and the like, which yield all desired fruits, are certain;
they say that such [merit] is "daily" when it is given day after day.
Whatever is desired for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, women, or children—
that gift known as "desire" is designated as "kāmya" (motivated by desire).

It is traditionally taught that the occasional rite (naimittika) is of three kinds— dependent on time, dependent on action, and dependent on purpose— and it is said to be performed either with or without an oblation.
Among those, four are superior, four are middling according to their method, and the remaining ones are inferior; the wise know this to be the threefold classification.
The gifts of food, knowledge, honey, women, cows, land, gold, horses,
and elephants are the supreme gifts, because they consist of the most excellent substances.
One should know that knowledge, clothing, dwellings,
articles of enjoyment, and medicinal herbs are the most excellent gifts, because they are the giving of supreme substances.
Shoes, female servants, vehicles, umbrellas, vessels, and seats;
lamps, wood, fruits, and so forth—these last are [considered] multi-year-old.
Because the varieties of objects are so numerous, no specific enumeration is desired for the remaining gifts;
therefore, they know all other gifts to be inferior.
What is sacrificed, given, or studied perishes through boasting;
or, by praising oneself or grieving for the past, one’s splendor is broken and one comes to ruin.
"Therefore, one should not vainly proclaim the merit performed by oneself. Thus it is said.

Four types of giving—namely, the constant (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the desire-based (*kāmya*), and the pure (*vimala*)—are shown in the *Purāṇasāra*. The Blessed One has spoken of the distinctions such as the *sāttvika* and others:
"That gift which is given with the thought 'it ought to be given' to one who does not return a favor..."
That gift given at the right place, at the right time, and to a worthy recipient is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
But that which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with a view toward a fruit,
and which is given with a sense of distress— that is declared to be "royal" (rājasa).
"That gift which is given at an improper place and time, to unworthy recipients, without respect and with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness" (BhG 17.20–22).
Regarding that, the specific results are shown in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
A human being always experiences the fruit of tamasic actions in the state of an animal,
or else in old age due to the condition of mixed castes.
Whether in childhood or as a slave, there is no need for deliberation on this point;
otherwise, in human existence, the fruit would belong to those characterized by passion (rājasa).
"One enjoys the fruit of those characterized by *sattva* while in a divine state; there is no doubt in this matter.
Regarding that, Yājñavalkya states what constitutes a worthy recipient for a gift:
"Worthiness as a recipient does not arise through learning alone, nor even through austerity alone."
"Where both of these find their livelihood, that indeed is declared to be a worthy recipient. Thus [it is said].
Yama also says:
"One who is endowed with learning, virtuous in conduct, tranquil, patient, self-controlled, truthful, and grateful..."
One who is devoted to sacred study, possessed of fortitude, a refuge for cows, a giver, and a performer of sacrifices—such a Brahmin they call a worthy recipient.

[185] Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "One vessel is distinguished by its knowledge of the Veda, another vessel is composed of austerity; but among all vessels, that is the most excellent vessel in whose stomach the food of a Śūdra has never entered. (VaDh 6.26)
Bṛhaspati said:
"Whichever vessel shall come, that vessel will cause one to cross over.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
"Because it protects one from falling, it is therefore proclaimed a *pātra* (vessel).
Thus, a specific type of vessel is described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"First, one should give the most excellent gift to the Guru in due order."
Then one should give to other Brahmins as well, according to their worthiness as recipients.
In the absence of the guru, [one should approach] his son, his wife, or likewise his daughter;
or his grandson, great-grandson, daughter’s son, or another born of that same lineage.
"If one fails to give to such a person, that gift instead leads to a lower rebirth.
Yama also says: "A gift given to a non-Brahmin yields equal merit; a gift given to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin yields double."
"One who has studied [the Veda] receives a hundred thousand-fold merit, and one who has mastered the Veda receives infinite merit.
Here, "one who has studied" (prādhīta) means one who has commenced the study. Saṃvarta says:
"The origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going..."
"He who knows both knowledge and ignorance shall be one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
And: "A gift given to a Śūdra is said to be equal [in merit]; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as twice that;
to a Kṣatriya, they say it is threefold; and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as sixfold."

The demonstration that Śūdras and others may serve as recipients [of gifts] pertains to the giving of food and similar items, based on the statement of Gautama: "Cooked food [may be given] to others. Vyāsa says:
"That which is given to one's mother and father, to brothers, sisters, and daughters, and that which is given to one's wife and sons—that is irreproachable and leads to heaven."
"A gift given to a father is said to be a hundredfold; to a mother, a thousandfold;
a gift to a daughter is infinite; and what is given to a uterine sister is inexhaustible. Thus [it is stated] in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Giving is praised not only for Brahmins, but in all cases,
even for sisters, nephews, maternal uncles, fathers, and sisters.
"And a gift given to poor kinsmen shall yield ten millionfold merit. Thus says Śātātapa as well:
"He who bypasses a nearby twice-born man who is studying..."
"In both eating and giving, it consumes [the merit] of the family unto the seventh generation.
Thus it is said; and also in the Mahābhārata:
"Those Brahmins whose property and wives have been seized during a regional upheaval..."
"They approach for the sake of wealth; what is given to them yields great fruit.
Regarding the unworthy recipient, Manu says:
"One should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat."
One who knows the Dharma should not give to one who follows the "heron-vow" (hypocritical conduct), nor to a sinner, nor to one who does not know the Vedas.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, when given to these three types of persons,
results in misfortune for the giver and likewise for the recipient in the next world.
He who pursues the practice of vows while setting aside the primary cause,
concealing his evil deeds under the guise of a vow— that is known as the "cat-vow" (baiḍāla-vrata).

"One who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends, treacherous, falsely humble, and one who practices the 'heron-vow'—such is the twice-born man. Thus [it is said]. Śātātapa also says:
"What is given to a temple-priest (*devalaka*) is lost; what is given to a usurer is without foundation;
and what is given to a merchant brings no fruit either in this world or after death.
Furthermore, the *devalaka* is described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:

"A Brahmin who, desiring wealth, is devoted to the worship of [other] gods for three years is indeed called a *devalaka*; he is censured in rites for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). Thus says Vṛddha-Manu.
Even if a Brahmin is a worthy recipient, if he accepts a gift and then employs it for improper purposes, nothing at all should be given to him.
"One who, having accepted [gifts] from all sides, makes a hoard and does not employ it for the sake of dharma— one should not honor such a thief. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The fruitless giving away of another's property and so forth is proclaimed to be entirely in vain,
as is that which is done for one who has fallen from his high station, or with wealth obtained through improper means.
A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin, to one who has fallen from his status, to a thief,
to one who causes displeasure to the guru, to an ungrateful person, or to a village priest is in vain.
[189] And that which is given to a seller of the Vedas, to one who has a paramour in his house,
to those conquered by women, and likewise to a snake-catcher;
"What is given to a Brahmin who is a mere nominal priest, what is given to the husband of a Vṛṣalī woman,
and what is given to attendants— these sixteen kinds of gifts are in vain. Thus it is stated in the Mahābhārata.
"Those who are lame, blind, deaf, mute, or afflicted by disease— these, O Great King, must be supported, but a gift should not be given to them.
Thus Manu prohibits both neglecting a worthy recipient and giving to one who is unworthy.

"What one gives to the undeserving, and what one does not give to the deserving— through such giving, due to ignorance of who is worthy and who is unworthy, one falls away from both [worldly] gifts and the Dharma" (MDh 3.99). In the *Bhaviṣyottara*, the nature of that which is to be given is described.
"Whatever is desired, whatever is excellent, and whatever may be rightfully obtained—that very thing should be given to one possessed of virtue; this is the definition of giving. (MDh 3.119).
Since this would imply that everything without exception must be given, Yājñavalkya states a qualification:

One may give away property without detriment to one's own family, except for one's wife and sons; however, when there is a lineage, one must not give away one's entire estate, nor that which has already been promised to another.
[190] Thus (YDh 2.175). Bṛhaspati also says: "That which remains after providing for the family's food and clothing should be given. In the Śivadharma:

"Therefore, one should set aside one-third of one's wealth for the sake of living, and two parts for the sake of dharma, since life is transient. It has been stated that "one should give without detriment to one's family"; Vyāsa states an exception to this rule:
"Even by causing distress to one's family, food must be given to a high-souled Brāhmaṇa and to a mendicant by one who desires his own prosperity. Thus [it is said].
Manu states that the excellence of the fruit depends upon the excellence of the gift:
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desirable offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of a horse attains the realm of the Moon and the realm of the Aśvins;
the giver of an ox enjoys cherished prosperity; and the giver of a cow reaches the world of the Sun.
The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda obtains the eternal Brahman.
"Of all gifts, the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*) is preeminent. (MDh 4.229–33).
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, specific items to be given according to the distinction of the recipient is shown:
"Likewise, one should give specific objects according to the distinction of the recipient."
One should give gifts of food to those who are distressed, and gifts of cows to a householder.
Likewise, for those who have lost their footing, the gift of land is preeminent;
gold for officiating priests, and knowledge for those of perpetual celibacy.
"And for those who give their daughters to childless men, there is the highest goal. Thus it is said. Also in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O King of Men, a man gives a vehicle to one who is weary, drink to one who is thirsty, and food to one afflicted by hunger."
"They shall give [him] a celestial chariot, and being praised by divine maidens, they lead him to the third heaven. Thus says Aṅgiras:
"Toward the gods, toward teachers, and likewise toward one's mother and father..."
"Merit should be bestowed with effort; demerit is never enjoined anywhere.
Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Whatever substance is useful to someone, that should be given to that very person."
Śātātapa states the occasions for giving:
