"At the beginning of the solstices, one should always give whatever desirable substance is found in the house,
as well as at the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti* periods and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun."
"Whatever *havya* and *kavya* offerings are given by donors at the time of the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*),
the Sun-god bestows those [fruits] eternally, birth after birth.
Thus says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha, who also indicates the solstices (*ayana*) and other such occasions.
The two transits of Pisces and Cancer are the northern and southern solstices;
Libra and Aries are the two equinoxes, and the others follow between them.
When the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, or Leo, this is called Viṣṇupada; its fruit is greater than that of the equinoxes.
"The Sun's transit through Virgo, Gemini, Pisces,
and Sagittarius is declared to be the six *ṣaḍaśītimukhas*, which possess the qualities of the sixty-eightfold fruits. Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
"The full moon days of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha yield great fruit.
On all full moon days, especially when conjoined with the lunar mansions of their respective months, the merit of gifts given here becomes tenfold. Thus it is said.

Manu says: "A gift given on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas becomes a thousandfold; likewise, rites such as the Śrāddha and others performed on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Manvantaras [yield a thousandfold merit]."
Yājñavalkya states:
"A gift of one hundred [cows] on the waning of the moon, but a thousand on the waning of the day;
at the equinox, a hundred thousand, and at the vyatīpāta conjunction, it is infinite."
Bhāradvāja says:
"That which is given during Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti becomes inexhaustible. Thus says Viṣṇu.
The end of a day, a gap in the day, the birth of a son and so forth,
as well as the conjunction of the planets beginning with the Sun with the lunar mansions.
"This time should be recognized as a period of merit after being examined by astrologers;
one should perform acts such as giving there for the increase of one's own merit.
Thus the definition of the day of loss (*dinakṣaya*) was stated by Vasiṣṭha.

When three lunar days (tithis) occur within a single solar day (sāvana), that is declared to be a "day of loss" (dinakṣaya), for which the merit is said to be equal to that of a hundred thousand [vows].
The definition of a "day-break" (dinacchidra) is stated in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*):

"Bhārgava has declared that the halves of lunar days, the conjunctions of lunar days, the [conjunctions] of asterisms, and the breakages of zodiac signs and parvans— these two similar types are known as 'day-breaks'."
The time for cutting [the hair] and other rites is said to be two ghaṭīs of the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (nakṣatra);
it is endowed with the conjunction of the asterism and so forth, and joined with the fruits of that cutting.

"Two nāḍikās joined with sixteen palas at the conjunction [of the sun and moon] is declared to be the time for the *cheda* and other rites; it bestows infinite fruit when used for giving. Thus they spoke. Śaṅkha and Likhita state the prohibited times for giving:
"One should avoid food, sexual intercourse, sleep, ritual action, teaching, as well as giving and receiving gifts during the twilight periods. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
A gift should never be given by anyone at night, because Rākṣasas carry it off; therefore, it brings fear to the donor.
"Especially at midnight, an auspicious rite does not lead to well-being;
therefore, a wise person should avoid the 'great night' (mahāniśā) for acts such as giving.
Regarding this, Devala states an exception:

"Gift-giving on the occasion of seeing Rāhu, at the solstices (saṃkrānti), during processions, and at births is to be known as occasional (naimittika); it is desired even at night. Here, the word *saṃkrānti* refers specifically to the [transits] of Capricorn and Cancer, because another Smṛti text, after introducing the prohibition of giving at night during the solstices, makes an exception by stating, "except for Capricorn and Cancer. In the Matsya Purāṇa, specific locations are indicated as particularly auspicious for giving.
"Having given at holy fords such as Prayāga, in sacred shrines, and in meritorious rivers and forests, one obtains inexhaustible [merit]. Thus also by Vyāsa:
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, at Avimukta, and at Puṣkara;
at Makara, at Aṭṭahāsa, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
What is given at Kurukṣetra, at the sacred site of Gayā, and likewise at Amarakaṇṭaka—
at such holy places as these, a gift becomes inexhaustible.
Thus ends the section on giving (*dāna*).

In this way, the section on giving, together with its prescribed procedures, has been explained. Now, the topic of receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) is being examined. Regarding this, the scriptural injunction was previously cited: "A Brāhmaṇa, while acquiring wealth, should accept gifts. In that regard, the discussion concerning officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) which was previously introduced should also be applied to the acceptance of gifts as far as possible.
But is it not the case that Manu has censured the acceptance of gifts?
"Receiving gifts is the lowest [means of livelihood], and it is censured for a Brāhmaṇa.
(MDh 10.109) It is not so; for this censure refers specifically to the acceptance of improper gifts, as is made clear by the subsequent statement:
"But the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra or one of the lowest birth. (MDh 10.110)

The meaning is that the acceptance of gifts from a base person is censurable; however, the acceptance of gifts from a virtuous person is permitted by that very [text]: "No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or from the acceptance of gifts—even if they are censurable—for they are like blazing fires" (MDh 10.103).
[196] Thus. The word *agarhitāt* is to be analyzed as *a-garhitāt*. Even compared to the acceptance of what is not censurable, non-acceptance is better. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Even one capable of accepting gifts, he who does not accept them, does not attain those abundant worlds that belong to those whose nature is to give" (YDh 1.213).
But surely, Yama praises the acceptance of gifts:
"Among receiving gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices, they say that receiving gifts is the most excellent;
one is purified from [the sin of] receiving gifts by means of recitations and burnt offerings, but the Vedas do not purify the sin of officiating at sacrifices."
Manu, however, states the opposite:
"The sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
but that caused by accepting gifts is removed by renunciation and austerity alone" (MDh 10.111).
This is not a fault, because the established rule—that accepting gifts from the twice-born is commendable, whereas accepting gifts from a Śūdra is censurable—is easy to maintain.
[Objection: But even in the case of accepting a gift from a worthy person, some degree of sin is understood, since it is said, "Acceptance of a gift is purified by recitations and burnt offerings.

[Reply: Certainly; there is indeed sin in accepting a gift for one who lacks the capacity such as mastery of the Vedas. It is with this very point in mind that the sin regarding the acceptance of gifts is ruled out for one who has mastered the Vedas in the Skanda Purāṇa.

[197] “If a Brahmin learned in the six limbs of the Veda should accept a gift, he would not be stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. This same principle should be applied to officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*). In the cases of officiating for those unfit to sacrifice, teaching for wages, or accepting gifts from the wicked, there is an abundance of sin (*enaḥ*). However, for one who acts while possessing only a slight deficiency in qualification, the transgression is minimal. The distinction is that for a primary qualified person engaging in the prescribed officiating at sacrifices and so forth, there is no sin whatsoever. Vyāsa distinguishes between the acceptance of good and bad gifts: * *satpratigraha* (good gift): A gift given by one who is pure in conduct, who follows the sacred law, and who possesses faith. * *asatpratigraha* (bad gift): A gift from one who is addicted to vice, who disregards the sacred law, or who is of evil character. The acceptance of a bad gift is like swallowing poison; it destroys the merit of many good deeds. Therefore, one should carefully examine the source of a gift before accepting it. Just as a man avoids a snake, so should he avoid an unworthy donor. It is said that a gift from a king is like fire, and a gift from a Vaiśya is like a thorn; but a gift from a Śūdra is like a heavy stone, and a gift from a fallen person is like excrement. Thus, one should always be discerning regarding the giver. The *Manusmṛti* further states: “Accepting a gift from a Śūdra is like eating the flesh of one’s own son; it burns the recipient even after death. One should not accept a gift from a king, nor from a Vaiśya, nor from a Śūdra; for these lead to ruin. But if one must accept, one should do so from a virtuous person, never from an unrighteous one. In summary, while the Vedic injunctions permit the acceptance of gifts for the maintenance of the priestly class, the scriptures strictly forbid accepting gifts from those of impure conduct or low status to prevent spiritual corruption. The wise should therefore exercise great caution in the matter of receiving gifts.

"A supreme among the twice-born should seek wealth from praiseworthy twice-born men, or even from those who are merely twice-born by birth, but never from a Śūdra. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Caturviṃśatimata*, the acceptance of gifts even from an unworthy person is permitted when no virtuous person is available.

"If one should accept [gifts] while sinking [in virtue], then [one should seek them] from Brāhmaṇas, then from the king, and then from Vaiśyas and Śūdras— such is the word of Śaṅkha. Regarding the specific rules for accepting gifts from a Śūdra, Aṅgiras says:
"But that grain which has been heaped together in a threshing floor or in a field may be taken even from a Śūdra; such is the statement of Aṅgiras.
Regarding this very point, Vyāsa states another distinction:
"But for the sake of one's family, one may accept what is unasked from a virtuous Śūdra;
however, for the sake of a sacrifice or for oneself, one should never ask at all. Thus says Manu as well.
"A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
even a sacrificer, having begged [thus], is born as a Caṇḍāla after death" (MDh 11.24). A particular state of being unfit to receive gifts from the unrighteous is shown in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"When a terrible famine has arrived and the family is perishing from hunger, one may, without indolence, accept gifts from even an unworthy person. Thus [says Manu]; Yājñavalkya also says:
"Even when fallen into distress, accepting and eating whatever comes his way, a Brahmin is not defiled by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun. Thus [says Yājñavalkya 3.41]. Manu also says:
"Manu has declared that aged parents, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be supported even by committing a hundred improper acts. One who,
having fallen into a life-threatening crisis, eats food from any source whatsoever,"
"He is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not smeared by mud" (MDh 10.104).
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, the quantity of the object to be accepted is shown:
"It should be such that the performer of the five sacrifices can maintain himself."
For he should take only as much as is necessary for his family and himself.
[199] Thus says Vyāsa as well:

"One should not have a desire for receiving gifts, but one may perform them for the sake of sacrifice. A Brāhmaṇa who accepts more than what is necessary for his maintenance goes to a downward state."
"One should seek the restriction of one's livelihood and not pursue the expansion of wealth;
for one who is intent upon the acquisition of wealth falls away from his very Brahminhood.
Thus Yājñavalkya censures the acceptance of gifts from a king when there is no distress.
One should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures;
for among those who receive gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, the prostitute, and the sovereign are the most censurable.
"These [types of acceptance] are increasingly ten times more wicked than each preceding one. Thus says Saṃvarta:
"Accepting gifts from a king is terrible; it has the taste of honey but is like poison."
"It is better to eat the flesh of one's own son than to accept the patronage of a king. Thus [it is said] in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In the waterless land of Maru, you became a Brahma-rākṣasa."
One who has been nourished by accepting gifts from a king does not undergo rebirth.
He who, deluded by greed for wealth and lusting after the bait of sensual objects, abandons his status as a Brahmin and accepts gifts from a king.
His fall into the terrible Raurava hell is certain;
yet trees burnt by a forest fire sprout again when the rainy season arrives.
"Those burnt by accepting gifts from a king never sprout again at any time. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"A maker of wheels is equal to ten slaughterers; a banner-bearer is equal to ten makers of wheels."
Ten courtesans are equal to one prostitute; ten prostitutes are equal to one king.
"A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is terrible. (MDh 4.75–76).
This censure refers to an unrighteous king, as it is specified in that very same context:
For those kings in whose realm the Brahmins do not worship Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, with sacrifices—
the fruit of this [negligence] has been declared by his son.
Those kings whose kingdom is crowded with heretics and not preeminent in Brahmins are partakers of ten thousand slaughterhouses.

"Those for whom the Supreme Person, the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa), is not the cause [of their merit], are indeed of sinful conduct and partakers of the sin of the slaughterhouse. However, accepting gifts from a king who is free from fault is not censured. For this very reason, in the Chandoga Śākhā, the absence of fault was presented by a king named Aśvapati in order to induce the great sages such as Prācīnaśāla and others to accept gifts from kings.

"In my kingdom there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard; no one who has not maintained the sacred fires, no one who is unlearned, and no libertine—how then could there be a wanton woman? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.5). Even in the words of Yājñavalkya, regarding the censure of accepting gifts from a king, it is understood from the qualification "of a greedy man who acts contrary to the scriptures" that accepting gifts from a king who is not corrupt is not censured. Likewise, Nārada also says:
For kings, the possession of subjects is superior to that of others, with the exception of the Brāhmaṇa.
Both the Brāhmaṇa and the king are observers of firm vows; between these two, there is no difference whatsoever in their protection of the people and the dharma. (41–42)
Just as the collection of pure and impure waters attains equality upon reaching the ocean, so too does the influx of wealth for kings.
And just as gold, when placed in fire, attains purity. (45)
"Thus, all acquisitions of wealth attain purity when [the recipient] is a king. (NSm 17.41–46).
If it is asked, "Why is it not assumed that even the acceptance of gifts from the righteous, like the acceptance of gifts from the wicked, pertains only to times of distress (*āpad*)," the answer is:
no, because in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the acceptance of gifts from the righteous is prescribed even when one is not in a state of distress.
Even when not in distress, a Brahmin who accepts gifts lawfully from a patron or a disciple does not fall away from dharma.
One should always receive [the gift] from a Brāhmaṇa who abides in proper conduct;
when given with faith and purity, one does not fall away from the path of dharma.
[202] Thus it is said. Regarding certain specific objects that have been offered unasked, Bhāradvāja states that there is no fault in accepting them:
"There is no fault in accepting things that come unasked;
the gods know that to be nectar (amṛta), therefore one should never reject it. Thus.
In this regard, Yājñavalkya specifies the particular items intended by Bharadvāja:
"Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water— these are not to be refused."
"Even from one of evil deeds, food brought unasked may be accepted, except from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, and likewise from an enemy. (YDh 1.214–15). Manu also says:
One should not refuse a bed, kusha grass, a house, perfumes, water, flowers, a gem, curd, fish, parched grain, milk, meat, or even vegetables;
likewise, one should not refuse fuel, water, roots, fruits, or food that is offered. (MDh 4.250)
"One may accept from anyone honey or a gift of safety" (MDh 4.247).
He himself stated who is ineligible to receive gifts:
"Gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, and clarified butter..."
"The ignorant man who accepts [a gift] is reduced to ashes like wood. (MDh 4.188). Yājñavalkya also says:
"A gift must not be accepted by one who is devoid of learning and austerity."
"By accepting [such a gift], one leads both the giver and oneself downward. (YDh 1.202)

In the Gāyatrī-vidyā of the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa, it is heard that for the wise man, no gift whatsoever brings about any fault: “Even if one who knows this should indeed receive many gifts, he does not reach even a single foot of the Gāyatrī. If he were to receive these three worlds full, he would obtain only its first foot. Then, if he were to receive as much as there is in the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā), he would obtain its second foot. And if he were to receive as much as there is in the three worlds and the threefold knowledge, he would obtain its third foot. But its fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust—that is this sun which shines. It cannot be reached by anything at all; how then could one receive so much? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.14.5–6).
Thus ends the section on receiving gifts (*pratigraha*).

Having considered the distinction between these acts—beginning with teaching (*adhyāpana*) and ending with receiving gifts—as distinct actions according to the principle of the section on "different words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*, PMS 2.2.1), it is stated that one should be "devoted to the six duties. That principle operates as follows: the examples are "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is there a single productive urge (*bhāvanā*) colored by the meanings of all the verbal roots, or is there a distinct productive urge for each meaning of the verbal root?

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denoting the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is one, and because the various meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), though distinct, function as subordinate elements such that they cannot differentiate the principal [efficient force], there is only a single efficient force. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since the efficient force is not cognized by the verbal suffix alone without being colored by the meaning of the verbal root, and since when the meaning of the suffix is already colored by one root-meaning prescribed at the time of origination (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), other root-meanings cannot enter into it, there is a differentiation of the efficient force for each respective root-meaning.

Thus, through the six—study and the rest—the meaning of the verbal roots is differentiated into a sixfold cultivation (*bhāvanā*); these constitute the six duties (*ṣaṭkarman*). Among them, "delight" (*abhirati*) is practice preceded by faith (*śraddhā*). Even that which is performed by one lacking faith would be fruitless. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever is offered, given, or performed as austerity, O Pārtha, if done without faith, it is called 'non-existent' (*asad*); it is of no account either after death or here. (BhG 17.28)

The word "constantly" (*nityam*) connects with what follows, not with what precedes it, because the three activities beginning with teaching are non-permanent. One should be a daily worshiper of both the deity and the guest (*devatātithī*). The nature of the deity has been investigated and determined in the *Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa* within the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya. Therein, Śākalya is the questioner and Yājñavalkya is the respondent; the subject matter to be inquired about consists of the expansion and contraction of the deities and their essential nature. Regarding this, there is the following scriptural passage (*śruti*).

Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? He answered with this very *nivid* (invocatory formula): "As many as are mentioned in the *nivid* of the Vaiśvadeva [hymn]: 'Three and three hundred, and three and three thousand. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Thirty-three. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Three. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Two. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "One and a half. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "One. "Yes," he said, "but who are those 'three and three hundred, and three and three thousand'? He replied: "These are merely their manifestations (*mahimāna*). There are only thirty-three gods. "Who are those thirty-three? "The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—that makes thirty-one; Indra and Prajāpati make up the thirty-third. "Who are the Vasus? "Agni, Earth, Vāyu, the Intermediate Space, Āditya, Heaven, the Moon, and the Stars—these are the Vasus. For in them all this wealth (*vasu*) is contained; they cause all this to dwell (*vāsayante*), therefore they are the Vasus. "Who are the Rudras? "There are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh. When they depart from this body, they cause one to weep (*rodayanti*); because they cause one to weep, they are the Rudras. "Who are the Ādityas? "The twelve months of the year are these Ādityas. For they take away (*ādadānāyanti*) all this; because they take away all this, they are the Ādityas. "Who is Indra? Who is Prajāpati? "Indra is the thunder, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. "Who is the thunder? "The lightning bolt (*aśani*). "Who is the sacrifice? "The cattle. "Who are the six? "Agni and Earth, Vāyu and the Intermediate Space, Āditya and Heaven—these are the six. For these are all this, and they are six. "Who are the three gods? "These three worlds themselves, for in them all these gods reside. "Who are the two gods? "Food and the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Who is the one and a half? "He who blows here (the wind). Regarding this they say: "Since he blows as if he were only one, how is he 'one and a half'? "Because all this is contained within him, he is 'one and a half' (*adhyardha*). "Who is the one god? "The vital breath (*prāṇa*); they call him Brahman. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.1–9.

The meaning of this Śruti passage is as follows: When asked how many gods there are in their numerical expansion—those deities worthy of worship—Yājñavalkya, being engaged in a debate with those seeking victory, gave an answer by means of a *nivid* in order to confound the understanding of his opponents. According to Vedic convention, the word *nivid* denotes the collection of words expressing numbers found within a specific liturgical recitation (*śastra*) called the Vaiśvadeva. Thus, it is implied that however many gods are mentioned in the *nivid* of the Vaiśvadeva, so many are to be meditated upon; these words are "three and three," and so forth. The expansion of the gods consists of three hundred, three thousand, and six. By the use of the particle *eva* ("only") in the phrase "how many indeed," any suspicion regarding other intervening deities is excluded. The meaning of the question in each instance is: "Of those very gods previously expanded, how many are there in brief? "How many" is a question regarding number; "Which ones are they" is a question regarding their specific nature. Among them, the gods numbered in the hundreds and thousands are not all primary. Rather, through the power of yoga, the thirty-three principal gods—who are the consumers of the oblation (*havis*)—assume voluntary forms at will; therefore, their specific individual forms are not distinct from the Vasus and others well-known in the Purāṇas. Their designation by names is based on etymological derivation (*yaugika*). "Prāṇas" refers to the external senses; "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The terms "Indra" and "Prajāpati" function metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote thunder and sacrifice, respectively; but by secondary metaphor (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), they refer to lightning and cattle. "Food" and "Life-breath" (*prāṇa*) refer to the deities presiding over the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer. The word "Adhyardha" primarily denotes a number, but by etymology it signifies the Wind (*Vāyu*) who is fully developed. The Wind is the Sūtrātman, according to the Śruti: "O Gautama, the Wind indeed is that thread" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.2). At the end, the word "Prāṇa" denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). To clarify this, it is said, "That is Brahman. The word "that" (*tat*) expresses something remote; for a person who has not yet investigated Brahman, Brahman is "remote" because it is accessible solely through the scriptures. In that context, the one god who is the "mouth" is the Supreme Self alone, denoted by the word "Prāṇa. And the Śvetāśvataras declare His true nature quite clearly.
The One God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
He is the overseer of actions, the dwelling place of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities.
(ŚveUp 6.11) [209] Thus it is said. Those skilled in the scriptures describe this very God in many ways through various specific terms. And so says a collection of mantras:
"The wise poets, with their hymns, conceive the one Being as manifold—the Suparṇa. Thus it is said.
And those specific words are clearly heard in another mantra:
"They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
The sages speak of the One Being as many; they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan. Thus it is said.

Now, an objection is raised: words such as Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa denote distinct deities and do not refer to a single deity; otherwise, an *aindra* mantra would have to be employed in a sacrifice dedicated to Varuṇa.

This is not a fault; for even though the deity is one, the systematic application of mantras is established through the distinction of forms (*mūrti*). Just as in the Śaiva Āgamas, although Śiva is one, mantras such as Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Cintāmaṇi, and Mṛtyuñjaya are established for specific forms according to their respective images; or just as in the Vaiṣṇava Āgamas there are mantras such as Gopāla and Vāmana—why should it not be the same with respect to the Lord?

Now, an objection is raised: the substance and the deity constitute the very nature of a sacrifice, and it has been established that a difference in ritual action follows from a difference in form. Just as in the passage, "He pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* is for the Vājins," there is a distinction between the two substances, *āmikṣā* and *vājina*, so too one must admit a distinction between the Viśvedevas and the deities who are the Vājins.

"Certainly; for it is indeed admitted that there is an adventitious (aupādhika) distinction of a single, real Deity during the state of performing ritual acts. For this very reason, in the *Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa*, within the section on the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, having referred to the well-known plurality of deities among those who perform rituals, the text establishes the real unity of the Deity by means of a refutation of that [plurality]: 'As for what they say, "One should sacrifice to that one, one should sacrifice to that other"—this is merely an emanation (*visṛṣṭi*) of this one Deity alone, for he alone is all the gods.'"

Nor should it be suspected that a difference in results cannot be easily achieved from a single deity, for that is possible through differences in the modes of meditation (*upāsti*), according to the Śruti: "In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become. Just as even a single king is the cause of a difference in results depending on the different modes of service, such as the use of the royal umbrella or chowries, so it is here. [211]

Now, it may be objected that the Mīmāṃsaka does not accept the view that "the deity bestows the fruit. For this was investigated in the ninth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]. The doubt is as follows: is the fruit [obtained] from a deity propitiated by the sacrifice, or is the sacrifice's status as a means to the fruit mediated by the *apūrva* (unseen potency)? In this regard, since a perishable sacrifice cannot logically be the means for a fruit that occurs at a later time, some intermediate medium must necessarily be postulated. And the favor of the deity would be that medium, based on both scripture and reasoning. The scriptural authority is: "Indra, being satisfied, satisfies him with offspring and cattle" (*TS* 2.5.4.3). Reasoning is also stated: because it is the most desired object to be attained through an action, the object (*karman*) is the primary factor (*kāraka*). Because it is that which is pervaded by the action, the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is even more primary than that. Since deities such as Indra possess primacy by virtue of being recipients, they deserve worship. Furthermore, because a sacrifice is of the nature of worship, it should be a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the deity, just as a meal is for a guest. Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the deity bestows the fruit, just like a king or similar authority.

To this it is replied: This relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) that has been proposed between the sacrifice and the deity is reversed when following the requirements of the verbal expression (*śabdākāṅkṣā*). To explain: by the verb *yajeta* (“one should sacrifice”), the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is denoted. And that [activity] sequentially requires three parts—characterized as the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—in the form of "what?", "by what?", and "how?". Among these, although the sacrifice is presented within the same word [as the verb], it cannot be the end to be achieved because it is unsuitable for that role. However, heaven (*svarga*), although presented only by the sentence, can be the end to be achieved because it is suitable as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). When that heaven requires an instrument, the sacrifice connects with it as the instrument. And since that instrument is of the nature of something to be accomplished, it takes the established substance and deity—which bring about its own production—as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, the sacrifice is the principal (*aṅgin*) and the deity is its subordinate (*aṅga*). This being the case, the deity is not propitiated by the sacrifice as one propitiates a guest. As for the scriptural text, “He indeed satisfies him,” that does not have its primary purport (*tātparya*) on its literal meaning, because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge. For no embodied deity is perceived through perception to eat the oblation, become satisfied, and bestow a fruit; on the contrary, the absence of such a thing is established by perception or by the non-perception of the perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*). Furthermore, in the Horse Sacrifice (*Aśvamedha*), specific deities such as cows and frogs are heard of in the texts as the consumers of the sacrificial materials—the horse’s limbs, teeth, and so forth—[in passages like] “the cow [consumes] the teeth and other substances, the frog [consumes] the teeth. Yet, it is not possible for them to be the bestowers of the fruit.

In passages such as, "Svāhā to the plants! Svāhā to the trees! Svāhā to the roots! (TS 7.3.19), the status of deities is heard to belong to insentient things—plants, trees, and their parts. In that case, how could there be the consumption of the oblation? How much less could there be satisfaction? And how much less could there be the granting of results? Therefore, since there is an absence of gods possessing a physical form and so forth, the grace of a deity cannot be the means by which a sacrifice yields its fruit. Rather, the means is the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is postulated because the stated efficacy as a means to the result would otherwise be inexplicable. Furthermore, in the mantras, *arthavādas*, *itihāsas*, and *purāṇas*, there are accounts of the accomplishment of desired goals for deities themselves through the practice of austerity, the performance of sacrifices, and the application of Vedic mantras such as the *Brahmāstra*. Thus, it is established that the god is not the bestower of the fruit. However, the followers of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadas*) maintain that the Lord (*īśvara*) is the giver of the fruit. For instance, this is discussed in the third chapter of their own scripture (*śāstra*). There is a doubt: does *dharma* bestow the fruit, or rather, does the Lord?
In this regard, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is that dharma bestows the fruit, according to the reasoning stated by the Mīmāṃsakas.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Does dharma bestow its fruit independently of anything else, or is it presided over by some conscious being? It cannot be the first, because that which is insentient and ignorant of gradations is incapable of bestowing appropriate fruits. In the second case, however, let that very being by whom it is presided over be the giver of the fruit. Nor should it be suspected that this renders dharma useless; for dharma is required in order to avoid the charge of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*). For if dharma did not exist, how could the Lord not be considered partial by leading some to supreme happiness, others to middling, and others to inferior states? Or how could He not be considered cruel by inflicting various forms of suffering? If He brings about those results in accordance with dharma and adharma, then, like teachers, fathers, or kings, He incurs neither partiality nor cruelty. Indeed, partiality and cruelty are not attributed to kings and others who provide discipline to the wicked and protection to the virtuous. As for the objection that "it is illogical for animals such as cows and frogs, or for stationary things such as plants and trees, to bestow fruits," that remains true in their own case. But what obstacle is there to the Lord being the giver of fruits? Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Indra, being satisfied himself, satisfies him with offspring and cattle" (*TS* 2.5.4.3), even there it is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) residing within the deity Indra who is intended as the giver of the fruit, according to the Vedic revelation: "He has entered within, the ruler of people. Therefore, the grace of the Lord alone is the door to the fruit. Nor is there any mutual contradiction between the views of Jaimini and Vyāsa, for that is resolved through a difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣā*). Just as, although Devadatta is the actual agent, the expression "the wood cooks" is used when one intends to emphasize the thorough blazing of the fire, why should the expression "dharma bestows the fruit" not be used when one intends to emphasize the predominance of dharma as the instrumental cause for producing those gradations, even though the Supreme Lord alone is the giver of the fruit? Thus, since there is no contradiction, the Lord of the Universe alone is the giver of fruits and the one God to be worshipped everywhere; enough of this digression.
Thus concludes the section on the definition of the nature of the deity;

the definition of a guest (*atithi*) he himself will state later. We shall explain the manner of worshipping both in the following verse: “One who worships the deity and the guest does not perish” [215]. From this statement, it is understood that in the absence of such worship, one perishes. And so it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: “He who, out of delusion or laziness, fails to perform the worship of the deity...”

"He who eats [without offering] goes to hell and is born among pigs. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.121) "If a best of the twice-born eats without having performed the worship of the gods and the great sacrifices, that deluded soul enters the womb of an animal. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.119)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated, he departs having given that person his own misdeeds and taken away their merit. Thus it is said.
Devala also says:
"The guest who returns from a house having been unhonored and disappointed destroys that family instantly."
[216] Thus it is said. In the case of worship, however, there is not only the absence of evil, but also spiritual advancement (*abhyudaya*). Accordingly, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Those who always worship Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace, being liberated from all sins, they enter into Brahman. Thus it is said.

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, as well as the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and likewise the worship of the gods, quickly destroy sins."
Manu also says:
"It is my view that he who honors a guest who is weary and pure of mind has, by that act, given away a hundred cows along with their bulls" (VaDh 27.7).
Viṣṇu also says: "A householder does not attain such worlds through Vedic study, the Agnihotra, sacrifice, or austerity as he does from honoring a guest" (ViDh 67.44).

Having cooked rice for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva offering, when the oblation has been performed with it, the rice that remains is the "remnant of the offering" (*hutaśeṣa*). One should eat only that; one should not cook rice for the purpose of one's own meal. As the Blessed One said:
"The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins;
but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin. (BhG 3.13)
Regarding the term "hutaśeṣam" (the remnant of what has been offered), the word *huta* is explained in the Mahābhārata:
"The wise call the Vaiśvadeva and other such offerings *huta*.
The remnant of that is *hutaśeṣa*. Furthermore, this term *hutaśeṣa* indicates what remains after being used for the worship of gods, sages, humans, and others. As Manu says:
Having honored the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains.
“He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice. (MDh 3.117–18).
Regarding the phrase “the Brāhmaṇa does not perish,” the definition of the Brāhmaṇa intended therein is shown in the Mahābhārata.
Truthfulness, charity, austerity, purity, kindness, self-restraint, and compassion—
where these are seen, O best of Brahmins, he is remembered as a true Brāhmaṇa.
The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who has conquered his senses, is devoted to dharma, intent on the study of the Vedas, pure, and has brought desire and anger under control.
The gods know him as a true Brahmin who, knowing the Dharma and possessing a noble mind, treats the world as his own self and conducts himself according to righteousness.
The gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa who either teaches or studies, or officiates at sacrifices or performs sacrifices himself, or gives according to his ability.
"Forgiveness, compassion, discernment, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility,

delight in the inner self, and knowledge— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa. Thus, even in the case of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the meaning of the statement culminates in the fact that a Brāhmaṇa characterized by the aforementioned qualities does not perish.

By the two statements, “of all four castes” and “devoted to the six duties,” the common and uncommon duties have been briefly indicated. Although only the triad beginning with teaching (adhyāpana) is unique to the Brāhmaṇa, and not the triad beginning with studying (adhyayana), because that [latter triad] is common to the three other castes; nevertheless, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that devotion to the six duties belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. (38)
Now, in connection with the common study of the scriptures and so forth, he briefly states the common daily observance that has come to mind:
"Sandhyā, bathing, recitation, fire-offering, worship of the deities and guests, hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice—these are the six duties to be performed day after day. (1.39)

Regarding the phrase “the twilight bath” (*saṃdhyā-snāna*), the priority of the bath is to be explained according to the logic of cooking gruel (*yavāgū-pāka-nyāya*). That logic is established in the first section of the fifth chapter. It is heard in scripture: “One offers the *agnihotra* with gruel; one cooks the gruel. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the sequence between the *agnihotra* offering and the cooking of the gruel unrestricted, or is it restricted? Furthermore, if it is restricted, is it restricted by the order of the text (*pāṭha*) or by the sense (*artha*)? On this point, one prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the sequence is unrestricted because there is no regulator of the order, since the two injunctions terminate merely in the performance of the acts themselves. Another prima facie view is that there is a restriction according to the order of the text, because in previous sections—such as “Having initiated the householder, the *adhvaryu* initiates the *brahmā*”—it was accepted that the order of the text serves as a regulator, and that possibility exists here as well.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the instrumental case in the word "with gruel" (*yavāgvā*) reveals that gruel is the means for the oblation (*homa*), and since an oblation cannot be accomplished in the absence of a substance, the cooking of the gruel necessarily precedes it. Likewise, in this context as well, since bathing is the cause of purification and only one who is purified is entitled to perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), it should be understood that bathing occurs first. In this regard, "bathing" is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those acts that precede it, such as rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflecting on what is beneficial for oneself. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should reflect upon what is beneficial for oneself."
"One should not neglect virtue, wealth, and pleasure at their proper times according to one's ability. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:
"One should wake up during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā and reflect upon dharma and artha."
"And the bodily afflictions rooted therein, as well as the true meaning of the Veda" (MDh 4.92).
Here, "the true meaning of the Veda" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus it is said in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should reflect upon dharma and artha."
"One should meditate upon the Lord of the mind, having subdued the bodily afflictions arising therefrom.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O King, having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, the wise man [should reflect] in his mind..."
Having awakened, one should contemplate the Dharma and the purpose that is not in conflict with it.
A king may certainly consider both of these [pleasure and wealth] without causing harm to dharma; however, he should abandon wealth and pleasure if they cause injury to dharma.

"Even a dharma that results in unhappiness and is indeed despised by the world. (ViP 3.11.5–7) Two *muhūrta*s, half a *prahara*, prior to sunrise: the first is the *brāhma* [period], the second is the *raudra*. Regarding that *brāhma* period, Viṣṇu indicates the specific object of reflection:
"Rising again and again, one should consider: 'What good deed has been performed today?'"
Whether it was given, or caused to be given, or even truthful speech was spoken.
“Rising again and again, one must remain vigilant: a great danger has arrived.
Which of death, disease, or sorrow will fall upon me today?
As for the injunction that “one should meditate on the Lord with the mind,” a specific method for doing so is shown in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*.
"May Brahmā, Murāri, the destroyer of Tripura, Bhānu, Śaśin, the son of the Earth, Budha, Guru, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu— all of them— grant me a beautiful dawn. (Vāyu Purāṇa 14.23), and so forth.
Thus ends the section on contemplating one's own welfare during the *brāhma-muhūrta*.
Immediately after contemplating one’s welfare, one should look upon a *śrotriya* (a Vedic scholar) and others, but not upon the most wicked and so forth. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"A *śrotriya*, a fortunate person, a cow, fire, and likewise one who has maintained the sacred fires (*agnicit*)."
He who, having risen in the morning, beholds [this], is liberated from calamities.
"He who, having risen in the morning, sees one who is most wicked, unfortunate, blind, naked, or whose nose has been cut off—that is a characteristic sign of the Kali age. Thus [it is said].
After that, he should void urine and feces. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:
Having risen in the latter part of the night, he should then sip water and cover the ground with grass,
veiling his head with a cloth.
Restraining his speech with effort and avoiding spitting or exhaling,
he should void urine and feces in a clean place with a concentrated mind.

[222] Thus it is said. In that regard, he specifies the rule concerning grass: "One should perform the voiding of feces and urine after covering the head and having covered the ground with sacrificially unfit grass that is not moist. So it is said.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the rule for the direction according to the difference in time:

"During the day and at the twilights, one should void urine and feces facing north with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) placed over the ear; however, if it be at night, one should face south. (YDh 1.16)

"And Karna: 'Having placed the purifier (pavitra) on the right ear, one should void feces and urine,' because another Smṛti text states that the purifier is to be located on the right ear. That same location is likewise appropriate for the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). However, Aṅgiras mentions another location as an alternative."
“Having placed the sacred thread behind him so that it hangs from the neck, a householder should void urine and feces; or, being composed, he may place it in his ear.

In this regard, placing it in the ear applies only to the case of wearing a single garment. Thus says Sāṅkhyāyana: “If one is clad in a single garment, he should place the sacred thread on his ear and then perform the evacuation of urine and feces. [223]
Now, an objection: the restriction regarding direction has not been established, because others remember it otherwise. Regarding this, Yama says:
"In the forenoon one should face west, likewise in the afternoon one should face east;
at midday one should face north, and at night one should face south."
In this matter, some establish [the rule] by resorting to an option (*vikalpa*).

That is incorrect, because an option is inadmissible between a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) and a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*). For the general rule is the statement of Yājñavalkya, since it prescribes facing north throughout the entire day; whereas the statement of Yama is a specific rule, as its prescription of facing north is understood here to be restricted to the midday period. If it is argued: "Let there be no option then; rather, let the settled rule (*vyavasthā*) be that which is stated in the words of Yama," [the response follows].

That too is not correct, because Devala himself specified the term "always" (*sadaiva*) precisely to exclude facing either east or west: "Always facing north in the morning, and facing south in the evening.
Here, the words "morning" (*prātaḥ*) and "evening" (*sāyāhna*) refer to day and night respectively. And so says Manu:

"One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day; at night and during the two twilights, one should face south, as during the day" (MDh 4.50). If this is so, then what is the status of the prescriptions for facing east or west mentioned by Yama? We reply that it is a statement intended to indicate the prohibition of facing the sun. This has been stated in the Mahābhārata:
"Those who urinate facing the sun, facing fire, facing a cow,
or facing a twice-born man on the roads, their life-span comes to an end.
As for that which was stated by Devala:

"One should always void excrement and urine, but one should avoid doing so during the *saṃdhyā* periods"—this [injunction] refers to cases other than when one is constrained; for there are Smṛti texts stating, "One should not suppress a natural urge," and "One who is constrained should not perform a ritual act. Furthermore, as Manu has said:
"Whether in shade or in darkness, by night or by day, the twice-born..."

"One may act according to one's comfort in cases of danger to life," as stated in MDh 4.51; even that refers to situations where one has lost one's sense of direction due to mist, darkness, and the like. The restriction regarding place is declared in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Beyond the range of an arrow-shot in the southwest of the earth..."
"One should perform urination and defecation at a distance from one's dwelling" (ViP 3.11.8–9).
Āpastamba also says: "One should void urine and feces at a distance from the dwelling, toward the southern direction or the western one" (ĀpDh 1.11.31.2). Manu also says:
"At a distance from the dwelling one should void urine; at a distance [from water] one should pour out the water used for washing the feet."
"And one should perform the disposal of food remnants from afar. (MDh 4.151).
He [Manu] himself states the forbidden places:
"One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen. (45)
Neither on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain;
neither in a ruined temple, nor ever on an anthill;
nor in pits containing living creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing. (46)
"Having approached neither a riverbank nor a mountain peak,
one should never discharge feces or urine while looking at wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, or cows. (MDh 4.45–48)
The repetition of the phrase "on a mountain peak" is for the purpose of indicating an excess of fault. Yama also says:
"Dust, charcoal, potsherds, temples, royal roads, cremation grounds, fields, and threshing floors..."
One who is under restraint should not frequent the shade of trees, visible crossroads, water, or the edge of a body of water; he should avoid the path as well.
"One should avoid the roots of trees, as well as shrines, pits, and holes. Thus says Hārīta:
"One should always take one's food and perform one's movements in private."
One who keeps [the senses] concealed shall be endowed with fortune; if they are exposed, one is deprived of prosperity.
[226] Thus it is said. Āpastamba also states: "And one should not void urine or excrement while wearing shoes" (ĀpDh 1.10.30.18). Yama also says:
"One should not urinate facing the sun, nor look at one's own feces;
having seen them, one should gaze upon the sun, a cow, fire, or likewise a Brāhmaṇa."
Then, having cleansed his anus and genitals with a clod of earth or similar substance, and having grasped his penis, he should rise. Thus says Bharadvāja:
"Then, having removed the feces and urine with a clod, a piece of wood, grass, or the like, he should rise with his lower garment tucked up, firmly holding his penis."
Thus ends the section on the voiding of feces and urine;
now begins the section on purification. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having risen with the penis still held [in the hand], one should [purify oneself] with earth and water drawn up from [the ground]."
"One should perform purification untiringly so as to remove the smell and the stain. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, YDh 1.17]. Devala also says:
"One should wipe the penis until the end of the purification, even after urination or defecation."
One should repeatedly cleanse the anus and the hands with earth and water.
[227] Thus says Dakṣa as well:

"One should not perform purification at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha); one should perform it with water drawn up. Regarding the case where drawing up water is impossible, Vivasvat states this specific rule:
"Having left aside water to the depth of one *ratni*, one should perform purification over ground that has not been excavated;
afterwards, one should clear away that [excess] from the sacred spot (*tīrtha*), for otherwise one would become impure.
Thus [it is said]. Yama speaks of the clay suitable for purification:
"A Brahmin should take earth from a bank that likewise contains sand.
Regarding this very point, Marīci states a specific rule:
"For a Brahmin, white earth is prescribed for purification; for a Kṣatriya, red [earth] is ordained."
"One should prescribe yellow-colored [earth] for a Vaiśya, but black for a Śūdra. In the absence of these specified [colors], any [earth] whatsoever may be taken. Regarding this, Manu says:
"In whatever region there is water, and whatever clay is found there..."
"That alone would be commendable there; by it, purification is ordained" (MDh 10.47).
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, specific types of earth to be avoided are shown:
earth dug up from an anthill, from a rat's hole, or likewise from within water.
Nor should one take what remains after purification from the house, as it may be smeared with impurities.
"Nor from mud dug up by a plow, nor from that inhabited by living creatures within it. (ViP 3.11.15–16).
The prohibition against using clay from within water, however, applies to sources other than ponds, wells, and the like. For this very reason, Yama says:
"One should take clay from the outside of ponds, wells, and tanks."
"One should take [earth] from within the water, beyond the wrist.
Devala also shows certain types of earth that are prohibited:
"That which is mixed with charcoal, husks, insects, bones, gravel, or sand..."
[The earth] originating from an anthill, from the edge of water, from a wall, from a ploughshare, or from a cremation ground [is not to be used].
"One should take sand from the area between the interior and exterior of a village, appearing as dust, which has been brought for the purpose of another's purification, but one should not take clay.
Thus [it is said]. Devala states the rule regarding the hands:
"One who knows the Dharma should not employ the right hand for cleaning the lower parts;
likewise, one should not cleanse above the navel with the left hand.
Thus, the rule regarding the directions is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
"Having drawn out water and taken earth, one who is restrained in speech should face north during the day, and if at night, he should face south. Thus [it is said].
Śātātapa states the number of applications of earth:
One application on the penis, three on the left hand, and two on each of the two hands—this is declared to be the purification for urination; for defecation, it shall be triple that amount.
[229] Thus it is said. Manu also states: "One application of earth should be made to the penis, three to the anus, ten to one hand, and seven to both hands, by one desiring purity."
"This is the purification for a householder; it is twofold for a student, threefold for a forest-dweller, and fourfold for ascetics" (MDh 5.136). Baudhāyana also says:

"Five applications of earth should be used for the anus, and likewise three each on the left foot and the hand; these should be applied in sequence by one desiring to perform purification properly. Thus says Vasiṣṭha as well.
Five applications of clay are prescribed for the anus, ten for each of the two hands,
seven for both feet together, and two are proclaimed for the penis.
"Twenty in one hand, and fourteen should be known for two. (VaDh 6.18).
This number beginning with twenty pertains to the student (*brahmacārin*), because it has been stated that "for a student, it is double. In the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"For women and Śūdras, half the measure of purification has been declared by the wise."
Half of the purification prescribed for daytime is ordained for nighttime; on a journey, it is reduced to one-quarter.
"One who is distressed should act according to his ability; one who is capable should act as prescribed. Baudhāyana also says:
"The place, the time, as well as oneself, the substance, and the purpose of the substance..."
"Having understood the circumstances and the situation, one should determine the appropriate purification. Thus [says] Vṛddha-Parāśara:
"But he who, while seated, is unable to void excrement or urine..."
"He should always perform half of his own purification.
Thus, in the *Anuśāsana-parvan*, the procedure for purification is shown:
"The wise man should perform purification slowly, with full awareness, and without confusion."
And the drops should likewise be such that they do not touch the thigh.
"With conscious effort, one should ensure that the buttocks are not touched at all. Dakṣa also says:
"Six other applications of clay should be given for the purification of the nails by one desiring purity."
"One should never perform purification with streams of rainwater. Thus [says the law]. Marīci also says:
"The feet should be cleansed with three [applications of earth] below the ankle, and likewise from the ankle upwards."
"And the hands up to the wrists for removing the smell and the smear.
Thus it is said. When purification has been performed according to the rule, if the smell does not depart, then Manu says:
"As long as the smell and the smear caused by that [impurity] do not depart from the part smeared with the impure substance..."
"In all purifications of substances, water should be applied with such softness as is appropriate. (MDh 5.126).
However, Devala says that in the absence of mental satisfaction:
"Purification is ordained for as long as one considers it to be pure."
"An authoritative rule regarding the number of purificatory acts is not taught by the Brahmins.
So too Pitāmaha:
"As long as the twice-born, as well as Śūdras and women, have not been initiated..."
For them, purification is prescribed as that which removes odor and stains.

[232] Thus it is said. Here, the mention of women and Śūdras refers to those who have not yet performed their marriage rites, because they are mentioned in conjunction with twice-born men who have not yet been initiated. Regarding the quantity of clay, Śātātapa says:
"The morsels for one established in the lunar vow (induvrata) should be the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit;
likewise, all the oblations and the clay used for purification should be of that same measure."
As for the different measurements stated by Dakṣa and Aṅgiras:
"The first clay is prescribed as being the measure of half a *prasṛti*;
the second and the third are proclaimed to be half of that."

"The first handful is to be known [as such], the second as half of that, and the third as earth sufficient to fill three parts of the hand. (Daśasmṛti 5.7). In all these cases, if the fragrance and other qualities have not yet vanished despite a smaller quantity, a larger quantity should be understood as necessary. Even when the fragrance has vanished, the number prescribed by the scriptures must certainly be fulfilled. As Dakṣa says:
"One desiring purity and cleanliness must not perform purification either deficiently or excessively;
one becomes purified by penance when a prescribed rule has been transgressed. (DaŚm 5.13).
Vyāghrapāda says that even when such purification has been performed as described, there is no purity for one who lacks purity of intention.
Purity is said to be twofold: external and internal.
External purity is traditionally defined as cleansing with earth and water, while internal purity is the purification of one's disposition.
"Even if one performs purification until death with the entirety of the waters of the Gaṅgā and with loads of earth like mountains,
one who is defiled in heart is not purified.
Thus Dakṣa demonstrates, through both positive and negative concomitance, that both types of purity are the cause for eligibility to perform all ritual acts.
"Effort regarding purity must always be made; the twice-born is said to have purity as his foundation.
For one devoid of purity and proper conduct, all ritual acts are fruitless. (Daśanirṇaya 5.2).
Thus ends the section on purity.
Now follows the procedure for gargling. Regarding this, Āpastamba states:
"Having thus performed the rules of purification, one should afterwards perform the gargling;
[this is required] after voiding urine, semen, or feces, and after the act of cleaning the teeth."
[234] While eating foods, one should perform mouth-rinsing (gaṇḍūṣa) in sequence with four,
eight, two, six, two, eight, and likewise sixteen rinses.
One should perform the purification of the mouth; otherwise, one incurs fault.
All the deities are in the east, and likewise the ancestors are in the south.
The sage-gandharvas are in the west; one should perform the *gaṇḍūṣa* (mouth-rinsing) on the left.
At the time of the *gaṇḍūṣa*, the Brahmin should strike his face with the index finger.

"If a foolish soul should do so, he would go to the Raurava hell. Thus ends the rule for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa). Now follows the rule for sipping water (ācamana). Regarding this, Vṛddha-Parāśara says:
Then, having performed purification by washing his feet and hands with earth and water,
the twice-born man, having tied up his topknot and his waistband, should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
"Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should be restrained in speech, mind, and body. Thus [says the law]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"With the hands between the knees, seated in a clean place facing north..."
Or, a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha on the front part [of the hand]. (YDh 1.18)

Gautama also says: "Sitting in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having washed his hands up to the wrists, remaining silent, he should sip water three or four times so that it touches his heart; he should wipe his mouth twice, sprinkle his feet, touch the apertures of the head, and apply [water] to the crown of his head" (GDh 1.11). In this regard, the option of "three or four" is a matter of personal choice. Yājñavalkya distinguishes the *brahmatīrtha* from the other *tīrthas*:
"The bases of the little finger, the index finger, and the thumb, and the tip of the hand [are the *brahma-*, *prājāpatya-*, *daiva-*, and *ārṣa-tīrthas* respectively]."

"The *prājāpatya*, *pitrya*, *brāhma*, and *daiva* tīrthas follow in this order" (YDh 1.19). This very point has been clarified by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "The *brāhma* tīrtha is on the north side of the base of the thumb, along the line running toward the east. Between the forefinger and the thumb is the *pitrya*. Between the little finger and the palm is the *prājāpatya*. On the first joint of the fingers is the *daiva*. [236] Thus, Śaṅkha specifies the water to be used for sipping (*ācamana*):
"With waters that have been drawn up, but which are free from foam and bubbles..."
"One should not sip water that has been heated by fire or that is alkaline. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 9.6). Yājñavalkya also says:
"But with water that is in its natural state, free from foam and bubbles..."
But by [the drops] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate, respectively, the twice-born [attain their status].
"A woman and a Śūdra are purified by water that merely touches the extremities once. Thus [says Yājñavalkya]. Manu also says:
"A Brāhmaṇa is purified by water reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat."
"A Vaiśya [is purified] by water that has been sipped, but a Śūdra by water touched at the extremity. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.62). Pracetas also says:
"With water that is not hot, free from foam, and pure to the eye and cloth..."
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three or four times with silent [mantras] directed toward the heart.
[237] Thus it is said. Regarding this, Yama states an exception:
"For the wise, purification is declared even by looking at water while on a journey;
likewise for the sick, and for those who drink hot water, by means of hot water. Thus it is said.
Bharadvāja describes the manner of taking water and its quantity:
"Having made his hand long like a mountain and shaped like a cow's ear,
the twice-born man should take water with his hand, the fingers of which are closely joined."
"One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with the remaining fingers, excluding the thumb and the little finger;
having taken up water in an amount sufficient to submerge a bean, one should drink it three times.

And it should be understood that this hand is the right hand, based on the Purāṇic statement: "One should drink water three times with the right hand. Dakṣa describes the procedure to be followed immediately after drinking the water.
Conventionally, one should wipe the mouth twice with the base of the thumb;
then, first of all, one should touch the mouth with the three fingers joined together.
Immediately after touching the nose with the thumb and the index finger,
one should then touch the eyes and ears with the thumb and the ring finger.
"One should touch the navel with the little finger and the thumb, the heart with the palm, the head with all [fingers], and finally the arms with the tips [of the fingers]. Thus [it is said].
However, Vṛddhaśaṅkha describes the touching in another way.
One should touch the two nostrils with the union of the index finger and the thumb;
then, one should touch the two eyes with the union of the middle finger and the thumb.
"Likewise, one should touch the navel and the heart with the palm of the hand, and then touch the head; this is the rule for *ācamana*. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 9.5–7).
Others also describe it in various other ways; in such cases, the settled rule should be observed according to one's own *śākhā*. Manu states the occasions for *ācamana*:
"Having voided urine or feces, one who has rinsed the mouth should touch the cavities [of the head];
so too when about to study the Veda and always when eating food. (MDh 5.138).
Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
[239] In conversing with Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas, in speaking with women or Śūdras while they are left-over from a meal,
or upon touching a person who is impure from food, or likewise any such food;
One should sip water (perform ācamana) upon the falling of tears or likewise of blood;
also upon touching fire, cows, or indeed one who is impure.
“Furthermore, upon touching women or oneself, or having put on indigo-dyed clothing. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.13.4–8).
The rule regarding “speaking with the remnants of food of women or Śūdras” applies to the context of recitation (*japa*) and similar acts. Likewise, in the Padma Purāṇa:
“Having seen Cāṇḍālas and others while reciting or performing a fire-oblation (*homa*), the best of the twice-born should sip water for purification (*ācamana*).”
Manu also says:

"Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken a falsehood, and having stepped upon a carriage road or a cremation ground, one should sip water for purification even if one is already pure. (MDh 5.145)
Bṛhaspati also says:
Upon the emission of downward wind, upon crying out, upon the arising of anger,
upon touching a cat or a mouse, upon laughing, and upon speaking untruths;
"Even while performing his work, he should touch [water] during all these occasions. Yama also says:
"Having emerged from water, one should sip water; likewise, having entered it."
"Thus Varuṇa also, endowed with splendor, is well-honored.
Hārīta also says: "One should not cross [water] without having touched water. Vasiṣṭha also says:
"[One becomes impure after] sneezing, spitting, sleeping, putting on a garment, or shedding tears."
"And among these five, one should sip water or touch the right ear.
This touching of the right ear is to be understood as applicable when sipping water is impossible. Likewise, the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa states:
"Having properly sipped water with [pure] liquid, one who is pure should indeed perform the ritual acts. (67)
One should diligently perform the sipping of water (ācamana), touch the back of a cow, look at the sun, and also touch the right ear for the sake of the deities, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors. (68–70)
"For according to one's means, this [is to be done]; in the absence of the former, the latter follows.
When that which was mentioned previously exists, the attainment of the subsequent is not desired. (MārkPur 34.67–71).
Furthermore, he will speak of the praise of the right ear with the words "the holy fords such as Prabhāsa," and so forth; or else, that which was stated by Baudhāyana should be consulted.
"Having loosened the knot of the lower garment and put it on, one should touch water;
or one should touch moist grass, cow dung, or the earth. (BDh 1.10.16–17).
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, the occasions for performing the second sipping of water (*ācamana*) are shown.
"At the time of eating at home, as well as during both twilights,
one who has already sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again during recitation, burnt offerings, worship, and so forth.
Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.

"Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road, and after putting on a different garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 1.116]. Baudhāyana also says:
In eating, in offering oblations, in giving gifts, in presenting offerings, in receiving gifts,
and at the time of consuming sacrificial food (havir), that twice-sipping of water (dvir-ācamana) is prescribed by tradition.
[242] Thus it is said. Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Having washed his hands and feet, one who is eating should sip water twice;
seated in a clean place, and having finished eating, he should likewise sip water twice. (KūrPu 1.2.12.64)
Having touched the lips when they are hairless, having changed one's garment,
after voiding semen, urine, or feces, and upon speaking what is improper;
Having yawned at the commencement of study, or likewise upon the onset of coughing or asthma,
the best of the twice-born, having approached a crossroads or a cremation ground, [should perform purification].
"Likewise, at both twilights, even though one has already sipped water, one should sip again. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.13.1–3).
[This refers to] speaking what is improper and speaking harshly. Regarding an exception to the rule for sipping water, Baudhāyana says:
"In the case of food particles stuck between the teeth, there is the same requirement as for the teeth themselves; they must be held [until removed]."
"When these have been swallowed, one should not sip water; they become pure by the mere removal of the substance," (BDh 1.4.1.24).
Thus, there is a distinction between what is "stuck" (*dantalagna*) and what is "adhered" (*danta-sakta*), based on whether it can be removed or not. For this very reason, Devala says:
"During a meal, having removed what is stuck to the teeth, one should perform the sipping of water."
One should consider a coating that has adhered to the teeth as being like the teeth themselves, and not removable.
"One should not exert great effort again in extracting [the object] from there;

for if a wound is made by piercing with grass, the impurity (āśauca) would become excessive. This refers to those [objects] which, having been swallowed, have fallen from their place—that is, having been ingested. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Regarding food stuck between the teeth, it is pure as long as it does not come into contact with the tongue, like [food on] the teeth;
but once it has fallen from its place, one becomes pure only by swallowing it.

(MDh ?? And this should be understood to apply when the taste is not perceived. As Śaṅkha says: "Regarding food stuck between the teeth, it is treated like [food on] the teeth, provided there is no contact with the tongue other than that. Regarding fruits, roots, and so forth, Śātātapa states a specific rule:
"A twice-born man does not become impure by what remains stuck to his teeth, nor by fruits, roots, remnants of oil that has been consumed, betel-leaf, or a stalk of sugarcane.
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* as well.
In the case of betel, the *soma* plant, and what remains after oil has been consumed; and upon touching a morsel stuck between the teeth—a man does not become impure by these.
“By means of bark, leaves, roots, flowers, or likewise [objects] made of grass or wood, as well as fragrant substances, a twice-born man does not become impure by what remains [in the mouth].

This refers to the remnants of things consumed for the sake of oral fragrance and the like, because of its association with betel (*tāmbūla*). Regarding the phrase “upon contact with what is stuck to the teeth,” the meaning is: upon contact of the tongue with that which is stuck to the teeth and cannot be removed. Yājñavalkya also says:

"Saliva from the mouth, drops [of water], likewise droplets from sipping, and beard-hair that has entered the mouth—having removed what is stuck to the teeth, one is then pure. (YDh 1.195) If drops issuing from the mouth fall upon a limb, they do not necessitate sipping (*ācamana*). Thus says Gautama: "Drops from the mouth do not cause impurity if they fall upon a limb" (GDh 1.16). However, droplets from sipping are pure even when they touch a limb. Thus says Manu:
"Those drops which touch the feet of one who is giving water for sipping to others are to be known as equal to those [drops] on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. (MDh 5.142).
Here, the mention of "feet" is intended as an illustration for other parts of the body as well. And so says Yama:
"Those drops that fall upon the body of men while they are sipping water—there is no fault of impurity from remnants in this case; they are considered equal to the earth," so it is said.

Regarding the matter of the beard, Āpastamba states a specific rule: "One does not become impure by virtue of hairs [of the beard] remaining inside the mouth, as long as one does not touch them with the hand" (ĀpDh 1.5.16.11). Bhṛgu declares those things to be avoided during the act of sipping water.
[246] If one sips water (performs ācamana) without the sacred thread, or with unwashed clothing,
or having released the topknot, the entire rite must be performed again.
"One who wears a turban, one who is seated in the full lotus posture, one whose feet are raised, one traveling in a vehicle,
or one who has gone to an improper place— none of these attain purity by merely sipping water."

Baudhāyana also says: “One should not sip water with the residue remaining from washing the feet. If one must sip water, one should do so after pouring it onto the ground. One should not sip water with the fingers, nor with water containing bubbles, nor with foam, nor with warm water, nor with alkaline water, nor with discolored water, nor with foul-smelling or foul-tasting water, nor with turbid water. One should not sip while laughing, nor while talking, nor while standing, nor while looking around, nor while stooping, nor while bowing, nor with the hair-tuft untied, nor with the neck wrapped, nor with the head covered, nor with the girdle tied, nor with the knees exposed, nor in haste, nor without the sacred thread, nor with legs outstretched; rather, without making a sound, one should drink water that reaches the heart three times. (BDh 1.5.12–19). Devala also says:
"A man should not sip water while wearing shoes, or while standing in water, or with his hair loose, or wearing a turban, or having bound his head with a cloth.
Āpastamba also says: "One should not sip water [while standing] under the fall of rain" (ĀpDh 1.6.15.4). Yama also says:
"If a twice-born man sips water that has been touched by the nails of his hands, he clearly drinks liquor; such is the word of Yama. Thus it is also stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.

"Having covered one's neck or head, or even while standing on a street or in a marketplace, one becomes impure even after sipping water (ācamana) if one has not washed one's feet. So says Gautama: "One should not drink from joined palms, nor should one sip water with water drawn up [in a vessel] while standing" (GDh 9.3). The rule "not while standing" refers to dry land; however, in water, one may sip water even while standing. Thus says Viṣṇu:

"Standing in water up to the knees, one who has sipped water (ācānta) attains purity; even if one sips water a hundred times while standing below that level, one does not become pure. Thus says Kauśika as well.
If any Brāhmaṇa who has not purified his hands should sip water,
all that [ritual] of his, as well as the sipping itself, becomes as if unperformed.

"If one performs the *ācamana* with the right hand while the *darbha* grass remains in the left hand, that water becomes blood; having drunk it, one must perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Thus [it is said].
Mārkaṇḍeya, however, prescribes that the right hand should be provided with the *pavitra* ring.

"One should perform the act of sipping water (ācamana) with a hand that holds a *pavitra*; however, that *pavitra* does not become defiled by it, though one should avoid using it after it has been used for eating. Thus [says Gobhila]. Gobhila also commends the *pavitra* even when held in both hands.
The twice-born who sips water with *darbha* grass placed on both [hands] obtains the fruit of drinking the Soma juice,
and having eaten, he shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
[249] Thus, Dakṣa states a specific rule regarding the sipping of water (ācamana) that occurs immediately after bathing:
"Having bathed, a Brahmin should sip water while standing both in the water and on dry land;
having done so, he becomes pure in both states and fit for performing his duties."
Hārīta says: "One wearing wet clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation in the water;
one wearing dry clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation on land."
A specific rule regarding land is shown in another Smṛti:
