"In the absence of a copper vessel, having taken a water-pot or a water-jar, a man should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) himself; he shall not remain impure."

One should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) with one's own hand using vessels such as those made of gourd or wood, or with a leaf-cup from the *tāmraparṇī* tree; furthermore, one should avoid oily substances and ointments.
"And that water which is in a leaf-cup, and that water which is in a copper vessel,
as well as in one of gold or silver— that is indeed remembered as never impure.
Thus, Vyāghrapāt speaks in praise of the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) characterized by such [rules]:
In this way, whatever Brahmin should constantly practice ritual ablution would satisfy the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
[250] Thus says Vṛddhaśaṅkha as well: "One should sip water three times; by that, the deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—are pleased for him. So we have heard."
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are pleased by the wiping [of the feet];
Viṣṇu is pleased by the two feet, and Brahmā is proclaimed to be pleased by the head.
When both nostril passages are touched, the Nāsatyas and Dasras are pleased;
when the pair of eyes is touched, the Moon and Sun are pleased.
Likewise, when the two color-sets are touched, Vāyu and Agni are pleased;
by the mere touching of the shoulders, all the deities are pleased.
The Nāgas are constantly pleased by his touch,
and when his heart is touched, all the deities are pleased.
"By touching his head, that person shall become pleased. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 9.9–13).
The sin incurred by failing to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) is shown in the *Purāṇasāra*:
"That atheist who, out of delusion, performs religious rites without having sipped water..."
"For all his ritual actions are indeed in vain, there is no doubt.
Thus ends the section on sipping water (ācamana).
Now, the procedure for cleaning the teeth. Regarding this, Atri says:
"When the mouth is stale, a man is constantly impure;
therefore, he should consume a tooth-cleansing twig, whether moist or dry."
Vyāsa also says:
Having thoroughly washed his hands, feet, and face, being well-composed,
he should then raise his right arm and place it between his knees.
"One should avoid milky trees, shrubs, and the like that are bitter, astringent, pungent, foul-smelling, or thorny for use as a toothbrush. Thus says Viṣṇu.
Made from a thorny milky tree, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length,
as thick as the little finger, and with a brush formed by half a joint.
The cleaning of the teeth and likewise the tongue-scraper have been prescribed;
for one with very fine teeth it should be very fine, and for one with even teeth it should be of medium size.

For one with uneven teeth, the tooth-stick should be thick; thus the wise declare that there are three types of tooth-sticks, and for a Brahmin, they say the wood should be twelve finger-breadths long.
"For those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, [the measures are] nine, six, and four aṅgulas respectively. Thus says Aṅgiras:
"Of the Āmra, Punnāga, Bilva, Apāmārga, and Śirīṣa..."
Having risen in the morning, one should, maintaining silence, chew the tooth-stick.
One should avoid the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *arka*, *khadira*, and *karavīra* trees;
likewise, one should avoid *jāti*, the roots of *bilva* and *khadira*, and the *kakubha*.
Having washed the *arimeda*, the *priyaṅgu*, and likewise the *kaṇṭakini*,
one should first eat them, and having washed them again, one should discard them.

"Facing either north or east, having become pure in the morning and remaining silent, one should consume an astringent or bitter tooth-stick. Thus Kātyāyana shows the mantra for consecrating the wood used for cleaning the teeth.
"O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us long life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and retentive memory. Thus [it is said].
Uśanas speaks of those who are to be avoided:
A man should never clean his own teeth with his fingers;
he should not eat facing south, nor should he eat blue, white, or kadamba flowers.
A tooth-stick made from *tinduka*, *iṅguda*, *bandhūka*, *moca*, *āmra*, *jaba*, *valvaja*,
or cotton (*kārpāsa*) takes away even the fortune of Viṣṇu.
"One should not eat *palāśa*, nor cotton, nor even vegetables; yet he who would eat these—cotton and even vegetables [is at fault]. Regarding the days and other factors to be avoided, Viṣṇu says:
"One should avoid using a tooth-stick on the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the new moon, on the sixth, on the fourteenth and eighth days, on the ninth, and on Sundays.
Thus [says] Yama as well.
On the fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, the full moon, and during the sun’s transit,
one should avoid oil, meat, and tooth-sticks when in the company of women.
"One should avoid cleaning the teeth with a twig during a *śrāddha*, on one's birthday, at a wedding, due to indigestion, and during a vow or a fast.
Thus says Vyāsa as well.
A woman whose husband is away from home should not eat according to the prescribed rules at a *śrāddha* or a sacrifice;
this prohibition applies to the performer of the *śrāddha*, but never to the one who eats it.
"In the absence of tooth-sticks, or on a prohibited lunar day, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water. Thus says Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya. [254]
"One should avoid using bricks, clods of earth, or stones, as well as the other fingers—
excepting the ring finger and the thumb— for cleaning the teeth.
Thus ends the section on cleaning the teeth.
Now, since bathing, recitation, fire-offerings (*homa*), and other rites must be performed with *darbha* grass in hand, the rules regarding *darbha* are stated first. Regarding this, Hārīta says:

"A twice-born man should procure auspicious *kuśa* grass for the sake of rites for the ancestors, the gods, and recitation—grass that has uncut tips, possesses leaves, is together with its roots, and is tender."

"That which is recited with *kuśa* grass in hand, as well as the gift given together with *kuśa* grass, and he who eats with *kuśa* grass in hand—for him, there is no limit to the merit. Thus it is said. Also in the Purāṇa:
"Bathing with *kuśa* grass becomes purifying; a twice-born man should sip water using *kuśa*;
water drawn up with *kuśa* is equal to the drinking of Soma. Thus [says] Gobhila as well.
"Brahmā resides at the root of the *kuśa* grass, Janārdana in the middle of the *kuśa*, and one should know Śaṅkara at the tip of the *kuśa*; thus the three gods are established. Thus says Kauśika.
Having become pure and standing in a clean place facing the northeast,
the best of the twice-born should touch the *kuśa* grass with the mantra consisting of the syllable *oṃ* alone.
[255] Thus. As for the mantra for uprooting: "O Darbha, born together with Viriñci, produced from the emission of Parameṣṭhin, drive away all my sins; may you bring me well-being! Thus.

Kātyāyana states the distinction in application according to the difference in color: "Green *darbha* grasses are for the *yajña*; yellow ones are for the *pākayajña*; those with roots are for the ancestors (*pitṛdaivata*); and speckled ones are for the Viśvedevas. (KSm 1.2.3)
"In the absence of *kuśa* grass, [one may use] *śaṅkha* grass;
in the absence of *kuśa*, O best of the twice-born, one should diligently perform the rites such as libations (*tarpaṇa*) with *kāśa* grass,
for *kāśa* is traditionally held to be equal to *kuśa*."
Yama also says: "Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, barley, dūrvā grass, as well as rice, balvaja grass, and puṇḍarīka grass— this is called the sevenfold sacrificial grass (barhis)."

Hārīta states those [types of *darbha*] that should be avoided: "One should avoid six kinds of *kuśa* grass: those on a funeral pyre, those on a path, those on sacrificial grounds, and those used for spreading, as seats, or for *piṇḍas*."
Those darbha grasses used in the Brahma-sacrifices and those used in the libations to the ancestors which have been defiled by urine or feces— their disposal is prescribed.
[256] "One should carefully avoid *darbha* grass that is impure, contemptible, or cut by the fingernails, as well as *kuśa* grass that has been boiled or scorched by fire. Thus [it is said].
Hārīta states the rule regarding the proper time for uprooting *kuśa* grass:

"On the new moon day of the month of Nabhasya, the gathering of darbha grass is prescribed; these darbha blades, being of undiminished potency, may be employed again and again. Thus says Śaṅkha as well.
"Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, mantras, and especially Brahmins—
these do not lose their potency and may be employed again and again.
Regarding the fruit of wearing the *pavitra*, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"A Brāhmaṇa should always remain with *kuśa* grass in hand, even when devoid of *darbha*;
he constantly destroys his sins just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. Thus says Śātātapa.
"In recitation, burnt offerings, giving, self-study, and the libation to the ancestors, one should ensure that the hand is not empty, using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass. Thus [it is said].
Kātyāyana describes the manner of the *pavitra*:

“[The *pavitra*] should be known to be without an inner core, with its tip intact, made of *kāśa* grass, consisting of two blades, and measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in length, wherever it may be used.
Thus [says the text]. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
The purifier for a Brāhmaṇa consists of four blades of *darbha* grass;
it is prescribed that there be one less blade for each successive social class (*varṇa*) in due order.
"Performing the rite of pacification (śāntika) with three blades of *darbha* grass, likewise the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika) with five,
and the rites of malevolent magic (abhicāra) with four— one should prepare the purifier (*pavitraka*). Thus said Atri.
"In the *brahmayajña* and in silent recitation (*japa*), the *brahmagranthi* (Brahma-knot) is prescribed; during meals, it is said to be circular. Thus, the dharma is not lost.
Thus ends the section on the rules for *darbha* grass.

[258] Thus, in this statement, "The twilight bath (*saṃdhyā-snāna*)," the rites beginning with rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and ending with the ritual of the *kuśa* grass—indicated by the word "bath"—have been defined. Now, the bath mentioned in the root text is explained in detail. Regarding that, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* states:
"Having washed the tooth-stick and having chewed it according to the rule..."
"Having sipped water and being purified, one should always perform the morning bath. Thus [says the Kūrma Purāṇa]. Vyāsa says:
"When the time of dawn has arrived, the wise man, having performed his necessary duties..."
"One should bathe in pure rivers after having performed purification according to the rule" (VySm 1.2–3). Dakṣa also says:
"Without bathing, one should not perform any rite whatsoever, such as recitation (*japa*) or fire-offerings (*homa*)."
A man who has risen from his bed is covered with saliva and sweat;
the body is extremely impure, endowed with nine apertures, and indeed flows [with secretions] day and night. Morning bathing is the means of purification. (9–10)
"They praise the morning bath, for it indeed yields both visible and invisible fruits.
One who has purified their soul through the morning bath is worthy of all [ritual acts] such as the recitation of mantras (*japa*) and so forth. (DaSm 2.7–12) — Vyāsa.
The state of being a seer among seers is eternal for those who bathe in the morning; of this there is no doubt.
Misfortune, Kālakarṇī, bad dreams, and evil thoughts [are all dispelled].
"By bathing at dawn, sins are purified; there is no doubt about this. Thus [it is said]. Dakṣa also says:
"If, through ignorance or delusion, an evil deed has been committed during the night..."
"By means of the morning bath, the twice-born purify all of that.
The method of bathing is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"The bath [should be performed] with earth and with mantras addressed to the Waters (*vāruṇa*) and to the Seasons (*abdaivata*)."
"Or one should perform it with the *vyāhṛtis*, or even with whatever [verse] from the *Ṛgveda*. Thus says Kātyāyana as well:
"Just as during the day, so too in the morning should one always bathe without sloth."
"Having rinsed one's teeth in a river or similar body of water; if at home, then without mantras.
(KSm 1.19.1) By "without mantras," an abbreviation of the mantras is intended. For he himself says:
"Because the time for the fire-oblation is brief and the ritual of bathing is extensive..."
"In the morning, the bath should be performed briefly; the omission of the *homa* is censured. Thus [it is said].
Jābāli states the rule regarding the time:
"Having always risen in the morning and preceded by the cleansing of the teeth..."
"One should perform the bath at dawn and offer libations to the gods and humans. Thus it is said. Also in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"The bath which is performed at every dawn, or during the twilight, or even after sunrise..."
"It is equal to the Prājāpatya [penance] and destroys all sins.

The term "at sunrise" (udite) means facing the rising [sun]. If one were to bathe even after the sun has risen, the *saṃdhyā* would also be postponed; for the *saṃdhyā* is preceded by the bath. Furthermore, the postponement of the *saṃdhyā* is prohibited by Yogiyājñavalkya:
"One should perform the *saṃdhyā* at the junction [of day and night], neither when the sun has set nor when it has risen."
At the time prescribed, while performing the bath, one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite. Thus says Śaunaka:
"Having bathed and sipped water, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* three times in the midst of the water.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as an ancillary part of the bath is enjoined.
"Daily, occasional, and optional—bathing is said to be threefold.
Libation (tarpaṇa), however, is proclaimed as being an ancillary part of it. Thus says Yama as well.
"Having joined the two hands together, one should fill them with a handful of water;
having drawn up water to the height of a cow's horn, one should pour it into the midst of the water. Thus says Kārṣṇājini.

"Standing in water reaching up to the navel, reflecting with an upward-turned mind"—the word "should satisfy" (*tarpayet*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Also, in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"Then, one should satisfy the gods and others with water through one's own *tīrtha*."
To the gods and the hosts of gods, and also to the sages and the hosts of sages.
"Then one should constantly satisfy the ancestors and the groups of ancestors. Thus [it is stated]. In the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Immediately after bathing, one should first offer libations to the ancestral deities."
"Having crossed over, one should wring out the garment; thereafter, the sandhyā-rite follows. Bharadvāja also says:
"Those who died while performing the service of slaves expect [the use of] water from their garments."
"Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the water to fall upon the ground.
Thus [it is said]. As for the mantra for wringing out the cloth:
"Whosoever have been born in our family, childless kinsmen who have died,"

"May they accept this water squeezed from my garment, which I have offered. Thus ends the section on bathing. Immediately after bathing, one should put on a garment; and so it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Having bathed in this manner, and thereafter having sipped water according to the rule, one should rise and put on two clean, white garments. (MatPu 112.13).
The word "should perform ritual action" (*karma kuryāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin.
"Having bathed in this manner and put on two clean, unwashed garments,
one should wash the thighs with earth and water, and thereafter wash the hands.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states a specific detail:
"A wise man should not wear a garment that has been worn below as something to be worn above,
nor should he ever dwell in a lower garment without an inner one.
Regarding this, a specific detail is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"One should not wipe one's limbs with clothes or hands after bathing,
nor should one shake the hair, nor should one shake the garment. Regarding this, Gobhila states the reason:
The gods drink from the head; the ancestors drink from the mouth;
all the gandharvas drink from the middle; and all living beings drink from below.
"Therefore, having bathed, one should not wipe oneself with a bathing cloth nor with the hand. Vyāsa also says:
"There are three and a half crores of body hairs."
"All sacred fords dwell therein; therefore, one should not wipe oneself. Thus says Jābāli:
"If, having bathed while still wearing wet clothes, one voids excrement or urine..."
"Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one becomes pure again by bathing.
Regarding the matter of clothing, Bhṛgu states a specific rule:
"The garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be white; that of a king should be red and brilliant."
"Yellow [is prescribed] for a Vaiśya, and blue for a Śūdra; it is held that [the latter] should be like a soiled garment. Thus says Prajāpati as well:
"They praise linen cloth, provided it has a border, for the ritual libation (tarpaṇa)."
"Or one may wear saffron-dyed [robes], but never anything ostentatious.
Devala also says:
"A wise person should perform religious rites with robes washed by himself."

"But not with one washed by a washerman, nor with an unbleached [cloth], nor anywhere else. Here, "nāhatena" (not with an unbleached) is a compound word. Pulastya states the definition of an *ahata* [cloth]: "That which is slightly washed, new, white, with its fringes intact, and which has not been worn."
"One should know that to be unsoiled, which is purifying for all ritual acts.
Thus says Baudhāyana as well:
"An upper garment must be worn during these five types of rites."
"During private recitation, the relinquishing [of breath], and giving; likewise during eating and sipping water.

This is intended as an illustration for all ritual acts (*sarvakarma*), because there is a prohibition against performing any rite whatsoever without an upper garment (*anuttarīya*). Thus it has been stated by Bhṛgu:
"One who is without a lower garment, without an upper garment, naked, or even without any clothing at all..."
One should not even contemplate Śrauta or Smārta rituals while naked.

"One may be naked, or wear soiled garments; one is also considered naked if wearing a half-robe (*ardharapaṭa*). One is naked if wearing burnt garments, and likewise naked if wearing a stitched robe (*sūtpaṭa*). Thus it is said. Also in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:

"A twice-born man should not engage in rituals such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the worship of deities, nor in recitation, nor in sipping water (*ācamana*), nor in silent prayer (*japa*) while wearing only a single garment. Thus [says the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, 3.12.20].
Gobhila also [states]:
"One should not eat nor perform the worship of the deities while wearing only a single garment.
Regarding this, Yogiyājñavalkya states the alternative rule:
"In the absence of a washed garment, [one may use] those made of hemp, linen, or wool."
One should have a water-strainer and a meditation-band; one must certainly not go about naked.
[266] Thus; the ellipsis is that one should wear a kutapa and a yogapaṭṭa.
This concludes the section on the wearing of garments;
next is the rule for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, which is shown in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*.
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, especially in my sacred field,
on the shore of the ocean, at an anthill, or at the root of a *tulasī* plant.
These types of clay should be prepared, while one should avoid any other kind of earth;
black clay is said to bring about pacification (śānti), and red clay brings about subjugation (vaśya).
They say that yellow brings prosperity, while white is said to belong to Viṣṇu;
the thumb is declared to bestow nourishment, and the middle finger shall grant long life.
The ring finger always bestows food, and the forefinger bestows liberation;
one should perform [the ritual] with these various fingers, but one must not touch the fingernails.
Or likewise in the shape of a wick-lamp, or similarly in the shape of a bamboo leaf,
as well as in the form of a lotus bud and a water-lily bud.
[267] Or likewise the shape of a fish or a tortoise, or beyond that the form of a conch;
measuring ten finger-breadths, it is called the most excellent of the excellent.
The middle [size] should be nine finger-breadths; beyond that, eight finger-breadths is also [middle].
The middle *puṇḍra* is traditionally said to be of three kinds: seven, six, and five [finger-breadths].
The *puṇḍra* may be of three types, measuring four, three, or two finger-breadths;
one should know Keśava on the forehead and Nārāyaṇa on the belly.
Having placed Mādhava in the heart and Govinda at the base of the shoulder,
Viṣṇu is said to be in the belly and on the right side.
One should remember Madhusūdana at the side between the arms,
Trivikrama in the region of the throat, and Vāmana in the left side of the abdomen.
One should remember Śrīdhara on the left upper arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the ear, Padmanābha on the back, and Dāmodara on the hump.

"Having concentrated his mind, one should, at the evening and morning fire-oblations, utter these twelve names according to the rule and wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka). Thus also says Satyavrata.

[268] "He on whose forehead a bright vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) made with clay is seen—even if he is a *caṇḍāla*, he is a pure soul and is indeed worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the section on the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*).
Now, in connection with the morning bath (*prātaḥsnāna*), other types of bathing are described. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:

"Bathing is declared to be of two kinds, distinguished as secondary (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*). Of these two, the *vāruṇa* (bath by immersion in water) is the primary; that, moreover, is of six kinds."
In this regard, the sixfold nature of the primary bath (*mukhyasnāna*) is shown in the *Āgneyapurāṇa*:

"The daily (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), that which is a limb of ritual action (*kriyāṅga*), the removal of impurities (*malakarṣaṇa*), and likewise the sixth, the ritual bath (*kriyāsnāna*); thus the bath is proclaimed to be sixfold. (AgPu 155.3–4)
Śaṅkha states their characteristics:
"A man who has not bathed is unfit for recitation, fire-offerings, and other such rites;
therefore, the morning bath is proclaimed as the obligatory daily bath (nityasnāna)."
Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a corpse, or a sacrificial post, or having touched a menstruating woman who has not yet bathed,
when one who is otherwise fit for bathing performs a bath, that is indeed an occasional (naimittika) bath.
[269] That which is enjoined by the rules of the astrologers, such as the Puṣya-bath and others, is indeed designated as optional (kāmya); one should not perform it without desire.
He who, desiring to recite purifying prayers or intending to worship the deities and ancestors,
performs a ritual bath— that is proclaimed as the bath that is an integral part of the rite.
The bath called *malāpakarṣaṇa* (removal of impurities) is preceded by anointing with oil;
its application is for the purpose of removing impurities and not otherwise.
In lakes, natural reservoirs, sacred fords, and rivers, the ritual bath is prescribed;
therein, the ritual itself is considered the act of bathing.

Although this is not the present occasion for the midday bath (*madhyāhna-snāna*), it is nevertheless mentioned here incidentally because, like the morning bath (*prātaḥ-snāna*), it is obligatory (*nitya*). Its obligatoriness was stated by Vyāghrapāda: "One should always be a morning bather; one should be a midday bather. Thus [it is said] in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
Then, at the time of midday, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing,
as well as flowers, unbroken grains of rice, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and pure cow dung.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and in hollows or springs.
"One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others; however, if no other option exists, one may bathe after having removed five lumps of earth. Thus [it is said].
Regarding this, Vyāsa distinguishes between those who are qualified and those who are unqualified:
"One should bathe on the sixth day of the lunar fortnight when food is well-digested and one is free from disease;
one should not bathe after eating, nor while adorned, nor if sick, nor in water that is unknown, nor while distressed.
Thus [it is said]. Dakṣa states the regulation for bathing according to the different stages of life (āśrama):
"Bathing at dawn and at midday is prescribed for forest-dwellers and householders;
for an ascetic, it is said to be three times a day, while for a student of sacred knowledge, it is once.
Vyāsa states that bathing should be accompanied by mantras, as established through both positive and negative concomitance.
"They say that bathing in water purified by mantras bestows the fruit of bathing;
it does not yield that result for those who merely immerse themselves in water like aquatic creatures. Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin.
[271] "Fish, turtles, and frogs remain submerged in water day and night;
yet, because they dwell there, they never obtain the fruit of bathing. This requirement of being accompanied by mantras applies specifically to the twice-born. As Viṣṇu says:
“Bathing with mantras is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
however, O joy of the Kurus, it is for the Śūdra and for women to be done silently.
Regarding what was stated, “One should fetch clay for the purpose of bathing,” Śātātapa states a specific rule therein:
Earth should be collected from a pure place, free from gravel, stones, and the like;
it is traditionally held to be of three kinds: red, pale-yellow, and white.

Seven kinds of earth should not be taken: that from a pit, from a heap of refuse, from what has been smeared [with cow dung], from water, from a road, from a tree, and that which remains after purification has been performed.
"A wise man should not collect clay or cow dung at night, nor should he take up cow urine or excrement. Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin as well.

Having gone to the edge of the water, the wise man should place that earth separately on the ground according to the rule; having divided that earth into three parts, he should likewise divide the cow-dung.

"One should perform the washing of the lower, upper, and middle parts of the body with those [parts] separately; in the act of washing, there must be no mixing of the earth. Thus says Śaunaka as well.

"Being self-restrained, having taken earth, dūrvā grass, apāmārga, and cow dung, one should place them separately in one spot; there must be no mixing of the earth used for washing. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.

The head should be washed with one portion of clay; likewise, the area above the navel should be cleansed with two portions, and the area below it with three; the feet should be washed in the same manner with six portions.
Having washed the entire body and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice according to the rule. Thus.

Śaunaka states the duties to be performed immediately after washing the body: "The deity of the Gāyatrī is known to be Āditya; therefore, one should consecrate the clay with the mantra *ato devā*. Then, having taken up the clay while reciting the mantras *yata indra*, *svastidā viśaspatir virakṣo vimṛdha*, and *idaṃ sumejarita*, one should throw it toward each direction in order, beginning with the east. Thereafter, one should perform the sweeping with clay, first using the mantras. The mantras for taking the clay, such as *aśvakrānte* and others, are well-known in the Yajurveda.
And again, with cow dung, saying "the tip,
the tip," he [anointed] the tips of the herbs as they grew in forest after forest.

"O cow dung, you are the purifier of those wives of the Ṛṣabhas, cleansing the body; drive away my diseases, sorrows, and sins. (Ā 3.5)—this is the mantra for the cow dung. Regarding the taking of *dūrvā* grass: "With the two verses beginning 'From joint to joint,' one should touch limb by limb"—the remainder [of the instruction] is that this is done with two blades of *dūrvā*.
O Apāmārga, drive away from us evil, impurity, misfortune, and sin;
drive away the fear of the wicked.
Saying "Svāhā," he should then touch each limb with *apāmārga* grass.

Then, having worshipped the waters with the verses "O divine waters" and "Within the waters," and having touched the water with "May they be well-disposed toward us," he should cast [the *apāmārga*] outside with "May those who are ill-disposed toward us.
Thereafter, having entered the water with the verse "Indra is pure," he should mutter it mentally.
There he should sing the Sāman chants, or else mutter the Vyāhṛtis.
"Having recited 'śivena me,' one should plunge into the water with the mantra 'āpaḥ. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.
A wise person should invoke the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) with the two verses beginning 'ye te śatam.'"
"Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Gaṅgā, Prabhāsa, and likewise Naimiṣa. Thus says Śaṅkha:
"I take refuge in the god Varuṇa, the lord and master of the waters."
Grant me the sacred ford that I have requested, for the removal of all my sins.
I shall invoke the sacred ford that destroys the flood of all sins;
by my grace, let your presence be established in these waters.
"I take refuge in all the Rudras, the givers of boons, as well as those who dwell in the waters;
I take refuge in the holy and purifying Waters, and likewise in Varuṇa.
May they quickly pacify my sin and protect me at all times. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 8.3–7)
Vasiṣṭha says: "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," "Idam āpaḥ," and "Drupadād iva," as well as the "Hiraṇyavarṇā" verses and finally the "Pāvamānī" hymns.
"Then, having looked at the sun and submerged the syllable *oṃ* within the water, the wise man should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), as well as the *gāyatrī* and the *aghamarṣaṇa*.

Viṣṇu also says: "Then, submerged in the waters, he should mutter three times the *aghamarṣaṇa*, or the verse 'That supreme step of Viṣṇu' (*tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*), or the *drupadā*, or the *sāvitrī*, or the section beginning with 'They harness [the mind]' (*yuñjate namaḥ*), or the *puruṣasūkta*. Having bathed and while still wearing his wet garment, he should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods, sages, and ancestors while remaining in the water" (ViDh 64.19–24). Medhātithi also says:
"Then, submerged in water, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
likewise, one should offer water upon the head with the Mahāvyāhṛtis. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.
Having bathed and taken up another garment, he should cleanse his thighs with earth;
for they have been defiled by the water used for washing the privities.
"Whatever twice-born man bathes in any water whatsoever according to this rite, he obtains the fruit of a sacred ford (tīrtha); however, at an actual sacred ford, the fruit is twofold.
Regarding this, Yogiyājñavalkya states the secondary alternative (anukalpa):
If one is unable to perform this extensive and supreme procedure for bathing that has been described, then this [following] procedure is prescribed.
Bathing within the water, as well as sprinkling and sipping water,
the consecration of the water, and the visualization of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
"By means of the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta recited three times daily,
this practice of bathing has been taught by the great-souled ones.
Thus ends the midday bath.
[277] Now, the bath for those who have seen an ill omen. Regarding this, Manu says:
"A professional bard, a woman in her courses, an outcast, and likewise a woman who has recently given birth..."

"Having touched a corpse or one who has touched it, one becomes pure by bathing. (MDh 5.85). A *divākīrti* is a *caṇḍāla*. Aṅgiras states: "A person who has touched a corpse, as well as a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, and likewise an outcast..."

"Having touched [such a person], one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on; of this there is no doubt. Gautama also states: "Upon touching those who have touched an outcaste (*patita*), a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), or a corpse, or having been touched by one who has touched them, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on and performing ritual ablution (*udakopasparśana*). (GDh 7.16). Starting from the third person who has touched those such as an outcaste, there is bathing with one's clothes on; however, for the fourth person, purity comes from ritual ablution. Thus says Marīci: "The fourth person should perform ritual ablution (*upaspṛśet*); beyond that, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is prescribed."
As for the fact that Saṃvarta has stated that bathing is prescribed for only two cases:
"But he who touches one who has touched [an impure person], bathing is ordained for him;
beyond that, sipping water (ācamana) is declared, as well as the sprinkling of objects."
That refers to the subject of intentional contact. And so says the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"In the case of unintentional contact, bathing is prescribed for two;
but in the case of intentional contact, the principle of 'contact with the one who touched it' (*tatspṛṣṭinyāya*) is applied to three."

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "If one should touch, through negligence, something touched by a Cāṇḍāla, a woman recently delivered, or a corpse, then, having sipped water (performed ācamana), one should perform recitation (japa) with a concentrated mind."

"Having intentionally touched one who has been touched by that [impurity], the best of the twice-born should perform ācamana for the sake of purification; so said the Lord Grandfather (Brahmā). Thus [it is stated in] Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.33.69–70. Yājñavalkya also says:
"One who has been touched by a woman in her courses or by those who have recently given birth shall bathe; one touched by them shall merely sip water.

He should mutter verses containing the word 'water' and recite the Gāyatrī once mentally. (YDh 3.30). This refers to cases of contact mediated by a staff or similar object; otherwise, it would contradict the rule stating that "both must bathe" [in the case of direct contact]. Regarding contact mediated by a cloth, however, when the principle of mediation by a staff applies, Pracetas says:
[279] "When there is contact mediated by a cloth, it is designated as direct contact;
and that which is prescribed for direct contact applies even when there is contact mediated by a cloth.
Thus, another occasion for bathing is also stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
Having touched Buddhists, Pāśupatas, Jains, Lokāyatikas, Kāpilas, or twice-born men who persist in forbidden acts, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
"But having touched Kāpālikas, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is considered superior. Regarding the specific rule for bathing necessitated by touching a Cāṇḍāla or others, Viṣṇu says:
"One who is entitled to bathe due to a specific cause, having merely immersed himself in water..."
"Having sipped water (ācamana) and become pure, one should thereafter perform the bath according to the rules.
Thus [says] Yogiyājñavalkya as well:
"When a man is impure, he should simply carry out the ablution silently."
"Having sipped water and become purified, one should thereafter perform the bath according to the prescribed rule. Thus says Gārgya as well:
"One should perform an occasional (naimittika) bath with cold water, and likewise a bath for the fulfillment of a specific desire (kāmya)."
"One should always perform [the bath] as occasion arises and according to one's inclination. Thus ends the section on occasional baths.
Now, regarding the optional bath (*kāmyasnāna*). On this point, Pulastya says:
"On the day of Puṣya, on one's birth-star, during Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti, and on the new moon day, bathing at a river site purifies the family up to the seventh generation."
He who bathes in the presence of Śiva on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra—
especially in the Gaṅgā— does not attain the state of a preta.
"That water standing before one near a Śiva-liṅga should be known as the Śiva-liṅga; having bathed there, one shall go to heaven. Thus [says the scripture]. Yama also says:
One who has bathed at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika is liberated from all sins;
one who has bathed at Prayāga on the full moon day of Māgha is likewise released from all impurities.

"In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the tenth day conjoined with the asterism Hasta, Gaṅgā destroys the sins of ten births; therefore she is remembered as the remover of evil. Thus says Viṣṇu.
The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to a solar eclipse;
bathing on that day at the time of dawn yields great fruit.

"The eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, conjoined with the asterism Punarvasu and the moon, one who bathes according to the rules in flowing waters shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus it is stated; and likewise in the Āditya Purāṇa:
One who bathes daily throughout the entire month of Kārttika, having conquered the senses, reciting prayers, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and being self-controlled, is liberated from all sins.
"One should always bathe at dawn during the months of Tulā, Makara, and Meṣa;
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and practicing celibacy destroy even the greatest sins.
Thus it is stated in the Matsyapurāṇa as well.
During the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should bathe every morning;
having given food to Brahmins, he should become a donor of cows on the full moon day of Kārttika.
"He indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Viṣṇu-vow. Thus [it is said]. Mārkaṇḍeya also [states]:
"The sage Vyāsa declared that bathing with sesame seeds at all times is meritorious."
May Viṣṇu be pleased by the offering of hair, especially on the eleventh day.
"A man desiring prosperity should always perform a bath with *āmalaka* fruits;
however, he should avoid doing so on the seventh and ninth lunar days, as well as on festival times. Thus says Viṣṇu.
Children, the young, and the elderly— men, women, and eunuchs alike—
having bathed in the auspicious Māgha at a sacred ford, obtain their desired fruit.
"Having bathed at dawn in the month of Māgha, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the optional ritual bathing (kāmyasnāna).

Now follows the bath for the removal of impurities (*malāpakarṣaṇasnāna*). Regarding this, the *Vāmana Purāṇa* states: "One should avoid oil massage on Sundays and on Tuesdays; one should avoid shaving on Fridays and Saturdays; and one should avoid sexual intercourse with women on Wednesdays. On all other days, one may always perform all these acts. (VāyPu 14.49–50)

In the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) as well, it is said: "From anointing oneself with oil on the days of the Sun and the other planets, there result respectively: distress, splendor, short life, wealth, poverty, ill health, and the fulfillment of all desires."
Manu also says: "One who is anointed with oil on the first day of the lunar fortnight, on a Sunday, on the sixth lunar day, or likewise on the Raktā tithi, is deprived of wealth and long life."
Garga also says: "One should avoid contact with oil on the fifteenth, the fourteenth, the eighth, during the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), and on the twelfth, seventh, and sixth [lunar days]."
Baudhāyana also says:
"On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially the ninth day,
as well as at the junction of the lunar phases (parvan), one should avoid anointing the head."
Garga also says: "A wise man seeking eternal prosperity should not perform [the rite] on the third, the thirteenth, nor likewise on the tenth lunar day."
Thus, although the prohibition of oil massage applies to all lunar days (tithis), Pracetas grants an exception for specific types of oil:
"Oil made from mustard seeds, scented oil, oil perfumed with flowers,
and oil mixed with other substances— these never cause any fault."
Yama also says: "There is no fault in using ghee, mustard oil, or any oil scented with flowers for daily bathing and anointing, provided they are cooked oils."
Thus ends the ritual of anointing and bathing;
however, the bathing as an ancillary part of the rite (kriyāṅgasnāna) should be performed according to the rules for the daily bath.
Having bathed with white sesame seeds in the morning, the wise one should perform worship at midday.

This and similar passages should be understood as referring to the bath that is an auxiliary to ritual action (*kriyāṅgasnāna*). Its status as an auxiliary to ritual action is made clear in the Purāṇa:

"One who intends to perform a religious rite (*dharmakriyā*) should first perform a bath; that bath is designated as an auxiliary to ritual action by the twice-born who are devoted to the Vedas. [284]
Thus concludes the ritual bath as a constituent part of the rite;
now follows the ritual bath itself. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"I shall explain the ritual bath exactly according to the prescribed rules."
At the outset, purification must be performed with earth and water according to the prescribed rule.

Having submerged in the water and emerged, and having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the rules, one should perform the invocation of the sacred ford (tīrtha); I shall explain that hereafter.
I take refuge in the god Varuṇa, the powerful lord of the waters;
grant me the sacred bathing place I have requested for the removal of all sins.
"I shall invoke the sacred ford that destroys all sins;
by my grace, let your presence be established in these waters. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, regarding the specific types of water for each of the six types of baths, both the primary and secondary alternatives, they are described in detail in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.

"One should always bathe for the sake of ritual action in rivers, streams, and tanks, in waters dug by the gods, and in mountain springs; or one may perform the bath on the ground using water drawn from wells. (ViP 3.11.24–25)
Mārkaṇḍeya also said:
"One should perform the ritual bathing of ancient kings, high-souled sages, and deities in wells and ponds."

The merit of water drawn from the earth is greater than that which remains on the ground; the merit of spring water is greater than that; the merit of lake water is greater still; and therefore, river water is said to be the most meritorious of all.
"Then the water of sacred fords (tīrtha) is meritorious, and the water of the Gaṅgā is so in every respect. Thus says Marīci:
"Whether situated on the ground or drawn up, whether cold or even warm..."
"The water of the Gaṅgā quickly purifies sin committed until the end of one's life.
Regarding forbidden water, Vyāsa says: "One should not bathe in waters that have not been released [by a priest], nor likewise in those that have not been consecrated."
One should not bathe even in waters that belong to oneself, nor likewise in waters that are scanty.
"One should avoid water that has fallen from a river, water that has flowed out from a river,
and water that has returned after having gone away. Thus says Śātātapa as well.
"Even when a well, a bridge, a pond, or similar structure has been constructed by others, one should perform the expiation after bathing and drinking there. Thus [it is said].
Manu states an exception to this rule:
"In the absence of divine pools, lakes, or rivers, one should perform the bath in water belonging to another after having drawn out four handfuls [of earth]. Thus [it is said].
Śaṅkha prohibits the use of hot water.
"Even so, for one who has bathed with water heated by fire,
the purification of the body should be understood [to have occurred], but the fruit of the ritual bath would not arise. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
[287] As for the rule regarding hot water: water itself is always pure, and fire is its purifier;
therefore, at all times, hot water is traditionally held to be purifying.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Water is pure by its very nature, how much more so when joined with fire? Therefore, the virtuous praise bathing with warm water."

Thus—this refers to the subject of bathing for the sick. And so says Yama: "Water that has been purified by the rays of the sun and further purified by fire, as prescribed for the bath of the sick, is recommended."
But when rivers and the like are unavailable, even for one who is not ill, bathing with warm water is not forbidden; thus says Yama:

"Whether it be daily, occasional, part of a ritual act, or for the removal of impurities, if a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) is absent, it should be performed with warm water or other [suitable] waters."
Furthermore, as stated by Vriddha-Manu:
"Upon death, at birth, during the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), at a śrāddha ceremony, on one's birthday, and likewise upon touching the untouchable, one should not bathe with warm water."
On the day of a solar transit, on Sunday, on the seventh lunar day, and during an eclipse,
one who desires health, sons, friends, or wealth should not bathe with warm water.

"He who bathes with hot water on the full moon day or likewise on the new moon day incurs the sin of killing a cow; of this there is no doubt. Regarding this, it has been stated that during the aforementioned occasions such as death and so forth, one should not bathe with hot water, but rather with water drawn from another source; thus, there is no contradiction. Vyāsa states a specific rule concerning bathing with hot water:
"Hot water, infused with the collection of mantras, poured into cold water—even at home—is praised; the wise know it to be equal to bathing in a river.
As for the secondary form of bathing (*gauṇa-snāna*), he will explain it himself later on.
Thus concludes the ritual bath;
now follows the procedure for the *saṃdhyā*. Regarding that, Dakṣa describes the nature of *saṃdhyā*:
"The junction of day and night, devoid of both sun and stars,"
"That, however, is declared as *saṃdhyā* by the sages who perceive the truth.

Although here the word *saṃdhyā* is understood as denoting time, nevertheless, the deity to be worshipped at that time is indicated by the word *saṃdhyā*. Thus, having indicated the worship of the deity, the word *saṃdhyā* is employed in the root text with reference to the ritual action (*karman*). Alternatively, *saṃdhyā* is the rite (*kriyā*) occurring at the junction (*saṃdhi*). For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"One worships at the juncture-time of night and day."
"Therefore, the wise call that very [period] 'saṃdhyā' (the junction).
Regarding that very rite, Yājñavalkya the Yogin prescribes:
"One should perform the saṃdhyā worship at the junction, neither when the sun has set nor when it has risen."
And that *saṃdhyā* is of three kinds. As it was said by Atri:
"The knower of the Self who is twice-born must always perform the three *saṃdhyās*.
Regarding this, Vyāsa states the difference in the names of the deity according to the distinction of time:
In the forenoon she is named Gāyatrī, at midday she is Sāvitrī, and in the evening she is Sarasvatī;
thus that very Sandhyā is remembered as threefold.
Because it protects one from the faults of accepting gifts, from mortal sins, and from minor offenses, the Gāyatrī is so called; for it saves that which sings it.
Because she illumines the sun, she is celebrated as Sāvitrī;
or, because she is the progenitor of the world and consists of the form of speech, she is Sarasvatī.

[290] Thus, the distinction of colors is stated in another Smṛti: "Gāyatrī should be red, Sāvitrī white in color, and Sarasvatī likewise black; they are to be meditated upon according to this distinction of colors."
"Gāyatrī is the form of Brahmā, Sāvitrī is the form of Rudra, and Sarasvatī is the form of Viṣṇu; she is to be worshipped according to these distinct forms. Thus it is said.

*Upāsana* means meditative contemplation (*abhidhyāna*). For this very reason, the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* states: "A learned Brāhmaṇa, performing [the rites] while contemplating the sun as it rises and as it sets, attains all that is auspicious, [realizing]: 'This sun is Brahman. Being Brahman indeed, he goes to Brahman—he who knows thus. The meaning is as follows: Performing the ritual acts such as breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) in the manner that will be described, and meditating on the sun—which is denoted by the word *saṃdhyā* and endowed with the aforementioned name, syllables, and form—as Brahman, one attains all that is auspicious, both of this world and the next. He whose internal organ has been purified by this aforementioned meditation perceives Brahman directly; having previously been Brahman itself, he attained the state of an individual soul (*jīvatva*) due to ignorance, and upon the removal of that ignorance through the aforementioned knowledge, he reaches Brahman itself. Vyāsa also spoke with this very intention.
"One should not practice the *gāyatrī* separately from the *brahman*;
one should worship with the thought 'I am that,' by whatever means prescribed.
[291] Regarding this, Dakṣa states the duration of time for the morning twilight (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*):
"The period beginning with the twilight (saṃdhyā) is said to consist of two nāḍīs at the end of the night;

its conclusion is recorded by the sages as occurring upon the sight of the sun's disc. Up to the time of *saṅgava* is the secondary period for the morning twilight (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*), and up to the end of *pradoṣa* is that for the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*). Thus says Bṛhan-Manu:
"Neither at dawn nor at twilight is the time for the *saṃdhyā* neglected;
both the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*anukalpa*) methods are prescribed for every ritual act.
Thus, the method for the performance of the *saṃdhyopāsti* is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.

"Then, standing on darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward and being well-composed, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and meditate upon the twilight (saṃdhyā); such is the Vedic revelation.
Thus [says] Yājñavalkya as well.
"Having restrained the breaths and sprinkled [himself] with the three verses addressed to the waters," so [says Yājñavalkya, YDh 1.24].
Bṛhaspati says:
"Having assumed the posture, having restrained the vital breaths, and likewise having remembered the Ṛṣis and the rest..."
"With eyes closed and observing silence, one should practice prāṇāyāma.
Regarding the definition of prāṇāyāma, Manu says:
"The Gāyatrī, together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras..."
"One who recites [the Gāyatrī] three times while restraining the breath—that is called prāṇāyāma. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti). Yājñavalkya says:
"One should mutter the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras), preceded by the vyāhṛtis."
"Accompanied by each *praṇava*, this threefold restraint of breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*) is performed. Thus [says Yājñavalkya].
Yogī Yājñavalkya also says:
"Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahar, janaḥ, tapaḥ, and likewise satyam."
Likewise, it is joined with the individual *oṃ*s and that which is beyond "tat savituḥ."
"Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ"—one should employ this as the head [of the mantra] at the end;
through the practice of repeating it three times, it is proclaimed as *prāṇāyāma*.
And that *prāṇāyāma* is to be known as threefold, distinguished by *pūraka*, *kumbhaka*, and *recaka*. Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin:
Inhalation, retention, and exhalation constitute the threefold prāṇāyāma.
Inhalation drawn through the nostrils while the breath is held is called pūraka.
"Kumbhaka is motionless breath; when it is being exhaled, it is recaka.
Regarding *mārjana*, Vyāsa says:
"One should perform *mārjana* with water from *kuśa* grass while reciting the verses beginning with 'āpo hi ṣṭhā'."
One should cast [the seed-syllable] joined with the Praṇava at every step, at the gateway.
One should sprinkle eight drops upwards and downwards for the destruction of those [faults] born of passion,
darkness, and delusion, whether they arise in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep.
"One should burn these nine defects born of speech, mind, and body with the nine [verses]. Thus [it is said]. Prajāpati also [said]:
"With a concentrated mind, one should perform the *mārjana* at the end of each *ṛc* or at the end of each quarter-verse."
"Or one may perform it at the end of the *ardharca*; such is the opinion of the learned.

Regarding the specific sacred part (*tīrtha*) for the ritual rinsing (*mārjana*), Hārīta says: "One should perform the rinsing, worship, offering of oblations (*balikarma*), and eating with the *devatīrtha*. Furthermore, that rinsing should not be performed with water falling from a continuous stream. Thus says Brahmā: "The twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*) is rendered defective by water falling from a stream."
The ancestors do not praise it, nor do the deities praise it.

[294] Thus it is said. How, then, is purification performed? To this, the same author replies: "In a river, at a sacred ford, or in a lake, or even in a vessel made of clay, or one made of udumbara wood, or of gold, silver, or wood."
"Or, having placed [the water] in the left hand, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*).

The word "having placed" implies "water," as is understood from the context. However, when vessels made of clay or other materials are available, the use of the left hand is prohibited. For it is said:
"Those who perform the twilight worship having placed water in their left hand..."
That twilight is to be known as a Vṛṣalī; by her, the Asuras were gratified.

This is because of the traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*); however, in the absence of materials such as clay, the left hand is prescribed by the rule: "Or, having taken [the water] in the left hand. Having thus performed the purification (*mārjana*) according to the stated method, one should drink water with the mantra: "And the Sun" (*sūryaś ca*). Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Having gone to a holy bathing place (*tīrtha*), being self-restrained, bathed, and having washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water according to the rule, he should drink water in the evening with the mantra 'Agni and Wrath' (*agniś ca mā manyuś ca*), and in the morning with 'The Sun and Wrath' (*sūryaś ca mā manyuś ca*). With his hand holding a *pavitra* [strainer], having sprinkled himself with verses addressed to the Earth (*vasumatī*), those containing the word 'water' (*abliṅga*), those addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*), those of golden color (*hiraṇyavarṇā*), the *pāvamānī* verses, the *vyāhṛtis*, and other purificatory texts, he becomes pure. (BDh 2.4.1–2)
Bharadvāja says: "Having said 'Agni and I' in the evening, and 'Sūrya and I' in the morning, one should drink water;
at midday, one should say 'The waters purify me,' and thereafter perform the ritual sipping (ācamana)."
Kātyāyana also says:
One should perform the sprinkling of the head with *kuśa* grass and drops of water,
[reciting] the *praṇava*, *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, and the two *gāyatrīs* as the third.
"And with a verse having the waters as its deity—this is the fourth [step], the *mārjana*. Thus [it is said].
After the *mārjana*, Prajāpati says:
"One should likewise place the hand, filled with water, at the tip of the nose."
"Having recited 'ṛtaṃ ca,' one should then cast that water upon the ground.
Then, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun. And so Vyāsa says:
"Taking water with both hands, it should be consecrated with the *gāyatrī* mantra."
"Standing facing the sun, one should cast [water] upwards three times at the two junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*).

This statement from Kātyāyana—"Having risen, one should offer a handful of water toward the sun with the *trika* [mantra]" (KSm 2.11.10)—refers specifically to the midday *saṃdhyā*. Hārīta also says: "One should cast water mixed with flowers, consecrated by the *Sāvitrī*, with the hollowed palms. Another mantra for the offering of the *arghya* is stated by Viṣṇu:
"Having formed a hollowed palm (*añjali*) with both hands, filled with water, and being composed..."
"One should pour that water onto the ground with the mantra beginning 'ud u tyam'.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should touch water. This is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"In the evening, having sipped water (ācamana) according to the mantra and having sprinkled [oneself], one should offer a handful (añjali) to the Sun."
"Having given [the gift], having performed circumambulation, and having touched [it], one becomes purified. Thus [says the tradition].
The Śruti also states: "In that they proceed by way of circumambulation, thereby they shake off evil. The Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Then, with a concentrated mind, one should worship the rising sun."

"But with various solar mantras originating from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the ritual of worship (upasthāna) should be performed with the mantras prescribed in one's own Vedic branch;
indeed, one should cause the worship of Āditya to be performed with the mantras belonging to oneself.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Vasiṣṭha. In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, this is elaborated upon beginning with the words, "The worship (*upasthāna*) is indeed with the hymns (*sūkta*)," and so forth.

That which has been described for the morning twilight (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*)—starting from "on blades of grass pointing eastward" up until the worship of the Sun—is the same for both of the other twilights as well. Regarding that, Nārāyaṇa has stated the specific procedure for the midday twilight (*madhyāhna-saṃdhyā*):
the sprinkling (*mārjana*) is performed with the mantra "May the waters purify me" (*āpaḥ punantu*) and the verse "O Waters, you are best" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*).
Having properly joined his palms in añjali, he should also recite "ud u tyam" and "citram".
With the mantra "That eye, O God," and also "The swan dwelling in purity," he should recite this with his arms raised, gazing at the sun with a concentrated mind.
"Having worshipped the Sun with the Gāyatrī according to one's ability.
A specific time for this is shown by Śaṅkha:
"The morning twilight [should be observed] while the stars are still visible, and the midday [twilight] during the performance of the bath."

"One should perform the evening twilight worship (saṃdhyā) facing the west with the sun present, according to the prescribed rule. Regarding the phrase "in the ritual of bathing," the meaning is "after the midday bath. Dakṣa states the secondary time for the midday twilight worship:
"The midday [twilight] is accepted as extending until one and a half watches (yāma) before the evening twilight."
Vyāsa states the specific distinctions of location according to the gradations of the three junctions (saṃdhyā):
"The twilight prayer performed at home is said to have a single merit; at the edge of a village, it is tenfold;
by a river, it is a hundred-thousandfold; and in the presence of Viṣṇu, it is infinite."
"The twilight prayer performed outside [a village] is tenfold [meritorious]; at wells and springs it is likewise;
at a famous sacred ford (tīrtha) it is a hundredfold; and on the bank of the Jāhnavī it is a thousandfold. Thus says Śātātapa as well.
"Falsehood, the smell of liquor, and sexual intercourse during the day—
even the food of a *vṛṣala* is purified by performing the *saṃdhyā* outside.

Regarding this, Atri states that when there is a lapse in the ancillary rites such as the ritual circumambulation (*viharaṇa*) while performing the *saṃdhyā* outside, then the three *saṃdhyās* must be performed within the house itself.
"The three twilight prayers (sandhyās) must always be performed by a twice-born who knows the Self;
however, both twilight prayers may be performed by Brahmins even within their homes.

Although it is established that the three twilight prayers should be performed outside because that is the more commendable practice, nevertheless, because the act of moving about [to the sacred site] is enjoined by Śruti and thus possesses greater authority, the evening and morning twilight prayers are permitted within the home in accordance with that injunction. Regarding the specific mantra for the worship during the evening twilight prayer, Nārāyaṇa says:
"Having thus worshipped the Sun with the Vāruṇī verses, one should perform a circumambulation and pay homage to the quarters and the lords of the quarters individually.

The Vāruṇī verses are those beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.6.1). Although the worship of Varuṇa by means of the Vāruṇī verses is established by the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), nevertheless, because direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful, it sets aside the indicative mark and enjoins them specifically for the worship of the Sun. This has been deliberated upon in the third chapter [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra].

For instance, it is heard in scripture: "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with an *aindrī* [verse]. An *aindrī* is that *ṛc* in which Indra is revealed as the deity by virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, such as "Never art thou barren, O Indra; never dost thou fail us" (*kadācana starīr asi nendra saścasi*). In that case, by virtue of the indicative mark, the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra is understood for the worship of Indra. However, by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the accusative case, "the Gārhapatya," its application is for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire. Herein arises a doubt: are both to be worshipped together, or only one? Even if only one, is it whichever one is desired, or is it Indra alone, or is it the Gārhapatya alone?

Regarding this, one position is that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) because *śruti* and *liṅga* possess equal authority and no contradiction is perceived. A second position is that the choice is optional, because once Indra has been invoked, the mantra’s requirement is satisfied; thus, due to the contradiction characterized by the fulfillment of its expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), and because no subsequent restrictive factor is seen, the choice is arbitrary. A third position is that Indra alone should be invoked, because *śruti*, being of the nature of a word, follows the capacity of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*), and since that capacity is what the *śruti* depends upon, it possesses greater force.

The word *indra* occurring in the mantra denotes Śakra by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Because it is derived from the verbal root *idi* in the sense of "supreme sovereignty," it denotes the Gārhapatya fire as being endowed with supreme sovereignty over its own sphere of activity. According to the principle that "there may also be denotation based on a quality," the gender (linga) gives rise to doubt because it is common to both [possibilities].

Now, it might be argued that according to the maxim, "Conventional usage (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga)," Indra alone should be understood here because conventional usage, which produces immediate cognition, is more powerful. If that were so, then in this case, it is *śruti* itself—by virtue of its capacity to produce immediate cognition—that performs the application (*viniyojikā*), rather than the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For thus it has been stated by the Teachers:

"Having understood the meaning of the mantra from the mantra itself, and having subsequently ascertained its power (*śakti*), one postulates a *śruti* for its status as a subordinate element through the force of the mantra's requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*)."
When the mantra has already attained its status as an auxiliary to the Gārhapatya fire through direct Vedic revelation (śruti),
and has thereby been rendered free of expectancy, the postulation of a further Vedic text (śrutikalpanā) is devoid of foundation.
Therefore, because it operates more rapidly, direct assertion (śruti) sublates indicative mark (liṅga).
Therefore, it is established that one should pay homage specifically to the *gārhapatya* fire. Yama praises the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*):
"Those who constantly perform the twilight devotions, their vows well-praised, go to the eternal world of Brahman, their sins shaken off."
Whatever evil one commits by deed, mind, or speech during the day,
one destroys that by sitting for the evening twilight prayer with breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever evil one commits by deed, thought, or speech during the night,
one dispels it by performing the morning twilight devotions with breath-control exercises.
"By virtue of the long *saṃdhyā*, the sages attained long life,
as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Thus, Dakṣa has shown that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform it.
"One who neglects the twilight prayers is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever other rite he performs, he shall not partake of its fruit. Thus says Gobhila as well.

"He by whom the twilight [devotions] are not known, and he by whom the twilight [devotions] are not performed, remains a Śūdra while living and is reborn as a dog after death. Thus it is stated; and likewise in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Those evil-minded ones who do not attend upon the morning and evening twilights (*saṃdhyā*), O King, go to the Tāmisra hell.
Thus [it is said] in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* as well.

"O best of the twice-born, that foremost of the twice-born who, having abandoned the salutation of the *saṃdhyā*, exerts effort elsewhere in religious duties, goes to ten thousand hells. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.31). All of this refers to one who is not in a state of distress; and so says Yājñavalkya:
"But that Brahmin who would abandon [his wife] while she is not afflicted is equal to a Śūdra;
he must perform penance and becomes censured in the world.
Thus says Atri as well.
"Those twice-born who do not attend upon the twilight prayers while in a state of health surely harm the blessed Sun, the Lord.
Thus it is stated; and also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Attendance at the two twilights is required of a king at all times, except in cases of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), ritual impurity (*āśauca*), confusion, illness, or fear. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.97).
Regarding the period of birth-impurity and similar states, Marīci states that even if one possesses the capacity, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) must not be performed.
"In the state of impurity (sūtaka), the abandonment of rituals such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and others is prescribed.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Pulastya:
"One should perform the twilight prayers, the sacrifice (iṣṭi), and the fire-oblation (homa) for as long as one lives."
One should not abandon [the fire] even during a period of impurity; by abandoning it, one goes to a lower state.
Thus, this refers to the intention of mental *saṃdhyā*. For it has been stated by that very [author]:
"During both birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), one should not abandon the *saṃdhyā* rite;
O twice-born ones, one should mentally recite the mantras, with the exception of *prāṇāyāma*."

"Having understood this, he who performs the twilight devotions with firm vows shall obtain long life and be liberated from all sins. Thus ends the procedure for the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā-vidhi*).
[303] Now follows the procedure for the recitation (japa) as an ancillary part of the twilight rites (saṃdhyā). Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having sipped water (ācamya), being pure and composed, one should constantly perform both twilights."
"In a pure place, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of what is to be recited according to the rule.

When the question "How? arises, Śaṅkha says: "Seated upon a mat of *kuśa* grass, or on a seat made of three *kuśa* blades, with *kuśa* blades as a sacred ring (*pavitra*) in his hand, facing north or facing the sun, and taking up a rosary, he should perform the recitation while meditating upon the deity. Vyāsa also says:
"Then one should recite the Gāyatrī together with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*."
Yogiyājñavalkya, however, states even at the end [of the recitation] for the purpose of the yoga of the *praṇava*:
"Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, one should utter the *gāyatrī* and the *praṇava* at the end; thus is the recitation described."
Baudhāyana also says: "One should mutter [the mantra] with the *praṇava* at both ends and accompanied by the *savyahṛti*.
In the Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa, the different types of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) are set forth.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is of three kinds; learn its divisions:
it is traditionally held to be threefold—vocal, whispered, and mental.
[304] "Of the three types of recitation-sacrifices (*japayajña*), each subsequent one is superior. Thus it is said (NṛPu 58.78–79).
The characteristics of the vocal (*vācika*) and whispered (*upāṃśu*) forms are stated in the Purāṇa:
"That which is uttered with words raised and lowered, with clear syllables and words..."
One should recite the mantra with the voice; this is known as vocal recitation (vācika-japa).

"One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly, so that it is not heard by others even a little; this is known as *upāṃśu-japa*. Thus [it is said]. Viśvāmitra has stated the definition of mental (*mānasa*) recitation:

"When one repeatedly contemplates the meaning of words, moving from syllable to syllable and from word to word by means of the intellect through a sequence of phonemes, that is called mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*).
The relative gradation among these three [types of recitation] has been stated by that same author:
[305] The twice-born say that among all mantras, mental recitation is the best, whispered recitation is considered middling, and vocal recitation is said to be the lowest.

"One [recitation] is said to be for the verbal, a hundred for the whispered, and a thousand for the mental; thus it was declared by Manu, Tri, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. Regarding the rules for recitation, Śaunaka says:
Having placed the hands palms-upward in the morning and likewise palms-downward in the evening,
with the hands at shoulder-level in between— thus is recitation prescribed.

"Satisfaction of mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra, freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of japa. Thus [it is said]. Manu also [says]:

"One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but during the evening, one should remain seated until the stars are clearly visible" (MDh 2.101). The rule for recitation at midday is shown in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Likewise, at the midday twilight, one should recite while seated, facing the east.
Regarding those things to be avoided, Vyāsa says:
"Neither walking, nor laughing, nor looking toward the side..."
Neither leaning against anything, nor talking, nor likewise with his head covered;
"One should not recite while stepping with one foot upon the other, nor likewise with the hands;
nor with an unconcentrated mind, nor while making others hear [the words]. Thus also says Baudhāyana.
"One engaged in ritual action should avoid contact below the navel. Thus [says Baudhāyana] (BDh 1.5.18). Vyāsa also says:
"One should not speak at the time of recitation (*japa*), nor during vows, fire-offerings (*homa*), and the like."

"But if a most excellent twice-born man should arrive while one is occupied with these very [tasks], then, having saluted the brahmin, one should inquire after his *yogakṣema*. Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin as well.
"If at any time during the recitation (*japa*) and other rites there should be a lapse in the restraint of speech,
one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu. Thus says Saṃvarta as well.

"Having heard worldly gossip and the like, having seen, touched, or spoken it, and that which is muttered without counting—that all shall be fruitless. Here, "spoken" (prabhāṣita) means a person who speaks much. Gautama also says:
Whether walking or standing, or performing actions according to one's own will,
or being impure— without this counting, all that becomes fruitless.
One should avoid anger, greed, sleep, spitting, yawning, and the sight of dogs or low-born persons during the act of recitation.
One should sip water; if these [substitutes] are available, one should remember Viṣṇu, who is worshipped by the gods;
or one should praise the luminaries, or perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
"One should [recite] before a fire, cows, Brahmins, or even ascetics for the sake of purification.
Regarding the restriction of place, Yājñavalkya has stated:
"One should recite in a fire-sanctuary, at the edge of water, or even in a temple."
"At a sacred bathing place, in a cow-pen, in a field of the twice-born, or in one's own home. Śaṅkha also says:
"Recitation performed at home is said to have a single merit; at a river and the like, it is remembered as having double the merit."
In a cow-pen it is tenfold; in a fire-sanctuary, it is more than a hundredfold.

"In the fields of the Siddhas, at sacred fords (tīrthas), and in the presence of a deity, [the merit] is a hundred thousand times ten millionfold; in the presence of Viṣṇu, it is infinite. Thus it is stated, and also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Since Guhyakas, Rākṣasas, and Siddhas carry it off by force, one should therefore always perform the recitation (*japa*) in a solitary and auspicious place. Thus [it is said].
Yogi-Yājñavalkya states the number for the recitation:
"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) and one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should recite it one hundred and eight times;
a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and an ascetic (yati) should recite it more than a thousand times. Thus it is stated in another Smṛti.
"At the new moon, at a *śrāddha*, and at nightfall, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* ten times;
during the periods of non-study (*anadhyāya*), twenty-eight times; and on auspicious days, according to the sequence. Thus says Yama as well.
"One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī, the goddess who has a thousand as her maximum, a hundred as her middle, and ten as her minimum, which destroys all sins.

Thus [it is said]. Āpastamba also says: "Seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, with his hands containing water and facing the east, one should repeat the Sāvitrī a thousand times, a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times."
Thus ends the rule for recitation.
Regarding the rosary which is an auxiliary to the recitation, Hārīta says:
"A rosary made of conch-shell or silver, or one made of gold or blue lotuses."
And with lotus seeds, rudrākṣas, corals, gems, and pearls.
"A rosary made of silver, *indrākṣa* seeds, or likewise the joints of the fingers,
as well as a rosary made of *putrajīva* fruit, is indeed recommended for the practice of recitation (*japa*).
Thus says Gautama as well.
Counting with the fingers is declared to be a single unit;
with a line it is eightfold, and with *putrajīva* seeds it is ten times more.
With conch shells and coral, it should be one hundred; with crystal, one thousand;
with sphatika stones, ten thousand; and with pearls, it is said to be one hundred thousand.
"Ten lakhs with lotus seeds, but with golden ones it is said to be ten million;
with knots of *kuśa* grass and *rudrākṣa* beads, an infinite fruit is said to be obtained. Thus [it is stated].
Now, Prajāpati states the number of beads in the rosary:
One should perform [the rite] with one hundred and eight [verses], or likewise with fifty-four;
it should be performed with twenty-seven, but it is not recorded as being fewer than that.
A rosary of one hundred and eight beads is proclaimed as the best;
that which consists of fifty-four beads is proclaimed as the middling.
"The twenty-seventh [finger] is always declared to be the lowest. Thus [it is said]. Gautama also says:
"One should know that the thumb bestows liberation, while the index finger destroys enemies."
The middle finger is for those desiring wealth, and likewise, the ring finger is for nourishment.
The little finger is said to be for protection and is auspicious for the act of recitation;
one should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers.
"Recitation performed without the thumb shall be fruitless.
Thus [it is said]. Vyāsa praises the recitation of the Gāyatrī:
"If that [Gāyatrī] is recited ten times, whatever has indeed been done [over the course] of three days [is accomplished]."
That evil is swiftly dispelled; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
When that goddess is recited one hundred times, she is known as the pacifier of the flood of sins;
when she is recited one thousand times, that goddess is the destroyer of minor offenses.
"By a hundred thousand recitations, it likewise destroys great sins;
by ten million recitations, O King of Kings, one shall obtain whatever one desires.
Thus [says] Yama as well.
"There is no recitation higher than the Gāyatrī; there is no muttering higher than the Gāyatrī;
there is no meditation higher than the Gāyatrī; there is no oblation higher than the Gāyatrī.
Thus [says] Manu as well.
"He who studies this day after day for three years without sloth, he attains the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind yet possessing a form. (MDh 2.82). Gautama also says:
[311] By this method, one should constantly perform the recitation with diligence.
Being pleased, he attains abundant enjoyments, as well as worldly experience and liberation. Thus ends the section on the twilight prayers and the recitation.
Now, the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*). Regarding this, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"Then, having returned home, the brahmin, having sipped water according to the rule, shall kindle the fire and offer oblations to Jātavedas according to the prescribed rite. (KūPu 1.2.18.50)
Dakṣa also says:
"At the conclusion of the twilight rites, however, the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed to be performed by oneself;
whatever fruit may arise from a self-performed oblation, that cannot be obtained by another."
Whatever fruit has been declared for one who offers oblations himself at home,
half of that fruit is obtained when the oblation is offered by another.

"The officiating priest (ṛtvij), a son, a teacher (guru), a brother, a sister’s son (bhāgineya), and then the husband of a daughter (viṭpati)—whatever is offered by these as well is indeed considered an offering made by oneself. Here, "husband of a daughter" (viṭpati) means a son-in-law (jāmātṛ). The offering performed by oneself is primary; in its absence, the offering may be performed by the officiating priest and others. A specific rule regarding this is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"A priest, a son, a wife, a disciple, or even a uterine brother—having obtained permission, they may especially offer oblations according to the rule. Thus [it is said].
The Śruti demonstrates the gradation of the officiating priests (*hotṛ*).
[312] One oblation offered by a disciple is better than a hundred oblations offered by others;
one oblation offered by a son is better than a hundred oblations offered by disciples.
