"Indeed, a single oblation made by oneself is better than a hundred oblations made by one's sons.

Thus, even in the case of oblations performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, they must take place in the presence of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This has been stated by Kātyāyana: "The oblation must not be offered by the officiating priests and others in the absence of the husband and wife."
"But if it should be offered in the absence of both, the *huta* offering becomes useless.
(KSm 3.20.1) The presence of both is primary; however, in its absence, it can still be offered even with the presence of only one. And so he [the author] himself says:
"Having entrusted the fire to his own wives, and likewise having appointed a priest..."
"A Brahmin who has business may travel abroad, but he should not dwell there for long without purpose. Thus it is said.
(KSm 2.19.1) The time for the *homa* sacrifice has also been indicated by that same authority:
"As long as the constellations in the sky have not become clearly visible on all sides..."
And its redness does not depart; it is offered in the evening at that time.

[313] Thus says Āpastamba as well: “This day-and-night is indeed like the ocean; its two junctions (*saṃdhi*) are its easily accessible landing-stairs (*gādhatīrtha*). Therefore, one should offer at the junction—so says the *Śailālibrāhmaṇa*. Having seen the stars, or at twilight (*pradoṣa*), or at night (*niśā*), [one offers] in the evening. The two junctions of the day-and-night, which has been characterized as an ocean, are the easily accessible landing-stairs; therefore, the junction is the primary time for the oblation (*homa*). The three times beginning with the sight of the stars are the secondary options (*anukalpa*) for the evening oblation. The rising of a single star is "the sight of the stars"; the rising of all the stars is "twilight" (*pradoṣa*); and the hour of sleep is "night" (*niśā*). The time for the morning oblation is also fourfold, as shown by that same author: “At dawn (*uṣas*), at the rising of the sun (*uṣodaya*), when the time has passed (*samayādhyuṣita*), and in the morning (*prātaḥ*). Manu, however, having combined the first and second [options], speaks of three times.
"When [the sun] has risen, when it has not yet risen, and likewise when it is the time of twilight—sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation" (MDh 2.15).
Vyāsa states the definition of these [times]:
When the sixteenth part of the night has arrived, adorned with planets and constellations, at that time before the sun has risen, the wise man should perform the fire-oblation.
Likewise, at the time of dawn, when the circle of stars has vanished but the sun is not yet visible— that interval is called *samayādhyuṣita*.
"If even a mere line [of the sun] should be seen, accompanied by its rays, one should recognize it as having risen; there, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa). Thus it is said.

Āśvalāyana, however, states another secondary alternative (*anukalpa*): "The morning [time] is until the time when the oxen are yoked. The phrase "the time for the *homa*" is understood to carry over. Alternatively, all these specific times are established as primary according to one's own *śākhā*, just like the cases of the *homa* performed after sunrise or before sunrise. But when, for some reason, the primary time is exceeded, then that which was stated by Gobhila should be observed: "Now, if one should not obtain either the sacrificial offering (*havya*) or the officiant (*hotṛ*) for the evening and morning *homas* or for the New and Full Moon sacrifices in the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*), how should he act? The morning oblation does not expire until the evening oblation, nor does the evening oblation expire until the morning oblation; the Full Moon day does not expire until the New Moon day, nor does the New Moon day expire until the Full Moon day. Baudhāyana also [says the same].

"From the evening rite until the morning, and from the morning rite until the evening, the oblation should not be omitted; likewise, the *pārvaṇa* [rite] should not be omitted until the next *pārvaṇa*. One who has fallen into such a state of distress should perform the fortnightly homa (*pakṣahoma*). And so says Marīci:
"Where bodily misfortune occurs, or where distress arises from fear, as well as in other calamities, the *pakṣahoma* (fortnightly oblation) is prescribed.
For one performing the *pakṣahoma*, if the misfortune ceases within the middle of that fortnight, then from that point onward, the oblation must be performed again. Regarding this, Marīci says:
"Having performed the fortnightly offerings (*pakṣahoma*) and then departed from that place, if he returns, he should perform the oblation (*homa*) again; thus he shall not be a partaker of fault.
Thus, even for one performing the *homa* in this manner, if he crosses the boundary (*sīmollaṅghana*), a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādhāna*) must be performed. Kātyāyana states this:

"If one goes beyond the boundary with his wife after leaving the sacred fire, the re-establishment of the fire (*punarādheya*) is prescribed for him when the time for the *homa* has passed. (KSm 3.20.2). However, if the time for the *homa* has not passed, there is no re-establishment of the fire. Regarding this, Śaunaka says:
"But when the husband has gone abroad, if the wife should go to another village, and she arrives at the time for the *homa*, she is not joined with any fault.
Thus [it is said]. He (the same author) states the substance for the *homa*:

Cooked food such as rice-meal and the like is called *kṛta*; rice grains and the like are *kṛtākṛta*; and unhusked grain such as paddy is declared *akṛta*. Thus, the sacrificial offering (*havya*) is said by the wise to be of three kinds.
Among sacrificial offerings, barley is primary; in its absence, rice is prescribed.
In the absence of both rice and barley, one may use either curd or milk.
In the absence of that, one should offer either barley-gruel or water;
when the prescribed substance cannot be obtained, that which resembles it should be accepted.
Just as wheat is to barley and rice is to paddy,
so is clarified butter prescribed as the sacrificial oblation when no specific material is designated among the offerings.
"The established rule is that Prajāpati is the deity of the mantra. Thus [it is said].
Bṛhaspati states the measure of the oblation:
"A prastha of grain is proclaimed to be the measure for sixty-four oblations."
"Half of that [the quantity for sesame] should be for sesame seeds, and half of that again should be for ghee. Thus says Baudhāyana:
"A hundred oblations of either rice or barley are prescribed."
The manner of the fire-oblation (homa) is to be understood according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra. Thus it is stated in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"One should perform the oblation according to the rule prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, in accordance with the injunction. Viṣṇu also says:
When the fire has abundant dry fuel, is well-kindled, is a blazing consumer,
and when it is smokeless and flickering, one should offer oblations for the successful accomplishment of the rite.
"The man who offers oblations into a fire that has no flames and lacks glowing embers is born with weak digestion, afflicted by disease, and suffers from ringworm.
(KSm 1.9.12) This must be performed only after understanding this; otherwise, a fault is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus Aṅgiras says:
"Whatever action is performed according to one's own whim, devoid of knowledge, is like the play of children; all that is purposeless. Thus it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*.
"Knowledge devoid of action is lost, and the actions of the ignorant are lost;
one who does not see is burned by darkness, and even one who sees is lame if he is paralyzed. Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya states the arrangement of the fires according to the Śruti and Smṛti:

"A householder should perform the *smārta* rites daily in the marriage fire (*vivāhāgni*), or in the fire brought at the time of inheritance; however, the *śrauta* rites should be performed in the *vaitānika* fires. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.97). The *vaitānika* fires are the *gārhapatya* and the others. Regarding the procedure for one who possesses both the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, Bharadvāja states:
"Having performed the Vaitānika Homa, the wise man should perform the Smārta [Homa];
because the Smṛtis are rooted in the Vedas, some have known the Smārta as such from of old. Thus says Śātātapa as well.

"That which is prescribed by the Śruti he himself should perform; another may also perform that which is prescribed by the Smṛti. In case of incapacity, even another may perform the Śrauta rite, and at the very least, the customary practice (ācāra).
Regarding the aforementioned fire, Garga states its necessity:
A twice-born man who has taken a wife must not remain even for a moment without the sacred fire;
if he should so remain, he becomes a *vrātya* and likewise falls from his status.

"Just as bathing, as a wife, and as the study of the Veda, so too is the performance of worship (upāsana) prescribed; one should not remain separated from it. Thus, when the capacity for Vedic practice exists, one should not be satisfied with merely that which is ordained by Smṛti. Regarding this, he (the same author) says:
That Brahmin who, out of delusion, disregards Vedic rites and performs only those prescribed by the Smṛtis and Itihāsas, is not joined with merit.
"Vedic action is primary, while other [action] is subordinate;
however, one who is devoted to the subordinate, having abandoned the primary, goes to a downward state.
Regarding one who is incapable [of the former], Vyāsa said:
"If one is unable to perform the *śrauta* rites, one should practice the *smārta* rituals;
if one is also unable to perform those, the wise person should adopt the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*).
Thus Aṅgiras praises the fire-oblation (*homa*).
"Whether one should give Mount Meru of gold and the earth together with its oceans, that may or may not be equal to the morning and evening *homa*.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, the sacred ash (*bhasman*) should be worn. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"The sacred ash (narya) must indeed be worn by those who maintain the *agnihotra* at the conclusion of the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), that which arises from the *aupāsana* fire is called *brahma*.
And there is another *smṛti* passage beginning with: "And having offered [the oblation], one should [mark oneself] with ash," and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the fire-oblation (*homaprakaraṇam*).

In this manner, within the fundamental statement, "The twilight bath, recitation, and oblation," the rites ending with the oblation have been defined. These are to be completed during the first division of the day, which is divided into eight parts. Although the midday bath and other such rites have also been defined, they are not to be performed in the first division because they were defined in connection with the morning bath and subsequent rites. Dakṣa demonstrates the eightfold division of the day and the specific duties to be performed therein.
The duty for him is prescribed for the first part of the day,
as well as for the second, third, fourth, and fifth parts.
"And in the sixth, seventh, and eighth [stages] respectively—
in these divisions— I shall explain the duties in their entirety," and so forth. (DaŚm 2.3–4)

Now, the worship of the deities should be described in accordance with the root text. Regarding that worship, some say it occurs immediately after the morning fire-oblation (*prātarhoma*). Marīci states this:
"Having performed the worship of the deities immediately after the morning fire-oblation.
"Others say that [the worship of the deities] should follow immediately after the recitation of the *brahmayajña*. And so says Hārīta:
'One should perform the worship of the deities immediately after the *japayajña*.
This is also stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:"

"Having wrung out the bathing cloth and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), being restrained in speech, one should worship the gods with their own mantras using leaves, flowers, and likewise with water. (KūP 1.2.18.90).

In this regard, we shall describe the worship of the gods following the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*). Since it occurs immediately after the morning fire-oblation (*prātarhoma*), those rites which follow the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*)—though not explicitly mentioned in the root text—are now stated because they are established by the sequence of the daily observance (*āhnika*). Dakṣa states the duties to be performed after the fire-oblation:

"Then, having performed the duties toward the gods and having beheld auspicious objects and the guru. (DaSm 2.23) "Auspicious objects" refers to mirrors and the like. This is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Yellow pigment, sandalwood, gold, a deer-horn, a mirror, and a gem..."
"A wise man should always look upon his guru, fire, and the sun at dawn.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), a person should attend to the grooming of his hair."
"And the touching of a mirror, collyrium, auspicious *dūrvā* grass, and so forth" (ViP 3.11.21).
Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If one desires long life, one should behold one's own self in clarified butter."
Nārada also said: "In this world there are eight auspicious things: a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, fire, gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise a king as the eighth."

"Whoever should constantly behold these, bow down to them, worship them, and perform circumambulation around them—in this way, indeed, his lifespan does not diminish. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:

"The builder of the fire-altar, a tawny cow, one who has completed a sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify merely by being seen; therefore, one should look upon them constantly.
Thus it is said, and also in the Vāmana Purāṇa:

Having performed the *homa* and the touching of auspicious objects, it is recommended that he then go outside. [He should touch] *dūrvā* grass, *sparśī*, curd, a water-pot, a cow with its calf, a bull, gold, clay, cow dung,
a *svastika* diagram, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), oil, honey, and a Brahmin girl.

[322] “One should touch white flowers, as well as the *śamī* tree, fire, sandalwood, the orb of the sun, and the *aśvattha* tree; thereafter, one should perform the duties pertaining to one’s own caste. Thus [says the Vāyu Purāṇa, 14.35–36]. Bharadvāja also says:
"Having scratched his back and performed obeisance to the Aśvattha tree, he should approach all his elders and likewise salute the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus [it is said]. When there is a gathering of Brāhmaṇas and a desire arises as to who should be saluted first, Manu says:
"Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should first salute the person from whom that knowledge was received. (MDh 2.117).
He [Manu] himself states that at the time of salutation, one should announce one's own name.
After the salutation, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name."
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name. (MDh 2.122–24)

[323] Thus: the meaning of the phrase "after the salutation" (*abhivādāt param*) is that after uttering the word "I salute" (*abhivādaye*), one should subsequently utter the words "O sir, I am so-and-so by name. Āpastamba describes the manner of salutation: "A Brāhmaṇa should salute, extending his right arm level with his ear; a Kṣatriya level with his chest; a Vaiśya level with his waist; and a Śūdra should remain low with palms joined in reverence" (ĀpDh 1.2.5.16–17). Viṣṇu prohibits saluting with only one hand: "Whatever dharma one may perform with the mind from birth onwards..."
"All that indeed becomes fruitless from saluting with only one hand. (MDh 2.118).
And this must be done after rising; regarding that, Manu says:
"For the vital breaths of a youth depart upward when an elder arrives."
"By rising to meet them and by saluting them, one regains those [merits]. (MDh 2.120).
Regarding the blessing that must be spoken by one who has been saluted, that same author says:
"A Brahmin, when being saluted, should be addressed as 'May you be long-lived, O gentle one! (MDh 2.126).
"And the letter 'a' should be uttered at the end of this name, with the preceding syllable protracted. (MDh 2.125)

That which has a preceding syllable is "pūrvākṣara. And by implication, the preceding syllable is a consonant (*vyañjana*), because it is impossible for vowels to be preceded by other vowels. Consequently, the final vowel situated at the end of the consonants within the name of the person offering salutation is to be protracted (*plāvanīya*). By means of the letter *a*, only the final vowel is indicated, since it is impossible for all names to end in the letter *a*. When this is the case, the usage is as follows: "May you be long-lived, O gentle Devadatta! He himself states that one who does not know the manner of returning a salutation is not to be saluted.
"A Brahmin who does not know how to return a salutation should not be saluted by a learned man; he is just like a Śūdra" (MDh 2.126).
Furthermore, the fault of one who, despite knowing [the proper form], does not offer a return salutation is shown in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"But he who, when a salutation has been performed, does not return the salutation or the blessing,
O best of the Kurus, goes to many hells.
Thus [says] Yama as well.
But he who does not offer a blessing to one who has first saluted him incurs a share of whatever evil that person may have committed.
Therefore, one who knows the Dharma should be the first to speak even to a Caṇḍāla;
he should say, "Drink wine," for in this way the Dharma is not lost.
"A Brahmin should say 'Svasti' (May it be well); a Kṣatriya, 'Āyuṣmān' (May you be long-lived);
a Vaiśya, 'Vardhatām' (May [it] increase); and a Śūdra should say 'Svāgatam' (Welcome). Thus [says the law]; Manu also [says]:
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, about his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, about his prosperity; and a Śūdra, about his health alone.
"But a woman who is the wife of another and not related by birth, one should address her as 'lady' (*bhavati*), or as 'fortunate one' (*subhage*), or as 'sister' (*bhaginī*). (MDh 2.128, 129).

It was stated [above] that "one should salute an elder" (MDh 2.122); when it is asked how much time constitutes being an elder, Āpastamba says: "A *śrotriya* who is three years senior deserves a salutation. (ĀpDh 1.4.14.13). Manu also [says]:

Friendship with fellow citizens is based on a ten-year age difference; that with artists, on a five-year difference; that with Vedic scholars, on a three-year difference; and among those of the same lineage, even a very small difference [qualifies as friendship]. (MDh 2.135)

[326] Thus: among residents of the same city, one who is ten years older becomes a senior friend (*pūrva-sakha*); one more than that is a superior (*jyāyān*). Among those who possess the arts, such as those learned in music and so forth (*kalābhṛt*), one five years older is a senior friend; among those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one three years older is a senior friend; one more than that is a superior. Regarding one's own kin, such as brothers and others, even if they are only slightly older in age, they are senior friends; one more than that is a superior—this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: since Yājñavalkya has declared that the officiating priests and others are worthy of honor in the verse, "These are to be honored" (YDh 1.35), does it not follow that they must be saluted even if they are younger? If this is argued:

That is not so, because respectability is established through rising to meet and addressing [the elder]. For this very reason, Gautama states that they are not to be saluted: "But for officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger, there is only rising to meet and addressing" (GDh 6.4). Addressing (*abhivādana*) means speaking to (*abhibhāṣaṇa*). And as Baudhāyana says: "But for officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger, there is rising to meet and addressing" (BDh 1.2.3.45). And this refers specifically to Brahmins. Thus also says Śātātapa:
A Brahmin must always be saluted with reverence, honored with prostrations, and indeed venerated with the head by Kṣatriyas and others who desire prosperity.
A Brahmin must never salute Kṣatriyas and others under any circumstances,
even if they are endowed with knowledge, action, and virtue, and are highly learned.
"Having saluted a Śūdra, a twice-born man should perform a bath with his clothes on;
by properly saluting one hundred Brāhmaṇas, he becomes purified. Thus says Viṣṇu as well.
"In all assemblies, at sacrifices, and in royal palaces, one should perform a salutation (*namaskāra*), but one should not offer a formal greeting (*abhivādana*).

Regarding the clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) toward teachers and others, Gautama says: "The clasping of the teacher's feet [should be performed] in the morning" (GDh 1.19). Here, "teacher" refers to the *ācārya*, because he himself says: "[It applies] to the mother, the father, their relatives, those born before oneself, teachers of knowledge, and the teachers of those [knowledge-teachers]" (GDh 1.19). Manu states the definition of the clasping of the feet:
"The clasping of the Guru's feet should be performed with crossed hands;
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand" (MDh 2.72).

The meaning is that the Guru’s left and right feet are to be touched by one's own left and right hands respectively. Baudhāyana also states: "Having touched the ears and composed the mind, [one should perform the clasping] below the knees down to the feet" (BDh 1.2.3.27); the words "one should perform the clasping" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. And this [rite] must also be performed for the wives of the Guru. Thus says Manu:
The wives of one's teachers who are of the same caste should be honored like the teachers themselves;
those of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by greeting them.
"A wife of one's brother may be saluted day after day, even if she is of the same caste;
however, upon returning from a journey, the wives of kinsmen and relatives must be saluted. (MDh 2.210, 132).
Since salutation would thus appear to apply without distinction, the same author states an exception in certain cases:
A young wife of the guru, however, should not be saluted by touching her feet here by one who is twenty years of age and capable of discerning virtues and faults.
"Anointing, bathing, the rubbing of the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these must not be performed for the wife of one's guru. When it is asked what, then, should be done in that regard, he [Manu] says the following:
[329] However, on this earth, a young man should duly perform a salutation to the wives of his elders who are young women, saying, "I am so-and-so."
"Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet [of the teacher] and offer salutations every day to the teacher’s wives, remembering the dharma of the virtuous. (MDh 2.216–17)

Regarding those whom one should avoid when offering salutation, Āpastamba says: “One should not offer salutation while wearing shoes, with the head wrapped, or with the hands not washed” (ĀpDh 1.4.14.22). Śaṅkha also says: “One should not offer salutation with a water-pot in hand, nor while wandering for alms, nor with flowers or food in hand, nor while impure, nor while reciting prayers, nor while performing rites for the gods or ancestors, nor while lying down. Āpastamba further states: “Likewise, salutation should not be offered to a teacher who is on uneven ground, nor to one who is unpurified; and one should not return a salutation to one who is unpurified. [This applies to] women who are of equal or greater age” (ĀpDh 1.4.15, 19, 20, 21). He says the same elsewhere as well.
A twice-born man who has sacrificial fuel, flowers, kusha grass, clarified butter, water, earth, rice, and unbroken grains in his hands,
while performing recitation or fire-offerings, is likewise not to be saluted.
One should never, under any circumstances, offer salutation to a heretic, one who has fallen from his caste, an outcaste, a perpetrator of a mortal sin, a rogue, an atheist, or an ungrateful person.

A preeminent twice-born man should not offer salutation to one who is running, to one who is intoxicated, to one who has just voided urine or excrement, to one who is eating, or to one who is afflicted by illness.
One should not offer salutation to one who is vomiting, yawning, brushing his teeth, or about to bathe with his head still anointed with oil.

"One should not salute one who holds a ladle in his hand, one who is unknown, one who is incapable, an enemy, one who is afflicted by illness, a yogin, one devoted to austerity, or a younger person. Thus says Śātātapa as well.

"Having saluted out of delusion a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a wife-killer, or a destroyer of the embryo, a twice-born man becomes pure after a day and a night. Regarding the statement, "The clasping of the Guru's feet," when the question arises as to what kind of person is a Guru, Manu says:
"He who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the rules, and supports him with food—he is called the *guru* among Brahmins. Thus [says Manu, MDh 2.142]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"He is a guru who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him. (YDh 1.34).

Teaching pertains specifically to Brahmins; however, the rites beginning with *niṣeka* (conception) are common to all castes. Manu describes the figurative status of a guru for those other than one's father:
"He who benefits another with his learning, whether little or much..."
"One should know him also as a guru here by virtue of his instruction in the revealed scriptures" (MDh 2.149). Hārīta also says:
"The sub-teacher, the father, the elder brother, and likewise the king..."
The maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the protector, the maternal grandfather, and the paternal grandfather.
The eldest by caste and the paternal uncle are remembered as teachers among males;
likewise, the mother, the maternal grandmother, the teacher’s wife, and the uterine sisters of both the father and the mother.
"The mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, an elder sister, and a nurse are like gurus among women.

In this context, the mention of the father and mother is for the purpose of showing that these [women] are also to be honored in the same way. For this very reason, the same author says: "One should follow their will through the actions of mind, speech, and body."
Vyāsa also says: "The maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the paternal uncle, the father-in-law,
the teacher, an elder brother, and a *snātaka* who is not a relative— these are always to be honored like gurus."
"A maternal aunt, the wife of a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, a nurse,
a paternal aunt, a grandmother, the wife of a paternal uncle, and the wife of a teacher— one should behave toward these as toward one's mother. Thus [says] Manu as well.
One should behave toward one's father's sister, one's mother's sister, and one's elder sister as toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they.
"An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya; a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya; but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect. (MDh 2.133, 145).
As for that which...
[333] According to the Dharma, there are two gurus for a person in this world: his father and his mother.
Of these two, the earth is more weighty, and the mother is even more weighty than that.
Between those two as well, the father is superior, because the predominance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.

This statement from the Purāṇa refers to the father who is the instructor, preceded by all the sacraments beginning with *niṣeka*. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement, "The mother alone is more venerable. Vyāsa establishes her greater venerability:
"She who, having carried him in her womb for ten months while tormented by piercing pains, gives birth in a state of fainting due to various agonizing sufferings..."
"A mother who is devoted to her children considers her sons dearer even than her own life;
who is able to repay her for that, even in hundreds of years?
Thus it is said. Regarding the statement, "An Ācārya is ten times [more venerable than] an Upādhyāya," Manu states the defining characteristics of the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya:
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or alternatively the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
"But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*. (MDh 2.141, 140).
Furthermore, even the *ācārya* is indeed more venerable than the father, mother, and others; as he himself says:
"Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world" (MDh 2.146).
Furthermore, he [Manu] himself stated that even one who is a child, if he teaches an elder, is likewise more venerable than him.
Even a young Brahmin becomes a father to an elder if he imparts the sacred mantras;
the child Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his elders,
for having embraced them with knowledge, he said to them, "O my sons!"
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."
The ignorant one is indeed a child, while the giver of mantras is a father;
for they call the ignorant one a "child" and the giver of mantras a "father."
"Neither by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) is great among us. (MDh 2.150–54).

Likewise, Viṣṇu states: "One should behave toward a teacher who is a child or of equal age as one would toward a guru" (ViSm 28.31). Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Purāṇasāra* that one must behave toward an elder brother as one would toward a guru.
O Brahmins, when the father has died, the eldest brother is equal to a father;
all the younger brothers, following his will, should pay him homage.
"And they should depend on him alone, just as they would on a father. So too says Manu:
"The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father."
"And they should behave toward him just like a son, as they do toward their own father.
He [Manu] says the same regarding the teacher's teacher: "When the teacher's teacher is present, one should behave toward him as one does toward the teacher" (MDh 2.205).
The same author states that one who has not yet completed his studies (*asamāvṛtta*) should not salute maternal uncles and others without the permission of his teacher:

"And one should not salute one's own elders without being dismissed by the teacher" (MDh 2.205). For one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*), however, there is no need for such permission. To this effect Āpastamba says: "By one who has returned home, all elders are to be saluted with clasping of the feet upon returning from a journey" (ĀpDh 1.4.14.7–8); and: "In the event of a meeting between the teacher and the sub-teacher (*prācārya*), having saluted the sub-teacher, he should desire to clasp the feet of the teacher" (ĀpDh 1.2.8.19). The same author praises the act of salutation:
"For one who is habituated to salutation and who constantly serves the elders, four things increase: life-span, wisdom, fame, and strength" (MDh 2.121). Thus ends the section on salutation.
Now, the duties for the second part of the day are described. Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
"And likewise, in the second part [of the day], the study of the Vedas is prescribed. (DaSm 2.26). In the Kūrma Purāṇa:

Then, O best of the twice-born, the twice-born man should diligently practice the study of the Vedas according to his ability; he should recite them, teach them to disciples, retain them in memory, reflect upon them, and examine the scriptures concerning dharma and other subjects. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.55–56)
[337] Thus Manu praises the study of the Vedas:
"The best of the twice-born, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda alone;
for the study of the Veda is declared here to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin."
"The Veda is the eternal eye of the sages, gods, and humans" (MDh 2.166–67). Vyāsa also said:
"Dharma is not known from any other source; it has shone forth from the Veda alone."
"Therefore, with every effort, one should rely upon the Veda for the sake of Dharma. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Of sacrifices, of austerities, and indeed of auspicious deeds..."
"The Veda alone is the supreme means for bringing about the ultimate good of the twice-born" (YDh 1.40).
Likewise, Manu demonstrates that all ritual acts of one devoid of the Veda are fruitless:
"Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, and just as a cow is fruitless with another cow," so too is he.
"Just as a gift given to one who lacks knowledge is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows no Rigvedic verses fruitless. (MDh 2.158).
Regarding this very same period, Dakṣa states another duty:
"That is declared to be the time for gathering fuel-sticks, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth. (DaSm 2.28).
Thus ends the duties of the second watch.
Now follows the duties of the third watch. Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
"And likewise, in the third part [of the day], one should accomplish the welfare of those to be supported. Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Then, for the sake of securing one's well-being (*yogakṣema*), one should approach the Lord."
"Then the twice-born man should accomplish various aims for the sake of his family. (KūP 1.2.18.57).
And the group of those to be supported has been shown by Dakṣa:
"The mother, the father, the teacher, the wife, the offspring, the indigent, and the dependent."

"The guest who has arrived and the sacred fire are declared to be among those who must be supported" (DaŚm 2.29). One should acquire wealth for the sake of subsistence according to one's own prescribed mode of life. Thus Manu says:
"For the sake of accomplishing mere subsistence, by means of one’s own irreproachable occupations..."

"One should accumulate wealth without causing distress to the body" (MDh 4.3). "Blameless occupations" refers to teaching and so forth; these have already been defined. Now, one might object: "These occupations belong only to the Brāhmaṇa, not to the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya. To this, Manu says:
Three duties would cease for a Brāhmaṇa with respect to a Kṣatriya:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts.
"In the same way, these [means] would cease for a Vaiśya; such is the established rule. (MDh 10.77–78).
Therefore, teaching and the like are not means of acquisition for those two [the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya]. Certainly. For this very reason, another means has been stated by that same author:

"Bearing weapons and missiles is the duty of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya" (MDh 10.79). Here, "trade" (*vaṇik*) means commerce, and "cattle" (*paśu*) means the tending of livestock. Yājñavalkya also states:
"The primary duty of the Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects."
"Laziness, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are recorded as the [duties] of the Vaiśyas" (YDh 1.119).
Manu states the other means [of livelihood]:
"There are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest," and so forth.

"Usury, the practice of agriculture and trade, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous" (MDh 10.115). Here, *dāya* is wealth inherited through lineage; *lābha* is the discovery of a treasure-trove. Acquisition through inheritance, discovery, purchase, and lineage belongs to all four castes (*varṇas*). Victory belongs to the Kṣatriya alone. *Prayoga* is the lending of money for the sake of interest. *Karmayoga* is agriculture and trade. The practices of usury and agriculture/trade belong to the Vaiśya alone. The acceptance of gifts from the virtuous belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. Also, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "The householder should be known to be of two kinds: the seeker (*sādhaka*) and the non-seeker (*asādhaka*)."
They say that teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts belong to the former [type].
Furthermore, a householder who is a seeker of spiritual perfection may subsist by gathering grains or picking ears of corn;
however, he who is declared not to be a seeker of perfection remains established in the householder stage of life.
"Two modes of subsistence, *śila* and *uñcha*, have been declared for him by the supreme seers. Alternatively, one may live on *amṛta* or even on *mṛta* in times of distress.
That which is unasked for is *amṛta*; but alms obtained by begging is *mṛta*. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.25.1–2)
Manu also says:
"One may live by means of *ṛta* and *amṛta*, or by *mṛta* and *pramṛta*, or even by *satya* and *anṛta*; but never by the livelihood of a dog."
[341] One should know that *ṛta* is the gleaning of grains; *amṛta* is what is obtained unasked;
*mṛta* is alms-food obtained by begging; and agriculture is traditionally known as *pramṛta*.
"Trade involves both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed subsist by it;
service is declared to be the 'dog's livelihood,' therefore one should avoid it. (MDh 4.4–6).
*Uñcha* is the gathering of single grains that have fallen and been discarded. *Śila* is the gathering of ears of rice and other crops that have fallen and been abandoned. Yājñavalkya also says:

"Whether he possesses a granary or a jar, or one who provides for three days, or even one who does not provide for tomorrow; or he may live by gleaning ears and picking grains—among these, each subsequent one is superior. (MDh 4.7) A *kuśūla* is a small storehouse; one who collects grain sufficient to fill it is a *kuśūladhānya*. One who collects grain sufficient for three days is a *tryāhika*. One who has no concern for the morrow (*na śvastana-cintā*) is an *aśvastana*, meaning one who procures what is needed for the immediate present. The modes of livelihood for these, ending with the *aśvastana*, are to be understood as those declared by Manu. Thus he says:

"One among these performs the six duties; another proceeds by means of three; one by means of two; but the fourth lives by the *brahmasattra*. (MDh 4.9) The meaning of this is as follows: One, who possesses grain sufficient for a granary (*kuśūladhānya*), should perform the six duties beginning with officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*). Another, the second, who possesses grain sufficient for a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*), should subsist by officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts. A third, who has grain for three days (*tryāhika*), should subsist by two [of the duties], excluding receiving gifts. But the fourth, who does not store enough for the morrow (*aśvastana*), lives by the *brahmasattra*, which means by teaching. The livelihood of a Śūdra, however, has been shown by Uśanas.
"Service to the twice-born, or all crafts,
as well as the sale of all commodities— this is declared to be the duty of a Śūdra.
Thus [says] Yājñavalkya as well.

“The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born; if unable to subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born. (YDh 1.20). Here, the word *ajīvan* is to be split as *a-jīvan* (if not living). Hārīta also says: “The duty of a Śūdra consists of service to the twice-born, avoidance of [forbidden] acts, the maintenance of his wife and others, agriculture, cattle-rearing, carrying loads, trade in commodities both permitted and forbidden, painting, dancing, singing, and playing the flute, lute, and drum.”
Thus concludes the duties for the third part of the day;
now the duties for the fourth part are stated. Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
"In the fourth part likewise, one should take earth for the purpose of bathing. (DaSm 2.36)

The procedure for the midday bath has already been described previously in its proper context. Now follows the procedure for the *brahmayajña*. Its essential nature is shown in the *Taittirīya-Brāhmaṇa*: “If one should study even a single *ṛc*, *yajus*, or *sāman* as one's own sacred recitation (*svādhyāya*), that constitutes the completion of the *brahmayajña*. It is also stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*: “O Brahmin, the study of one’s own Vedic branch is traditionally known as the *brahmayajña*” (LiPu 1.26.16). Regarding its time, Bṛhaspati says:

"And that [offering] should be performed either before the satiation of guests, or after the morning oblation, or at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva; it is not to be done on any other occasion except for a specific cause.
Here, by the word "Vaiśvadeva," the ritual ending with the *manuṣyayajña* (the sacrifice to humans) is intended. For this reason, it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"If the Brahmayajña has not been performed prior to the libation (tarpaṇa), one should perform the Manuṣyayajña and then begin the study of the Veda (svādhyāya). (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.104)

And the Śruti mentions direction, place, and time: "One who is about to perform the *brahmayajña* [should go] from the village toward the eastern direction, the southern direction, the northern direction, or the intermediate direction between east and north, when the sun has risen and the roofs are no longer visible. By the expression "when the roofs are no longer visible," a specific location is indicated; the meaning is: "in a place where roofs—that is, coverings for houses such as grass, mats, and so forth—are not seen. By the phrase "when the sun has risen," it prohibits the time prior to sunrise, but it does not enjoin immediate sequence after sunrise, because that [moment] is the time for the *homa*. Manu also describes the procedure regarding place and other factors.
Having gone to the forest, self-controlled and composed, he should recite the Sāvitrī, following the daily rule near water. (MDh 2.104)

[345] Thus, the Śruti declares the duties to be performed, beginning with the *avīta* (the non-exclusion) rite: “Having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*upavīya*), having sat down, having washed both hands, one should sip water three times, wipe the mouth twice, and touch the body once—touching the head, the eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, and the heart. And: “Having spread out a great quantity of *darbha* grass, having assumed the *upastha* posture, and sitting facing east, one should study the Veda (*svādhyāya*”). And: “Having placed the right hand over the left and having held them along with the *pavitra* blades of grass, one begins with ‘Oṃ’. And: “One should employ exactly these three: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*. And: “Then one recites the *Sāvitrī* Gāyatrī three times—verse by quarter, then by half-verse, and finally without pausing. And: “In a village, one should study the Veda mentally, both by day and by night. And: “Whether the hands are impure, whether in the forest or in the open, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, one should indeed study the Veda. [346] And: “At midday, one should study with great vigor. And: “Reciting the concluding verse ‘Salutation to Brahman’ three times, and touching water, he goes home; then whatever he gives is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The phrase “having gone to the right” means having performed a circumambulation from left to right. And so says Yogiyājñavalkya:
Having circumambulated [the sacred site], paid homage,
and sat down upon *darbha* grass with *darbha* grass held in both hands joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*),
one should perform the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) according to one's ability for the sake of the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). Thus it is said.
Śaunaka, however, states another procedure:
"Having burned away his faults through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), wearing white garments and being pure,
having sipped water according to the rule, he should ascend the layer of darbha grass."
"Having placed the sacred grass in his hand, he should place his right hand over his left [upon his lap]. Thus it is said.

In the cited scriptural passage, immediately after the phrase "having touched [water] once," the words "he should sprinkle his left hand and his feet" must be supplied, because they follow in that same sequence in the subsequent statement regarding the results: "By the fact that he sips water three times, he gratifies the *ṛc*s; by the fact that he wipes [his mouth] twice, he gratifies the *yajus* verses; by the fact that he touches [himself with water] once, he gratifies the *sāman*s; by the fact that he sprinkles his left and right hands and his feet, and touches his head, eyes, nostrils, ears, and heart, he gratifies the *Atharva-aṅgiras*s, the *Brāhmaṇa*s, the *Itihāsas*, the *Purāṇas*, the *Kalpas*, the *Gāthās*, and the *Nārāśaṃsīs*. The meaning of the scriptural passage beginning with "of *darbha* grasses" has been shown by Śaunaka: "Having gone out from the village either toward the east or the north, having bathed in water, being in a pure place, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), having sipped water, and wearing unwet clothes, one should spread a large quantity of *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward; sitting upon them facing east, placing the knees together, joining the right and left hands which hold the *pavitra* strainers, and looking at the junction of heaven and earth, or closing his eyes, in whatever way he considers himself composed, so composed he should recite his *svādhyāya*. He should recite the *Sāvitrī* preceded by the *Vyāhṛti*s and the syllable *Oṃ*: first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, then the whole verse; this is the third time—thus says Śauceya. Śauceya is the son of Śuci; he states that the seer was indeed Ātreya. The connection is with the word "self" (*ātman*) according to the scripture.
One may study mentally in a village or even in a dense forest;
one may study mentally by day or by night,
whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.

In every way, one should certainly study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*). The meaning is that the primary rite must not be abandoned simply because of an incapacity regarding its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). Regarding the recitation (*japya*) for the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), it is shown in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]:
"Beginning with the Veda, whatever one studies day by day according to one's ability, proceeding further and further in sequence, that they call *svādhyāya*."
"Whether it be a Ṛc verse, or a Yajus formula, or even a Sāman chant,
or the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, one should not neglect them according to one's ability. Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.
"One should recite the Vedas, the Atharva, the Purāṇas, along with the Itihāsas, according to one's ability;
for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should recite the spiritual knowledge (ādhyātmikī vidyā). (YDh 1.101).
Regarding the study of the Brahmayajña, Manu states that just as with formal instruction and study, there would otherwise be the contingency of abandoning it on days when study is prohibited.
There is no obligation regarding the study of the Vedas, whether it be the auxiliary sciences or the daily recitation,
nor indeed regarding the fire-oblation mantras, when one is unable to perform them.
In the daily recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice.
It is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call even during times when study is otherwise suspended. (MDh 2.105–06)

[349] Thus: Brahman alone is the substance of the oblation; by that it is offered. An *adhyāya* is that which is studied—the collection of mantras beginning with the *yājyā*. The offering is performed together with that and with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, because there is no time unfit for study (*anadhyāya*). For this very reason, the Śruti, having referred to specific occasions unfit for study, praises the recitation (*japa*) during them: “He who, knowing thus, studies his own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) when the clouds rain, when lightning flashes, when thunder rolls, or when the wind howls at the new moon—verily he performs austerity; for the study of one’s own Veda is austerity” (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15). On those occasions unfit for study, only a small amount should be recited. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: “Now, if the wind blows, or if it thunders, or if it flashes with lightning, or if it crashes with thunder, let him recite a single Ṛc, a single Yajus, or a single Sāman” (ĀpDh 1.4.12.5). When either oneself or one's location is impure, the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) must be avoided; and so the Śruti says: “For this sacrifice, there are two occasions unfit for study: when one is impure, and when the location is [impure]. The Śruti praises the sacrifice to Brahman: [350] “He ascends to the highest heaven; he becomes the best among his equals. As much as one wins the heavenly world by giving away this earth full of wealth, so much a world does he win. Moreover, he conquers a greater and inexhaustible [world], overcomes untimely death, and attains union (*sāyujya*) with Brahman. Yājñavalkya also [says]:
"Whatever sacrifice one studies, one shall obtain the fruit of that very sacrifice;
one enjoys the fruit of giving away the earth filled with wealth three times over. Thus ends the section on the *brahmayajña*. (YDh 1.47–48)
Now follows the procedure for libation (tarpaṇa). Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Having recited the mantras to be chanted prescribed in the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda, as well as the Yajus formulas, one should then perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"For the sake of accomplishing the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayajña), one should mutter knowledge concerning the supreme self;
having muttered either that or the Praṇava, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa)."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa as well:
"Having bathed and wearing clean garments, one should, with a well-composed mind, perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors using the very *tīrtha* belonging to them."
One should offer water three times for the sake of gratifying the gods;
likewise for the sages according to the rule, and once also for Prajāpati.
"O Lord of the Earth, one should offer water three times for the sake of pleasing the ancestors. Thus [says] Vyāsa:
"The gods [receive] one handful each; Sanaka and the others, however, receive two each."
"The ancestors deserve three handfuls each, and women one each. Thus [it is said]. In the *Āgneya Purāṇa*:
"One should satisfy the gods with water poured toward the east, and humans in the middle."
"But for the ancestors, [one should offer] one, two, or three handfuls of water with the tips of the blades pointing south.

In this regard, the number of handfuls is determined according to one's own Vedic school (*śākhā*). Where no specific rule regarding the number is heard in a particular *śākhā*, there is an option (*vikalpa*). In that very context, the specific manner of arranging the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) is shown:
"Rites for the gods are performed with the left [hand], and the libation for the ancestors with the right."
"The satiation of human beings is performed with the *nivīta*.
This means with the *savya*, the *upavīta*, or the left [hand], that is, with the *prācīnāvīta*. And so Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Facing east, wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), [one should offer] with both hands."
"One should perform the libation to the deities with *kuśa* grass blades pointing eastward, using the *devatīrtha* [part of the hand]. Thus [it is said]. Viṣṇu also says:
"Then, having placed the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) around the neck [in the *nivīta* fashion], one should act without sloth."

"One should satisfy human beings individually with the *prājāpatya* tīrtha," so [says] Baudhāyana: "Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one satisfies the ancestors with the formula, 'Svadhā! Homage! I satisfy the ancestors,' and so forth" (BDh 2.5.10.1). As for that which says: "He who offers water with both hands..."
That fool goes headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell.

Thus, the statement of Vyāghrapāda refers to the context of faith (*śraddhā*) and similar matters. For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini says: "In the *śrāddha* rite and at the time of marriage, [the gift] is given with one hand;
however, in the libation (*tarpaṇa*), it must be done with both hands—this is the ancient rule."
And one standing on dry land should not perform this libation (tarpaṇa) in water. Thus says Gobhila:
"Water offered neither in [other] waters nor in vessels, neither by one who is angry nor with only one hand, does not reach [the ancestors], provided it is not poured upon the ground."
[353] Now, one standing on dry land should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) upon the ground itself, and not in water or similar places. And so says Viṣṇu:
"That man who, while standing on dry land, offers water into the water..."
"That water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless.
Regarding this, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"Having put on dry clothing upon a wide expanse of sacrificial grass on dry ground..."
One who knows the ritual rules should perform the libation, but never in a single vessel.
Or, having taken water from the vessel, one should pour it into another auspicious vessel,
or into a pit filled with water, but not onto bare ground without sacrificial grass.
"Because the surface of the earth would become strewn with hair, ashes, husks, charcoal, thorns, and bones, for that reason there is the spreading of sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
As for what was stated by Kārṣṇājini—"One should offer handfuls of water to the deities and the ancestors in water"—that refers to impure locations. Viṣṇu says this:

"Wherever there may be an impure place, one should satisfy the deities and ancestors with water; for everything is established in water. Thus [it is said]. Pitāmaha speaks regarding the specific vessel:
"A vessel made of gold or silver, or originating from copper or bell-metal, is suitable for the libation (tarpaṇa) to the ancestors; however, one should avoid a vessel made of clay. Thus says Marīci.
"Whatever is given to the ancestors in a vessel made of gold, or one made of copper or silver, or in a vessel of udumbara wood, or in a sword-shaped vessel, becomes inexhaustible.
Thus [it is said]. He (the same author) further states: "One should not perform [the offering] with empty hands."
"Without silver and gold, without copper and sesame seeds,
and without mantras and *darbha* grass, [the offering] does not reach the ancestors.
Thus it is said in another *Smṛti*.
"The libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) should be performed with a sword, pearls, or [other items] in hand;
or with jewels, gold, and *darbha* grass; never with empty hands.
Intending that there is neither a conjunction (*samuccaya*) nor an equal option (*samavikalpa*) here, Marīci said:
"But in the absence even of sesame seeds, [one should sprinkle] accompanied by gold and silver;
in the absence of those, one should sprinkle with *darbha* grass or again with the mantra.
Regarding the taking of sesame seeds, Yogi-Yājñavalkya states a specific rule:
"If one sprinkles [water] that has been drawn up, one should mix sesame seeds into the water;
otherwise, the wise should take the sesame seeds with the left hand. This refers to a hairless area. And so says Devala:
"He who offers libations to the ancestors by making sesame seeds appear as if covered in hair—
by him the ancestors are gratified with blood or with filth.
Thus, that same author shows the specific application of sesame seeds according to their different colors.

"A twice-born man should satisfy the gods with white sesame seeds, humans with variegated sesame seeds, and the ancestors by satisfying them with black sesame seeds on all occasions. Thus it is said. Furthermore, a specific distinction regarding the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors is shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
"One should satisfy the gods and the brahminical seers with water containing unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
and the ancestors with devotion using black sesame seeds according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *sūtra*" (KūP 1.2.18.88).
Vyāsa, however, prohibits the libation of sesame seeds on specific lunar days (*tithi*) and other such occasions.

"On the seventh lunar day, on Sunday, at home, and likewise on one's birthday, one who desires servants, sons, or a wife should not perform the libation with sesame seeds. Thus it is said; and also in the Purāṇa:
"O King, on both fortnights, on the seventh day, at night, and during the two twilights—
one who desires wealth, sons, or a wife should avoid sesame seeds on these five occasions. Thus says Baudhāyana as well.
One whose father is living should not perform libations with black sesame seeds on the seventh lunar day,
on Sundays, or on the days of one's birth asterism.
Libation with sesame seeds, which is prohibited inside the house, should be performed outside;
this applies respectively during marriage, the initiation ceremony, and the tonsure ceremony.
"Some say that the libation of sesame water (*tilatarpaṇa*) should not be performed for one year, half a year, or even half of that;

however, it must always be performed for the deceased on specific lunar days (*tithi*) and at special sacred sites (*tīrtha*). Thus [it is said]. Satyavrata indicates those who are to be offered libations:
Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods,
one should then place it around the neck (nivītin) and satisfy the humans with devotion, as well as the sons of Brahmā and the sages.
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and having bent the left knee to the ground,
one should satisfy the deceased (pretas) with darbha grass in hand according to the prescribed rule.
Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin as well.
First, one should satiate Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati;
as well as the Vedas, the meters, the gods, and the sages whose wealth is asceticism.
The Gandharvas who are teachers, as well as the sons of teachers,
the year with its constituent parts, and the divine Apsarases.
Likewise, he [beheld] the gods, the mountains, the nāgas, the oceans, and even the peaks;
as well as the rivers, human beings, yakṣas, and indeed the rākṣasas.
And the Piśācas, the Suparṇas, the spirits (bhūtas), as well as the beasts,
the trees, the medicinal herbs, and the fourfold classes of living beings.
Then, having touched his left knee and facing south,
he should satisfy all the hosts of ancestors with mantras containing their respective names.
“A twice-born man should always satisfy his maternal grandfathers with faith.

Thus says Śaunaka, beginning with: “Agni, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati,” and so forth. For those belonging to the Yajurveda branch, however, the libation to the *kāṇḍarṣis* (the seers of the sections) is prescribed:
“Then, being pure, [one should satisfy] these *kāṇḍarṣis* with handfuls of water.”
"Being undistracted, one should always perform the libation with the mantra consisting of the eight names.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) and standing while facing the direction of the ancestors..."

"One should satisfy the divine and non-divine ancestors with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* [of the hand]. Here, the "divine" are the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas; the "non-divine" are the father and other ancestors. Yogi-Yājñavalkya states:
"The Vasus, Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas, accompanied by salutations."

The word "should satisfy" (tarpayet) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The names of the Vasus and others have been shown by Paiṭhīnasi: Dhruva, Dharma, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Nala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāta—these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata;
Hara, Bahurūpa, and Tryambaka, the lord of the gods.
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita—
these are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the most excellent of the gods.
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Mitra, Varuṇa,
Aryaman, Arcis, Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu.
"These twelve Ādityas are indeed considered the foremost among the gods;
they are the twice-born ancestors who should be worshipped by everyone with great effort.
Thus [it is said]. Thereafter, one should offer libations (tarpaṇa) to one's own ancestors and others. Regarding the procedure for this, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"For each individual person, one should repeatedly cast three handfuls of water with sesame seeds into the air, pronouncing their name and lineage.
Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin.
"Water should be given to those of the same caste, and certainly not to those of a different caste;
one should satisfy them in due order with their lineage names (*gotra*), personal names (*nāman*), and the exclamation *svadhā*.
Regarding the specific procedure even for the utterance of names, Āśvalāyana says:
A name ending in "śarman" is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, one ending in "varman" for a Kṣatriya,
one ending in "gupta" for a Vaiśya, and one ending in "dāsa" for one born as a Śūdra.
"For all four castes, [the libation is offered] to the ancestors according to the father's gotra;
for unmarried daughters, it is according to the father's gotra, and for married women, according to the husband's gotra.
Thus [it is said]. Satyavrata states the sequence for the libation to the ancestors:
"One should offer [the śrāddha] every day to the fathers, and then to the mothers;
then to the maternal grandfathers, and also to the son of the paternal uncle.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well.
One should give with the *paitra* (ancestral) *tīrtha*; now hear from me regarding other [offerings] made for specific desires.
"To one's mother, to the knower of the truth (*pramātṛ*), to one's maternal aunt, and likewise to the wife of the guru, O King;

to the guru, to the maternal uncles and others, to a dear friend, and to the sovereign. (ViPu 3.11.29–30). Hārīta also says: "One should offer libations to the father and others, the mother and others, the maternal grandfather and others, paternal uncles and their wives, elder brothers and their wives, maternal uncles and their wives, as well as to the guru, the *ācārya*, the *upādhyāya*, friends, relatives, kinsmen, those who provide wealth, food, or support, heirs, and their wives. (HāSm 12.4). Regarding the specific rule for libations when the father is still living, Yogi-Yājñavalkya states:
Kavyavāḍ, Anala, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman,
as well as the Agniṣvātta, the Somapa, and the Barhiṣad ancestors.
If one has a father still living, he should regard those as his ancestors;
or else, the offering is given to the same ancestors to whom his own father would give.
“And a twice-born man whose father is still living should offer these very same [libations] for those who have passed away.

The word “should offer” (*tarpayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Kātyāyana states regarding the final *añjali*: “I offer libations to those belonging to my paternal lineage, those belonging to my maternal lineage, and whoever else deserves water from me; this is the final *añjali*” (KSm 2.12.2). Also in the Ādityapurāṇa:
“For those who have perished anywhere, their selves afflicted by hunger and thirst...”
May this water offering of sesame seeds be inexhaustible for them.
"May this water with sesame seeds, which is being offered, be inexhaustible for those in my family who have had their funeral offerings (piṇḍa) interrupted and who are bereft of sons and wives.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"May those who were kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and those who were kinsmen in another birth—
may they go satisfied, as well as whoever desires water from us. Thus,
for one unable to perform the rite in detail, a concise libation (*tarpaṇa*) is described in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.

"Reciting, 'May the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, be satisfied,' one should cast three handfuls of water; thus one should perform the abbreviated libation (saṃkṣepatarpaṇa). As for the libation to Yama, it has been stated by Vṛddha-Manu:
The libation to Yama should be performed on the fourteenth day of the festival of lamps (Dīpotsava),
or it may always be performed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight known as Kṛṣṇāṅgāra-caturdaśī.
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, and to the Ender;
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.
"Salutation to Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, Parameṣṭhin, Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, the rule is set forth in the Skanda Purāṇa:

"Facing south, with sesame seeds in his left hand, being composed, he should perform the rite with the *daivata-tīrtha* because of its divine nature; for by means of sesame seeds, the Lord of the Dead (Yama) is propitiated.
Regarding the fruit for one who acts in this manner, Yama says:
"Having bathed in any river whatsoever on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kṛṣṇa, and having offered libations to Dharmarāja, one is liberated from all sins. Thus it is said.
One should perform the *bhīṣma-tarpaṇa* on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
Whoever offers water to Bhīṣma on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
the sin committed during that year perishes at that very moment.
To Bhīṣma, son of Gaṅgā, belonging to the Vaiyāghrapāda lineage and the Sāṃkṛtya pravaras, I shall offer this water with sesame seeds.
"I give this water to Bhīṣma Varman, who is without a son.
Thus, the praise of the libation (tarpaṇa) is shown in the *Purāṇasāra*:
"In this manner, the twice-born who should daily satisfy all beings..."
"He shall go to the supreme abode, the embodiment of splendor, free from all ailment. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the sin incurred by failing to perform this is shown in the Purāṇa:
"He who indeed does not offer libations to the deities, the ancestors, and the sages..."
"Having become a debtor to the gods and others, he goes down to hell. Thus [it is said]. Yogi-Yājñavalkya also says:
"He who, out of an atheistic disposition, does not indeed satisfy those ancestors..."
"His ancestors, seeking water, drink the discharge from his body. Thus says Hārīta as well:
"Both the gods and the ancestors long for the *añjali* of water mixed with sesame seeds."
"But when they receive nothing, they depart as they came, their hopes dashed. Thus [it is said]. Kātyāyana also says:
"Just as one afflicted by the summer heat desires shade, one thirsty desires water, and one hungry desires food in abundance," [363] ... so too do those who have been wronged desire justice.
The fool [sees] his mother as his father, the woman the man, and the man the woman.
In the same way, all beings, both stationary and moving, desire water from a Brahmin; indeed, all are seekers of water.

"Therefore, this must always be performed; by not performing it, a Brahmin incurs great sin, for by performing it, he sustains this entire universe. Regarding this, there are these verses of the ancestors (*pitṛgāthā*):
"May there be born in our lineage one who shall offer us a handful of water, especially in rivers abounding with cool waters.
After the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the wringing out of the garment must be performed. Regarding this, Yogī Yājñavalkya says:
As long as a twice-born man who has bathed does not offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors, he must not wring out his garment.
"The Brahmin who wrings out his bathing garment without having offered libations [to the ancestors] causes the ancestors to depart in despair after uttering a most terrible curse. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the wringing out [of the garment] should be performed on dry land. This has been stated in another Smṛti:
"The water squeezed from a cloth is the portion for those who eat the remnants at a *śrāddha* feast;
so says the *Śruti*. Therefore, one should squeeze it on dry ground.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should then offer a handful of water with both hands joined (añjali) to the Sun, saying:
"Salutations to Vivasvat, O Brahman, the radiant one, the splendor of Viṣṇu."

"To the progenitor of the world, the pure one, to Savitṛ, the bestower of action. (ViPu 3.11.37–38). Thus ends the section on libations (*tarpaṇa*). Now follows the worship of the deity (*devārcana*). In this manner, the rites ending with libations, which were not mentioned in the root texts, have been described. Now, the worship of the deity, as stated in the root texts and following in due order, is described. And so says the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"Having paid homage to the water-deities, the wise man should then go home;
he should then worship Viṣṇu with the Pauruṣa Sūkta.
Thus it is said in the *Āgneya Purāṇa* as well.
With Vaiṣṇava, Raudra, Sāvitra, and Śākta mantras,
one should likewise [worship] Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, Śiva, or Bhāskara.
"With concentrated mind, one should worship all the gods with their respective characteristic marks and mantras.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Sūrya, and likewise Madhusūdana..."
And a man who is free from anger should worship other desired deities with devotion.
"One should worship daily with one's own mantras, using leaves, flowers, and likewise water. Thus [it is said]. In another Smṛti:
"The Sun, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara..."

And so forth. Although it was previously explained at great length in the commentary on the root text that "the God who is to be worshipped is indeed one alone," nevertheless, the presentation of distinctions such as Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, and others is not contradictory when based upon the differences between philosophical systems (*darśana*). Furthermore, these differences between philosophical systems are described in the *Purāṇasāra*: "The Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Saura, Vaināyaka, and likewise the Skānda—these are indeed the six philosophical systems of the path of devotion."
[366] Thus it is said. In that regard, the sequence of worship according to the Vaiṣṇava system is described in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]:
"Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to all that regarding the sequence of your own worship:
having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*)."
Either by means of the eight-syllable formula, or else with twelve-syllable [mantras],
or with Vedic mantras, or again with my own hymn (sūkta).
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the wise man should worship me established therein,
as well as Puruṣa, Satya, and Acyuta.
People who know the Vaikhānasa scriptures call me Aniruddha;
but others, O King, the followers of the Pāñcarātra, understand me in this way.
O king of kings, they declare Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha to be the fourfold form.

"O Indra among kings, know that these and other forms, through their various designations, are indeed solely devoted to the inner self (adhyātma); thus should the wise man worship me. Thus it is also stated in the Āgneya-purāṇa.
[367] I shall now fully describe the worship of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable,
by performing which all sages attain the supreme state that is beyond all qualities.
The sages have declared that the proper worship of Hari is performed in these six locations: in water, in fire, in the heart, in the sun, on the sacrificial ground, and in images.
For those who perform rituals, Hari is the deity in the fire; for the wise, he is the deity in heaven; for those of limited intellect, he is in images; and for yogis, he is in the heart.
And because he is omnipresent, for those who have cultivated their selves upon the sacrificial ground,
the Puruṣa-sūkta from the Ṛgveda is praised as the supreme secret.
The meter of this hymn is Anuṣṭubh, its deity is the Triṣṭubh,
and the seer is remembered as Nārāyaṇa, who is Puruṣa, the seed of the universe.
One should place the first [syllable] on the left hand and the second on the right hand;
one should place the third on the left foot and the fourth on the right.
One should place the fifth on the left knee and the sixth on the right;
the seventh on the left hip and likewise the eighth on the right.
The ninth [digit] is in the center of the navel, the tenth likewise in the heart;
the eleventh is in the middle of the throat, and the twelfth on the left arm.
One should place the thirteenth on the right side, the fourteenth on the mouth,
the fifteenth on the two eyes, and the sixteenth on the head.
Just as in the body, so too in the deity, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rule;
by that very placement, he indeed becomes Janārdana himself.
Having thus performed the ritual of placement (nyāsa), one should thereafter carry out the sacrifice (yāga).
One should invoke the deity with the first [mantra] and offer the seat with the second.
One should cause water for washing the feet to be offered with the third [verse], and the arghya with the fourth;
one should give water for sipping with the fifth, and perform the ritual bath with the sixth.
On the seventh day, however, there is the dwelling; on the eighth, the sacred thread;
on the ninth, the application of fragrant paste; and likewise on the tenth, the flower.
Likewise, one should offer incense on the eleventh day, a lamp on the twelfth,
an offering of food on the thirteenth, and a prostration on the fourteenth.
One should offer fifteen prostrations while circumambulating and sixteen while bowing;
likewise, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth after the bath, the garment, the food offering, and the water for sipping.
Having offered sixteen oblations of food with sixteen mantras,
one should again offer sixteen flowers with sixteen mantras.
One should recite all of that, as well as the supreme Puruṣasūkta, repeatedly;
by worshipping in this very manner, one attains perfection within six months.
Nārāyaṇa, seated upon a lotus throne, residing within the orb of the sun, should always be meditated upon—
wearing armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, and a diadem.
"Golden-hued, with a body made of gold, bearing the conch and the discus"—thus [says the scripture].
Baudhāyana also [states]:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the daily service of the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa). Having bathed and become pure, having smeared a clean place with cow-dung and fashioned an image, one should worship it with unbroken grains and flowers as they are available. Together with water and flowers, one should invoke the Great Person: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I invoke the Puruṣa. Having thus invoked him, one says: "May the Blessed Great Person come. Then he welcomes him with a greeting: "Welcome now to the Blessed Great Person! This seat has been prepared for the Blessed Great Person; may the Blessed Great Person sit here," and he offers a grass mat (kūrca), saying: "This is the Blessed One’s grass mat, made of Darbha grass, triple-stranded, green and golden; please enjoy it. Here he prepares the places below: "In front, I prepare a place for Śaṅkha; behind, I prepare a place for Cakra; to the right, I prepare a place for Gadā; to the left, I prepare a place for Vanamālā; to the west, I prepare a place for Śrīvatsa and for Garutmant; to the north, I prepare a place for Śrī, Sarasvatī, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi. Then, having consecrated the vessel with the Sāvitrī, washed it, sprinkled water around it three times, and filled it with water, he should show it to the sun together with the purifier (pavitra) while saying "Oṃ. When about to bathe him, he should say "Ṛtam" and offer water for the feet (pādya) with the verse "He strode out his three steps. He should offer the respectful oblation (arghya) with the Praṇava. Then, having removed the remains of previous offerings (nirmālya) with the Vyāhṛtis, he pays homage to Viṣvaksena on the north, saying "Salutation to Viṣvaksena. Then he bathes him with the three verses beginning "Āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ," or with the "Brahmajajñānam" verse, the Vāmadevya hymn, and the Yajus-pavitra—having bathed him with these six, he then satiates him with water. Having satiated Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara, he then gives these garments, sacred thread, and water for sipping with the Vyāhṛtis. Having sprinkled water clockwise with the Vyāhṛtis, he should offer perfume with the verse "Idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame. He should offer flowers with "Tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam," unbroken grains (akṣata) with "Irāvatī," incense with the Sāvitrī, and a lamp with "Ud dīpyasva. He should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) as food with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I present this pleasing caru to the Blessed Great Person. Then he should offer twelve flowers with the names beginning with Keśava. [He offers them with: "Salutation to Śaṅkha, salutation to Cakra, salutation to Vanamālā, salutation to Śrīvatsa, salutation to Garutmant, salutation to Śrī, salutation to Sarasvatī, salutation to Puṣṭi, salutation to Tuṣṭi. Having adorned the Brahmins with common perfumes and garlands, he should praise the Lord with the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan hymns, muttering the Dhruva-sūkta or the Puruṣa-sūkta, or other Vaiṣṇava mantras, according to some teachers. Having set aside the caru with the formula: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ, I set aside the caru for the Blessed Great Person," at the time of setting it aside, he says: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I set aside the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I set aside the Puruṣa; Oṃ suvaḥ, I set aside the Puruṣa; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I set aside the Puruṣa. Then he says: "May the Blessed Great Person Hari depart, satisfied by this offering, for the sake of returning again and for being seen again. In cases where there is no image, such as in water or fire, everything is the same except for the invocation and dismissal. "This is the great auspicious rite," so they call it; "This is the great auspicious rite," said the Blessed Baudhāyana. Thus it ends.
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"There is no Vedic rite more meritorious than the worship of Viṣṇu;
therefore, one should worship Hari daily at the beginning of the day and at midday."
