"By means of the mantra *tad viṣṇoḥ* and the *Puruṣasūkta*, there is no mantra equal to these two mentioned even in all four Vedas. (KūPū 1.2.18.94–95).
In this way, worship according to the Vaiṣṇava system should be understood.
Alternatively, one who is purified by inner disposition should worship the divine Lord, the eternal Bhagavān Mahādeva, the Great Īśvara.
With the Rudra-Gāyatrī mantra, or again with the Praṇava,
or with the Īśāna mantra, or with the Tryambaka Rudras, one should remain composed.
One should worship Maheśvara with flowers, leaves, or water, or with sandalwood and other offerings, using either this mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya."
One should pay homage to Mahādeva, the Lord, saying "Truth, Reality";
and one should offer oneself to Brahmā, the Lord, saying "I am He."
"A twice-born man should perform circumambulation, or he should mutter the five Brahmans;
he should meditate upon the Lord Īśāna, Śiva, situated in the midst of the sky. Thus [says the Kūrma Purāṇa]. Baudhāyana also says:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the daily ritual service of Mahādeva. Having bathed, having smeared a clean place with cow-dung, and having fashioned an image, one should worship it with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and flowers as they are available. One should invoke Mahādeva together with water and flowers: [373] *Oṃ bhūr mahādevam āvāhayāmi* (I invoke Mahādeva from the earth), *Oṃ bhuvo mahādevam āvāhayāmi* (I invoke Mahādeva from the atmosphere), *Oṃ suvaḥ mahādevam āvāhayāmi* (I invoke Mahādeva from heaven), *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ mahādevam āvāhayāmi* (I invoke Mahādeva from the three worlds). Having thus invoked him, one says: "May the Blessed Mahādeva come. Then one welcomes him with a greeting: "Welcome, and a further welcome to the Blessed Mahādeva! A seat has been prepared; may the Blessed Mahādeva sit here. Here he offers a grass mat (*kūrca*), saying: "This is the Blessed One’s grass mat, made of *darbha* grass, triple-stranded, green, and golden; please accept it. Here he prepares the stations: "In front, I prepare a station for Viṣṇu; I prepare a station for Brahmā. To the south, I prepare a station for Skanda; I prepare a station for Vināyaka. To the west, I prepare a station for Śūla; I prepare a station for Mahākāla. To the north, I prepare a station for Umā; I prepare a station for Nandikeśvara. Having thus prepared them, he consecrates a vessel with the *Sāvitrī*, washes it, sprinkles water around it three times, brings pure water along with the strainers (*pavitra*), and shows it to the sun, saying *Oṃ*. Saying *Ṛtam*, when about to bathe, he should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *Tvaritarudra*; with the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*), the water for honor (*arghya*). Then, having removed the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*) with the *Vyāhṛtis*, he says to the north, "Salutation to Caṇḍeśa. Then, having bathed him with the three verses beginning "The waters which are most healing" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*), with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored, pure, purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), and with the section beginning "Pavamāna, of beautiful luster" (*pavamānaḥ suvarcanaḥ*), he satisfies him with water: "I satisfy the god Bhava; I satisfy the god Śarva; I satisfy the god Īśāna; I satisfy the god Paśupati; I satisfy the god Rudra; I satisfy the god Ugra; I satisfy the god Bhīma; I satisfy the god Mahānta. Having thus satisfied him, he gives these garments, sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the *Vyāhṛtis* and water, sprinkling the water clockwise with the *Vyāhṛtis*. He should offer perfume with the verse "Homage to you, O Rudra, to your wrath" (*namas te rudra manyave*). He should offer flowers with the verse "Thousands upon thousands" (*sahasrāṇi sahasraśaḥ*). He should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the verse "You, the lord of beings, the glory above all" (*īśānaṃ tvāṃ bhuvanānām adhiśriyam*). He should offer incense with the *Sāvitrī*. He should offer a lamp with the verse "Be kindled" (*uddīpyasva*). He should offer the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I present this pleasing sacrificial pap (*caru*) to the Blessed Mahādeva. Then he should offer eight flowers with the eight names: "Salutation to the god Bhava; salutation to the god Śarva; salutation to the god Īśāna; salutation to the god Paśupati; salutation to the god Rudra; salutation to the god Ugra; salutation to the god Bhīma; salutation to the god Mahānta. [375] Salutation to Viṣṇu; salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Skanda; salutation to Vināyaka; salutation to Śūla; salutation to Mahākāla; salutation to Umā; salutation to Nandikeśvara. With the remainder of the sacrificial pap, he performs eight oblations with the eight names, beginning with "To the god Bhava, svāhā," and so on. Having offered these and having adorned the Brahmins with the remaining perfumes and garlands, they praise him with the *Ṛg-, Yajur-, and Sāma-veda* hymns. Having muttered the section beginning "Thousands upon thousands" and other Rudra-mantras according to his ability, he dismisses the sacrificial pap for Mahādeva with the formulas beginning "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ, I dismiss the sacrificial pap for Mahādeva. At the time of dismissal, he dismisses Rudra with each mantra, saying: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I dismiss Mahādeva."
May the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign honored by all the worlds,
depart satisfied by this oblation, for the sake of returning once again.

"Or for the purpose of seeing [the deity] again. In the case of images, everything is the same as in the [other] locations, with the exception of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*visarjana*). "This is called the Great Auspicious Rite," says the venerable Baudhāyana.
Thus [ends the section]. Nandikeśvara praises the worship of Śiva:
"He who might give a hundred thousand milch cows to one who has mastered the Vedas..."
The merit of one who worships the Liṅga for even a single day is greater than that.
"O Brahmins, he who worships the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Umā, even once, obtains a fruit greater than that of a horse-sacrifice. Thus it is said.

Even the fragrance of the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering) should be worn, because of the injunction in the Smṛti texts such as: "Having worshipped the gods with fragrance... The fault incurred by failing to perform the worship of the gods is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
"He who, out of delusion or laziness, eats without having performed the worship of the deities, goes to hell and is reborn among pigs. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.121).
Thus ends the section on the worship of the deities.

Now begins the section on the worship of the Guru. Thus has been described the worship of the deity as stated in the root text. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of the deities and" (*devatānāṃ ca*), the Guru is included; for the Guru is to be worshipped just like the deity. Therefore, the Śruti says:
"For one who has supreme devotion to the deity, and as to the deity, so to the Guru—for that high-souled one, these meanings thus explained become manifest. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23)
Also in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; that which is the Mantra is Śaṅkara.
Between Śiva, the Vidyā, and the Gurus, there is no distinction whatsoever."
For one whose devotion toward the auspicious mantra, the deity, and the guru is equal,
enjoyment, liberation, and spiritual accomplishment will certainly and swiftly be attained.
"Garments, ornaments, garlands, beds, and seats—whatever things are dear to oneself, those indeed should be given to the guru.
One should strive to please him with mind, action, and speech. (Śiva Purāṇa 5.1.1916–20)
Manu also says: "By devotion to one's mother, one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world;
and by service to one's teacher, one attains the world of Brahmā."
All dharmas are honored by him who honors these three;
and for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless.
"As long as those three live, he should not attend to anyone else; he should constantly perform service toward them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare. (MDh 2.233–35).
Thus ends the section on the worship of the guru.
[378] Now begins the section on the Vaiśvadeva offering. Regarding that, Dakṣa states the duty pertaining to the fifth part:
"And likewise, in the fifth part, there should be a distribution according to what is appropriate."
"It is prescribed for the ancestors, the gods, human beings, and even insects" (DaŚm 2.42).

Although the priority of the *ātithya* (hospitality to guests) over the *vaiśvadeva* is stated in the root text by the phrase "the *ātithya* and the *vaiśvadeva*," nevertheless, the fact that the *vaiśvadeva* occurs immediately after the worship of the gods is declared in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"And then one should worship Viṣṇu with the *Puruṣasūkta*."
"Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, and likewise the Bali offering. (NṛPu 58.93)

In this regard, the sequence is understood from the word "tataḥ" by virtue of the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī-śruti*). However, in the root text, it is understood merely by the order of recitation (*pāṭha*). It has been established in the *Śruti-liṅga-sūtra* (PMS 3.3.14) that direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than proximity based on the order of recitation. Therefore, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed first. This being the case, the Vedic order of recitation is also upheld. Furthermore, it is understood through the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*; PMS 1.3.2) that the Vedic order of recitation is stronger than the Smṛti order of recitation, such as: "The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to humans, and the sacrifice to Brahman" (ĀśGṛ 3.1.2). For these reasons as well, the Vaiśvadeva comes first. Regarding this, Vyāsa prescribes the Vaiśvadeva.
Thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā),
using various kinds of consecrated cooked foods accompanied by sacrificial oblations (haviṣya) and side dishes (vyañjana).

"With those very same foods, one should offer the *bali*; having sprinkled the remainder with water, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should present the *kavya* to the south with the utterance 'svadhā'. Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: "thereafter," that is, immediately after the worship of the gods. Nārāyaṇa also [says]:

"But having bathed with his wife, being pure, having sipped water according to the rule and restrained his speech, he should enter and perform the Vaiśvadeva rite in a well-kindled fire. Thus it is said; and also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed either in the domestic fire, or in the common fire, or even in water or on the ground; this is indeed remembered as the Devayajña.
"If the cooking were done on a worldly fire, then food would be offered therein;
however, one should cook the food on the domestic fire (*śālāgni*). This is the eternal rule.
Thus [says] Aṅgiras as well.

"One should always cook food either in the hall-fire (śālāgni) or in the common fire (laukika). In whichever fire one cooks the food, in that very fire the oblation (homa) is prescribed. Thus says Śātātapa as well.
Whether in a worldly or a Vedic context, the Vaiśvadeva offering must be performed with water poured onto the ground for the removal of the five slaughtering grounds.
[380] Thus Yama points out the five slaughterhouses: "Five slaughterhouses exist for the householder day after day, always:
the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom."
"By driving these [senses], a Brahmin is indeed bound again and again;
for the sake of purifying them, the five sacrifices were ordained. Thus it is said.

*Sūnā* refers to places of violence. *Kaṇḍanī* refers to the mortar, pestle, and so forth; *peṣaṇī* refers to the grinding stone, millstone, and so forth; *cullī* is the hearth for cooking; *jalakumbha* is the water-jar; and *upaskara* refers to winnowing baskets and other such implements. If the reading is *avaskara*, it should be understood as referring to brooms and similar items. The meaning is that one becomes joined with sin by causing these *sūnās* to perform their respective functions. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that the Vaiśvadeva rite must be performed at both times: "The Vaiśvadeva and the Bali-offering must be performed in the evening and in the morning."
"Even by one who does not eat constantly, otherwise he would become a sinner. (KSm 2.13.10)

Āśvalāyana describes the manner of the *homa*: “Then, in the evening and morning, one should offer oblations of prepared sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) to the deities of the *agnihotra*: to Soma, to Vanaspati, to Agni and Soma, to Indra and Agni, to Heaven and Earth, to Dhanvantari, to Indra, to the Viśvedevas, and to Brahman—*svāhā*” (ĀśGṛ 1.2.1.3). The term *haviṣyasya* means that which is fit for sacrifice. “To the deities of the *agnihotra*” means to Sūrya, Agni, and Prajāpati. Āpastamba also says: “[381] One should offer with the hand, using each of the first six mantras, either in the *aupāsana* fire or the cooking fire; there is sprinkling of water on both sides as before” (ĀpDh 2.2.3.16–17). “With the first” refers to those stated at the beginning of the section, starting with “*agnaye svāhā*” and ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. “On both sides” means at the beginning and the end of the ritual act. Pāraskara also says: “Having sprinkled water around the food from the *vaiśvadeva* meal, one should offer oblations with the *svāhā*-utterances: to Brahman, to Prajāpati, to the *gṛhya* deities, to Kaśyapa, and to Anumati” (PārGṛ 2.9.2). In this matter, the arrangement follows one’s own *śākhā*. Vyāsa describes the consecration of the food to be offered:
"One should offer oblations smeared with clarified butter, excluding oil and alkali;
or smeared with curd, or smeared with milk, or in its absence, even with water.
Thus is the substitution for the ritual substance shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*.
In the absence [of these], one should perform the Vaiśvadeva with whatever is available— such as fruits, vegetables, water, and so forth— or with milk, curd, and ghee, using a *sruva* ladle.
"One should perform [the offering] with food and other substances using the hand; in water, one should do so with a handful of water."

That which is eaten is itself with which one should sacrifice. This has been stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: “[382] Whether it be a vegetable, or a leaf, or a root, or a fruit—whatever one intends as food, with that very thing one may also offer oblation. A sacrifice in the fire must not be performed with anything mixed with alkaline substances, salt, or inferior food, nor with what is unfit for sacrifice (*ahaviṣya*). Rather, having silently removed some hot ashes from the north of the fire-pit, one should offer therein. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: “There is no sacrifice with alkaline substances or salt; likewise, there is none with what is mixed with inferior food. When there is an offering of something unfit for sacrifice, one should remove the hot ashes toward the north and offer therein; that becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire” (ĀpDh 2.6.15.15–17). It is also stated in the *Pariśiṣṭa*.

"With the hand turned upward, pressing with the tip of the thumb and with fingers joined together, one should offer the oblation while remaining silent. Regarding the specific rule for one who maintains no sacred fire (*anagnika*) during the *vaiśvadeva* rite, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:

"But that Brahmin who is without a sacred fire, having himself offered food with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *śākala* mantras, should offer the remainder as the *kākabali*. The *śākala* mantras begin with "The sin of the god-given" (*devakṛtasyainasaḥ*). Viṣṇu also says:
"Having offered food with the *vyāhṛtis* and with the *śākala* mantras,
and having offered the oblation to Prajāpati, one should then honor the guest.
Thus is the *bhūtayajña* (sacrifice to beings) shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.
“From the food remaining after the oblation has been offered to the gods, one should present the *bhūtabali*.

That is indeed declared to be the *bhūtayajña*, which bestows prosperity upon all embodied beings. (KūP 1.2.18.108). Hārīta also says: “The offering of the *bali* to the guardians of the dwelling-place (*vāstupāla*) and to the spirits (*bhūta*) is the *bhūtayajña*. (HārSm 15.3). Kātyāyana also says:

"Having taken up the oblation and poured clarified butter or other sacrificial substances over it, one should offer the oblation according to the rules of one's own Vedic school and then present the *bali* offering with what remains. Thus [it is said].
Atri states the secondary agents [of the rite]:

"A son, a brother, a sacrificial priest, a pupil, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, a wife, a Vedic scholar, and one for whom one performs sacrifices— these are permitted [to perform] the *balikarman* when they are present.
Regarding this, Baudhāyana states that in the absence of another performer in the house, one who is traveling abroad must perform it himself.
"He who has no performer of these five great duties in his house when departing on a journey departs together with those sacrifices. Thus it is said.

Āśvalāyana describes the manner of offering the *bali* oblations: “Now follows the *baliharaṇa*. To these very deities: to the Waters (*adbhyaḥ*), to the Herbs and Trees (*oṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ*), to the House (*gṛhāya*), to the Deities of the House (*gṛhadevatābhyaḥ*), to the Deities of the Site (*vāstudevatābhyaḥ*). To Indra and Indra’s attendants; to Yama and Yama’s attendants; to Varuṇa and Varuṇa’s attendants; to Soma and Soma’s attendants—to each of these in their respective directions. To Brahmā and Brahmā’s attendants—in the center. To the Viśvedevas. To all beings who roam by day—thus during the day. To those who roam by night—thus at night. To the Rākṣasas—in the north. *Svadhā* to the Fathers—thus with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he should pour out the remainder toward the south. (ĀśGṛ 1.2.3–11) Āpastamba also says: “To the west of the fire, he makes offerings with the seventh and eighth [formulas], ending toward the north. Near the water-jar, with the ninth. In the middle of the house, with the tenth and eleventh, ending toward the east. In the north-eastern part of the house, with the four following [formulas]. At the place of the bed, with the formula containing the word ‘desire’ (*kāma*). On the threshold, with the formula containing the word ‘intermediate space’ (*antarikṣa*). To the north of the covering, with the following [formulas]. To the south, with the formula containing the word ‘Fathers,’ wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he should perform it with his hand turned downward. [385] The offering to Rudra is in the north, as in the case of the other deities. For those two, the sprinkling of water is separate because of the difference in ritual rule. Only at night, with the following [formula], he makes an offering in the air. (ĀpDh 2.2.3–4, 20, 8) It is also stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Having thus performed the domestic offering (*gṛhabali*), the head of the household, being pure,
should respectfully perform the ritual release (*utsarga*) for the nourishment of all beings.
Thus [it is said] in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* (29.22–23).
"O best of the twice-born, one should place food on the ground outside for dogs, for those who cook dogs, for the outcastes, and likewise for birds. Thus [it is said].
Manu also says:
"And for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms, one should slowly scatter [food] upon the ground" (MDh 3.92).
The word "food" (*anna*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The mantra for the offering of food is shown in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
Gods, humans, animals, birds, Siddhas, along with the hosts of Yakṣas, Uragas, and Daityas;
Pretas, Piśācas, and all trees—whatever beings desire food, may it be given here by me.
May ants, insects, moths, and the like, who are hungry and bound by the fetters of karma, attain satisfaction; this food has been offered by me to them—may they be happy.

For those who have no mother, no father, no kinsman, and for whom there is neither the preparation of food nor food itself—may this food given upon the earth lead them to satisfaction; may they attain contentment and be joyful.
All beings, as well as this food and I myself—Viṣṇu—are not other than that.
Therefore, for the welfare of all beings and for their prosperity, I bestow this food upon the earth.
This fourteenth class of beings, and whatever hosts of spirits dwell therein—for their satisfaction this food has been offered by me; may they be joyful in it.
"Having uttered this, a man endowed with faith should offer food for the benefit of beings upon the earth; for the householder has become the refuge of all. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.47–53).
The *pitṛyajña* is shown by the Śruti: "In that one offers the *svadhā* to the ancestors, even though it is merely water, that *pitṛyajña* is completed. Kātyāyana also [says the same].

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the Pitṛs; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali-offering is the sacrifice to beings; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.

"Or the *śrāddha* may be the *pitṛyajña*, or even the *balir* offering to the ancestors. (KSm 2.13.3–4). Here, the arrangement is according to one's own *śākhā*. And the *śrāddha* mentioned here is the obligatory *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*). Thus says the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"O best of men, one should feed at least one Brahmin with reference to the ancestors."
"That is designated as the *nitya-śrāddha*, a sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛ-yajña*) that bestows a [favorable] state of existence. Thus [it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa, 1.2.18.111].
Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya [Purāṇa]:
"One should perform the *śrāddha* day by day with food, grain, or even with water."
"One should feed Brahmins or even a single Brahmin with the ancestors in mind" (MārPu 29.33).
The method for the daily *śrāddha* is shown in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"I shall now describe the daily [śrāddha], which is devoid of the *arghya* offering and the invocation."
"One should know that to be *adaiva* (without the gods); it is remembered as the *pārvaṇa* rite to be performed on the *parvan* days. (Matsya Purāṇa 16.5–6).
Pracetas says: "There is no invocation (*āvāhana*), no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), no funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), and no dismissal (*visarjana*)."
Vyāsa also says:
"In the daily *śrāddha*, having honored the twice-born with water for the hands (*arghya*), perfumes, and other offerings according to one's ability,
one should feed them all properly while duly designating them along with all the hosts of ancestors."
The invocation, the utterance of *svadhā*, the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), the ritual of placing [the food] into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and so forth;
likewise, the observances such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the Viśvedevas.
"In the daily *śrāddha*, one should exclude these [unfit persons] and prepare food fit for consumption;
having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should dismiss them with prostrations.
A householder should always feed at least one person daily, even if it be from the six [classes of ancestors]. Thus it is said.
Kātyāyana, however, states an alternative procedure in that regard:
"For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), one should feed even a single Brahmin;
for there is no other recipient or food [for the rite] apart from the divine (adaiva)."
Having set aside some food according to his ability and in accordance with the rules,
he should give it day after day to the ancestors and to human beings, O twice-born one.
"Having said, 'This for the ancestors,' one should utter the word *svadhā*.
For humans, one should say *hantakāra*, and one should pour water into half of that. (KSm 2.13.68).
One should give the food that has been set aside to a Brāhmaṇa. This is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Or, having set aside some food according to his ability, being composed, he should present it to a twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.112)

These three—the *devayajña*, *bhūtayajña*, and *pitṛyajña*—are all designated by the term *vaiśvadeva*. That ritual in which the *Viśvedevas* are worshipped is a *vaiśvadaivika* rite. Since the formula “*svāhā* to the *Viśvedevas*” (*viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ svāhā*) is recited in the *devayajña* (ĀśGṛ 1.2.2–3), this name applies primarily to it. However, for those whose *śākhā* includes this same mantra in the *bhūtayajña*, the name applies primarily to that as well. In the *pitṛyajña*, however, the name is applied by way of the "umbrella-logic" (*chatrinyāya*). Alternatively, in the root text’s phrase “and the *vaiśvadeva*,” the word “and” (*ca*) includes the *pitṛyajña* and other rites not explicitly mentioned. Although the statement “one should offer the prepared sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) in the evening and morning” (ĀśGṛ 1.2.1) suggests that the *vaiśvadeva* is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the food, its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) must nevertheless be accepted; for this is understood from the supplementary passage: “One should perform these sacrifices day after day” (ĀśGṛ 3.1.4). One should not suspect it has a dual purpose, as that would involve a mutual contradiction. If it were a consecration of food, the food would be primary and the *vaiśvadeva* secondary. If it were a human goal, the reverse would be true. This being the case, the simultaneous predominance and subordination of a single thing would be contradictory. If it is argued, “Let it then be merely a consecration of food; let it not be a human goal,” that is not so.
By means of the great sacrifices and the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman. (MDh 2.28)

This is because Manu records that this is for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). As for the citation, “One should offer what is already prepared as an oblation” (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* 1.2.1), that can be explained otherwise. In that context, “one should offer” (*juhuyāt*) is the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*); “of what is already prepared as an oblation” (*siddhasya haviṣyasya*) is the applicatory injunction (*viniyoga-vidhi*); and “one should perform these day after day” is the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*). Furthermore, if it were a consecration of food (*anna-saṃskāra*), repetition would result at every cooking, according to the maxim: “The subordinate element is repeated with each primary element. Therefore, its status as a human purpose alone is logical. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Even when away from home, one should perform the refinement of the self without hesitation. Thus says Gobhila:

"If rice and barley should ripen at the same time, having offered [the oblation] of either one, one may consider the duty fulfilled. If food should be cooked again and again at the same time, one should perform the *bali* offering only once. If much food should be cooked in various ways at the same time, one should perform a single *bali* from the householder’s kitchen alone."

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning: even when cooking food consisting of various ingredients, or when cooking food repeatedly, or even when many undivided persons such as brothers cook separately, one must offer from that very same substance—namely, from the single cooking performed by the householder.
Thus concludes the section on the Vaiśvadeva;
now the sacrifice to humans (manuṣyayajña), also known by the name *ātithya*, is described. That the *ātithya* is a sacrifice to humans has been stated by Kātyāyana.

"Teaching is the *brahmayajña*; the *pitṛyajña* is the libation (*tarpaṇa*); the *daivayajña* is the burnt offering (*homa*); the *bhūtayajña* is the bali-offering; and the *nṛyajña* is the honoring of guests. (KSm 2.13.3). The Śruti also states: "In that one gives food to Brāhmaṇas, the *manuṣyayajña* is completed. Baudhāyana also says: [392] "Day after day one should give food to Brāhmaṇas, even down to roots, fruits, and vegetables; thus one accomplishes this *manuṣyayajña*. Kārṣṇājini also says:
"Whether it be abundant alms, or even a morsel of food (hantakāra), or if such is unavailable, one should likewise give even a vessel of water.
Thus it is said; and also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:

"A twice-born man should always give an *hantakāra*, or the first portion of food, or alms according to his ability to the guest, and should thus perceive him as the Supreme Lord. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.18.144).
Manu has stated the definition of alms and so forth:
"A single morsel shall constitute *bhikṣā*; four morsels are the *agra*;
and by quadrupling the *agra*, the *hantakāra* is prescribed.
Thus it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa that one should remain for some time in the courtyard of the house to await a guest.
[393] And having sipped water, the wise man should then look toward the door;
for a guest may appear during even the eighth part of a muhūrta. Thus it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (29.24–25). It is also stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

"Then he should remain in the courtyard of his house for a period of time equal to the milking of a cow, or for half that time, or as he desires, for the purpose of receiving guests. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.55). Thus concludes the sacrifice to human beings (*manuṣyayajña*).

Thus, in this root text stating "the twilight bath" (*saṃdhyā-snāna*), the six rites beginning with bathing and ending with hospitality (*ātithya*) are defined. Nor should it be suspected that the number six is contradicted by the appearance of the number seven here; for, according to the principle of the *sammārjana* (sprinkling), the number residing in the subject of the enunciation (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant. This is because those rites which reside in the subject of the enunciation are to be performed day after day, as they are enjoined as being obligatory (*nitya*). And the principle of *sammārjana* is established in the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "One cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) for one cup, or for all? For that purpose, the inquiry is: is the number residing in the object of reference (*uddeśya*) intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*), or unintended? Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), where by the force of the heard singular ending, the number residing in the animal—which is the thing to be taken up (*upādeya*)—is intended to be significant; likewise, by the force of the heard singular ending in "the cup" (*graham*), the number residing in the object of reference ought also to be intended to be significant. Therefore, when it follows that the cleansing applies to only one cup, we reply: In the case of the animal, since its connection to the sacrifice is understood through this very statement, the animal is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) with respect to the sacrifice. Because there is no repetition of the principal (*pradhāna*) for every subordinate, when there arises an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "by how many animals," the number one is connected as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Thus, it is logical that the number residing in the thing to be taken up is intended to be significant. However, in the case of the cups (*graha*), since their connection to the sacrifice is understood through another sentence, and because in the sentence concerning cleansing, the cup is understood to be the principal (*pradhāna*) with respect to the cleansing due to the hearing of the accusative case-ending, the quality (*guṇa*) of cleansing must be repeated for each principal. Consequently, since there is no arising of an expectancy such as "how many cups are to be cleansed," the number residing in the cups—the objects of reference—is not intended to be significant. Therefore, all cups are to be cleansed. In the present context as well, the number six residing in the Sandhyās and so forth, which are the objects of reference, is not intended to be significant.

Now it may be argued: since in this *Parāśara-smṛti* there is no establishment of the *saṃdhyā* and other rites through another statement, it is logical that their number is intended to be significant—just like the "oneness" of the animal in a sacrifice—because they are produced by this very sentence as things to be enjoined (*upādeya*). If this is so, then when the compound *saṃdhyā-snānam* (the twilight-bath) is understood as "the bath together with the *saṃdhyā*," the *saṃdhyā*, which is the primary element (*aṅgin*), is counted as one along with its subsidiary (*aṅga*) the bath; thus, it should be understood that the number six is not contradicted here.

The obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the twilight rituals (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth is understood through their being required to be performed as long as one lives, just like the *agnihotra* sacrifice; and their status as a qualification (*adhikāra*) based on the condition of living is understood through the repetition (*vīpsā*) in the phrase "day after day" (*dine dine*), just as that understanding is derived from the repetition in the passage: "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* every spring. (39)
It has been stated, "The guest-offering (ātithya) and the Vaiśvadeva [rite]," and in response to the inquiry as to what kind of person constitutes a guest, he says:
Whether beloved or even hated, whether a fool or indeed a scholar—whoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite is a guest who leads one to heaven. (40)
A "dear one" refers to a friend and so forth. Regarding their being worthy of a feast, Yājñavalkya has stated:
"One should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time" (YDh 1.108).
However, Manu has censured the feeding of an enemy.
"One should honor a friend even if he is not handsome, but never an enemy;

for an oblation consumed by an enemy becomes fruitless after death" (MDh 3.144). This being so, just as a distinction is made regarding an excessive friend, the same applies when such a possibility arises regarding a guest; therefore, to exclude that [undesirable case], it is said: "Whether he be beloved or even hateful. Furthermore, the feeding of a fool is prohibited in another Smṛti.
"When food is being given to a Brahmin who has lost his purity, who has fallen from his vows, and who is devoid of the Vedas, the food weeps: 'What evil deed have I committed? (Vyāsa Smṛti 4.52).
Thus, the worthiness of a learned man as a recipient of food has been praised by Manu.
"Sacrificial offerings to the gods and ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit. (MDh 3.128)

This being the case, since there might arise a confusion between the learned and the ignorant even at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva—just as there is during the Śrāddha and other rites—it is said, "Whether he be a fool or indeed a scholar," in order to dispel that [confusion]. By the term "at the end of the Vaiśvadeva," a period of time measuring only a quarter of a *ghaṭikā* (three minutes) following the Devayajña, Bhūtayajña, and Pitṛyajña is intended. Accordingly, the statement from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa has been cited: "The eighth part of a *muhūrta*" (MārPu 29.25). For this very reason, arriving at that time is the defining characteristic of a guest (*atithi*), and not [merely] possessing learning and so forth. It is called a *saṃkrama* because one passes through it (*saṃkramyate ’nena*); "the passage to heaven" (*svargasaṃkrama*) means the cause for attaining heaven. And so it is stated in the Aśvamedhika [Parvan]:
"One who desires the fruit of sacrifice should respectfully provide food to one afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, and who has arrived at the proper place and time. (40)
He specifies that very guest:
"One who has arrived after a long journey, exhausted, and appears during the Vaiśvadeva rite—one should recognize him as a guest; one who arrives before [that time] is not a guest. (41)
[397] One who has come from a long journey, arrived from another village, exhausted, and tormented by hunger and thirst; for this very reason Vyāsa said:
"One who has come from a great distance, being weary and emaciated by hunger, thirst, and fatigue."
"He who is properly honored as a guest is indeed an unprecedented sacrifice.
Regarding this, the phrase "a guest who has arrived before" means that he is a guest on that very day and not on the following day. And so Manu says:
"A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally known as a guest. (MDh 3.102)

The phrase "the Vaiśvadeva has arrived" refers to the daytime. However, in the evening, at the time of the Vaiśvadeva rite or at any other time, it is specifically the guest (*atithi*) who has arrived. Thus says Manu:
"A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating. (MDh 3.105)
"Sūryoḍha" means that by the setting sun, having rendered him incapable of traveling to another place, he has been brought home; such is the meaning. Yājñavalkya also says:
"A guest is not to be turned away even in the evening, [by providing] at least speech, grass, and water. (YDh 1.107) Pracetas also says:
"He who arrives at the end of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice in the evening, or who comes to the house in the evening—he is to be honored like a god; such a guest is known as a *sūryoḍha*. [41]
He speaks regarding those who have turned back from a long journey:
"One should never consider a guest as belonging to the same village;
because he has arrived unexpectedly, he is therefore called a 'guest' (atithi). (42)

One for whom no specific lunar day (*tithi*) exists is a guest (*atithi*). And so says Yama: "That great-souled one by whom all lunar days, festivals, and celebrations have been abandoned is a guest for all beings; they know the others to be mere visitors."

Those who come for the purpose of obtaining wealth on specific lunar days (tithis) such as those marking the beginning of the Manvantaras and Yugas are called *abhyāgatas* (guests who arrive by appointment). One who arrives at any time whatsoever, regardless of such specific lunar days, being afflicted by hunger, thirst, or other needs, is an *atithi* (unexpected guest). This being the case, one who belongs to the same village and arrives only on predetermined lunar days is not an *atithi*. However, he who comes unexpectedly from another village, having no prior agreement and being hungry, is one who has arrived "not [regularly]" (*anityam āgata*); it is precisely him that one should receive with the status of an *atithi*, and no other. Thus says the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
One should properly honor a guest who has arrived from elsewhere and belongs to a family other than one's own, provided that he does not reside in the same village.
"One who possesses nothing, has no kin, and has arrived from another land" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.58–59).
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"One should not make a friend an *atithi* (guest), nor one who dwells in the same village."
His family name was unknown, and he had appeared at that time.

"One who is hungry, who has arrived weary, who is begging and possesses nothing—a Brāhmaṇa such as this is called a guest; he should be honored according to one's ability by the wise. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:

"One should not recognize as a guest a Brahmin who lives in the same village, nor one who is merely an acquaintance, even if he has arrived at the house where the wife or the sacred fires are present" (MDh 3.103).

One who resides in the same village does not become a guest even if he arrives according to the rules for guests. Likewise, an "acquaintance" (*sāṅgatika*) is one who moves in company, or one with whom there has been a prior association—meaning, one who has been seen before. Nor is anyone who arrives according to the rules of hospitality a guest merely because he has come to some place or other; rather, he becomes a guest only when he arrives in that very place where his own wife or the sacred fires are located, whether that place be his own or another's.
Having described the true nature of a guest, he now states what should be done when such a guest has arrived:
"One should honor the guest who has arrived there with a welcome and so forth, by offering water for the feet (*arghya*), a seat, and by washing his feet. (43)
[400] With faith, by the gift of food, by pleasant inquiries and replies,
and by following one who is departing, the householder should generate joy.

These two verses have been explained by the preceding commentary. This [rule] pertains specifically to Brāhmaṇas, because it is cited from both Śruti and Smṛti: "When one gives food to Brāhmaṇas," and "One should give food to Brāhmaṇas day after day" (BDh 2.5.10.5). However, Kṣatriyas and others do not deserve the hospitable reception due to a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa; rather, they are entitled only to a meal. Thus says Manu:
"A Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, nor are a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, nor a friend, nor kinsmen, nor even a teacher."
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may,
if desired, feed him even after the Brahmins have finished eating.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who are not [otherwise] entitled [to such hospitality] arrive at his household as guests, he should feed them along with his servants; thus he should practice benevolence.

"Furthermore, one should, together with one's wife, feed friends and others who have come to the house out of affection, providing them with food according to one's ability as is natural. (MDh 3.110–13).
He states the specific rule regarding the offering of seats and other items as follows:

"One should provide a superior seat, lodging, bed, escorting, and attendance for those who are superior; inferior for those who are inferior; and equal for those who are equal. (MDh 3.107) || 43 – 44 ||
He states the transgression incurred by failing to honor a guest:
"If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated, that person's ancestors do not eat for fifteen years. (45)
[402] For him whose guest departs with disappointed hopes, even a thousand loads of wood and a hundred jars of ghee make his burnt offering useless. 46.

If a guest who has arrived with the expectation, "I shall eat in this man's house," should turn away from that house without receiving food, then the ancestral rite (*paitṛka*) performed by the householder would become fruitless; likewise, even a rite for the gods (*daivika*), though endowed with the prescribed materials and other required factors, would be rendered fruitless. And so says Manu:
"Even if he gathers grain by hand or by picking ears, and even if he constantly offers oblations into the five fires—the Brahmin dwelling unhonored takes away all his merit. (MDh 3.100)
Also in the *Āśvamedhika*:
"Even if he recites the Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs here day after day,
yet does not honor a guest, that twice-born man recites in vain."
Those who perform the *pākayajñas*, the great sacrifices (*mahāyajñas*), and the *soma* rites,
and who honor and worship the guest who has arrived at their home;

"For those who desire fame, whatever may have been given or sacrificed becomes in vain; it is destroyed by the hand of expectation. In this passage, the mention of the loss of merit (*sukṛta*) is also an indication of the acquisition of demerit (*duṣkṛta*). And so says Viṣṇu:
"If a guest departs from a householder with his hopes frustrated, he takes away that person's merit and bestows upon him their demerit. Thus it is said;
and also in the *Aśvamedhika*:
He who does not honor a guest who has arrived at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite immediately attains the state of a Caṇḍāla; of this there is no doubt.
"He who expels a brahmin who has arrived at his house at the proper time and place becomes an outcast at that very moment; there is no doubt about this. (45–46)
He praises the honoring of guests:
"One should sow seed in a fertile field and deposit wealth with a worthy recipient;
for what is sown and given in a fertile field and with a worthy recipient does not perish. (47)
Just as seed sown in a fertile field does not perish but leads to a great harvest, so too food and other gifts given to a worthy guest yield inexhaustible fruit; this is the meaning. As Manu says:
"One should never eat that which one would not first offer to a guest;
honoring a guest brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven" (MDh 3.106).
Thus it is said. Also in the *Āśvamedhika* [Parvan]:
"O King of kings, that man who honors a guest with the gift of water for washing his feet is, by that act, honoring me here; of this there is no doubt."
Śātātapa also says: "A householder does not attain such worlds through Vedic study, the Agnihotra sacrifice, other sacrifices, or asceticism as he does from honoring a guest. (47)
He states the rule for the host:
"One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or learning;
one should conceive of him as a deity in one's heart, for he embodies all the gods. (48)
For it has been shown by Manu that at the very beginning of a *śrāddha*, a Brāhmaṇa must be examined:
"One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; he is the proper channel for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and he is remembered as the true guest. (MDh 3.130)
The King himself should also first examine Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
who are purified of defects arising from the body, and who have observed their vows.

Therefore, by the same principle as that applied to *śrāddha* rites, when the examination of lineage (*gotra*) and other such factors would otherwise apply to the rite of hospitality (*ātithya*), it is here prohibited. *Gotra* is the connection with a great seer (*maharṣi*) who founded a lineage. *Caraṇa* refers to conduct (*ācāra*). It also denotes a specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*) or one's own recited scripture (*svādhyāya*). *Śruta* refers to grammar, Mīmāṃsā, and so forth; this serves as an illustration for place, name, and other such details. For this very reason, Yama says:
"One should not inquire about the lineage, conduct, country, name, family, or learning of a Brahmin who has arrived from a journey and stands before one for the purpose of a meal."
It is not only that one must avoid questions concerning lineage and the like; rather, one should also cultivate the perception [of the teacher] as a deity. As Śātātapa has said:
"One should contemplate within the mind that Vyāsa himself has arrived there.
And likewise in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Without inquiring into his Vedic study, lineage, conduct, or family, the householder should regard that guest with the thought that he is Hiraṇyagarbha. (ViP 3.11.60).
The reason for regarding him as the object of the thought "he is a deity" is that he embodies all the gods; and this has been demonstrated in the *Purāṇasāra*.
"Dhātṛ, Prajāpati, Śakra, Vahni, the Vasu-gaṇa, and Yama—
these indeed consume the food after having designated the guest, O best of the twice-born. Thus,
an objection regarding the inquiry into [the guest's] lineage and so forth has been shown by Yama.
"He who gives food after asking about one's country, name, family, or learning does not obtain the fruit thereof; having given it, he does not go to heaven.
Thus, just as the host should not ask about the lineage and so forth, so too the guest should not speak of them. Regarding this, Manu says:
"A Brahmin should not announce his own family and lineage for the sake of food;
for by proclaiming them for the sake of food, he is called by the wise a 'vomit-eater' (one who eats what has been vomited). (MDh 3.109) || 48 ||
By means of the illustration of the guest, he declares the venerability of the two types of mendicants—the ascetic (yati) and the student (brahmacārī):

"Just as a brahmin who observes excellent vows is unprecedented, and likewise a guest is unprecedented, so too those two who are constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas are unprecedented day after day. (49)

A *suvratī* is an ascetic (*yati*) who possesses a "good vow" (*suvrata*); that is, the duty of an ascetic which is the cause of liberation. A *brahmacārī* is one devoted to the study of the Vedas, because that is the purpose of his stage of life (*āśrama*). The meaning is that both of these should be honored every day like unprecedented guests; and thus Yājñavalkya says: "Having paid respect, alms should be given to a mendicant and to one of good vows. (YDh 1.108). And in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:

"And one should give alms to a mendicant, a wandering ascetic, or a student of sacred knowledge, having set aside from the unprepared food a portion provided with all kinds of condiments. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:

"And a householder twice-born man should give alms according to the rule to a mendicant student of sacred knowledge; he obtains that same fruit of merit which one obtains by giving a cow to a teacher according to the rule. (MDh 3.94–95)
Yama says: "The Blessed Yama has declared that for that person who respectfully bestows alms upon a mendicant, the merit is equal to the gift of a cow."

Having caused the religious student (*brahmacārin*) to recite "May there be well-being," and having given water into his hand, the offering of alms (*bhikṣā*) should be performed. Regarding this, Gautama says: "After having had [him] recite 'May there be well-being,' the going for alms is preceded by water" (GDh 5.7).

[408] When an ascetic (*yati*) and a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) arrive at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* offering, let it be so; but when they arrive before the *vaiśvadeva*, how should one proceed? To this he says:
"But when the *vaiśvadeva* has commenced, if a mendicant (*bhikṣuka*) arrives at the house..."
Having set aside food for the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should dismiss the mendicant.
"When it has arrived" means when it has presented itself and not yet been attended to. And so it is said in the *Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa*:
"But when a mendicant has come to the house while the Vaiśvadeva offering has not yet been performed, alms must certainly be given; it acts as a staircase to heaven."
Having set aside the food for the Vaiśvadeva and having given alms, he should dismiss [the mendicant].
(NṛPu 58.100) Having separated as much food as was used for the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, and having given alms from the remaining food, he should dismiss the mendicant. || 50 ||
He states the transgression incurred by failing to do so:
"Both the ascetic and the student are the masters of cooked food.
Having eaten without giving food to those two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (51)

We shall describe the characteristics of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance in the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta*). From the prescription of expiations, it is understood that there is transgression (*pratyavāya*). Since those two [the moon and the sun] are the owners of cooked food, it is logical that there is transgression in taking their food. For this very reason, it is said in the *Purāṇa*:
"Having eaten without having offered oblations to the fire and without having satisfied the ascetic who has approached him, one eats one's own flesh in the next world. (51)
Anticipating the question of what should be done when many mendicants have arrived and one is unable [to satisfy them all], he says:
A wandering ascetic (parivrāj) and a student (brahmacārin) should each be given three portions of alms.
Beyond that, if there is wealth available, one may give as much as desired without restriction. (52)
This has been explained by the preceding words. The giving of alms according to one’s means is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"One should indeed give alms according to the rule to a mendicant who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*);
free from greed, one should give food to those in need according to one's ability. (KūPu 1.2.18.117)
He states the rule for the offering of alms to an ascetic:
"One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, then give the alms-food, and again give water.
That alms-food is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is like the ocean. (53)
[410] This is clear. And that alms-food should be given in abundance when one has the means. Thus it is said in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"He who bestows upon ascetics alms sufficient to fill their bowls..."
"Being liberated from all evils, he shall not fall into an evil rebirth. Thus it is said.

Just as hospitality must necessarily be shown to a mendicant who has arrived, so too must hospitality be shown by one desiring prosperity to a person endowed with power who has come to one's own home; thus he says:
"One whose parasol, horse, and elephant-riders are magnificent should occupy the station of Indra; therefore, one should not scrutinize him. (54)

One who performs hospitality for a guest who possesses an umbrella and horses shall attain the station of Indra. Because of this statement, and because the preceding and following statements concern hospitality (*ātithya*), the two words "performing hospitality" (*ātithyaṃ kurvan*)—though not explicitly mentioned in this particular verse—are understood here by the principle of *sandaṃśa* (enclosure within a context). The phrase *kuñjarāroham* means that station of Indra upon which one mounts an elephant. It is called *ṛddhimat* because it possesses prosperity such as drinking the nectar of immortality and serving the Apsarases. Even if a guest possessing an umbrella and other such things—a Kṣatriya or similar—is inferior in terms of birth, lineage, or conduct, nevertheless, because honoring him is a cause for attaining heaven, one should not examine or doubt that guest with the thought of his inferiority—wondering, "Is he worthy of honor or not?"—but rather should honor him with the thought that he is the Lord (*Īśvara*).

Although this ascetic did not practice austerities in this life like a mendicant, he nevertheless performed penance in a past life; otherwise, the attainment of such sovereignty would be impossible. For this very reason, the Blessed One has shown that one possessing such splendor is a portion of the Lord:
"Whatever being is possessed of glory, beauty, or power, know that to be born from a mere fragment of my splendor" (BhG 10.41).
Therefore, it is proper that hospitality be extended to one endowed with sovereignty. || 54 ||
Regarding the statement that alms should be given to ascetics and students even before the Vaiśvadeva rite, he states the reasoning for this:
"A mendicant is capable of removing the sin committed during the Vaiśvadeva;
however, the Vaiśvadeva does not remove the faults committed by a mendicant. (55)

The fault that arises from performing the Vaiśvadeva offering after [the meal] is removed by the giving of alms (*bhikṣā*). However, the fault that arises from the omission of alms is not removed even by a previously performed Vaiśvadeva. In this context, the word "mendicant" (*bhikṣu*) is indicative of students and others as well. Accordingly, their status as mendicants was stated by Vyāsa:

"An ascetic (*yati*), a student (*brahmacārī*), a seeker of knowledge (*vidyārthin*), one who supports his teacher (*gurupoṣaka*), a traveler (*adhvaga*), and one whose livelihood is exhausted (*kṣīṇavṛtti*)—these six are remembered as mendicants."
Also in the Purāṇa:
"For one who is diseased, for one who is destitute of wealth, for one who has fallen away from his family, and for one who has set out upon a journey—wandering for alms is prescribed. (55)
Having stated "it is called the Vaiśvadeva," he declares the transgression incurred by failing to perform the Vaiśvadeva because it is present in the mind:
"Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva..."
All those should be known as fruitless; they fall into an impure hell. || 56 ||

"Fruitless" means devoid of the results as previously described. Not only is there an absence of attaining the desired, but the attainment of the undesired is also shown by the words, "they fall into the impure hell. || 56 ||
By means of the example of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he states that there is sin even in failing to perform the rites for guests:
"Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva and excluded from hospitality—all of them go to hell and enter the womb of a crow. (57)
Having experienced hell, such as Raurava and others, they subsequently enter the womb of a crow. || 57 ||
Praising [the guest] as such, he speaks of others who are also worthy of being fed:
"Whether he be a sinner, an outcaste, a slayer of a Brahmin, or a killer of a father—if he arrives during the Vaiśvadeva rite, he is a guest who leads one to heaven. (58)

A "sinner" (*pāpa*) is one who commits minor offenses such as the killing of a cow; for these individuals, there is only the obligation to provide food, but not the right to receive the full honors of hospitality. With this very intent, it is described in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]:
"Whether it be a Caṇḍāla or a dog-cooker, whoeversoever arrives at the proper time, he should be honored with food by one desiring welfare in the hereafter."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Whether he be a Caṇḍāla, a sinner, an enemy, or even a patricide—
if he arrives at the proper place and time, he is, in my view, worthy of being supported."

Hārīta praises the five great sacrifices (mahāyajña) that have been described: "A Brahmin who gratifies the gods, the sages, the ancestors, the elemental beings, and likewise the Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rule, becomes fit for union with Brahman. (HārSm 4.22)
Also in the Purāṇa:
"Whatever fruit a wealthy twice-born man obtains through the Soma sacrifice,
a poor man may attain that same fruit by properly performing the five great sacrifices."
Vyāsa states that there is a transgression in failing to perform [these rites]:
"The householder who, out of delusion, does not perform the five sacrifices, for him neither this world nor the next exists according to dharma. (58)
With reference to the rules for eating following the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña), he states therein what is to be avoided by way of restatement:
"He who eats with his head covered, he who eats facing south, or he who places his hand upon his left foot—verily, the Rākṣasas eat that. (59)
[414] And the procedure for eating has been shown by Manu:
"When the Brahmins, as well as one's own servants, have indeed finished eating..."
"Then afterwards, the husband and wife should eat what remains. (MDh 3.116).
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Then [one should feed] women who have recently given birth, the distressed, pregnant women, the elderly, and children..."
The householder should first feed [the guests] with consecrated food.

"O King, he who eats while these [guests] have not yet eaten consumes a grave misdeed; having died and gone to hell, he is born as one who feeds on phlegm. Thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* as well. (ViPu 3.11.68–69)
Having honored his dear guests, kinsmen, relatives, and supplicants,
he should then feed those who are disabled, children, the elderly, and the sick.
"And another who is destitute, his soul overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, desires food.
Thus [it is said]. Baudhāyana states the procedure regarding the meal:
"On a smooth seat placed in a clean, level spot that has been smeared [with cow dung]."
It may be square, triangular, circular, or crescent-shaped.
"The maṇḍala should be performed in due order among the Brāhmaṇas and the others. Thus says Śaṅkha as well:
"The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and Brahmā, the Grandfather."
“They subsist upon mandalas; therefore, one should construct a mandala. Thus it is said.
Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
“Having washed both feet and hands in a clean, smeared place...”
"Having sipped water, with a moist face and free from anger, one should eat while being moist in five places. Thus [says the text]. Vyāsa also says:
"One should eat while moist in five places, facing the east, and observing silence."
"The hands, the feet, and likewise the mouth—in these, fivefold moisture is prescribed. (LVyāSm 2.72).
Also in the *Āśvamedhika*:
"One should eat with moist feet, facing eastward, and on a clean seat."
"Having touched the ground with both feet, or again, with only one foot. Furthermore, that meal should be taken from a clean vessel; as it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"A twice-born man, free from anger, should eat from vessels that are praised and clean."
And the vessels that are recommended have been shown by Paiṭhīnasi:
"In a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or of lotus leaves and palāśa leaves,
one obtains the fruit of an Atirātra sacrifice at every meal."
"But he who eats alone from a pure bronze vessel—his four qualities increase: longevity, wisdom, fame, and strength.
In this regard, eating from a lotus leaf or a palāśa leaf pertains to those other than householders.
"Having eaten from palāśa or lotus leaves, a householder should perform the *aindava* penance;
however, for celibate students (*brahmacārins*) and ascetics (*yatis*), they obtain the fruit of the *cāndrāyaṇa*.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Vyāsa. As for the bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), it pertains exclusively to the householder, since its use is prohibited for ascetics and others. Thus says Pracetas:
"A mendicant, a student of sacred knowledge, and a widow should avoid betel, ointments, and eating from a bell-metal vessel. Furthermore,
that vessel must be placed on the ground, as it is stated in the Kūrmapurāṇa:
"Having placed the vessel upon the ground, one should eat five mouthfuls while it is still moist;

Prajāpati Manu has declared that this is equal to a fast. This placing [of the vessel] lasts until the offering of the *prāṇāhuti* oblations. Thereafter, however, one should eat after having ascended the *yantrikā*. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
Having set down the vessel, O great sage, one should eat five morsels;
having set aside the remainder, it should be eaten—listen now to the reason for this.
"The touch of droplets, the contact of feet, and likewise the dust from the feet or clothing—a Brahmin may eat these with ease; indeed, the purpose of the rite is not thereby lost.

The meaning is that at a funeral feast (*paitṛka-bhojana*), the placing of the food upon the ground or in a vessel must not be omitted. One should pay homage to the food placed in the aforementioned vessels; this is stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa*.
"Having seen the food, one should first bow down; then, with palms joined in reverence (*prāñjali*), one should say:
'May this be ours forever. Then, with devotion, one should pay homage.

Gobhila states the duty following the homage: "Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*). Having consecrated [the food] with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *gāyatrī*, one says at evening: 'I sprinkle you, the Real, with Truth,' and in the morning: 'I sprinkle you, the Truth, with the Real.'"
You move within all beings, dwelling in their secret cave, facing every direction;
you are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, you are the waters, the light, the essence, and the immortal.

[418] “You are Brahmā; you are Prajāpati; you are Brahman, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Om! You are the under-layering of immortality”—having thus drunk water and mentally offered the *daśahotṛ* formula, he should quickly take five mouthfuls. With the words “Svāhā to Prāṇa,” he offers that very portion into the Gārhapatya fire. With “Svāhā to Apāna,” he offers that very portion into the Anvāhāryapacana fire. With “Svāhā to Vyāna,” he offers that very portion into the Āhavanīya fire. With “Svāhā to Udāna,” he offers that very portion into the Sabhya fire. With “Svāhā to Samāna,” he offers that very portion into the Āvasathya fire. These five mantras are to be preceded by the *praṇava*. And so says Śaunaka:
"The Vāyu-mantras consist of names preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*.
One should swallow food with the tongue alone and not touch it with the teeth. Thus [it is said].
A specific rule regarding swallowing with the tongue is shown in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]:
"Just as the tongue does not perceive taste during the offering of breath, O King, so should one who is composed perform the offering of breath without sloth. Thus [it is said].
Śaunaka states the rule regarding the fingers for the offerings of breath:
The offering to the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs when the index finger, middle finger, and thumb are joined;
thereafter, one should offer to the downward breath (apāna) with the middle finger, ring finger, and thumb.
One should offer the oblation into Vyāna with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb;
then, having placed the index finger outside, one should offer it into Udāna.
"When [the food] is equal, there should be a collective offering with the entire hand.
Thus, a specific detail occurring immediately after the sprinkling is shown in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"One should indeed offer a portion of the first morsel of food from the meal as a *bali* to Dharmarāja."
Then, having given [the offering] to Citragupta and to the departed spirits (pretas), one should utter this:

"Wherever they may dwell, for the satisfaction of those hungry ghosts whose selves are afflicted by hunger and thirst, may this be inexhaustible according to their pleasure. Thus it is said; and also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

"Having covered the food with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and with water, one should perform the *āpośana* rite with the formula: 'Thou art the spreading of nectar' (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*). Thus [it is said]. Baudhāyana, however, having summarized all of this, says:

At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having washed his hands and feet and sipped water, he should sit facing the east in a clean, enclosed place. Having offered reverence with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om" to the food being brought forth, he should restrain his speech. After the food has been set down, he should sprinkle water around it clockwise while reciting the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, and without releasing his hand from the left side, he should first drink water with the mantra, "Thou art the under-layer for the nectar. Then, he offers the five oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) with the food: "In faith, seated in the out-breath (*prāṇa*), I offer nectar; may it enter me auspiciously, not burning me; svāhā to the out-breath! The formula is to be applied accordingly to the other breaths, beginning with "seated in the in-breath (*apāna*)," "seated in the diffused breath (*vyāna*)," "seated in the upward breath (*udāna*)," and "seated in the equalized breath (*samāna*). Having thus offered the five oblations of breath with the food, he should eat further in silence. Meditating on Prajāpati in his mind, he should not release his speech in the interval.
Moreover, they cite this example:

"Seated, facing the east, one should eat food while remaining silent and not disparaging it; without spilling any, and with full attention, having eaten, one should touch fire and perform the ritual sipping of water."

One should not bite with the teeth any food, cakes, bulbs, roots, fruits, or meat. Nor should one eat when excessively satiated. Having drunk water afterwards with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of immortality" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), and having sipped water again (*ācāntaḥ*), he touches the region of his heart with the mantra: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; enter me as Rudra the Destroyer; through this food, cause me to swell. [421] Having sipped water once more, he pours out the water from his hand onto his right big toe with the mantra:
"The Person the size of a thumb resides within the thumb;
the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the All-Consumer, is pleased."

With hands raised, he should perform the consecration of the offered food (*hutānnānumantraṇa*) with five mantras: "Having entered into faith, may the offered nectar nourish the breath with food" (*śraddhāyāṃ prāṇe niviśyāmṛtaṃ hutaṃ prāṇam annenāpyāyasva*). Then, with the syllable *Om* (*akṣara*), he should unite his self with the mantra: "May my self be joined with Brahman for the sake of immortality" (*brahmaṇi ma ātmāmṛtatvāya*). It is said: "Among those who sacrifice in all rituals, the sacrificer of the self (*ātmayājī*) is preeminent.
(Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra 2.7.12.2–15). In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "Having become focused on that [food], one should eat, beginning first with a sweet flavor."
Likewise, salt and sour [tastes] are in the middle, and thereafter pungent, bitter, and so forth.
"One should eat liquid food first, solid food in the middle, and liquid food again at the end; thus, one is not deprived of strength and health. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.83–84).
Regarding the number of mouthfuls in a meal, Āpastamba says:

"A sage should eat eight morsels, a forest-dweller sixteen, a householder thirty-two, and for a student there is no limit. Thus it is said in the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra (2.4.9.13). It is also stated in the Aśvamedhika Parvan:
One should swallow morsels the size of the mouth one by one;
however, that morsel which exceeds the capacity of the mouth is called "one's own leavings.
Furthermore, food remaining from the morsels as well as that which has fallen from the mouth [is also included].
"One should know that to be unfit for consumption; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should never eat too much, nor ever eat too little.
One should always eat in such a way that no distress arises from the food. Thus [it is said].
Vṛddha-Manu says: "Having drunk water, one should eat food that has been placed on a vessel and is not censurable;
a twice-born man should leave over some of the remnants for his wife, his laborers, and his slaves."
The rule regarding leaving a remnant of the food, however, refers to items other than ghee and the like. Thus Pulastya says:
"A wise person should never leave his meal entirely without remainder, except in the case of curd, barley-meal, ghee, meat, milk, honey, and water."
And this meal must be taken both in the evening and in the morning. As it was said by Manu:
"For the twice-born, eating in the evening and in the morning is enjoined by the Veda;
one should not eat in between, for this rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice" (MDh 2.53).

Gautama states: "One should eat food offered in the evening and morning without finding fault with it" (GDh 9.4). Having restated the well-known practice of eating with its ancillary requirements through the phrase "he who eats" in the root text, [the author] prohibits such acts as covering the head and so forth by declaring them to be transgressions. This also serves as an illustration for other things to be avoided, which are shown in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "That which one eats from the palm of the hand, that which is eaten with a hissing sound, and that which is eaten with fingers spread apart—that is like beef."
One should not eat while food from a previous meal is undigested, nor should one eat when excessively hungry;
one should never consume food while mounted on an elephant, a horse, a chariot, or a camel.
Whether staying within a cremation ground, or having gone to a temple, or lying down, one should not eat; nor should one eat food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
Neither with wet clothes nor with a wet head, nor without the sacred thread,
nor with his arms or thighs crossed, nor while seated upon a couch.
Nor with his head wrapped, nor with a vessel held in his lap,
nor with only one garment, nor looking downward, nor wearing sandals or shoes.
One should not eat while sitting upon a skin, nor with one's sides wrapped in skin;
one should not consume the remnants of a morsel, nor drink the remnants of what has been drunk.
One should not eat vegetables, roots, fruits, or sugarcane with one's teeth;
nor should one eat in haste while many others are eating.
"One should not discard food in vain, nor should one go anywhere while still having remnants of food. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"While eating, one should never touch the food with the left hand."
"One should not touch the feet, the head, or the bladder, nor should one touch a vessel with the foot. Thus says Uśanas:
"One should not eat something sweet without first giving it to others while many are looking on."
"Many should not eat together, nor should they eat while another looks on. Thus it is stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"One who is impure from eating remnants should not cause [another] to take clarified butter, and one should completely abandon the remnants of a sacrifice."
"One should not eat what remains after a Śūdra has eaten, even if it is contained in a vessel.
Also, in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Neither at midnight, nor at midday, nor when one has indigestion, nor while wearing wet clothes..."
Nor indeed in a broken vessel, nor on the ground, nor in the hands.
One should not take ghee while still impure from food, nor even while touching one's head;
nor should one do so after reciting the Veda, nor when it is entirely exhausted, nor together with one's wife.
"Not in darkness, nor at twilight, nor in temples and the like. Thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya also says: "One should not eat while looking at one's wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing. (YDh 1.131)
But as for that which says:
"If one should ever eat with a Brāhmaṇī woman or consume her leavings,
the wise do not consider there to be any fault in him at all."
If a Brāhmaṇa should ever eat the leavings of other women, he should be known as one requiring atonement; he is a man of mixed caste and deluded intellect.

Thus, this [statement] does not intend to establish the absolute absence of fault in all circumstances, because of the use of the word "kadācana" (at any time). For this very reason, the *Ādityapurāṇa* states:
"One may eat with a Brāhmaṇa wife at some point while on a journey;
however, having eaten together with a woman of a different caste, one falls [from his status] at that very moment."
Vṛddha-Manu also says:
"A twice-born man should neither drink nor eat with his left hand;
he should not drink water offered by a Śūdra with only one hand."
If water, while being drunk, falls from the mouth onto the vessel, that food becomes unfit for consumption; the eater would consume only sin.
"A Brāhmaṇa shall not drink water that has been turned yellow;
if he should drink it out of delusion, the twice-born man must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus says Atri.
"A Brāhmaṇa shall never drink water touched by the nails of a living being;
that is equal to drinking liquor—thus Manu has declared. So says Śātātapa.

"Whatever water a twice-born man drinks after lifting it with his left hand, that is equal to the drinking of liquor; so said Manu, the Lord of Creatures. Thus [it is stated] also in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan].
"The best of the twice-born may drink from that vessel with which he drinks water;
it shall not be considered leftover (ucchiṣṭa) until he sets it down upon the ground.
Thus says Śaṅkha: "Even if not invited, one should not eat first while remaining seated; one should not give more than is required, nor should one accept more. Śātātapa also [says the same].
But that ignorant twice-born man who, seated at the head of the row, eats first while many look on, takes upon himself the sin of the entire line.
[427] Thus says Gobhila: "When Brahmins seated in a single row are eating together,
if even one should set aside his vessel, the others shall not eat either."
But he who eats there out of delusion should perform the *taptasāntapana* penance;
likewise, he who abandons his vessel while the Brahmins are eating [should do the same].
"He who creates an obstacle to one's meal is likewise called a slayer of a Brahmin. Thus it is said. Regarding the restraint of speech, the Purāṇa states:
"Varuṇa would take away the strength of one about to bathe, and Agni would take away the prosperity of one offering oblations."
"While eating, death [seizes] one's lifespan; therefore, silence is prescribed in these three cases.
As for that which was stated by Atri: "The vow of silence is extremely difficult to maintain; it is destroyed even by the utterance of 'hum'."
If that were so, there would be a great fault; therefore, one should practice that with constancy.
Thus, this refers to the intention of "wooden silence" (*kāṣṭha-mauna*). And this applies to the period prior to five mouthfuls. Accordingly, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"One should always eat food while remaining silent and without disparaging it;
[eating] five mouthfuls is 'great silence' (*mahā-mauna*), which greatly nourishes the vital breaths and so forth."
Also in the *Āśvamedhika*:
"Whether observing silence or not, the Brahmin, being joyful and with senses restrained, should eat according to the rule and should not chew his leftovers."
Śātātapa also says:
"Food given with the hand, as well as salt [concealed] from direct view,
and likewise the eating of clay, is declared to be equivalent to the eating of cow-meat."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"Salt, condiments, ghee, oil,
as well as various kinds of foods to be licked or drunk— one should not eat these when they have been given by hand."
Ghee, rice, and all varieties of side dishes should be served with a ladle;
likewise, water and cooked food—whosoever desires to give these should do so with a ladle.

"He is a killer of an embryo, a drinker of spirituous liquor, a thief, and one who violates the teacher's bed. Thus [it is said] in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]: "Even toward a woman in her courses, a Caṇḍāla, a dog, or even a cock..."
If, while eating, he should see that food, he must abandon it.

"One should know that food into which hair or insects have fallen, or which has been fanned by the breath of the mouth, is unfit for consumption; having eaten such, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus says Kātyāyana.

"Having heard the words of a Caṇḍāla, an outcaste, or a woman who has recently given birth, the best of the twice-born should eat only a single mouthful [of food] and then fast for one day. Thus says Gautama as well.
"As long as the sound of trumpets, the whirling of stones, a wheel, or a mortar is heard, for that duration there shall be no eating. Thus [it is stated]. Bṛhaspati also says:
One should not eat even in the same row as Brahmins, even if they are one's own kinsmen;
for who knows what secret sin another might possess?
"Whatever evil deed is committed by wicked-souled men sitting in a single row,
it belongs equally to all of them as long as the row is not broken.
He [the same author] also describes the manner of breaking the row:
"By fire, by ashes, by a pillar, by water,
