and by a door or a path— thus is the breaking of the row (paṅktibheda) declared by the wise. So too says Yama:
"Water, grass, ashes, a door, and likewise a path—having placed these as an interval, no defect in the row occurs.

Thus, the specific rules characterized by the avoidance of such things as having the head wrapped, as stated in the root texts, have been shown. The prohibition against facing south applies to daily meals, because that rule is prescribed for optional (kāmya) rites. And so says Manu:
"One who eats facing east gains long life; facing south, one gains fame;
facing west, one gains prosperity; and facing north, one eats the truth" (MDh 2.52).
However, Gobhila prohibits facing south.
"A Brahmin should sit facing the east, or facing the west as is comfortable;
however, for rites concerning the ancestors (pitṛkārya), he should face north and avoid facing south.

Regarding the phrase "with the hand on the left foot" (*vāmapādakara*): it refers to one whose hand is on the left foot. Whatever is eaten by those who eat with their hand on the left foot, or by those who eat while standing—all that is consumed by the *rākṣasas*. The meaning is that [the eater] does not himself obtain the fruit of the *prāṇāgnihotra* and other such rites. That food, once eaten, goes to the *rākṣasas*, is also shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.

"He who eats with his head covered, he who eats facing an intermediate direction, and he who eats wearing shoes—all that should be known as pertaining to the Asuras" (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.19.19). After the intended rule for eating, the subsequent subsidiary acts such as the offering of water for the remnants (*ucchiṣṭodaka*) and so forth must be performed. Regarding this, Devala says:
"Having taken a little of the remains from all [the food] after eating, and having sipped water,
one should offer it with water upon the ground to those entitled to receive the portion of leavings.
Regarding this, the mantra is as follows:

"In Raurava, the abode of pus, for those living in Padma and Arbuda, may it remain inexhaustible for all living beings who approach [the offering]. Thus [it is said]. Vyāsa also states in prose: "Then, being satisfied, having sipped water with the mantra 'Thou art the covering of nectar' (amṛtāpidhānam asi), and having moved slightly away from that place, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) according to the rules. And that method of rinsing the mouth has been shown by Devala.
"Having eaten, one should sip water according to the prescribed rule with a concentrated mind;
one should also cleanse the mouth and hands with earth and water, even by means of rubbing.
And that rubbing must not be performed with the index finger. Regarding this, Gautama says:
"At the time of rinsing the mouth, one should perform the cleansing of the face with the index finger;
if a foolish person fails to do so, he shall fall into the Raurava hell. (Gauḍa-smṛti 5.29). Vyāsa says:
That foolish person who, having washed his hands, drinks the rinsing water (gaṇḍūṣa) causes the gods, the ancestors, and even himself to fall.
One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) from that vessel in which one has eaten;
likewise, if one rises from the seat after eating without having performed ācamana, [one must do so].
"One should perform an immediate bath; otherwise, one would remain impure. Thus it is said. Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"With the mantra 'Thou art the covering of nectar,' one should drink water from above."
Having sipped water once, one should sip again with the mantra beginning "āyaṃ gauḥ."
Or, having recited the *drupadā* verse three times, which destroys all sins,
he should then touch his heart with the mantra, "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths."
Having sipped water, with his hands raised and composed, he should let the water from his hand flow out over the big toe of his right foot by means of the thumb.
One should perform the consecration of the oblation with the mantra beginning "In faith" (śraddhāyām);
then, one should unite oneself with the Imperishable (akṣara) by means of the syllable "Brahman."
"Of all yogas, the sacrifice to the Self (ātmayāga) is remembered as the highest.
He who performs it according to this rule goes to the station of Brahman. Thus [says] Atri. (KūPurāṇa 1.2.19.9–13)
Even after sipping water, one remains impure as long as the vessel has not been removed;
even when it has been removed, one remains impure as long as the ground is not wiped clean.
"For even on ground that has been smeared [with cow dung], a man remains impure as long as he has not touched the earth after rising from his seat. Thus says Śātātapa.
Having sipped water and set aside the vessel, and having touched the principal vital organs with his hand while it is still slightly moist,
as well as the navel with the palm of the hand;
Having eaten, one should not depart immediately, nor with wet hands;
rather, placing the hand upon the head and touching fire, one should remain composed.
"A man skilled in practice attains preeminence among his kinsmen.
Also, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Established in himself, with a tranquil mind, having taken up his seat..."
And a person should perform the recollection of their chosen deities.
May Agni, impelled by the wind, cause the food of the earth to swell;
may he, granted space by the ether, digest it, and may there be happiness for me.
May this food, transformed for me, serve for the strength of earth, water, fire, and air; may there be unimpeded happiness for me.
May food be nourishing for the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna breaths; may there be unimpeded happiness for me.
May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire digest without remainder the food eaten by me;
may they grant me the well-being arising from its digestion, and may my body be free from disease.
Just as the Lord Viṣṇu alone is the primary essence of all the senses, bodies, and embodied beings,
by that truth may this entire food become conducive to my health and undergo proper digestion.
Viṣṇu is the eater, and likewise the food and its transformation;
by that truth, may this food I have eaten be digested for me.
Having recited this and rubbed his belly with his own hand, he should perform his duties without weariness and with alertness. Thus [it is said in Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.11.87–98]. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"Having sipped water once more, one should then consume betel-leaf. Thus [it is said].
On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Betel-nut that is well-prepared, with excellent leaves, and provided with lime-powder..."
A wise person should refrain from chewing betel leaf without first having given it to the twice-born and the gods.
A single group brings happiness and health; two groups will be fruitless;
three groups are most excellent, and more than that does not cause any harm.
A disease arises from the base of a leaf; the occurrence of sin from the tip of a leaf.
A withered leaf takes away life, while a vein destroys the intellect.
Therefore, a wise person should eat betel, having specifically avoided the tip, the root, and the stalk, as well as withered leaves.
[435] Thus: this food which has been specified is forbidden at the time of its reception. Regarding this, Manu says:

"During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat; one may eat after bathing once they have been released. If they have not been released when they set, one should bathe and eat on the following day. (MDh 4.224)

"During an eclipse" means at the time of the seizing. The period of the eclipse begins from the moment of contact (*sparśa*) and lasts until the moment of release (*mokṣa*). During that time, one should not eat. Rather, one should eat after bathing once the moon and the sun have been released by Rāhu. However, when there is a total eclipse ending with sunset (*grastāstamaya*), then one should eat on the following day after seeing that both have been released. Not only is there an absence of eating during the time of the eclipse itself, but also prior to the eclipse. As Vyāsa says: "One should not eat before a solar eclipse during the day, nor before a lunar eclipse in the evening."
One should not eat during an eclipse, but one may eat after bathing once it has been released.

"One should eat when the moon has been released [from eclipse], provided it is not the dead of night; or, if both [sun and moon] have not been released or have set, one may eat after seeing them on the following day. (La-vyā-sm 2.77–78). Regarding the prohibition of eating at the aforementioned times, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states the following distinction:
If a lunar eclipse occurs during the first watch of the day, one should eat before midday;
if it occurs during the last watch, one should eat after midnight.
"But it must be after the sun has turned [in the afternoon] and before midnight;
if it occurs during the fourth watch, it must be prior to that fourth watch. Thus it is said.

If the eclipse occurs during the first watch of the night or after midday, one should eat before the *āvartana* (the turning point) of the day, that is, prior to midday. If it occurs during the last watch of the night, one should eat before the first watch of the night. The meaning is that if the sun is eclipsed during the fourth watch of the day, one should eat below—that is, before—the fourth watch of the night. *Viśītha* refers to midnight. The meaning is that if the sun is eclipsed after midday, one should eat only before midnight. In the case of a lunar eclipse, an interval of three watches is required; however, in the case of a solar eclipse, an interval of four watches is required—this is the essential point. And so says Vṛddha-Gautama:
"One should not eat for four watches prior to a solar eclipse,
but for three watches prior to a lunar eclipse, except in the case of children, the elderly, and the sick.
Regarding the specific case of children, the elderly, and the sick, there is a distinction stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"One should eat in the afternoon, but not at midday; if it be midday, then not during the *saṅgava* period;
if it be the *saṅgava* period, one should not have eaten previously.
Regarding the penance for eating when one is capable [of fasting], it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"Having eaten during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one is purified by a *prājāpatya* penance;
having eaten on that very day [of the eclipse], one is purified by a three-night fast. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the exception for a three-watch period during a lunar eclipse, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"One should not eat during the day prior to the eclipse of the moon.
Regarding the specific case of the eclipsed setting, Bhṛgu says:
"If both the sun and the moon reach their setting while being eclipsed..."
"On the day following those two, a man, having bathed at sunrise, should take his meal. Thus says Vṛddhagārgya as well:
"When Rāhu swallows the moon and the sun at the time of twilight..."
"One should not eat at all on that day, nor even at night. Thus it is said; and also in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"When there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one must not eat for a full day and night."

"Having seen [the food] being eaten, one should eat after having performed a bath. Now, if it is argued that visual perception is not possible when the food has disappeared from sight, we say no; for by the word "seeing," what is intended is knowledge derived from the scriptures. Thus said Vṛddhagautama:
"One should not eat on the day of an eclipse of the moon or sun, prior to that [time];
having recognized Rāhu’s release and bathed, one should take food.
If this is so, then—even in the case of an eclipse ending at sunset—eating would likewise follow, since it is possible to have knowledge of the scriptures even before sunrise on the following day.
That is not so;
on the day after those two [eclipses], a person, having bathed, may eat;
however, when there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one must not eat for a full day and night.
Because that [objection] is not applicable due to these two statements; as for what is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"O dear one, when a lunar eclipse occurs after midnight, one should eat in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), and never in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*)."
O Śikhivāhana, when an eclipse of the moon occurs before midnight, one should not take food during the day.

This refers to the intention of three watches (yāmas); however, regarding a lunar eclipse, Vṛddha-Gautama specifies "three watches" as a particular rule. One who desires the destruction of evil should fast on the day of the eclipse. To this effect, Dakṣa says:
"During the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses, one who has fasted for a day and night and bathed is liberated from all sins."

But a daughter should not fast. Regarding this, Nārada says: "A householder who has sons should not observe a fast on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun."

However, at the time of a total eclipse (*grasta-astamaya*), even those who have children must observe a fast, because of the prohibition against eating: "One must not eat for a day and night. Yet, in certain specific types of eclipses, bathing and other such rites should not be performed. This is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "When there is a solar eclipse at night, or likewise a lunar eclipse during the day, one should not perform a bath, nor should one ever give a gift."
And this is to be understood as applying when those situated in specific locations lack the capacity to perceive the swallowing and releasing [of the breath].
Thus ends the section on eating.

One should pass the fifth part of the day by means of the collection of duties to be performed ending with the meal as thus described. By this mention of the duties belonging to the five parts [of the day], the remaining duties of the day are to be indicated by way of illustration. And that collection of duties has been shown by Dakṣa:
"But having eaten, one should remain at ease and digest that food."
One should pass the sixth and seventh [periods] by means of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth.
"In the eighth [month], however, there is worldly activity; then, outside, the twilight [ritual] again.
Thus [says Atri]:
"One should not sleep during the day, and one should indeed avoid women."
Sleeping during the day destroys longevity; sexual intercourse with a woman during the day destroys merit.
"One should study the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras;
one should avoid idle disputatious speech and slander.
Thus [it is said] also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
One should perform tasks without weariness and with diligence,
diverting oneself with the study of authentic scriptures and other such activities that do not conflict with the true path and similar virtues.
"Then he should pass the day and, with a concentrated mind, perform the twilight worship. Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"He should spend the remainder of the day with learned and beloved kinsmen."

"Having performed the evening twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), having offered oblations into those fires and attended to them, and having eaten surrounded by his dependents, he should then go to bed without being overly full. (YDh 1.113–14) By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and having performed" (*upāsa ca*), [the author] includes the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice and other rites. The evening twilight devotions and the fire-oblation have been described. A certain specific detail regarding the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites is shown in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
Furthermore, O lord of the earth, having prepared the evening meal,
one should offer the bali-oblation for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva rite together with one's wife.
[440] Even there, one should likewise offer food to outcastes and others;
furthermore, a wise person should honor a guest who has arrived there according to his own ability.
O King, whatever sin is incurred when a guest turns away at daybreak,
that very same sin is multiplied eightfold for men when the sun has risen and he turns away.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, a man should honor a guest who has arrived with the sun according to his own ability; when he is honored, all the deities are honored.

"O King, having performed the purification of his feet and other parts and having eaten in the evening, the householder should then go to a bed that is not cracked, even if it is made of wood. (ViP 3.11.101–07).
Thus ends the section on duties for the remainder of the day and so forth.

Now Hārīta describes the manner of going to bed: “Having thoroughly washed the soles of his feet, having performed protective rites (*rakṣā*), and being accompanied by auspicious items such as a jar filled with water, he should ascend the bed that is comfortable for himself and free from defects, reciting the verse ‘sutramāṇam. Having muttered the *Rātrisūkta*, paid homage to Viṣṇu, and recited the verse ‘Sarpāpasarpa bhadraṃ te,’ he should remember his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), enter into meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and after muttering other Vedic mantras and the *Sāvitrī*, while listening to auspicious sacred texts and the sound of a conch shell, he should sleep with his head toward the south. The phrase “with his head toward the south” is intended as an illustration; likewise, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:

"The head is recommended toward the eastern direction, or else toward the south, O King, for a man who is always sleeping; however, the opposite brings about disease. (ViP 3.11.109). Gārgya also says:

"One should sleep in one's own home with the head toward the east for longevity; with the head toward the south [in the same place]; with the head toward the west while traveling abroad; and occasionally with the head toward the north. Thus it is said, and also in the Purāṇa:
"Having remembered and recited the *Rātrisūkta*, and having paid homage to the imperishable Viṣṇu, one should sleep at night established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus [it is said].
Those who cause peaceful sleep have also been shown by Gobhila:
"Agastya, Mādhava, the great sage Mucukunda, the sage Kapila, and Āstīka—these five sleep in peace. Thus it is said.
Mārkaṇḍeya speaks of those who must be avoided at the time of sleeping:
[442] One should not sleep in an empty house, in a cremation ground, under a solitary tree, at a crossroads, in the temple of Mahādeva, or in the dwelling of the Mothers.
Nor in a shrine of yakṣas or nāgas, nor likewise in a shrine of Skanda; nor in the shade of riverbanks, nor on gravel, clods of earth, or dust.
One should never sleep in a pit without necessity, nor should one ever sleep upon grain,
cattle, Brahmins, deities, or one's teachers.
Nor should one study on a broken bed, nor in an unclean place, nor while being oneself impure;
nor while wearing wet clothes, nor naked, nor with the head pointing toward the north or the west.
"Neither in the sky, nor in that which is entirely empty, nor likewise in a sacred tree. Thus it is said.

Viṣṇu also says: “One should not sleep with wet feet; nor with the head toward the north or the west; nor naked; nor on a wet bamboo bed; nor in the open air; nor on a bed of *palāśa* leaves; nor on one made of five kinds of wood; nor on one made from wood broken by an elephant; nor on one burnt by lightning; nor on a cracked one; nor on one scorched by fire; nor on one made from a tree watered by a jar; nor in cremation grounds, empty dwellings, or temples of the gods; nor in the midst of fickle people; nor in the midst of women; nor above grain, cattle, one’s teacher, fire, or the gods; nor while impure from food remnants; nor should one sleep during the day, nor at the two twilights, nor on ashes; nor in an unclean place, nor on damp ground, nor on a mountain peak. (ViDh 70.1–17). It is also stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.

"One should not occupy a bed that is not spacious, nor one that is broken, uneven, dirty, infested with insects, or uncovered. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.108). Uśanas says: "One should not sleep with oil smeared on the head, nor, if uninitiated, on a black antelope skin. Dakṣa says:
[444] “He should spend the final two watches of the night devoted to the study of the Vedas;

by sleeping for only two watches, he becomes fit for union with Brahman. (DaŚm 2.54). Thus, beginning with the words “The twilight bath” and ending with “he who has his head wrapped,” this section of the text has concisely defined the daily ritual (*āhnika*) through the indicative marks of the Śruti. By performing this, one attains spiritual welfare (*śreya*); by failing to perform it, however, there is transgression (*pratyavāya*). This has been stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
Thus, this entire collection of duties for Brahmins, which bestows the fruit of liberation, has been proclaimed by me day after day.
If a Brahmin does not perform [his duties] out of atheism or laziness,
he goes to terrible hells and is reborn in the womb of a crow.

"There is no other path to liberation except one's own prescribed stage of life (āśrama). Therefore, one should perform ritual actions for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.19.30–32) || 59 ||

Thus, having defined the specific duties (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of a Brāhmaṇa by means of the phrase "devoted to the six duties," and having concluded this daily observance (*āhnika*) in connection with the general duties (*sādhāraṇadharma*) such as study mentioned therein, he now states the specific duties of the consecrated Kṣatriya as they follow in due order:
"For where twice-born men wander for alms while remaining without vows and unlearned... [445]
The king should punish that village, for it is indeed a provider of sustenance for thieves.
For the Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapon in hand and wielding the rod of punishment, should conquer the enemy armies and protect the earth in accordance with dharma. (61)

“One should pluck flower after flower, but should not cause the cutting of the roots, like a gardener in a grove, and not like a charcoal-burner. (62) For the duty of a king is twofold: the punishment of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous. Of these, the first verse establishes the punishment of the wicked. By the word *vrata* here, the avoidance of honey and other forbidden things by a religious student (*brahmacārin*) is intended. And thus, Yājñavalkya, having stated “without causing pain to his vow” (YDh 1.3), clarified that very vow which he intended to express.
"One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, leavings of food, fermented acids, women, injury to living beings, looking at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and so forth. (YDh 1.33)

Alternatively, the four vows well-known in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, beginning with the *Prājāpatya*, are what is denoted here by the word "vow" (*vrata*). The king should punish that village where students (*brahmacārin*) who are devoid of both types of vows and do not even study their own sacred texts (*svādhyāya*) practice begging for alms; for that village provides food and sustenance to those who are like thieves. By this statement, it is indicated that all kings must punish everyone who fails to perform what is enjoined and performs what is prohibited. For this very reason, Nārada says:
Whichever caste should decline and whichever should attain preeminence—
having observed each such case, one should establish that person who has strayed from their own path back upon the path.

"And regarding other acts not prescribed by the scriptures that are joined with sin, the king, having deliberated within himself, shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment. (NSm 17.67). Thus says Yājñavalkya.

"Having disciplined families, castes, guilds, corporations, and even rural communities that have deviated from their own duties, the king shall establish them on the [right] path. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 1.361]. Manu also says:
"Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest is exempt from punishment by the king if they abide in unrighteousness. Thus [says Manu]; Yājñavalkya also [says]:
"Whether it be a brother, a son, a worthy guest, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle—there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king. (YDh 1.358).
Thus, Yājñavalkya praises the punishment of those deserving of punishment.
"The king who punishes those deserving of punishment and causes those deserving of death to be executed properly, has performed sacrifices with the most excellent sacrificial fees. (YDh 1.359).
Manu prohibits the punishment of those who do not deserve it.
"A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it, incurs great infamy and goes to hell" (MDh 8.128).
And punishment is of two kinds: corporal and monetary. As Nārada has said:
"Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporal and monetary.
Corporal punishment is proclaimed to range from flogging up to death; monetary punishment likewise ranges from a *kākiṇī* coin up to the forfeiture of all one's property. (NSm 21.53–55)
Manu establishes the king's role as the wielder of punishment through an extensive discourse:
"For when this world was without a king and everything had fled in every direction out of fear,
the Lord created the king for the protection of all this."
Having extracted the eternal portions from Indra, Anila, Yama, and Ārka; from Agni and Varuṇa; and from Candra and Vitteśa.
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore overcomes all beings with his splendor.
Like the sun, he scorches both eyes and minds;
no one on earth is able even to look upon him.
By his power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma;
he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra.
A king must not be despised even if he is a child,
for he is a great deity dwelling in human form.
Fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the king's fire consumes the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.
Having truly considered the task, his own power, and the place and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the Goddess of Fortune, in whose prowess dwells victory,
and in whose anger dwells death— for he is composed of all splendor.
But he who hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind upon his swift destruction.
Therefore, that lord of men should apply whatever law he desires toward those who are dear to him,
and he should not deviate from that law even toward those who are not dear.
For their sake, the Lord first created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the rod consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
"A king who conducts him [the minister] properly prospers through the three aims of life. (Manu Dharmaśāstra 7.3–27).
In the Mahābhārata:
"All deities are invisible; the king is the visible deity."
And whose favor and anger are seen to be directly perceptible.
The king is indeed both mother and father; the king is the lineage of those who possess lineage. The king is truth and righteousness; the king is the benefactor of men.
Either time is the cause of the king, or the king is the cause of time;
let there be no such doubt in you: the king is the cause of time.
"O Great King, the Dharma of the world is obtained with the king as its root; it is only through fear of the king that subjects do not devour one another. (MBh Śānti, Rājadharmaparvan 69.79).

Now, one might object: since it is stated that "the king should inflict punishment," the king's role as an inflictor of punishment has been mentioned; how then can this be the unique duty (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of the Kṣatriya?

Not so; for it has been determined in the *Aveṣṭyadhikaraṇa* that the word "king" (*rājan*) refers specifically to a Kṣatriya. To explain: in the second chapter, in the section on the *Aveṣṭi*, it is heard in the context of the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice—which is a part of the *Rājasūya* performed by a king—that "if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should place the offering to Bṛhaspati in the middle and, having offered the oblation, pour clarified butter over it; if a Rājanya, [the offering to] Indra; if a Vaiśya, [the offering to] the Viśvedevas. (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 2.1.5) [450] Thus, the term is restricted.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the *rājasūya* sacrifice for the castes such as Brāhmaṇas who are already included in the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, or is it for the Kṣatriya alone? To determine that, one must further investigate: Does the word "king" (*rājan*) denote all three castes, or only the Kṣatriya? Furthermore, one must consider whether the word "king" is based on the connection with sovereignty (*rājya-yoga*), or based on the status of being a Kṣatriya (*kṣatriyatva*). In this matter, the word "king" is based solely on the connection with sovereignty, because of its usage among the Āryas; for it is well-known to all the world and is used without contradiction. It is not, however, based on the status of being a Kṣatriya, because the usage among non-Āryas is weaker than the usage among Āryas, and because there is contradiction regarding the Draviḍas (where the term is applied even to non-Kṣatriyas). Moreover, it is not unknown among others. Thus, by virtue of the connection with sovereignty, all three [castes] can be kings. But the term "sovereignty" (*rājya*) refers by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) to the protection of the realm (*janapada-rakṣaṇa*); it does not depend on the connection with a king.

If it is argued: "Since the rule *'yak' is applied after words ending in *pati* and *purohita*, etc.* (Pāṇini 5.1.128) is governed by the heading *'in the sense of an action'* (*karmaṇi*), and since the word *rājan* is included therein—and because direct usage (*ācāra*) is stronger than traditional authority (*smṛti*)—the primary meaning of the term *rājya* is indeed the yoga of a king."

Since it is common usage alone that serves as the authority for determining the meaning of words, that alone—and nothing else—is the source even for traditional Smṛti. Furthermore, from actual usage, it is understood that the word *rājya* (sovereignty) is independent and that the word *rājan* (king) is derived from it as its cause. Therefore, the Smṛti rule following that usage must be explained as being concerned merely with the distinction between correct (*śabda*) and incorrect (*apaśabda*) forms of the word. Consequently, since all three [classes] are denoted by the term *rājā* and are thus applicable in the Rājasūya sacrifice, the scriptural mentions of them serve to define the specific occasion (*nimitta*). Moreover, the word "if" (*yadi*) is also proof that the word *rājan* has its basis in connection with sovereignty; otherwise, in the absence of such applicability, the word "if" would be illogical. Furthermore, Vedic indication is more authoritative than Smṛti. Thus, the conclusion reached is that the scriptural mentions serve to define the occasion. To this, we reply: [The rest of the passage follows: ...because the word *rājan* is used in the sense of one who possesses sovereignty, and because the word *rājya* is not used independently of the word *rājan*, the Smṛti rule is based on common usage. However, in the case of the Rājasūya, the word *rājan* is used in its primary sense of Kṣatriyas, while the word *rājya* refers to the Vaiśyas and others who have been appointed to the office of king. Therefore, the mention of the three classes is not for the purpose of defining the occasion, but rather for the purpose of enjoining the performance of the sacrifice for those who are already entitled to it. As for the word "if," it indicates a conditional application based on the specific context of the ritual procedure. Thus, the scriptural mentions are not merely for the sake of defining the occasion. This is the established conclusion.

A definitive conclusion cannot be reached here based on Vedic injunction alone, because that [usage] exists otherwise as well. For in the injunction regarding consecration—“one should consecrate the king”—the word *rājan* is used even before the connection with kingship, referring merely to a Kṣatriya; thus, the word *rājan* is determined to be based on conventional usage (*rūḍha*). Furthermore, because the particle *yadi* is indeclinable, and according to the traditional rule that “there is no fault in a restriction [of meaning] in any way whatsoever,” the word *rājan* is independent. Nor is it rootless, for the usage among the Draviḍas can serve as its root. Therefore, there is no evidence for the authority of the traditional rule regarding its literal sense. Since such usage is possible through the conduct of those who are experts, and since the application of the word might have spread from secondary or erroneous usage, the word *rājan* is applied by virtue of the connection with kingship. However, the independent word *rājan* denotes a Kṣatriya; thus, since Brāhmaṇas and others are not eligible for the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, the scriptural statements serve as the means of eligibility (*prāpaka*). In the same way, here too, the word *rājan* refers to a Kṣatriya.

Now, an objection may be raised: Is it not stated in the *Mahābhārata* that kingship arises from pleasing the people? "Indeed, kingship comes from pleasing the subjects and also from protecting them. Certainly; such a capacity to please is indeed possible for a Kṣatriya as well. By the second verse beginning with "For the Kṣatriya," the duty consisting of the protection of the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) is set forth. Since, among the duties of a king, the protection of the subjects is intended to be the primary one, it was mentioned first as "the protection of the subjects. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects. Thus [it is said].
Manu also demonstrates that very same point at the outset:
"The protection of subjects, as well as giving, sacrifice, and study..."
"And he enjoined upon the Kṣatriya non-attachment to sense objects" (MDh 1.89). Also, in the Śāntiparvan:
"The supreme duty of kings is indeed the protection of their subjects."
For a king who enjoys the fruits as they have been ordained is joined with righteousness.
The king becomes the protector of the social classes and the stages of life;
by enjoining his subjects to their respective duties, he should always protect them.
By the very protection of living beings, the lord of the earth fulfills his duty;
as one who protects them properly, he obtains a full share of merit.

Whatever [merit] one gains by being born, by studying, by giving, and by performing worship— the king, while protecting his subjects according to dharma, becomes the recipient of a sixth part of that.
The king should always protect all his subjects in accordance with dharma;
moreover, he should honor the righteous through diligence and graciousness.
"For when the King is honored, Dharma is thereby honored everywhere;
whatever the King practices is what pleases the subjects. Thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
My child, a king who has been consecrated to the kingdom must, from the very beginning, endeavor to delight his subjects without contradicting his own dharma.
"By the very protection of living beings, the lord of the earth has fulfilled his duty;
having protected them properly, he obtains a full share in meritorious deeds. Thus [it is said] in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* (27.4–31).
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The great fruit of the merit that a king, protecting his subjects with righteousness, performs during a single day, he enjoys for ten thousand years.
Thus [says] Manu as well.
A sixth part of all merit accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of even demerit accrues to him who does not protect.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices day after day with fees of hundreds and thousands.
“That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, and tolls—whether for the sake of personal pleasure, enjoyment, or punishment—he shall immediately go to hell. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the subjects who have fallen into danger must be protected. Their danger arises in two ways: from thieves, tigers, and the like, or from enemy armies. Therefore, for the purpose of warding off both of these, it is said that he is "possessed of firm punishment" and "having conquered enemy armies. Anticipating the objection as to why this protection is the exclusive duty of the Kṣatriya alone, the fact of his "having weapons in hand" is described as the reason for that. And that belongs to the Kṣatriya alone. Thus says Manu: "The bearing of weapons and missiles is the duty of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya."
"Furthermore, for the sake of livelihood, his duty consists of giving, study, and sacrifice" (MDh 10.79).
Also, in the *Ānuśāsana-parvan*, with reference to the Kṣatriya, it is recited:
"Zeal and the bearing of weapons—this is his eternal duty."

By the phrase "with weapons in hand," all the implements of war are indicated; these are shown in the Śāntiparvan: "Staves, lances, swords, and sharpened axes, as well as shields and armor, were prepared in great numbers."

By the term "possessing severe punishment" (*pradaṇḍavān*), the instruction of thieves and others is intended. Although this has already been mentioned in the preceding statement, there it was presented primarily [as a personal quality], whereas here it is presented as a means for protecting the subjects; thus, there is no tautology. Manu states the manner of punishment:
"Having examined the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature, and having considered the offense, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment. (MDh 8.126)
Viṣṇu [455]:
"In other offenses as well, having taken into account the caste, wealth, and age, the king shall determine the punishment after consulting with Brāhmaṇas. (ViDh 5.194)
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Reproach, verbal abuse, a beating, and the confiscation of one's own property—this punishment is ordained in four ways.
One should determine it after considering the nature and extent of the man's offense."
One should punish teachers, domestic priests, and Brahmins solely with the punishment of speech;
other litigants and offenders one should punish with a fine.
"And those who have committed great offenses, he should punish with the penalty of death.
Likewise, Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of friends and others, one should employ the punishment of words, such as 'Shame on you wretched ones!'"
They should do for him that which has been stated, and even that which is unstated but well-conceived.
"One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment."— Thus says Manu.
The Self-existent Manu has declared ten places for punishment;
these may be applied to the three social classes, but a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt.
The genitals, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
"Shaving the head is ordained as the punishment ending in death for a Brāhmaṇa, especially for men of noble birth and for women. (MDh 8.124–25).
Bṛhaspati also says:
One might destroy this entire world, yet that is equal to [the offense against] a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive of his slaughter in his mind.
"They say that Brāhmaṇas are not to be slain, even if they are established in all manner of sins. Whatever is beneficial for the Brāhmaṇas, that the king should practice.
He should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with his entire wealth intact and unhurt. Thus it is said.
Yama also said:
"For a king who thus proceeds according to Dharma and wields the rod of punishment,
his fame spreads throughout this world, and likewise his residence in heaven is imperishable."

The conquest of the enemy army, however, is shown in the Śāntiparvan. The mobilization of an army is recommended in either the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa; for at that time the earth is rich in ripened crops and abounding in water.
O Bhārata, the season is neither too cold nor too hot;
therefore, at that time, one should engage [in battle], or else when the enemies are in distress.
For these are the recommended formations for an army in the assault of the enemy;
a path that has water, grass, and is level is praised as suitable for marching.
With their movements well-observed by skilled scouts familiar with the forest,
they should fight like immovable mountains, having placed the Seven Sages behind them.

Where the wind blows, where the sun shines, and where the moon is bright, there lies victory. Those who are skilled in warfare praise a terrain for horses that is free from mud, free from water, without natural boundaries, and devoid of clods of earth.
A chariot ground that is level and free from water is praised; for those who fight on elephants, ground with low trees, thick undergrowth, and water is recommended.
The terrain was filled with many inaccessible places and great trees, obscured by bamboos and reeds; it was ground suitable for infantry, consisting of mountains and groves.
An army with a great abundance of infantry is firm, O Bhārata;
an army with a great abundance of chariots and horses is praised on fair days.
"In the rainy season, an army consisting largely of infantry and elephants is recommended.
Having reckoned these advantages, one should engage in battle against enemies. Thus [it is said in] MBh 12.100.10–25. Manu also [says]:
But when the lord intends to set out toward the enemy's kingdom,
he should then proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this following rule.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition,
or else toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra, according to his strength.
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives that victory is uncertain,
he should march forth only after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for his enemy.
Having performed the ritual at the base according to the rules, as well as the preparations for the journey, and having secured a residence and properly stationed spies; [458]
"Having cleared the three types of paths and his own sixfold force, he should slowly advance toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a prolonged campaign. (MDh 7.181–85).

The sixfold nature of the force was shown by Uśanas: "The root-force, the guild-force, the ally-force, the hired-force, the enemy-force, and the forest-dweller-force. Manu describes the preparation and arrangement of the army for the purpose of battle:
He should march along that path in the staff formation, or the wagon formation,
or the boar or crocodile formations, or the needle or the eagle formation.
From whichever direction he fears danger, in that direction he should extend his force;
then he himself should take up position in the lotus array.
The commander-in-chief and the general should station their forces in all directions;
and whichever direction one suspects danger from, that one should designate as the east.
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides—
men who are skilled in both their positions and in combat, fearless, and steadfast.
One should make a small number of troops fight in a compact formation, but one may extend a large number at will;
having arrayed them in the *sūcī* (needle) or *vajra* (thunderbolt) formations, one should cause them to fight.
[459] One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy terrain;
with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other weapons on firm ground.
One should station the men of Kaurukṣetra, the Mātsyas, the Pāñcālas, and those born in Śūrasena—
both tall and short— in the vanguard ranks.
Having arrayed his forces, he should encourage them and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the movements of the enemies as they engage in battle.
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain encamped and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, water, and fuel.
He should break down the tanks as well as the walls and moats;
he should also launch a sudden assault upon him at night and likewise cause terror.
One should instigate those who can be instigated and indeed observe their actions;
when fate is favorable, one who desires victory should fight, free from fear.
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension— either all together or individually— and never by means of war.
Since victory is seen to be impermanent for two who fight,
as is defeat in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
When even the three previously mentioned expedients are unavailable,
one who is well-prepared should fight in such a way that he conquers his enemy.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety.
But having understood the intended purpose of all these [claimants] in brief,
he should install a member of that lineage there and establish a formal covenant.
"And he should establish authorities for them according to the duties as they have been declared. (MDh 7.187–203)

Having conquered the enemy armies in the manner described, he should protect this eastern region, his own conquered land, according to the duty of a king (*rājadharma*). That very protection through righteousness is clarified by the third verse with the words "flower after flower. Just as a gardener, in a grove, plucks whichever flower blossoms at whatever time, but does not uproot the flowering creeper; so too, when collecting taxes from his subjects, the king should take a sixth part in accordance with their income. But a charcoal-maker uproots the tree and burns it entirely; he should not oppress the subjects in such a manner. And this has been demonstrated in the *Śāntiparvan*.
One should milk the kingdom like honey; one should not drive away the bees. One should milk it while having regard for the calf, and one should not crush the teats.
A king should drink from his kingdom gently, like a leech;
he should extract his son like a tigress, neither biting nor causing pain.
Just as a scribe [eats] a leaf and a mouse [eats] the skin of a foot,
so should one consume the kingdom by means of non-coercive methods.
"One should cause [the debtor] to pay by increasing the amount through very small increments;
then, one should apply an increase further and further in gradual succession. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of property and person, the king should cause merchants to pay taxes.
Just as the king and the doer of actions may be joined with their fruit,
so should the king, having duly considered [the people], constantly apportion taxes within his realm.
"Just as water, fire, a calf, and a bee take their food little by little, so should the annual tax be taken by the king from his realm in small amounts. Thus [says Manu, MDh 7.127–29].
Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"Just as the sun draws up water with its rays over the course of eight months, so too should the king [collect] taxes and the like by subtle means. (MārPu 27.23).
And this collection of taxes, illustrated by the analogy of the gardener, serves as an indicative example for all other duties of kings. Those duties have been set forth by Yājñavalkya.
One who possesses great energy, is liberal, grateful, a servant of the elders,
humble, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure.
One who is not procrastinating, possesses mindfulness, is not mean-spirited, nor harsh;
likewise, one who is righteous, free from calamity, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets.

"Having been disciplined in the protection of his own weak points (*svarandhragoptṛ*), likewise in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), and also in economics (*vārttā*) and the triple Veda (*trayī*), [he becomes] a lord of men. (YDh 1.309–11).

These are the internal duties of a king (*rājadharma*). They are also called the qualities of a king (*rājaguṇa*). For this very reason, in the course of explaining the aphorism "A king endowed with thirty-six qualities," Mahotsāha and the others were enumerated by Uśanas. Yājñavalkya has also shown the external duties of a king.
"He should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
with them he should deliberate on the kingdom, and then with a Brahmin, and finally by himself. (YDh 1.312). Manu also says:
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.
Together with them, he should constantly deliberate upon conciliation and the other [stratagems],
as well as peace and war, stability, the collection [of resources], protection, and the pacification of what has been acquired.
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions,
he should act for his own welfare in all matters concerning them collectively.
But the king should deliberate on the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brahmin among all his ministers.
"Always placing full confidence in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, he should then undertake his work. (MDh 7.54–59).
And the work to be undertaken is the construction of fortresses in specific locations, as shown by Yājñavalkya:

"One should dwell in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there, one should construct fortresses for the protection of the people, the treasury, and oneself. (YDh 1.321).
The different types of fortresses have been shown by Manu.
Having surrounded it with a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, or even a forest fort,
as well as a human fort and a mountain fort, one should dwell in a city.
"But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress" (MDh 7.70–71). The methods for the construction of fortresses are shown in the Śāntiparvan:
"One [should build] a fortress with strong walls and moats, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots."
It was filled with powerful men, elephants, and horses, and adorned with crossroads and marketplaces.
It was a place of well-established worldly conduct, tranquil and free from fear from any quarter;
it was rich with heroes, filled with the wise, and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.

"The king, with his ministers and forces under his control, should personally enter that city which is endowed with festive assemblies and where the deities are always worshipped. Thus [says Manu]. Manu also says:
That [fortress] should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
it should be provided with Brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, water, and fuel.

"In its center, he should have a sufficient dwelling built for himself—secure, suitable for all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees. (MDh 7.75–76). Having thus described the arrangement of the fortress, the same author also spoke of religious duties such as sacrifices:
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks,
born of a noble family, charming, and endowed with beauty.
He should appoint a domestic priest and indeed choose officiating priests;
they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires.
The king should sacrifice with various rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of sacrifice, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the Brahmins.
"Every year, he should cause the tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy men;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects as toward his own ancestors. Thus [says Manu].
Yājñavalkya also says:
He should appoint as his domestic priest one who is renowned for his learning, skilled in astrology,
proficient in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and likewise well-versed in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda].

For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis, one should indeed choose officiating priests and likewise perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
"He should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins;
he should always provide for the Vedic scholars with gifts, honor, and hospitality. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:
Even when dying, a king must not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling within his realm perish from hunger.
In whose kingdom a learned Śrotriya perishes from hunger,
his kingdom likewise perishes from hunger before long.
"Having ascertained his learning and conduct, one should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
and one should protect him in every way, like a father protects his own biological son. Thus [it is said in] MDh 7.133–35. Also in the *Ānuśāsanika* [Parvan]:
Excellent kings should construct assembly halls, water-stations, tanks, temples, and dwellings for Brahmins.
Brahmins must not be despised, for they are like fires covered by ashes;
these twice-born ones, when possessed by anger, could uproot an entire lineage.

"The punishment of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous must always be performed by the protector of the earth, as well as straightforwardness in all affairs. Thus it is said in the Śāntiparvan as well.
O best of the Kurus, one should provide protection for beings who are distressed and young;
one should maintain a composed mind and show compassion toward those who have come for refuge.
The support of all beings and their protection in every way, the constant performance of sacrifices according to the seasons, and the giving of gifts without causing distress— this is his duty.
One must perform the protection of the subjects and avoid reprehensible actions;
likewise, one should provide clothing, food, and vessels to those in the various stages of life at the appropriate times.
The king himself, having honored him according to the prescribed rites, should offer himself,
all his affairs, and even his kingdom to the ascetic.
He should offer [oblations] with diligence and remain perpetually humble;
having acquired the earth through valor, he should protect his subjects according to dharma.
"A king devoted to righteousness should meet his end in battle;
and having acquired land in battle, he should bestow it upon one learned in the Vedas. (MBh 12.86.21–26) — Manu.
The king who, out of delusion, neglects his own kingdom and oppresses it,
shall soon be deprived of both his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen.
"Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body, so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom. (MDh 7.111–12).
Furthermore, the daily routine has been shown by Manu:

"Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed purification and being composed, having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brāhmaṇas, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall. Thus [it is said in] Mānava Dharma Śāstra 7.145. Also in another Smṛti:
Having risen in the morning, the king should perform the cleansing of his teeth;
then, having gone to the bathing hall and bathed with pure water.
Having offered the *arghya* to the god Bhāskara with a concentrated mind,
he should then, with his body adorned, look at his own face while reciting the mantra.
"A king should give a vessel of ghee along with gold to a brahmin. Thus [says the law]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family priest, and the teachers..."
Having seen [the results], one should give cows, gold, and land to the astrologers and physicians.
"And then [he should give] household goods and houses to those learned in the Vedas" (YDh 1.332–33).
"Household goods" (*naiveśikāni*) refers to items such as ornaments for the bride that are used in marriage. Regarding the duty to be performed immediately after the gift, Manu says:
"Remaining there, having greeted all his subjects, he should dismiss them."
And having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Having ascended to a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place,
or in a forest free from undergrowth, one should deliberate on the counsel unobserved.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue,
he should contemplate the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, either together with those [pursuits] or entirely alone.
The giving away of daughters and the protection of sons.
The dispatching of envoys, as well as the remaining tasks to be accomplished,
the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.
He should [know] in truth the entire eightfold business and the fivefold group,
as well as affection and enmity, and the conduct of the circle of states.
Immediately after [the enemy], one should know the enemy's ally;
immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party.
He should win over all of them by means of conciliation and other such measures,
whether employed individually or collectively, through personal effort and statesmanship.
One should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge.

Having carefully considered the task at hand, he should employ sitting encampment (*āsana*), marching (*yāna*), peace (*saṃdhi*), war (*vigraha*), double-dealing (*dvaidha*), or seeking protection (*saṃśraya*).
"Relying upon these three—the pursuer, the goal to be pursued, and all the means in their entirety—one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose. (MDh 7.146–215).
Furthermore, the eightfold nature of action has been demonstrated by Uśanas.
In taking and in giving, likewise in commanding and in forbidding,
in the fifth [matter] of speaking for the sake of another's purpose, and in overseeing legal proceedings;
"By being joined with punishment and purification, the king possesses the eightfold course.

Here, "purification" (*śuddhi*) refers to atonement (*prāyaścitta*). The "fivefold group" (*pañcavarga*), however, consists of spies appearing as a traveler, a hypocrite, a householder, a merchant, and an ascetic. Alternatively, the fivefold group consists of: the means for initiating undertakings, the excellence of personnel and resources, the remedy for setbacks, and the successful accomplishment of the task.
Thus, having deliberated upon all this together with his ministers, the king—
Having exercised and bathed at midday, he should enter the inner apartments to eat.
One should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like one's own self, who know the proper time, who cannot be led astray, and who have neutralized poison with mantras.
One should apply all substances that counteract poison to him with anti-venomous medicines;
and, being self-controlled, he should always wear jewels that destroy poison.
And women who have been thoroughly examined, purified by their dress and ornaments, and composed in mind, should touch him with fans, water, and incense.
One should exert effort in this manner regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food;
likewise in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment.
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again deliberate upon his duties.
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the armed troops once more,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should, while bearing arms, listen within his inner apartments to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and properly dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to rest at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled.
"A king who is free from illness should maintain this rule;
if he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants. Thus [Manu] stated another duty. (MDh 7.216–26) Manu speaks further regarding another duty:
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects,
and service to the Brahmins— this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.

"He should conduct himself with complete sincerity and never with deceit; yet, being always well-guarded, he should recognize the deceit employed by his enemy. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 7.88–104). Also, in the Śāntiparvan:
"A king should avoid all vices;
for the sake of winning over the people, he should feign the indulgence in a vice.
These vices have been shown by Manu:

[473] Ten arise from desire, and likewise eight from anger: hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, intoxication, the three types of performance (song, dance, and music), and idle wandering— this is the group of ten born of desire.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault, and the corruption of wealth, as well as harshness of speech and severity of punishment— this is the group of eight born of anger.
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of his very self.
One should strive to conquer greed, which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these groups arise from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—
one should know this tetrad to be the most grievous among the group of vices born of passion.
One should always know that this triad— the infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the misappropriation of wealth— is always painful, even within the group born of anger.

"Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous; for one who suffers a calamity goes downward, whereas one who dies free from calamity goes to heaven. (MDh 7.45–53). Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
Having abandoned the seven vices and those things that destroy the very root,
one must protect oneself from enemies by ensuring that secret counsel does not leak outward.
A lord of men must possess knowledge of the stability, increase, and decline [of his power], as well as mastery over the sixfold policy; he must not be one who acts under the sway of passion.
First, the king must conquer himself, then his ministers, and thereafter his servants;
immediately after that, the citizens, and finally he may contend with his enemies.
"But he who seeks victory without first conquering these enemies—being one whose self is unsubdued and whose ministers are unsubdued—is oppressed by the host of his foes. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 27.5–11).
Thus, a king endowed with this aforementioned collection of dharmas should protect his subjects. This was stated by Manu:
"Having thus performed all these duties pertaining to himself, he should protect these subjects, being both disciplined and vigilant. (MDh 7.141).
Regarding the protection of subjects, the specific excellence of the king's welfare—both in this world and the next—is demonstrated in the Śāntiparvan.
And when the protector of the earth provides protection, women, unaccompanied by men and adorned with all their ornaments, travel the road without fear.
When the protector of the earth provides protection, people resort solely to righteousness, do not harm one another, and instead show mutual favor.
And when the king protects the land, the three social orders perform various great sacrifices and, being disciplined, study the Vedas.

"When the king takes up the foremost burden and carries the subjects with the application of great strength, then the world prospers. Thus [it is said] in the Mahābhārata (12.68.32–36). Also in the Rāmāyaṇa:
"The Kṣatriya who indeed rules the earth according to his own dharma, O hero, attains fame in this world and also after death. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the fault in failing to protect [the subjects] is shown in the Śāntiparvan.
Vehicles, garments, ornaments, and various kinds of jewels—
these the wicked would seize by force if the king did not protect them.
"Various kinds of weapons fall upon those who practice dharma in many ways, if the king does not uphold righteousness. (MDh 12.68.16–17). Thus ends the section on the duties of kings.

[476] Now begins the section on the duties of the Vaiśya. He states the specific duties of the Vaiśya as they follow in due order: "The work of acquiring profit, as well as gems and the protection of cattle."
Agriculture and trade are declared to be the livelihood of the Vaiśya. || 63 ||

"Business for profit" (*lābhakarma*) means livelihood through laziness and so forth. "Jewels" (*ratna*) refers to gems, pearls, and the like; by this, their examination, purchase, and sale are implied. "Tending cattle" (*gopālana*) includes providing grass and water, tethering and releasing them, milking, and so on. "Agricultural work" (*kṛṣikarma*) includes plowing the land, sowing seeds, and so forth. "Trade" (*vāṇijya*) consists of the buying and selling of betel nuts, grain, and other goods. Yājñavalkya states that these—money-lending and the rest—are the duties of a Vaiśya: "Money-lending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are declared to be the [duties] of a Vaiśya. (YDh 1.119) Manu also says:
"The protection of cattle, giving, sacrifice, study, trade, money-lending, and agriculture—these [were prescribed] for the Vaiśya. (MDh 1.90).
The word "he commanded" (*samādiśat*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Also, in the Varāha Purāṇa:
"A Vaiśya should perform Vedic study, sacrifice, giving, usury, cattle-rearing, cow-herding, agriculture, and trade according to the prescribed rule.

Here, "cattle-rearing" refers to the rearing of goats, horses, and so forth, since the word "cow" (go) is mentioned separately. Furthermore, the commodities for sale are also illustrated in the Anuśāsana Parvan.
“Sesame, hides, oils, as well as cattle and horses, are to be sold by Vaiśyas who follow the path of trade and abide in the way of Vaiśyas. (MBh 13.141.56).
In the Śāntiparvan, within the context of the Jājali-upākhyāna, the duties of Vaiśyas were thus declared by Tulādhāra.
What I give is not less than it should be, and what I receive is not more;
I sell the juices without deceit, with the exception of liquor.
"Having purchased it, he sells it back again later for much wealth. (MBh 12.261.7–8)

Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated a specific rule regarding the tending of cattle: "One should guard the cows. One should not drink until the cows have drunk. One should not sit while they are standing. One should not drive them up oneself. One should strike them gently from behind with a moist branch that has leaves. One should not lead them down to a watering place, nor to uneven ground, nor where there is little water. One should provide medical treatment according to one's ability for those that are young, old, or afflicted by disease; otherwise, there will be ruin" [478]. All those activities beginning with profit-making and ending with trade constitute the occupation of a Vaiśya; the meaning is that these are the means of livelihood for a Vaiśya. This has been stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
"Charity, study, and sacrifice—these three also belong to the Vaiśya.

Trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are his means of livelihood. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 28.6). The knowledge of prices and so forth should also be understood as duties of the Vaiśya; for this very reason, they have been enumerated among the duties of the Vaiśya by Manu.
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the purificatory rites and taken a wife,
should be constantly devoted to his livelihood through trade and to the protection of cattle.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
yet it should not be the desire of the Vaiśya that he should not protect the cattle.
If a Vaiśya desires [to trade], they must by no means be protected by anyone else;
[this applies to] gems, pearls, corals, metals, and woven textiles.
One should understand the relative value and strength of fragrances and flavors,
as well as the defects and virtues of the soil, according to the manner in which seeds are sown.
He should know the combinations of weights and all the combinations of balances;
he should know the value and worthlessness of commodities, and the merits and defects of various regions.
The profit and loss of merchandise, and the increase of livestock.
[479] He should know the wages of servants and the various languages of men; he should also know the storage and application of goods, as well as their purchase and sale.
"And he should exert the greatest effort toward the increase of his wealth through righteous means;
and he should diligently provide food for all living beings. (MDh 9.326–327)

Agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are designated by the term *vārtā*. The *mānayogas* consist of measures accomplished by means of the *añjali*, the *prastha*, and so forth. Regarding the root text, where some read "the work of metals" (*lohakarma*) instead of "the work of profit" (*lābhakarma*), it should be explained as the knowledge of the value and the buying and selling of metals such as gold and silver; this is because the word "metals" (*lauha*) is included in the list of Manu's recitations. The fruit resulting from the performance of the aforementioned duties is described in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]:
"One who does not abandon the duties of a merchant, and who honors the gods and Brahmins..."
"That merchant attains heaven, being honored by hosts of apsarases.
Conversely, the fault in the opposite case is shown in the Śāntiparvan:
"He who causes virtuous people to be cheated in the business of trade..."
He goes to a terrible hell, and his wealth also perishes. Thus [it is said]. (63)
Thus ends the section on the duties of the Vaiśya;
now he states the specific duties of the Śūdra that follow in due order.
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is said to be the supreme duty;
if he does anything otherwise, that shall be fruitless for him. (64)

In this context, the word *dvija* refers to the Brāhmaṇa. Service to him is supreme because it is the cause of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). Thus Manu says: "Of learned Brāhmaṇas who are householders and renowned..."
For a Śūdra, however, service alone is the supreme dharma for attaining the highest good.
"Pure, devoted to excellent service, gentle in speech, free from egoism, and always taking refuge in Brahmins, one attains a superior birth. Thus [it is said in] Manu Smṛti 9.334–35.
Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:

"By serving the twice-born alone, this Śūdra is entitled to the performance of *pākayajña* sacrifices; devoted to his own duties, he conquers his worlds and is remembered as one who has attained prosperity. Thus it is stated also in the *Anuśāsana-parvan*.
Passion, hatred, and delusion; harshness and cruelty; deceit, long-standing enmity, excessive pride, and lack of integrity.
Untruth, excessive speech, slander, extreme greed, deceit,
and lack of discernment entered the Śūdra at his birth.
Seeing that the Śūdra was overwhelmed by the qualities of darkness (tamas),
the Grandfather prescribed service to the twice-born as the duty of Śūdras.
“Tamas-born dispositions perish through a Śūdra’s devotion to the twice-born;
by service to the twice-born, a Śūdra attains the supreme good (*paraṃ śreyaḥ*).

By the qualification “supreme,” it is understood that there are also certain other duties. These have been shown by Devala: “The duties of a Śūdra are service to the three castes, the maintenance of wife and family, agriculture, cattle-rearing, carrying loads, trade in merchandise, painting, dancing, singing, and playing the flute, lute, *muraja*, and *mṛdaṅga* drums. This is also stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
"Even a Śūdra may give gifts and perform *pākayajña* sacrifices;
indeed, a Śūdra may perform all rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*) and so forth by means of these.
Thus [says] Yājñavalkya as well.

"Devoted to his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and intent on the performance of *śrāddha* rites, he should not neglect the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) by means of the *namaskāra* mantra. (YDh 1.121).
Also, in the *Śāntiparvan*:
The mantra consisting of the utterance of *svāhā* and the salutation (*namaskāra*) is prescribed for the Śūdra;
by means of these two, the Śūdra, being himself without vows, should perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
A Śūdra should never, under any circumstances, amass wealth;
for by obtaining wealth through service, he should bring his superiors under his control.
"Or, permitted by the king, a righteous man may indulge his desires. Thus it is said in the *Anuśāsana-parvan* (MBh 12.60.28–37):
"One who is non-violent, of auspicious conduct, and a worshiper of the gods and the twice-born..."

"A Śūdra is joined with the desired fruits of dharma precisely through his own duty. (MBh Āśvamedhika 141.59). Service to Brāhmaṇas serves not only for the sake of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), but also for the sake of livelihood (*vṛtti*). For this very reason, the livelihood to be provided for him has been shown by Manu:
"A livelihood should be provided for him by them from their own family according to what is appropriate."
And having considered one's own power, as well as one's skill and the number of dependents to be maintained.
"Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, broken grains of rice from the harvest, and old household utensils. (MDh 10.124–25). Also, in the Śāntiparvan:
If any Śūdra should approach the twice-born seeking to serve them,
those who know the Dharma say that the twice-born must provide for his livelihood.
"An umbrella, a turban, a seat of *uśīra* grass, sandals, and fans—these, when worn out, should be given to a Śūdra servant. (MBh 12.60.31–33) [483].
Otherwise, if he should perform any rite such as a *pākayajña* without service to the twice-born, all of that would become fruitless. This has been stated by Manu:

"Service to a Brahmin alone is declared to be the distinguished duty of a Śūdra; for whatever else he performs, that shall be fruitless for him" (MDh 10.123). Therefore, service to the twice-born alone is his supreme dharma. Service to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, however, is a secondary dharma because it serves merely as a means of livelihood. For this very reason, Manu has shown that service to a Brahmin serves both purposes [dharma and livelihood], whereas service to others serves only the purpose of livelihood.
But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek to live.
"He should propitiate the Brahmins for the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both; for one who has acquired the title of 'Brahmin,' that indeed is his fulfillment of duty. (MDh 10.121–22) || 64 ||
[484] When one is unable to subsist by serving a twice-born man, what then should he do? To this, he says:
Salt, honey, oil, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk—
One should not find fault with those of the Śūdra caste; one may engage in trade with all of them. || 65 ||
If one is unable to live by means of service, one may sell salt and all other such items for the sake of livelihood.
But surely—do not these items, when sold, bring fault upon the seller? To this Yājñavalkya says:
"Fruits, stones, linen, soma, humans, cakes, and climbing plants..."
Sesame-water, rice-gruel, juice, alkali, curd, milk, ghee, and water.
Weapons, liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, and *barhis* grass;
earth, leather, flowers, *kutapa* wool, hair, buttermilk, poison, and land.
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals,
lead, vegetables, fresh herbs, oil-cakes, livestock, and perfumes— likewise [these are forbidden].
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, one must never sell lac,
salt, or meat, for these lead to a fall from one's status.
"Milk, curd, liquor, and things that cause loss of caste" (YDh 3.36–40). Here, "one of inferior caste" (*hīnavarṇa*) refers to a Śūdra.
This is not so, because this rule pertains specifically to Brāhmaṇas. For this very reason, Manu says:
"One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt;
by selling milk, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days" (MDh 10.92).

However, a Śūdra would not incur sin even by selling salt and such items. The word "selling" (*vikrīṇan*) should be supplied from the verse to be cited later and applied here. Yājñavalkya also states that for a Śūdra who is unable to subsist through service, trade and other such activities are permitted.

"For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born" (YDh 1.120). The meaning is: "by those occupations through which the twice-born are served. Manu also says:
But if a Śūdra is unable to perform service for the twice-born and has fallen into distress regarding his wife and children, he may live by manual crafts.
"Those well-performed actions by which the twice-born are served—
those are the occupations of craftsmen and various arts. (MDh 10.99–100) || 65 ||
[486] He also states those things to be avoided by a Śūdra: "Indeed, selling liquor and meat, as well as eating what is unfit to be eaten."
By having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, a Śūdra falls from his status at that very moment. || 66 ||
By drinking the milk of a tawny cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Vedas, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla. (67)

And various kinds of intoxicants, such as palm-juice, honey-wine, date-palm wine, and so forth; forbidden foods, such as beef and the like; and women who should not be approached, such as sisters and others. The rest is clear. 66–67.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Conduct of the Four Castes," in the Śrī Parāśara Saṃhitā. || 1 ||
For the Parāśara-smṛti is indeed renowned here; it proclaims the tradition of the Smṛtis and Āgamas, and its two dharmas are commonly accepted by the esteem of the four castes.
Of these, the first is designated by the name of the learned (śiṣṭa) [Parāśara], while the other is purified by the six duties.
The wise Mādhava has explained all of that which was set forth in the previous chapter. || 1 ||

Thus ends the first chapter of the Mādhavīyā, the commentary on the Pārāśara-smṛti, composed by Mādhava, the minister of Śrī Vīrabukka Bhūpāla—the illustrious sovereign of great kings, supreme lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and upholder of the imperial throne. || 1 ||
